title: On the ground in the English seaside town rightwing influencers say is being ‘invaded’ | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Some in Dover say their town is being exploited by content creators and politicians, but others claim there is a genuine problem
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Some in Dover say their town is being exploited by content creators and politicians, but others claim there is a genuine problem
Content: Tom Armstrong, who lives in the area, said it was good that rightwing politicians were drawing attention to small boat crossings.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Armstrong, who lives in the area, said it was good that rightwing politicians were drawing attention to small boat crossings.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianImmigration and asylumOn the ground in the English seaside town rightwing influencers say is being ‘invaded’Some in Dover say their town is being exploited by content creators and politicians, but others claim there is a genuine problemKevin RawlinsonSat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you believe rightwing influencers and politicians, Dover and the widerKentcoast has been the site of an “invasion” for years now. And, for an online audience of millions, they and their camera crews have been the vanguard in the nation’s defence.Indeed, if you believe all you see on the algorithms of amateur Channel watchers, the shadow home secretary,Chris Philp, braved a hail of French gunfire as he took to the water in a fishing boat this week; an attempt by the French authorities, he suggested, to deter him in his mission of highlighting the small boats crisis.The inconvenient truth behind Philp’s attempt to self-police our borders is that nothing of the sort happened. The French government said he simply passed by a routine training exercise that involved firing live rounds.With its sloping pebble beach and sunbathers and dog-walkers enjoying the summer sunshine by its marina this week, Dover does not look much like the frontline of a war zone. Are the rightwing figures who regularly visit the town to create social media content exploiting it for their own careers, or are they seeking solutions to a genuine problem? “They’re using Dover a bit,” said one resident, Alison Drake. “People making all these videos and that is not really doing much, is it?”View image in fullscreenThe frontline of a war zone? The Dover seafront, where rightwing influencers and politicians flock to make content for social media about an ‘invasion’.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianSome said that creating tension where there was none before was all part of the plan. “What they’re trying to do is play on fear with all of these stunts,” said Razia Shariff, who runs the Kent Refugee Action Network (Kran), a charity that provides education for refugee and asylum-seeking young people.Whether or not the selfie stick-toting influencers who descend on the south coast need to capture the supposed “invasion” is, for some, a moot point.Some of those living in the area insisted the relentless focus on the issue – and on the region – was at least keeping the problem in the public eye. “They’re letting the people know that the French are not doing anything,” Tom Armstrong said. Armstrong is avowedly anti-immigration and said the “country is being devalued” by it. He said rightwing politicians were helping that cause. “You’ve got to draw attention,” he said. Later, he added: “We’ve got to know the truth.”Philp claimed to have been exposing the small boats crisis during his jaunt across the Channel. While Drake agreed that rightwing figures highlighting the issue might prompt action, she added: “Everyone knows about it, it’s about time they did something about it. They don’t do anything. So, it’s all very well everyone keep going on about it, but no one does anything. They know it’s happening.”View image in fullscreenAlison Drake said despite the attention on Dover, no one was doing anything about the small boat crossings.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianFew people have had more opportunity to solve the small boats crisis than Philp who, as immigration minister in the early 2020s, oversaw a sharp increase in crossings.In contrast, organisations such as Kran are working to alleviate some of the challenges caused by the way migration has been handled by successive governments.The young people Kran helps are taking part in a summer scheme at an academy in Kent this week. Shariff spoke glowingly of some of their predecessors’ achievements. One, she said, had arrived in the UK as a child refugee and now worked as a nurse in local hospitals. “Others have set up their own businesses against all the odds. They get on with their lives and they try.”Carol, who lives in Dover and did not want to give her surname, suggested the focus should be more on the work of organisations such as Kran than on politicians such as Philp andNigel Farage.The Reform leader has repeatedly referred to small boat crossings as an “invasion”. Standing on the Dover seafront in 2024, he described the site as the “frontline of the great national debate on immigration”.Carol did not recognise the picture the Reform leader painted of the town, as she stood on almost the same spot he had occupied two years ago. “I mean, look, it’s pleasant enough,” she said, nodding towards the beach.View image in fullscreenCarol worries that Dover being used as the backdrop for content about small boat crossings could deter tourists from visiting.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianPeople there were sunbathing in the warm weather, while children played in the water and others took an opportunity to go out in the sea in small vessels. “I think it is unfair that Dover is headlined in that way. Because you can sit on the beach, enjoy the area.”Carol said it was frustrating that Dover and other nearby towns were so often used as the backdrop for social media content focusing on the small boats crisis and feared it could deter people from visiting an area that needs a lift.“It’s a bit rundown, like many towns. It’s a bit sad. So it’s not a great place to shop, by all means, but the seafront’s lovely. And the surrounding countryside is lovely. I’m sure it isn’t helping. Dover has got that image.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumKentChris PhilpNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: The great British switch-off: how floating retreats, mobile-free pubs and sauna book groups are liberating people from their phones  | Smartphones | The Guardian
description: Sick of doomscrolling? From venues with smartphone swear jars to cabins with absolutely no signal, here are the fun and freeing ways to ditch your device
Author: Isabelle Aron
Headline: Sick of doomscrolling? From venues with smartphone swear jars to cabins with absolutely no signal, here are the fun and freeing ways to ditch your device
Content: A Hawaii reading retreat with the Silent Book Club.Photograph: Silent Book ClubView image in fullscreenA Hawaii reading retreat with the Silent Book Club.Photograph: Silent Book ClubSmartphonesThe great British switch-off: how floating retreats, mobile-free pubs and sauna book groups are liberating people from their phonesSick of doomscrolling? From venues with smartphone swear jars to cabins with absolutely no signal, here are the fun and freeing ways to ditch your deviceIsabelle AronSat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a ritual at the start of every event hosted bythe Offline Project. Run by Pelé Zachariah, the activities vary – it could be a group walk, a collage‑making class or a supper club – but each one begins in the same way, *with an invitation to hand over your phone. Devices go in a lockbox. Once they’re all in, Zachariah closes the door and turns the key. “I don’t place them in for people, because it’s nice for them to physically put it in the box themselves, walk away, and think: for the next two or three hours, I’m fully present.”He has been running these screen-free events in London since August 2025. First-timers can be apprehensive about being separated from their phone. “You can sense the vibe when they’re putting it away,” says Zachariah. “People have said to me, ‘I felt really weird’ or ‘I felt super uncomfortable for the first few minutes not having my phone on me.’ Then they’ll say, ‘I didn’t know how much I needed that.’”Zachariah understands why people might find it difficult at first. “It’s very unnatural. You might put your phone in the living room while you work in the kitchen, but here you’re seeing it locked behind what is essentially a gate that you can’t access,” he says. But when people leave, they often say they would like to have their own phone lockbox, or tell him that they’re going to try to not look at their device until they get home. “It’s kind of sad that we have to literally lock our phones away. But people really crave that time.”View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignThis is true for Jarred Laros, 31, who lives in Essex and has been a regular at the Offline Project since it launched. One of the first events he went to was a “paint and sip” evening, where an artist taught everyone how to paint a landscape scene with mountains, a river and a sunset. People sat around a table together, working on their canvases while having drinks and snacks, and getting to know each other. “I liked the idea of getting off my phone and being more intentional with how I’m spending my time. I would never try to teach myself how to paint, but doing that in a community setting is very easy-going. The conversation flows.”Laros runs his own business, and spends a lot of time on his devices. “I’m always glued to a screen, whether it’s my iPad, my MacBook, my phone, or all three at the same time,” he says. “Outside of work, there’s the doomscroll that you succumb to. I go on Instagram without intending to. Half an hour later, I’m, like, ‘What am I still doing on this app?’ My average daily screen time is seven and a half hours. My relationship with my phone is not what I want it to be.”The Offline Project is part of a new wave of digital detox communities that host events to give people time away from screens. It’s not hard to understand the appeal: adults in the UK now spend an average of four and a half hours online a day, and most of that is on their phones, according to Ofcom’s 2025Online Nation report.In 2025, theannual TouchPoints surveyby the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that British adults were spending more time on their phones than watching TV for the first time. The government hasrecently announcedthat in spring 2027 it will bring in asocial media banfor under-16s, which will include platforms like Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. When the news was announced, a teenage girl went viral when asked by a news reporter how she would spend all her newfound free time. Her answer?“Stare at a wall.”Thankfully, if you want a break from your phone, there are plenty of things to do that are much more engaging. As our lives are becoming ever-more online, people are starting to push back against the hold that technology has on us. Sick of looking out at a sea of screens, some musicians are enforcing a no phones policy at their gigs. Bob Dylan’s 2025 UK and Ireland tour, Fred Again’s gigs at Alexandra Palace in February, and Harry Styles’s one-off gig in Manchester in March this year all had rules against using phones. It’s happening at comedy events, too – phones were placed in locked pouches at Sarah Silverman’s London Palladium gig last year, and Russell Howard’s current Don’t Tell the Algorithm tour promises “no phones, no distractions, just humans and jokes”.double quotation markNightclubs are meant to be dark for that dual sense of losing yourself and finding yourself at the same time. Phones inhibit both of those thingsView image in fullscreenAnnie Mac’s club night Before Midnight, where stickers are placed on phone cameras to prevent people taking photos or videos.Photograph: Karen StanleyAccording todata from Eventbrite, attendance at phone-free events in 2024 to 2025 increased by 121% globally. At broadcaster and DJ Annie Mac’s club nightBefore Midnight, stickers are placed on phone cameras so you can’t take photos or videos. “It reminds people to be in the moment. You’re only going to get so much satisfaction out of blurred videos with distorted sound, or dark, fuzzy photos,” she says. “Nightclubs are traditionally places where you go to feel a sense of freedom – to be whoever you want to be. They’re meant to be dark for that dual sense of losing yourself and finding yourself at the same time. Phones inhibit both of those things.”While some are seeking out pockets of time at events and venues where they can escape their smartphones, others are going one step further and ditching them altogether. Cody Ramone, 31, from Derby, was using an old flip phone from 2015 until the pandemic, when life became more online than ever and he needed a smartphone again. In 2024, he switched back to a “dumb phone”. “I got tired of all the notifications and being constantly online,” he says.Abandoning his smartphone has been transformative and given him time for more enriching activities. “I get bored more. Being bored is what drives you to try new things, pick up an old hobby, or think creatively. My attention span has improved, so I read more and spend more time doing creative hobbies, like crochet. I call people or hang out with them more often,” he says.What is it that makes our phones so addictive? “Digital media activates the same reward pathway as drugs and alcohol, releasing dopamine, our reward neurotransmitter, in a key area of the reward pathway in the brain,” says Anna Lembke, professor of psychiatry at Stanford University School of Medicine and the author ofDopamine Nation. “Moving images are like catnip for the mammalian brain, leading to video-chaining, akin to ‘chain smoking’. Once we begin, it’s hard to stop, even when we want to.”The more time we spend on our phones, the more we become “desensitised to what we are seeing” and look for more “potent rewards to recreate that original experience of pleasure”, says Lembke. “At the same time, we lose our ability to take joy in other more modest rewards, like watching a sunset, sharing a meal with friends, or reading a good book. We spend more time scrolling alone. We become increasingly dissatisfied and lonely.”While that might sound like a bleak state of affairs, the good news is that it doesn’t have to be this way. With the rise of phone-free experiences, it’s possible to detach yourself from your device, even if it’s temporarily. “Part of having a healthier relationship with technology must include discrete periods of time when we are not using it, and instead fully present and interacting with the people and the world around us,” says Lembke. “This means creating collective spaces where we come together device-free.”From off-grid, tech-free cabins to the pubs where devices aren’t allowed, these are the places to escape your phone in the UK.View image in fullscreenOn arrival at the Digital Detox Club, devices are put in the ‘phone hotel’.Photograph: Celie NigoumiDigital detox clubsSet up in Amsterdam in 2024 by friends Jordy van Bennekom, Valentijn Klok and Ilya Kneppelhout, the Offline Club has 14 chapters in cities across 10 countries, including London and Bristol in the UK. Events start with everyone putting their devices in the “phone hotel”, a lockable metal box with slots. For the first hour, there’s music playing but no talking, and everyone does their own thing. For the second hour, people are encouraged to chat.The demand for these kinds of events is growing. In London there’sthe Switch Off– quiet, phone-free sessions for women where they can journal, collage or read a book – whilethe Offline Projecthosts screen-free walks, talks and workshops.Logging Off Clubis a UK initiative – with local groups in London, Bristol, Brighton, Southampton, Cambridge and the New Forest – that has now expanded to Sydney, Mexico City and Winnipeg.In Bath, friends Nicola MacDonald and Laura Hughes startedthe Digital Detox Clubin early 2025. They host events every two months at The Den cafe in Bath – phones go into the “tech motel” on arrival, and the pair provide optional activities like board games, journalling and crafts. “We’ve been struck by the diversity of attendees, from university students to retirees, which suggests this isn’t a niche concern,” says MacDonald. “It reflects a broader cultural fatigue with constant connectivity.”View image in fullscreenDigging clay for wild pottery with Native Hands in Sussex.Photograph: Natasa LeoniCraft sessionsIf you’re trying to spend less time on your phone, a craft class does some of the work for you by keeping your hands busy. But there are specifically phone‑free classes, too.Native Handsoffers basketry, pottery and bushcraft sessions, held outside in an ancient woodland in Sussex. AtCurious Housein East Sussex, classes range from basket weaving to portrait painting. All sessions start with a mindful breathing exercise to help people switch off.In November last year, Dan Palmer launchedAirplane Mode– a monthly phone-free event at his organic restaurant and natural wine bar, Eat Your Greens, in Leeds. The free events include workshops hosted by local creatives, doing things like painting, collage and origami.Rather than locking phones away in a safe, they use a swear jar system. “Every time I catch anyone on their phone, I fine them 50p,” Palmer says. “All the fines go to a charity called Positive Action for Refugees and Asylum Seekers. So far, I’ve issued three fines – and one of them was for me! No one wants to be on their phones when they have something more interesting to do.”The idea of using your hands to make something tangible rather than doomscrolling is what inspired Nadia Butt fromInner Canvasto host art sessions for women at her home in Reading without the distraction of screens. “The screen-free element is at the heart of the sessions,” she says. “We treat it like a ritual. At the start of each session, phones are silenced and placed in a box. I call it the ‘phone spa’. Framing it as something collective removes the anxiety around it.”View image in fullscreenThe Bath Thermae Spa. ‘All of my best ideas in the past two years have been while sitting in a sauna,’ says a regular.Photograph: Ellis Reed/We Are FoundSpas and saunasSpas are all about relaxing and switching off, but often these spaces aren’t phone-free. That is changing, though, with some spas now enforcing phone bans. TheBath Thermae Spahas a strict no phones policy – guests must put devices in a lockable pouch that’s kept in their locker. AtCareys Manorin the New Forest, there’s a digital detox spa break, which includes relaxing treatments, a complimentary journal and a phone amnesty box in the room.Phones have been banned atthe Bothyat Heckfield Place, Hampshire, since it launched in 2023. “Seeing someone on their phone in a space dedicated to restoration felt out of alignment. You are there to be with yourself, to listen inwardly, to slow down,” says the spa operations director, Reka Seres-Erdei.It’s not just at spas – as sauna culture rapidly grows, many people are finding these spaces offer a welcome break from technology. Ryan Haynes, 34, is a regular at London’sCommunity Sauna Baths, which has locations in Camberwell, Hackney Wick, Stratford, Walthamstow and Peckham. You can’t take your phone into the sauna, but you’re allowed to take photos outside, although they are considering a phone ban throughout.Haynes’s Wednesday morning sauna session is “non-negotiable” for him. “All of my best ideas in the past two years have been while sitting in a sauna. Everyone needs to slow down to hear what’s going on in their brain,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKelly Wickson, who runs a sauna book club in Shoreham-by-Sea, Sussex, says: ‘We do it on a Friday evening and it sells out.’Photograph: Petra HarringtonBook clubsAs an independent bookshop owner and a sauna enthusiast, Kelly Wickson had an inspired idea last year: a book clubina sauna. Wickson ownsChapter 34in Shoreham-by-Sea on the Sussex coast, and hosts the sauna book club once a month at the Nomadic Sauna on Kingston Beach. Creating a phone-free space was a big part of it, and the sauna conveniently ticks that box. “It will ruin your phone; you’ve got no choice,” she says.The books are always 250 pages or less, and there’s no commitment to go every month. Phones are left in waterproof tubs outside the sauna. The book club is an hour long, and they go in and out of the sauna throughout, with some having a quick dip in the sea during breaks. Wickson has been amazed at how popular it is. “We do it on a Friday evening and it sells out,” she says.While a book club in a sauna is particularly unusual, people increasingly value being given the time and space to switch off and read. This is the thinking behindSilent Book Club, where one of the mottoes is: “Put down your phone, pick up a book.” It’s a global network with about 2,000 chapters in more than 60 countries, and there are almost 150 in the UK and Ireland.View image in fullscreen‘The idea is to enter a fantasy world where you can enjoy the moment,’ says Camille Jetzer, co-owner of the Roses of Elagabalus in east London.Photograph: Ollie TomlinsonPubs and barsWhen Camille Jetzer and James Nasmyth openedthe Roses of Elagabalusin Dalston, east London, last year, they knew they wanted to minimise phone use. They refer to it as a “clubhouse” – there’s a bar, restaurant, dancing and cabaret. “The idea of having no phones is that you would walk into the Roses, leave the outside world behind and enter this fantasy world where you can just enjoy the moment,” Jetzer says.When you arrive at the Roses, a host explains that there’s no photography, and places a sticker over your phone camera. There are also reminders on the menus. “It’s a ‘you were there or you missed it’ situation,” Jetzer says, who has also noticed their regular punters reminding new visitors about the rule.While phones aren’t locked away, Jetzer says the stickers on cameras mean they are used less. “It creates an environment where phones are less desired. In a dream world, we’d lock away the phones. That’s maybe next year’s project,” she says.Elsewhere in London,Esmeralda’s Mayfairandthe Spy Bar at Raffles London at the OWOboth put stickers on phone cameras. In 2019, Samuel Smith’s pubs brought in a rule that customers couldn’t use phones or laptops in their establishments, of which there are more than 200 across the country. Atthe Barrel at Budein Cornwall, anyone who breaks its no phones rule has to donate £1, which goes to local charities. In Herne Bay in Kent,the Butchers Armshas been a phone-free zone since it opened in 2005 – there are no signs needed to enforce it, says owner Martyn Hillier. “A disgruntled look from other customers is enough. If that doesn’t work we all start saying, ‘Rhubarb, rhubarb, rhubarb’, louder and louder until they realise they can’t converse any more.”In Woking, Kim and Mike Jarred runBeyond the Screen, a monthly phone-free social at their local pub the Olive Tree. They set it up in March 2025 after talking about how they could model good phone habits for their teenage sons. They provide activities like puzzles and conversation starters, but mostly people just sit and chat. “Pubs are closing down and we’re just staying in our houses with our phones in front of our faces rather than getting out and meeting people. We’re human beings, and we need to connect with each other. Phones are getting in the way of that,” Kim says.View image in fullscreenAmber’s in Manchester. ‘People seen taking photos or videos are politely asked to leave,’ says co-founder James Hutchins.Photograph: Amber’sClubnights“Nights out now can feel like content creation exercises. We wanted to remove that layer entirely and return the focus to the room,” says James Hutchins, co-founder of Manchester clubAmber’s. It opened in December 2024 and has a no-photo, no‑video policy, with stickers placed over phone cameras. “If people are seen taking photos or videos inside the club, they are politely asked to leave,” Hutchins says.Amber’s is part of a growing trend in UK clubs, as more venues are making their dancefloors a phone‑free space. The policy is used atboth FoldandFabricin London,Lakotaand sister venueMoon Clubin Bristol, andDoppler Studioin Leicester. Some clubs ban phones completely. AtOffgrid, a monthly day party at House Party in Soho, London, co‑founded by Stormzy, phones are sealed in a locked pouch. At her club nightBefore Midnight, Annie Mac has noticed a palpable shift in atmosphere – something she experienced during the first phone‑free Before Midnight event at the Warehouse Project in Manchester. “People were more present and louder. They whooped, they hollered, they whistled. They reacted to the tunes in a visceral way.”View image in fullscreenThe Cottage in the Clouds, in the Lake District national park, where there’s no wifi and limited phone signal.Photograph: Canopy and StarsOff-grid staysIn 2019, Hector Hughes was working for a tech startup in London and feeling burnt out. “I ended up at a silent retreat at a Buddhist temple on top of a mountain in the Himalayas. When you got there, they took your phone off you. I spent 10 days cut off from the outside world. It was a revelation,” says Hughes.He came back from that trip, quit his job and started setting upUnplugged– off-grid cabins in the UK where you lock your phone away. It launched in the summer of 2020; there are now 60 digital detox cabins around the country (and they have expanded to Catalonia, too). The phone-free element is self‑policed, but each cabin has a lock box with a padlock, and the key is in a sealed envelope. They provide a Polaroid camera, a map and an old-school Nokia phone in case of emergencies. Hughes says that Unplugged’s customers often return for regular stays and go on to make changes in their daily lives, like having phone-free date nights or drastically cutting down their screen time.If you like the idea of escaping to an off-grid cabin and ditching your phone, there are various options around the UK.Unyoked’s cabins run on solar power, have no wifi and often no phone signal – there’s a “spice signal”, from mild to extra spicy, to set expectations for how remote a cabin feels, and how long it might take to walk to one. They also have Brick devices, which help you block certain apps from your phone for a set amount of time. Similarly,Shacks’ cabins are off-grid with no wifi, and lockboxes for phones.Alternatively, you could look for a remote cottage with no wifi and limited or no phone signal, like theCottage in the Cloudsin the middle of the Lake District national park, orWoodcock Cabinin the Cambrian mountains in Wales. If you want to escape dry land, too,Lilypodin Devon is a floating retreat with three solar-powered eco pods built on a platform next to a lake, where there’s no TV, wifi or phone signal, but there are board games, beanbags and a king-sized bed.View image in fullscreenWild dipping with Yoga Retreats and More. ‘I had to WhatsApp a guest after they left – they’d left their devices behind,’ says founder Florence AcheryRemote retreatsFlorence Achery, founder ofYoga Retreats and More, launched her “Retreat like it’s 1999” digital detox breaks, in Lancashire and Cumbria, in 2023. A recent guest enjoyed the break from her devices so much that she forgot to pack her laptop and phone when she left. “I had to WhatsApp the guest she was travelling with to get them to pick up her stuff,” Achery says.On arrival, guests hand over their devices before spending the next few days sharing meals together, going on long walks, doing yoga and star gazing. “They’re in charge, not their phones,” says Achery, who gives her guests a battery-powered alarm clock to take home, to encourage them to keep phones out of their bedrooms. She has also launched a parent and teen digital detox retreat to help younger people to change their relationship with technology.At its 223-hectare (550-acre) estate on the River Dart in Devon,the Sharpham Trusthosts retreats focused on mindfulness and connecting to nature; guests are encouraged to switch off their phones.And, in Suffolk, sisters Lauretta and Sharon Gavin host regular phone-free retreats atthe Detox Barn, where guests enjoy vegan food, yoga, sound baths and countryside walks. “For many people it’s a huge relief to step away from their phones for 48 hours,” Lauretta says. “People open up, share stories and properly connect.”Explore more on these topicsSmartphonesMental healthSocial media banMobile phones (Technology)Mobile phones (Money)HealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The tangled financial web at the heart of Reform UK | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Nigel Farage’s £5m gift, the Cottrell family’s links and donations, and Richard Tice’s business dealings form part of an increasingly clear nexus of relationships
Author: Anna Isaac
Headline: Nigel Farage’s £5m gift, the Cottrell family’s links and donations, and Richard Tice’s business dealings form part of an increasingly clear nexus of relationships
Content: Faced with scrutiny, Nigel Farage has made unsubstantiated claims about the Guardian’s reporting.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenFaced with scrutiny, Nigel Farage has made unsubstantiated claims about the Guardian’s reporting.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianReform UKAnalysisThe tangled financial web at the heart of Reform UKAnna IsaacNigel Farage’s £5m gift, the Cottrell family’s links and donations, and Richard Tice’s business dealings form part of an increasingly clear nexus of relationshipsSat 1 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTShareIt has been three months since the Guardian revealed that Nigel Farage had accepteda £5m gift from Christopher Harborne, a billionaire donor to Reform UK.This was not the first story in our continuing investigation. But it has proved the most significant, and the consequences of the disclosure are still being played out.Little by little, a picture is emerging – one that shows howReform UKhas been funded and by whom. Each new detail raises more questions for Farage and the coterie around him.Aside from the “gift”, the Guardian has revealed details of secret donations, a behind-the-scenes loan from a donor and how theMetropolitan police have interviewed two peopleunder caution.Sources have described how staff at several different banks were so concerned about a range of transactions, some of which are referenced above and involved senior figures at the party,that theyreported them to the National Crime Agency.Sources have now told us that George Cottrell, a convicted fraudster based in Montenegro, transferreda total of more than $2mto his mother, Fiona, in 2024, with each sum arriving shortly before she made substantial donations to the party.The stories have given voters a much clearer idea of the people and the financial transactions that underpin Reform.It is a financially and politically incestuous set of relationships.Farage is friends with George Cottrell, who is said to be an unpaid adviser to Reform. Cottrell is friends with Harborne, the billionaire who has given millions to the party, and to Farage himself.View image in fullscreenGeorge Cottrell (left), sometimes called an unpaid Reform adviser, is friends with Nigel Farage and Christopher Harborne, and has lent money to Richard Tice, Farage’s deputy.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/AlamyFarage’s deputy,Richard Tice, has known the Cottrell family, he says, for 50 years. Fiona is also a significant donor to the party. George has also lent money to Tice.These five people are at the heart of a party that believes it can form the next government.Without them and their money, Reform would not exist in its current form.Scrutiny has provoked Farage into an array of explanations for why he accepted the £5m gift, and broad declarations there is an establishment plot to undermine him.Rather than answering questions posed by the Guardian, he and other senior Reform figures have sent threatening legal letters, or attempted to “spoil” the Guardian’s stories with pre-emptive interviews with the Daily Telegraph, which reported what they said uncritically.Millions of pounds and many, many questions: the untold story of why Reform figures face NCA scrutinyRead moreFarage has also made unsubstantiated claims about the Guardian’s reporting – citing, without any evidence, illegal hacks involving Russia, or talking about state-orchestrated leaks.Throwing sand in the air is one way of distracting attention, but when it settles, certain facts remain unchanged, and certain questions remain unanswered.Several relate to George Cottrell, who is known as “Posh George”, and has been at Farage’s side for at least a decade.Many of those questions pertain to his wealth and business activity.In January, the Guardian reported on his alleged role as a frontman for the betting syndicate of the megastar gambler and football proprietor Tony Bloom.Court documents claimed that Cottrell, as well as raking in millions by allowing Bloom’s syndicate to place bets using accounts in his name,also had a financial interest in the offshore gambling outfit Tether.bet.The claims went further still: that he had approached gamblers in the UK to use Tether.bet, despite that outfit not holding a UK gambling licence.Lawyers for Cottrell repeatedly said he was not a director or shareholder of Tether.bet and had not commented on the court proceedings, as he was not party to them. The case relates to a former employee of Bloom’s gambling syndicate who claims he introduced Cottrell to Bloom.Cottrell, who was unable to pay for legal representation when he was initially arrested in the US in 2016, and then had to rely on family assistance, has seen a rapid reversal in his fortunes since his release from US prison in 2017.View image in fullscreenChristopher Harborne gave Farage a gift of £5m in April 2024, some of which was not transferred until just before Farage announced he would stand in the general election in July.Photograph: George Cracknell Wright/LNPIn recent years he has pursueda costly, jet-set lifestyle,often using Montenegro as a base.Then there are the questions around Farage, who said he was “skint” in 2017.Five pressing questions for Reform UK about its financesRead moreNot any more. He now owns a number of houses, and has shown flashes of anger when asked about this, and what he has done with the £5m given to him by Harborne.“Literally none of your business,” he said to the BBC.The £5m came via a deed of gift in April 2024, just as Farage, who was the main shareholder of Reform UK, weighed his political future.In fact, the Guardian would later report our sources’ claims that some of the £5m was not transferred to Farage until just before he declared he would stand in the 2024 general election.Lawyers for Harborne have said their client’s gift was unconditional and that, when it was made, Harborne did not foresee Farage returning to politics.The Guardian has since been able to shed more light on the tangled web of overlapping personal financial activity and donations to the party.Cottrell, whom the Guardian revealed issometimes called Farage’s chief of staff(Reform has said he has never held an official position in the party), was also providing financial support to Tice behind the scenes.View image in fullscreenRichard Tice’s company, Tisun Investments, borrowed money from Cottrell, which was repaid after a large donation was made via the same company to Reform UK.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAHe lent Tice’s company £78,100 in late 2024 when he was already a sitting MP. Tice says this money was then repaid, but only after he made a donation of £613,000 via the same company – Tisun Investments – to Reform. Tice has called it a “bridging loan”, a type of short-term loan.But the benefits and support Cottrell gave to Farage, and the £78,100 loan to Tice, were a drop in the ocean compared with the apparent largesse Cottrell may have extended to the party.As the Guardian revealed, his mother, a woman with aristocratic roots but who is understood to be of relatively modest means, had secretly given Britain Means Business – a fundraising vehicle for Reform solely controlled by Tice – £1m on 10 June 2024, just weeks before the July general election.Half the sum, £500,000, was almost immediately transferred into the party, despite queries from bankers to Tice about the origin of the funds. This was in addition to two more donations of £250,000 made in her own namein May of the same year.Get in touchContact Anna Isaac about this storyIf you have something to share about this story you can contact Anna using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.To send a message to Anna Isaac please choose the ‘Business (UK and Global)’ team.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can email: anna.isaac@theguardian.comMessaging appsYou can message Anna using the Signal Messenger app: 07341998403SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreOn Wednesday, the Guardian revealed that sums totalling more than $2m were transferred to Fiona by her son, according to financial industry sources.The pair have now been interviewed under caution as part of a police investigation into the 2024 donations from Fiona to the party and Britain Means Business.Fiona has not responded to multiple efforts by this newspaper to contact her. George has not denied giving his mother large sums of money. Instead, his lawyers said any political donations his mother had made had been entirely her decision and were a matter for her.Two parliamentary standards investigations are due to be concluded in the autumn, one into the £5m gift Farage received from Harborne; another into his benefits from Cottrell.There is an ongoing Metropolitan police investigation.Reform is learning that with great success comes ever greater scrutiny.Explore more on these topicsReform UKNigel FarageParty fundingChristopher HarborneRichard TiceanalysisShareReuse this content

title: The Manchester mayoral result holds the key to the future of progressive politics  | Neal Lawson | The Guardian
description: Voters on the left may be fragmented – but they will pull together behind a convincing cross-party message, says Neal Lawson, director of cross-party campaign organisation Compass
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Voters on the left may be fragmented – but they will pull together behind a convincing cross-party message, says Neal Lawson, director of cross-party campaign organisation Compass
Content: ‘When second preferences kicked in, it’s estimated that about seven in 10 progressives who had backed other parties piled in behind Craig.’ Labour's Bev Craig with a supporter at the Manchester mayoral vote count on Friday.Photograph: Gary Roberts Photography/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘When second preferences kicked in, it’s estimated that about seven in 10 progressives who had backed other parties piled in behind Craig.’ Labour's Bev Craig with a supporter at the Manchester mayoral vote count on Friday.Photograph: Gary Roberts Photography/ShutterstockOpinionPoliticsThe Manchester mayoral result holds the key to the future of progressive politicsNeal LawsonVoters on the left are more fragmented than ever – but they will pull together behind a convincing cross-party messageThe author is director of the cross-party campaign organisation CompassSat 1 Aug 2026 08.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.51 EDTShareThe results of the election for a new mayor to succeed Andy Burnham inGreater Manchestershow progressives standing at the threshold of a new era. But only if they work together.The new mayor,Bev Craig, was elected using the supplementary vote, which uses voters’ second preference if no one wins more than half the vote in the first round. Despite the Burnham bounce, Labour received only 47% of the vote in the first round, well down on Burnham, who never achieved below 63% in his three campaigns. But when second preferences kicked in,it’s estimated that about seven in 10progressives who had backed other parties piled in behind Craig.This confirms that we live in an age of bloc politics; left v right. Few now shift between blocs, but many move parties within their respective bloc. The Manchester mayoral vote saw the progressive bloc consolidate behind Labour, just as it did for Andy Burnham in Makerfield, but they backed the Greens inGorton and Dentonearlier in the year andPlaid Cymruin a Senedd byelection at the end of last year.Two things are happening at once in this progressive bloc: voters are becoming more promiscuous in who they really support and highly disciplined in how they actually vote. Voters seem to be backing the progressive candidate best placed to beat the right, but only when the candidate is deemed sufficiently progressive. This amorphous mix of progressive voters appears to be capable of ruthlessly flocking around the same candidate.Given that UK politics is likely to remain incredibly fragmented, two challenges face progressive parties and voters, in winning and governing. Within this fragmented bloc lurks the danger of “progressive tragedies”, where a majority progressive vote splits and lets the right bloc through. The bloc, rather than the party, that now wins today is the one that most efficiently organises its total vote.But it’s not just the quantity of the progressive vote that matters, it’s the quality. While majorities can be won on a small percentage of the vote, as in the general election in 2024, these victories don’t deliver strong government, because people are merely backing the least bad option. As soon as the going gets tough, this negative support melts away. Unless Burnham can reach and maintain something more like 40% backing, governing will remain treacherous.View image in fullscreen‘He built a long-term cross-party consensus in Manchester.’ The prime minister, Andy Burnham, with the newly elected mayor, Bev Craig, on Saturday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PALabour has been in this doom loop of failure for too long. Because it decides to go it alone and not work with other progressive parties, it can only win under first past the post by appealing to centre-right voters. This means promising little or no change. With no mandate for radical change, Labour sets itself up to fail and wonders why it loses the red wall, Scotland, Wales,support from Muslim votersand nowinner-city seats.The clever move would be to mobilise the country’s whole progressive majority based on a transformative offer. This fragmented landscape can and must be woven together in a way that combines values, policies and electoral performance.There are good omens for this, starting with Burnham himself. He built a long-term cross-party consensus in Manchester, which was the basis for sustained state and private sector investment and the fastest-growing economy in the country. His experience of the supplementary vote, where to secure second preferences he had to listen and engage with non-Labour voters, led him to back a fully proportional voting system.But the mobilisation of any latent progressive majority requires deeper roots than just transactional electoral politics. This is why Burnham’scross-party move on social carematters. While he should haveinvolved the Greens, he recognises that some big issues need a broad and permanent consensus. This principle should be extended, not least to delivering a low-carbon economy. Processes such as this build trust across parties and reveal just how much progressives have in common.Problems still abound. Progressive consolidation works in byelections where media attention and polling send a signal to voters about who to back. But unless progressives work out how to organise their bloc in a general election, the chaos of many progressive tragedies will ensue.In this regard, it’s Clacton that shows the way. It is woeful that the progressive parties have all pulled out, leaving the voters of Clacton with no serious choice about who represents them. As in Tatton in 1997, where theanti-corruption journalist Martin Bell stoodagainst the sitting Tory MP and won, moves should have been made to field a credible centre-right independent to challenge Reform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, a critical precedent has been re-established, that these so-called “national” parties don’t always put up candidates. Now they’ve stood aside, they can repeat it. Why stand a candidate in a seat that you have no hope of winning and by doing so only make it more likely that the national populist right wins? At the next election, local parties should be empowered to decide whether to stand or not.The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s speech: Rewiring Britain needs Westminster to give up real power | EditorialRead moreThe change to unlock all of this is proportional representation (PR), the promise of which massively helps consolidate the progressive vote at the next election. Burnham and the Labour party staunchly back it. Combined with manifesto promises from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens, a super-majority for change could transform our political system for good. This is why the vote in the Commons on 2September on an elections bill amendment setting up a national commission to pave the way for PR is a critical litmus test of Burnham’s commitment to a new politics for a new society.British politics has never been more volatile and will continue to be so. Yes, the Burnham bounce is welcome. But will it last? No one should think the resourceful and ruthless British right will simply sit back and let progressives win. They will unite the right if they must.As ever, the people are ahead of the politicians. If the parties can catch up and stop their self-defeating tribalism, then progressives won’t just beat Reform – they will beat the causes of Reform.Neal Lawson is director of the cross-party campaign organisation CompassExplore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionGreater Manchester mayoralty byelection 2026Greater ManchesterMayoral electionsLocal politicsProportional representationByelectionscommentShareReuse this content

title: Lost income, energy fears and a woolly mammoth: what Europe’s dried-up rivers have yielded | Drought | The Guardian
description: Heat and drought have affected shipping, power plants and tourism across eastern Europe – as well as unearthing some surprises
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Heat and drought have affected shipping, power plants and tourism across eastern Europe – as well as unearthing some surprises
Content: The dried-up Danube in Budapest, Hungary. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesHeat and drought have affected shipping, power plants and tourism across eastern Europe – as well as unearthing some surprisesByDeborah Colein Berlin and agenciesSat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBaking temperatures and drought across large swathes of central and easternEuropehave driven water levels on the Danube and Rhine rivers to record lows in some areas, hitting shipping, energy production and tourism hard.View image in fullscreenExtreme conditions aggravated by the climate emergency left Europe’s waterways from the Netherlands to the Black Sea parched, triggering compounding crises.For the first time in their history,Hungaryand Romania had to shut down atomic reactors normally cooled by the Danube.The largest nuclear power plant in Hungary, the 44-year-old Paks which supplies nearly half of the country’s electricity, has been cutting output since Monday.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe Paks power plant’s cold-water intake channel from the Danube.The prime minister, Péter Magyar, said the Paks plant was operating at less than ​50% capacity and was expected ​to be ​completely powered down next week. The shutdown could extend for weeks as Danube water ⁠levels are expected to remain too ⁠low to ​restart ‌it.“An energy crisis situation could arise beginning Monday,” he posted on X. “Coordinated steps and restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences. We are counting on everyone!”Map of the Danube running across eastern Europe with two nuclear power plants detailedA malfunction at Hungary’s largest gas-fired power plant in Százhalombatta was worsening the grid shortage, he said.Hungarian authorities have asked citizens to reduce energy use in the peak evening hours, including refraining from charging EVs and switching off air conditioners, while carmakers and battery manufacturers have been ordered to cut power and water consumption.In Romania, authorities shut down a reactor unit at the Cernavodǎ power plant earlier in the week for safety reasons and announced a second would be switched off soon after.The prime minister, Ilie Bolojan, said the shutdowns could last for one to two weeks and also urged Romanians to reduce power consumption in the evenings.View image in fullscreenPeople swimming near a sunken German warship in Prahovo,Serbia.The Danube, which flows through 10 countries, has receded to unprecedented lows in some areas, exposing rocks, old shipwrecks, a second world war bomb and even the remains of an ancient woolly mammoth.A resident of Ryahovo village in northernBulgariadiscovered the bones of the giant ice age beast on the riverbed and specialists at the Regional History Museum in the nearby ‌town of Ruse arrived to investigate the rare find.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenScientists examining the remains of an ancient mammoth on the dried-up riverbed.Last week, authorities in Budapest closed the Margaret Bridge after a wartime bomb was exposed at its base by the dropping water levels.The record low level of the Danube has forced Budapest cruise ships to dock upriver and sightseeing cruises to be cancelled. Cargo ship operations have ground to a near halt, according to Hungary’s ministry of transport and investment.View image in fullscreenCattle sit on sand dunes visible after the Danube’s level fell substantially, near Calarasi, Romania.The river is expected to further ebb in the coming days, with no significant rain in the forecast and temperatures expected to exceed 38C across the region.From Slovakia and Hungary to Romania and Bulgaria farther east, ships on the Danube were unable to travel fully loaded along the waterway, and faced lengthy waits.At the Vidin-Calafat Bridge connecting Bulgaria and Romania, Bulgarians said they were out of work because the low water levels had trapped their boats onshore.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenA fisher tries to move his boat, blocked by algae on the bottom of the Danube, in front of the Calafat-Vidin Bridge.“It’s never dried up this much before,” Rossen Dobrev, a fisher, told Agence France-Presse. “Now we can even walk all the way to Romania.”Water levels on the Rhine inGermanyalso fell to near record lows on ⁠Friday, triggered by a heatwave and prolonged dry weather, the country’s WSV navigation agency said. Shallow water has forced reductions of cargo on ‌vessels to about 20% of their normal capacity.View image in fullscreenThree former vessels, including a sailing ship and an eel-fishing boat, connected by a bridge and now serving as a cafe at the old confluence of the Wupper and the Rhine.The Rhine is a crucial shipping artery ​for grains, minerals, ores, coal and oil products, including petrol, creating potential bottlenecks for companies in the EU’s top economy.Dutch officials said the Rhine had dropped to its lowest recorded level at the point where it flows into the Netherlands, and was due to recede further.The Netherlands has suffered from an officially recognised water shortage since mid-July, leading to use restrictions across most of the country, particularly in farming.In Serbia, hundreds of small boats and dozens of cargo ships were marooned on the dried-out riverbank near the northern city of Novi Sad.One houseboat owner, Radovan Segrt, who runs river excursions on his vessel, told the Associated Press that the water in the Danube had withdrawn about 15 to 20 metres from its shore.“The summer season is over now, as far as boat riding is concerned,” he said.Agence France-Presse, The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this reportExplore more on these topicsDroughtRiversGermanyBulgariaHungarySerbiafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ​What makes a good comic novel? Andrew Sean Greer on the joy of funny writing  | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The Pulitzer-winning author of Less and Villa Coco explores the art of writing humour – plus 10 of the best novels to make you laugh
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Pulitzer-winning author of Less and Villa Coco explores the art of writing humour – plus 10 of the best novels to make you laugh
Content: Comedy​What makes a good comic novel? Andrew Sean Greer on the joy of funny writingThe Pulitzer-winning author of Less and Villa Coco explores the art of writing humour – plus 10 of the best novels to make you laughAndrew Sean GreerSat 1 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTShareView image in fullscreenIllustration: Javi AznarezIn March 2020, when the mayor of San Francisco instructed all citizens to remain in their houses due to a pandemic, the first thing I did was order all the books of Agatha Christie. I was not alone; I think many of us immersed ourselves in reliable narratives to drown out the chaos. It did not matter if it ended in marriage or murder; the reliability was what mattered. Later when I realised I would need to hole up for some time, my reading shifted to a different kind of novel. And because, like Christie, our world has an endless supply of new terrors, it is the comic novel that still fills my reading hours.Nobody knows what a comic novel is. And once you start discussing it, all the fun runs out. EB White compared it to dissecting a frog (you’re left with innards and a dead frog) but I would compare it to turning all the lights on at a party: everyone looks terrible and you’ve ruined the party. Most would agree, of course, that Wodehouse wrote comic novels, but I turn to books hardly anybody would classify that way – Moby-Dick by Herman Melville, for instance – that yet seem to me to be a hoot. I think they are books thatdecidesomething is funny, as Jerry Seinfeld once defined comedy. In Moby-Dick, it’s a coin nailed to a masthead. In Vladimir Nabokov’s Pale Fire, it’s the worst best poem you’ve ever read. And yet we feel we’re getting at something the most solemn narratives aim for: an understanding of the human condition, of grief, of love, of death. All the big stuff. The comic novels I love are books that could just as easily have been tragedies. It is simply that the author hasdecidedit’s funny.It’s something I learned from a wise friend of mine who once, after I angrily related a publishing story of mine, responded: “That’s not a very funny story.” I was shocked. And then I understood that I had not processed the story at all, and was serving this dish to her raw. I had to learn to turn an old outrage into a funny story. And then she would be willing to listen. I did learn to do this. And I have put the very scene I have described to you into my latest novel. A comic novel, if you like.I have written both comic novels and novels where you would not crack a smile – serious novels, I suppose. And I can relate that, for me, writing the comic ones is a much more pleasant, though very different, kind of work. But the plots are no funnier than the serious ones. See if you can guess which one is comic and which is serious:A young woman in 1952 San Francisco joins with her husband’s gay lover to remove obstacles to her liberation and gain a small fortune.A middle-aged writer travels across a troubled United States while struggling to maintain his recently renewed relationship with a younger man.Even if you guessed, you see my point: I have to decide it’s funny. And that takes double-processing. Like blond hair at the salon. First, I work out the hardships and frustrations of the characters as realistically, even tragically, as possible. People die in comic novels. Sometimes the world ends, or sometimes just the world we thought we knew, and I have to consider the real reactions of my characters because, after all,theydon’t know it’s a comedy. Second, I begin to write it as if it’s all just a funny story. That takes a great deal of struggle and sometimes feels impossible.double quotation markWhen writing comedy, a whole feast of words is spread before you: hullabaloo, brouhaha, hubbub and chivaree. Chivaree!In my last novel,Less Is Lost(that’s the one about the middle-aged writer), I found myself sitting with my notes on visiting three forced labour plantations in the American south. There was nothing humorous about them, yet I didn’t want to cut them; I knew my protagonist had to confront that part of American history. But then I read over the notes of my final visit and realised thatIwas the comedy: myself and the other white visitors, showcasing our guilt and anxiety through statements that were utterly absurd. In fact, I ended up portraying the visit almost exactly as I had it in my notes … but with a different emphasis. Is it “funny”? No. Is it “comic”? Definitely. Why? I don’t know. I don’t know. I can’t explain it any better for fear of turning on the party lights.In writing my latest novel,Villa Coco,I had a much easier time, since I was working off notes in my diaries from my time living in Tuscany, and those notes were already blond hair in a salon; I made a promise to myself that I would turn each day’s events into a “funny story”. And yet, in a way, I found myself sifting through these stories for the other thing: the real feeling. Because there was the death, in those days, of a dear friend. A turn of seasons. A broken heart. All the things I would have previously put down in my diary now had been expunged, and though I had processed them into lovely stories, the job (as a novelist now and not a diarist) was to get to the hardships and frustrations of my characters. Because, to me, comedy is only great fun if it is about something hard and true.“I don’t think of you as writing a comic novel,” a writer friend told me. “I think of you as working through something in whatever way you have to.” He meant that my books are not “about” women in 1952 or middle-aged writers or olive harvests in Tuscany. They are about marriage and growing old and the terror of death. It is just that, in a comic novel, those issues are temporarily resolved, often in a flagrantly artificial fashion. As if to say: life is a vale of tears, and there’s no fixing it, but just for fun let’s fix this one small piece. Let’s decide, briefly, to lift the weight of being. You can’t successfully do that, I think, without being honest about it first.View image in fullscreenTuscany, Italy, an inspiration for Andrew Sean GreerAnd yet – what a lovely time I have working on these books. Because everything has to be processed in this way, each awful moment of the day becomes more material for comedy. Thus I become, somehow, more resilient; a trip on the sidewalk is no less embarrassing than before but, instead of trying to play it off, I laugh with anyone who notices (and peopledo notice). What would normally be a dull wait at a bus stop (or a mind‑numbing trip through the internet) becomes a delightful experience with my notebook. “Cheese rolling contest May 20,” I might copy down from a poster, “Prize is the wheel of cheese.” Or “lady in black sequined dress yelling at a mailbox at nine in the morning. I think she mailed her purse by mistake.” I am not a person who particularly lives in the present tense, but comedy forces me there. A good place to be.Language also achieves a new richness. People assume writers think about plot or characters, in the way they assume painters or photographers think about their subjects. But painters think about paint. Photographers think about light. And writers think about words. There is something so utterly delicious about being able to make use of words that are otherwise forbidden to touch. I don’t mean curse words; I mean fancy ones. Take for instance something like “noise”. In a serious novel, you would have to say “down the street came a noise”. Anything more elaborate would be a red flag of pretentiousness. So you settle for the austerity of “noise” and move on. But when writing comedy, suddenly a whole feast of words is spread before you: hullabaloo and brouhaha and hubbub and chivaree. Chivaree! Banging pots and pans together to publicly shame a citizen or tease a newly married couple! What a word! My language has not become simpler by writing comedy; it has become zestier. And if, like me, words are your favourite medium, it is akin to tomatoes finally coming into season after months of cabbage and kale.Villa Coco by Andrew Sean Greer review – fun in the Tuscan sunRead moreNo wonder what some consider the very first “novel” was one of the most rip-roaring, slapstick comedies around: Don Quixote. Chaucer himself was not above a fart joke, and Shakespeare could never resist a pun. There is a grand tradition, in fact, of great writers dabbling in comedy – Philip Roth, Saul Bellow, Thornton Wilder – and I think there is something about having seen the darkness that pulls so many to laughter. Certainly, in these difficult times, with endless apocalyptic films and novels appearing, many of us find ourselves picking upStella Gibbons’ Cold Comfort Farminstead.There is something dear and beautiful about the comic novel, something to love. A friend to hold your hand when the lights flicker out and tell you a story until they come back on again. And, for those of us who write them, a way to feel our way forward down the tunnel into the light. I know that it was a solace to imagine a much younger American man, finding himself delivered to a rural Tuscan train station that he says is “so fanciful one might unwrap it and find it was chocolate”. And to be seated next to a princess who cannot understand him because she has not mastered “the American dialect”. And throw a wild animal into his window at night. And make the septic tank overflow. All to get at a simple truth: the world is trouble, and full of sorrows, and we will not get out alive.But look closely: it is, in fact, made of chocolate.Villa Coco by Andrew Sean Greer is published by Sceptre. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Ten novels to make you laughCold Comfort Farmby Stella GibbonsThis is a satire of a genre that no longer even exists (the rural English romance) because it erased it with its perfect sense of humour.Pomp and Circumstanceby Noël CowardThe queen is coming to visit a far-flung island nation and everyone is aquiver.Pninby Vladimir NabokovThe poignancy of Nabokov’s tortured Russian academic makes one fall in love with poor Pnin.Bech: ABook by John UpdikeThe first of a series of books about a Philip Roth-like novelist adrift in the world. Like Nabokov, a wordsmith having great fun with the English language.The Selloutby Paul BeattyA brilliant example of taking the most serious of subjects – slavery in America – and turning it completely on its head.I Capturethe Castleby Dodie SmithI reread this book annually and both laugh and shed tears over the fate of our teenage narrator, Cassandra, whose diary this is.View image in fullscreenOur Man in Havanaby Graham GreenePersonally, I prefer Greene’s “entertainments” to his serious fiction, from Travels With My Aunt to this wonderful case of mistaken identity.Little Me: The Intimate Memoirs ofThat Great Star of Stage, Screen and Television, Belle Poitrineby Patrick DennisFrom the writer of Auntie Mame, a deliciously deluded memoir of an absolute nobody, complete with photographs!The Pursuit of Love/Love in a Cold Climateby Nancy MitfordEccentricity and delight mix with heartache in this classic fictionalised version of her famous family.Don Quixoteby Miguel de CervantesHilarious from beginning to end, and the sequel is even better, because suddenly Don Quixote and Sancho Panza are famous because everyone has read the first.

title: Devolution plans strengthen case for written UK constitution, says Burnham | Constitutional reform | The Guardian
description: PM argues for codified model of decentralisation that would fundamentally change centuries-old workings of state
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: PM argues for codified model of decentralisation that would fundamentally change centuries-old workings of state
Content: Burnham is inspired by Germany’s postwar basic law, which equalises finances across the regions.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenBurnham is inspired by Germany’s postwar basic law, which equalises finances across the regions.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAConstitutional reformDevolution plans strengthen case for written UK constitution, says BurnhamPM argues for codified model of decentralisation that would fundamentally change centuries-old workings of stateJosh HallidayandAletha AduSat 1 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said his programme of devolution strengthens the case for a written constitution for the UK, a move that would fundamentally alter the workings of the state that have developed over centuries.The prime minister has long believed the UK’s “antiquated” political system needs a dramatic overhaul if opportunity is to be shared equally across the country.The UK is one of only a few major democracies without a written constitution, a document that codifies how a nation is governed within a set of fundamental rules.In a potentially historic shift, Burnham said this weekend that his government’s programme of decentralisation – which includesgiving regional leaders much greater controlover their finances – strengthens the argument for a codified arrangement.“It will increase the case for a constitution because Britain is changing through this,Englandis certainly changing through this,” he said.Burnham said the UK needed to devise a codified model of devolution that works for Wales, Scotland,Northern Irelandand the English regions.“In the end, I think it does start to point towards a new constitutional settlement … with that commitment to equivalent living standards,” he said, adding that his pledge of “good growth in every postcode” was “more than just a soundbite”.Burnham described the further devolution measures outlined on Friday as the most radical departure from Britain’s overcentralised political establishment. The “rewiring” of the UK had “gone to a new level of seriousness” and was centred on shifting decision-making outside Whitehall to mayors and local authorities throughNo 10 North.Tim Bale, a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, said introducing a written constitution would be a “huge departure” for the UK. Historically, most countries did it “in the wake of a revolution or a war that has removed or delegitimised the former regime”.It is unclear how the UK government would go about such significant constitutional change at the same time as pursuingBurnham’s agendaon issues such as devolution, social care and public control of utilities.While it would bring the UK into line with other democracies such as the US, Bale said it could “represent a major constraint on the executive … because it would presumably put the rules of the game beyond the power of parliament to change with a simple majority”.He added: “One of the upsides is that it might better define the competencies of the various levels of government – local, regional and national. But there is no way he will be able to limit it to that.”In his 2024 book Head North, written with the Liverpool city region mayor, Steve Rotheram, Burnham said deep inequality had become entrenched in Britain partly because it had not evolved from a “feudal state” in which power is largely concentrated in Westminster.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it | EditorialRead more“Our failure fully to set out the rules for how the country should be run is one of the principal reasons why Britain is one of the most unequal major countries in the world,” he wrote.“Our unwritten and murky constitutional arrangements have had the effect of hoarding power in a small number of hands – in Whitehall and Westminster and, by extension, in the powerful networks of institutions and vested interests that surround them.”Burnham has cited as inspiration Germany’s postwarbasic law, orGrundgesetz, which stipulates there must be equivalent living standards in all the country’s states, with the wealthier regions redistributing their funds across the nation.Under devolution plans announced last week, by early 2028 regional mayors across England will be able to keep a share of income tax generated in their area.Under proposals to be published in late October, it is expected that economic powerhouses, such as London, Greater Manchester and the West Midlands, will hand some of their share to less prosperous regions, such as Hull and East Yorkshire.Dr Hannah White, the chief executive of the Institute for Government, said: “Adopting a written constitution – of the kind almost every other country already has – would represent a very significant constitutional shift for the UK and be a major exercise. A fully codified constitution would need to go far beyond devolution to encompass all the rules which structure the UK state.”Explore more on these topicsConstitutional reformAndy BurnhamDevolutionLabourWalesScotlandNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump offering early access to online posts in move seen as corruption | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Truth Social, where Trump’s account is by far the largest, to offer users early access for up to $100,000 per month
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Truth Social, where Trump’s account is by far the largest, to offer users early access for up to $100,000 per month
Content: Donald Trump holds up a printout from his Truth Social account, in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington DC on June 4.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenDonald Trump holds up a printout from his Truth Social account, in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington DC on June 4.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APDonald TrumpTrump offering early access to online posts in move seen as corruptionTruth Social, where Trump’s account is by far the largest, to offer users early access for up to $100,000 per monthMarina DunbarSat 1 Aug 2026 13.29 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpis now offering early access to his Truth Social posts in a move that has been seen as corruption benefitting a sitting president.Trump Media and Technology Group officially rolled out itsnew subscription-based data serviceon Saturday, giving paying customers faster, real-time access to Truth Social posts from Trump and other high-profile accounts.Called Truth API, the application programming interface is intended to provide businesses with “a direct, licensed, real-time feed of the platform’s most market-moving Truths”, interim CEO Kevin McGurn said in a release announcing the launch. Trading firms and other paying subscribers can now access the posts earlier than other users – for a fee of up to $100,000 per month.The new offering mirrors similar paid data services available on competing social media platforms, though with a particularly steep price tag. However, Truth Social stands apart because its most influential user is Trump, who is also the largest shareholder of the publicly traded parent company, meaning he could personally benefit from the service.Although the announcement does not specifically mention Trump, his @realDonaldTrump account is by far the platform’s largest. He frequently uses it to announce major policy decisions before making them elsewhere. As of Saturday, the account had 13 million followers.Criticsargue the serviceis blatant evidence of market manipulation and insider trading. Trump has repeatedly used Truth Social to reveal significant policy moves with the potential to shift financial markets, including posts involving tariffs and theIranwar.The launch comes just days after Democratic senators Adam Schiff and Elizabeth Warren called on the Securities and Exchange Commission to examine the new service. Ina letterdated Tuesday and sent to SEC chair Paul Atkins, the lawmakers urged the agency to investigate whether the company was breaking the law.“This appears to be an outrageous abuse of the President’s office for his personal benefit that undermines everyday investors and the integrity of our markets, while enriching Wall Street and other wealthy insiders,” they wrote.Last year, Trump published more than 100 Truth Social postsin a single daywhile global stock markets tumbled amid concerns that his economic agenda could trigger a “Trumpcession” in the US.His posts about Iran have drawn particular attention because investors remain concerned that rising oil prices could keep inflation elevated and potentially lead the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates.Trump Media’s stock has fallen by more than 70% since the president took office last year, wiping out roughly $6bn (£4.4bn) in shareholder value.Those losses, combined with billions more in investor losses connected to new Trump family cryptocurrency ventures, have come under increased scrutiny after Trump’s annual financial disclosure showedhe generated more than $1 billionin revenue last year from the same companies and offerings.On Friday, one day before Truth API’s debut, shares of Trump Media climbed 5.5% to $10.39 shortly before the market closed, reportedForbes. The president’s company has primarily depended on advertising revenue, but the new API service could expand its revenue sources if it proves successful.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpSocial mediaUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ultra-processed food companies hindering health drives by suing countries, says WHO | Ultra-processed foods | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Director general accuses corporations of obstructing efforts to tackle obesity crisis after investigation by Guardian and others
Author: Andrew Gregory
Headline: Exclusive: Director general accuses corporations of obstructing efforts to tackle obesity crisis after investigation by Guardian and others
Content: The investigation found 235 lawsuits were lodged over health policies targeting UPFs in Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, the US and the UK from 2010 to 2025.Photograph: Henry Romero/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe investigation found 235 lawsuits were lodged over health policies targeting UPFs in Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, the US and the UK from 2010 to 2025.Photograph: Henry Romero/ReutersUltra-processed foodsUltra-processed food companies hindering health drives by suing countries, says WHOExclusive: Director general accuses corporations of obstructing efforts to tackle obesity crisis after investigation by Guardian and othersAndrew GregoryHealth editorSat 1 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 12.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe world’s biggest ultra-processed food corporations are hindering global efforts to tackle the obesity crisis by suing governments that try to promote healthier diets, the head of theWorld Health Organizationhas said.Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, accused global food companies of obstructing the adoption of vital public health measures and costing countries billions of dollars in healthcare and legal costs in the process.Almost 1 billion people worldwide are living with obesity, and unhealthy diets are one of the main drivers of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and cancer. Ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption is soaring and now makes up half the average diet in many countries, including the UK, the US and Australia.Governments around the world, waking up to the health and economic impacts of the obesity crisis, have begun introducing measures designed to curb junk-food intake and promote healthier diets. These include front-of-pack warning labels, marketing and advertising restrictions on unhealthy products, and taxes on junk food.View image in fullscreenUltra-processed food consumption makes up half the average diet in many countries.Photograph: Kenishirotie/AlamyPublicly, the world’s biggest UPF companies insist they back the policies, want to help consumers make informed choices and are committed to being part of the solution.But aninvestigationby the Guardian, in collaboration with academics, the non-profit newsroom Lighthouse Reports and a coalition of media partners across four continents, found many of these same companies were taking governments to court to overturn, weaken or delay the policies.In total, 235 lawsuits were lodged over health policies targeting UPFs in Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, the US and the UK from 2010 to 2025,the investigation found.‘If all else fails, sue’: how ultra-processed food firms are using the courts to obstruct health rulesRead more“The findings of the global investigation by the Guardian and other outlets into ultra-processed food come as no surprise, but they are met with grim recognition,” Tedros said. “When harm and profit are tied to the same product, a familiar pattern of industry interference emerges: sowing doubt and obstructing regulation.”Of the resolved lawsuits, three-quarters were lost by the food corporations.
