title: ‘More than just objects’: Australian booksellers raise alarm over ‘horrific’ destruction of rare titles to feed AI | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Secondhand booksellers believe they may have been caught up in the AI supply chain that sees old books scanned then destroyed
Author: Stephanie Convery
Headline: Secondhand booksellers believe they may have been caught up in the AI supply chain that sees old books scanned then destroyed
Content: A 400-year-old document recording a Spanish Inquisition exorcism at the Antiquariat Forum BV and Inlibris stall at the 2026 Rare Book Fair.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA 400-year-old document recording a Spanish Inquisition exorcism at the Antiquariat Forum BV and Inlibris stall at the 2026 Rare Book Fair.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)‘More than just objects’: Australian booksellers raise alarm over ‘horrific’ destruction of rare titles to feed AISecondhand booksellers believe they may have been caught up in the AI supply chain that sees old books scanned then destroyedFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastStephanie ConverySat 1 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 21.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Sometimes books tell you more than the content,” says Tim White, as he lines up carefully dust-jacketed books and pamphlets in plastic sleeves on temporary shelves in Melbourne University’s Wilson Hall.He’s preparing his stall for this weekend’sMelbourne Rare Book Fair. For people like White, who runs independent bookshop Books for Cooks, the book as a physical object is just as important as what’s inside it.“We’re interested in where food and society connect … So we just keep pushing the boundaries, looking for things that show unusual aspects of that, things that tell us a bit more about what it is to be human,” he says.“That’s what most of us [rare booksellers] do. We handle things that have a story.”View image in fullscreenTim White of Books for Cooks says the issue raises ‘an interesting tension … If it’s a book that has that storytelling element to it, or it’s a one-off, it’s horrific.’Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianBut vendors and rare books experts are increasingly worried that these artefacts may be under threat of destruction by generative AI companies seeking to feed their ravenous technology with new texts.Fears stem from a copyright lawsuit brought against AI company Anthropic in the United States by book authors. Unsealed court files revealed earlier this yearthat the company was engaging in the practice of “destructive scanning”– buying physical books, slicing off the spines to more efficiently scan the pages, then pulping the remains – and had sought to keep it quiet. The judge ruled this was lawful under US copyright law, as it amounted to “transformative use”.The Melbourne man who loves libraries so much he created his own – and it’s so huge he needs two homes to house itRead moreThe practice is now understood to be widespread among generative AI companies, and recent reports suggestintermediaries are stepping upto facilitate the process. Australian secondhand booksellers are wondering if they have been caught up in the AI supply chain after they recently experienced waves of orders that did not fit with usual customer patterns.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsMultiple vendors confirmed to Guardian Australia they had received orders from a Canadian company called Zoom Books, which describes itself as a book recycler. The orders usually came through large secondhand marketplaces like Abebooks or Biblio, where inventory can range from cheap paperbacks to rare, expensive items.Delfina Manor, who runs Good Reading Secondhand Books in Benalla,Victoria, said she received orders from Zoom Books in May amounting to three full boxes, but had to write to the company and ask them not to order in such volume again.“They ordered, paid in advance, and they didn’t quibble over the postage … [but] it would have been about 30 to 40 books, and so finding them, packing them, making sure you hadn’t missed one out … It was just driving me nuts,” Manor said.View image in fullscreenA rare 14th-century coffret made for a book on display at the 2026 Rare Book Fair.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianJohn Sainsbury, owner of Melbourne’s Sainsburys Books, confirmed a slew of orders from Zoom Books had come through the store’s online listings around the same time. The orders were price insensitive and appeared entirely random – niche titles, “bottom-end” and sometimes decades-old stock. The orders resulted in Sainsburys shipping multiple boxes overseas.Sainsbury described his company as “a general bookseller at an antiquarian book fair”, as he doesn’t just deal in rare material. The profile fits the pattern of vendors who have received similar orders – high-end specialist sellers did not appear to have been approached.Some vendors speculated the company may be buying the books on arbitrage – common enough in the secondhand book trade – but the specific requests nevertheless seemed odd. In one order, a 1970s manual on soil mechanics was bought alongside a 2010 book called Born to Thunder: Champions of New Zealand Cycling, a collection of Early Australian Poetry (1982), and a local history of the Melbourne suburb of Hawthorn. The poetry book sold for $9 and had been on the shelf for 20 years.White says the issue raises “an interesting tension”. “If it’s a $20 book of which there’s … 500,000 copies in Australia, I wouldn’t cry,” he says. “I’d have different issues around copyright.”“If it’s a book that has that storytelling element to it, or it’s a one-off, it’s horrific.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJenny Dawes runs Grant’s Bookshop with her husband. They say they have about 500,000 books in their warehouses.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianFor booksellers struggling to catalogue their vast stock of books, let alone sell them, such sales aren’t necessarily bad.Nick Dawes, who runs Grant’s Bookshop with his wife, Jenny, estimates they have about 500,000 books in their warehouses.“If somebody wanted to come and buy all my books and cut them up, well … I’d be unhappy at one level, but I’d be happy at another,” says Dawes. “But if somebody said to me, look, this is the only known copy, I’m going to cut it up, then I’d say, I think I’d rather not send it to you.”AI companies are not the first to destroy books for profit. Some vendors source rare books in order to slice them up and sell the illustration plates individually.“When I sell a book and then find the prints available individually, I just find it physically abhorrent,” says rare bookseller Gwenyth Todd from Chatelaine Books. She screens buyers accordingly, so the books don’t go “to the wrong home”.“To me books are more than just objects.”View image in fullscreenZoom Books placed an order with John Sainsbury of Sainsburys Books for seemingly random books: niche titles, ‘bottom-end’ and sometimes decades-old stock.Photograph: Christopher Hopkins/The GuardianAn Anthropic spokesperson said the company has never bought from Zoom Books, but that “sourcing books is a widely used approach for training large language models across the AI industry”. Anthropic procures its books from mainstream commercial markets, the spokesperson said. “None of our data acquisition programs buy and destroy rare or antiquarian books.”Zoom Books’ co-founder, Manroop Gill, said ina recent LinkedIn postthat the company had been “expanding aggressively” in the past months.Zoom Books has previously denied it destructively scans books. A spokesperson told Guardian Australia: “We acquire secondhand books and resell them intact. We do not digitize books. Our priority is always reuse, and when a book can no longer be rehomed, it is responsibly recycled.”The company did not disclose if it sold intact books to AI companies for destructive scanning, saying: “Our commercial agreements require confidentiality, so we do not disclose or discuss our customers.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingVictoriafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The brief life and sudden death of Zyzz: why did the bodybuilding influencer die at just 22? | Australian film | The Guardian
description: Long before looksmaxxers, Aziz ‘Zyzz’ Shavershian was famous online for posting workouts and rage-bait – until he died in Thailand in 2011. A new documentary reveals what really happened
Author: Jenny Valentish
Headline: Long before looksmaxxers, Aziz ‘Zyzz’ Shavershian was famous online for posting workouts and rage-bait – until he died in Thailand in 2011. A new documentary reveals what really happened
Content: Aziz ‘Zyzz’ Shavershian, an Australia bodybuilder and YouTube influencer from western Sydney who died in Thailand 15 years ago. The exact circumstances of Zyzz’s death have never been revealed – until now.Photograph: StanView image in fullscreenAziz ‘Zyzz’ Shavershian, an Australia bodybuilder and YouTube influencer from western Sydney who died in Thailand 15 years ago. The exact circumstances of Zyzz’s death have never been revealed – until now.Photograph: StanAustralian filmThe brief life and sudden death of Zyzz: why did the bodybuilding influencer die at just 22?Long before looksmaxxers, Aziz ‘Zyzz’ Shavershian was famous online for posting workouts and rage-bait – until he died in Thailand in 2011. A new documentary reveals what really happenedJenny ValentishSat 1 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 20.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDecades before the extreme aesthetic trend of looksmaxxing, there was Zyzz. Aziz Shavershian was an Australian teenager who became a fitness influencer in the 2000s, filming his workouts and thoughts about the world on his Nokia and posting them to YouTube.Zyzz was big in all senses of the word: many of his videos would see him flexing into unabashedly vain bodybuilding poses, hair feathered like an anime character, as he mocked his audience’s envy with slang straight out of bodybuilding forums: “U mirin’, brah?” He was skilled in rage-bait long before anyone had heard of it, creating accounts to troll himself in case the haters ever forgot to hate. He started an anonymous Facebook page, titled “10,000 likes and I’ll bash Zyzz” and, when the goal was reached, switched the page to one advertising his protein brand.From bone smashing to chin extensions: how ‘looksmaxxing’ is reshaping young men’s facesRead moreThen Aziz made headlines in Australia when he suddenly and unexpectedly died in 2011, at the age of 22. By that point he’d attracted more than 60,000 Facebook followers who either loved him or loved to hate him. His global audience grew even more rapidly after his death as speculation grew about its cause. Fraudulent attempts to access the coroner’s report were made by people impersonating his family. Influencers made videos claiming he had faked his death. Zyzz “sightings” were posted for years.Now finally, in a new documentary being released on the 15th anniversary of his death, the truth is being revealed.Revealed – Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzzis a Stan documentary directed by film-maker Selina Miles, whose post-#MeToo documentary Silenced opened the Sydney film festival this year. But Poster Boy shares more DNA with her 2020 doco Harley & Katya, about two figure skaters who skidded into tragedy. “They both have vulnerable, impressionable young people that are willing to take risks and aren’t maybe informed about the extent of those risks,” Miles tells Guardian Australia.Poster Boy starts where the Zyzz phenomenon began: in a modest brick home in Carlingford, near Sydney’s Parramatta. The documentary includes a recreation of Aziz’s childhood bedroom, right down to the clothes strewn all over the floor; you can practically smell the hair gel and fake tan.Aziz and his older brother Said were born in Russia to Kurdish parents who then migrated to Australia where they worked long hours. In the film, the boys’ friends – many of them first-generation Australians – describe struggling to fit in, but finding community in bodybuilding. “We were a mixed bag,” one says in the documentary. “We aligned our values not on our ethnic background but on the camaraderie of training together.”View image in fullscreen‘We were a mixed bag’ … Aziz Shavershian (L) with friends.Photograph: StanThere was a community online too, within the massive forums of bodybuilding.com. Under the username Zyzz, Aziz commiserated with other young men about not being able to get girls and posted progress pictures of his physique. In 2007, when bedroom rants likeLeave Britney Alone!started going viral, Aziz unleashed his persona on YouTube. Not everyone was a fan, As Said remembers, there were some who wanted to beat them up, particularly when Aziz and his “aesthetics crew” stripped down to tiny shorts and flexed at music festivals.“I had the mindset of, ‘These guys are all just brutes,” Said tells Guardian Australia. “‘They don’t even look after their damn skin or have nice hair.’”Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThese days, Said is a fitness coach with 440,000 Instagram followers, who still goes under his forum name Chestbrah. He says he and his brother were “two nerds who built a simulation around these characters we invented”.But Aziz was also a born salesman. He had been dux of his high school, then enrolled in a marketing and commerce degree. His tactics to build and influence his audience, with stunts like the Facebook page, are common practice now, but in 2010 it was hard to monetise these new dark arts. So Aziz worked mundane jobs while he figured it out. Sometimes, as one friend recalls, he sold photographs of himself “to gross old men on the internet”.Aziz needed money to maintain his appearance: teeth whitener, tan and performance-enhancing drugs. He began to increasingly experiment with substances untested on humans, and without the recommended cycling on and off. As his fame grew, so did the gains. But the hateful comments from strangers also multiplied.“As a grown-up man, I look back and think, you bastards,” says Said. “He was one of the most beautiful men to walk the planet, not just physically, but internally. I hate that these people put these thoughts in his head.”View image in fullscreenZyzz’s brother, Said Shavershian, now.Photograph: StanFriends remember Aziz as obsessing over his perceived flaws, and using the benzodiazepine Xanax to soothe his social anxiety. His later videos veered on existential crises. “It’s a fucking act,” he says bleakly in one. “Zyzz is a fucking joke … Zyzz is a person who took over who I am.”In a rare win, he made $20,000 in two months from selling copy-and-paste training programs. “Literally the first thing he did was take that money and go for a trip to Thailand,” says Said.View image in fullscreenAziz (L) and Said (R) Shavershian.Photograph: StanOne friend worried that Pattaya City had pharmacies “like candy shops”, stocked with steroids and benzodiazepines, that would prove too tempting. Aziz reassured him he just needed to get away for a bit.The final footage Aziz took shows him wandering around the empty pool area of his hotel, alone. He had secretly booked himself in for nose and cheek reconstruction. When he died shortly after, the internet ignited with theories. The most widely circulated story was that Aziz had had a heart attack in a sauna due to a congenital heart defect; perhaps it was unthinkable that someone preaching fitness could die of anything other than natural causes, exacerbated by extreme heat.With the help of Aziz’s parents, Miles can reveal the findings of the toxicology report. While Aziz did have an enlarged heart, the cause of death was acute respiratory failure due to the combined use of morphine, cocaine and benzodiazepines. No sauna.The disturbing rise of Clavicular: how a looksmaxxer turned his ‘horror story’ into fameRead more“We don’t know what caused [the enlarged heart], whether it was his steroid use or something else,” says Miles. “And we don’t know what he took when. But it was a drug interaction that caused his death.”Poster Boy might act as a cautionary tale for a new generation, particularly since looksmaxxing influencer Connor Murphy died in Thailand in July, drowning in a lake amid just as much mystery; or looksmaxxing figurehead Braden Eric Peters AKAClavicular, who overdosed on a substance mid-livestream in April but was revived.Miles hopes people will be more curious and kind to young men like Aziz. “What I would give to be able to have a conversation with him,” she says. “But he lives on through his friends. They’re empathetic, self-aware men who have done a lot of self-reflection. They loved Aziz and he loved them. That speaks volumes as to who he might have been behind the scenes.”Said is certain that his brother would have pursued a more positive path than the looksmaxxing and manosphere influencers who followed in his wake.“Az was split between a rock and a hard place,” he says. “He loved the attention, but he was a good kid. With great power comes great responsibility and I think he started to feel that. We always just wanted to help everyone be the hero of their own story and to see the potential that they have.”Revealed – Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzzis available to stream in Australia on StanExplore more on these topicsAustralian filmDocumentary filmsBody imageHealth & wellbeingStanMen's healthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Purple reign: how shade became British gardeners’ favourite | Gardens | The Guardian
description: Britons move away from trend of grey paving and pristine lawns in an embrace of colour, with lavender a top choice
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Britons move away from trend of grey paving and pristine lawns in an embrace of colour, with lavender a top choice
Content: More than 11,000 visitors of RHS Garden Wisley’s Hilltop were asked to pick their favourite colour for plants.Photograph: Tim Graham/AlamyView image in fullscreenMore than 11,000 visitors of RHS Garden Wisley’s Hilltop were asked to pick their favourite colour for plants.Photograph: Tim Graham/AlamyGardensPurple reign: how shade became British gardeners’ favouriteBritons move away from trend of grey paving and pristine lawns in an embrace of colour, with lavender a top choiceHelena HortonSat 1 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you manage to spot a garden in bloom this summer, beyond the strips of bleached and torched grass, there may be one colour you see more than any other: purple, the horticultural hue of the season.Plants such as lavender, salvias and catmint are in vogue, according to the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS), which conducted extensive research into the colours Britons best love to see in their gardens.In one experiment at RHS Garden Wisley’s Hilltop, more than 11,000 visitors were asked to choose their preferred shades. Purple flower hues accounted for the strongest preference (26.67%), closely followed by red (25.24%).View image in fullscreenVisitors look at the crops at Warwickshire lavender farm.Photograph: Jacob King/PAThe purple patch has surprisedgardentrend watchers and marks a departure from recent less dramatic trends. Grey hues have been very popular in home and garden design over the last few years.Tom Massey, anaward-winninggarden designer based in London, said clients wanted bright colours, particularly purples. He said: “We’ve moved away from the era of large expanses of decking, paving and lawn towards richer, more naturalistic planting inspired by meadows and natural plant communities.”View image in fullscreenMore natural, colourful garden styles are growing in popularity.Photograph: Ros Crosland/AlamyLaura Carey, who co-owns Carey garden designs with her husband, Joe, has found that purple is the most popular colour with her clients, too. She said: “Purple is a favourite across the board with all of our clients. There are so many purple flowering plants to choose from, including national favourites like lavender, alliums and geraniums.”View image in fullscreenCatmint is also a popular purple plant.Photograph: John Glover/AlamyMassey added: “Purple has always been a hugely important colour in gardens because it combines beautifully with greens, silvers and the buff tones of ornamental grasses. It also attracts pollinators and tends to have a calming quality. Plants like salvias, nepetas, alliums and lavender remain incredibly popular for exactly those reasons.”The popularity of the colour may be related to the emotions it evokes in humans. Other research found that purples and blues evoke a sense of calm and relaxation, and yellows and oranges bring joy.Massey said: “I think people are becoming much more confident with colour generally. You can see this in high-profile public landscapes that have proved hugely popular, such as Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in London, parts of the High Line in New York, and the seasonal displays and borders at RHS gardens like Wisley, where bold combinations of colour are used to create planting schemes that are both beautiful and ecologically rich.”View image in fullscreenSalvia nachtvlinder.Photograph: Elf Photography/AlamyThe findings were published in the study Flower Power: How favourite flower colours shape how we feelinActa Psychologica.Dr Ashby Sachs, a wellbeing fellow at the RHS, said: “Colour is a key consideration when it comes to garden design, but little is known about how it interacts with our sense of wellbeing. That different shades of colour can elicit an anticipated emotional response in people is incredibly useful when it comes to designing spaces for specific purposes and people such as in schools and hospitals.”Explore more on these topicsGardensPlantsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Knickers in a twist: why M&S selling crotchless underwear isn’t as outrageous as it seems | Marks & Spencer | The Guardian
description: Some have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts say
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Some have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts say
Content: In 2024, M&S reported a third of underwear sales were made by people under 30.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenIn 2024, M&S reported a third of underwear sales were made by people under 30.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAMarks & SpencerKnickers in a twist: why M&S selling crotchless underwear isn’t as outrageous as it seemsSome have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts sayLauren CochraneSat 1 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe news that Marks & Spencer is selling Ann Summers crotchless knickers on their website has been greeted – as might be expected – with outrage online, being described as everything from “tawdry” to“S & M”.But it could be this is just the latest evolution in what the UK’s biggest underwear retailer has available for the smalls drawer. In recent years, the store has sold vastly different options through its own products, ranging from full-brief knickers to thongs, period knickers and those that can be used bywomen who wear stomas. The introduction of other brands in clothing came five years ago, with underwear included. Ann Summers – which is selling bras and chemises as well as knickers on the M&S website – lines up alongside lingerie brands including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein.Catherine Shuttleworth, the chief executive of retail consultancy Savvy, sees it as part of wider strategy. “They’ve started introducing brands to bring them into sectors that probably isn’t their core,” she says. “And this is another one. It’s just a little bit more eye-catching.”View image in fullscreenThe offending crotchless thong being sold by M&S, which has been called ‘tawdry’Photograph: M&SShuttleworth describes M&S underwear as a “national obsession” and there’s little doubt the store remains a must-visit for anyone restocking their underwear drawer. If its long-term popularity might have meant it was perceived as a bit mumsy for younger people, that has changed recently. In 2024, the store reported that people under 30 made up a third of underwear sales – double that of 2023.View image in fullscreenThe Ann Summers knickers are sold on M&S’s website alongside other retailers including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein.Photograph: M&SShuttleworth says the introduction of Ann Summers could be about continuing to engage this demographic. “They are always innovating for every stage of your life,” she says. “And I think this is a gap in their category. Ann Summers is a byword for sex, isn’t it?”This echoes the message coming from the retailer itself. In a statement, an M&S spokesperson said: “Our ‘brands at M&S’ strategy is all about giving customers greater choice through carefully selected third-party brands that complement our existing M&S offer. Ann Summers is one of the latest brands to join [M&S online], helping broaden our underwear and nightwear offer.”There is also, of course, the publicity factor. “It doesn’t really matter whether they sell any crotchless pants or not, we’re all going to be talking about it,” says Shuttleworth. “You might also go online to look. You might not buy those, but you’ll think: ‘I could do with replacing my pants.’”M&Shas sold underwear since the 1920s and fitted bras since 1947. It was the first retailer to sell pre-shrunk cotton underwear in 1965, and by 1976 knickers were the biggest export – nearly 4m pairs were sold internationally every year. Fashion dictated different styles – from the “hip-hugger” styles in the 60s to thongs, whichreached the apex of popularity in the mid-00s.In 2016, the store sold 60m pairs of knickers a year, with Brazilian knickers replacing the thong. The style, which reveals some of the wearer’s bum, made up 10% of those sales. By 2021,thongs were back, thanks to the popularity of low rise jeans. According to the retailer’s website, the No 1 bestseller now is a five-pack of white full briefs.View image in fullscreenExperts have said that M&S have always followed trends, including lace designs a world away from basics.Photograph: PR ImageLorraine Topper, a researcher atThe Underpinnings Museum, argues the reaction around the crotchless knickers is disproportionate – because the store does stock sexier styles along with basics.“M&S have always followed fashion with regard to their lingerie designs,” she says. “For some reason, it’s the multipack of full briefs that sticks in people’s heads when you talk about their underwear, rather than, for example, the beautiful lace designs from the Rosie Exclusively range.”She describes the outrage as “a fuss over nothing … Open-crotch underwear for women was the norm before the 1920s so this type of garment isn’t quite as scandalous as we might first think.”Explore more on these topicsMarks & SpencerRetail industryUnderwearnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I felt sick that he was near my mum’: a top amputation surgeon had his own legs removed due to a fetish. Were his patients safe? | Crime | The Guardian
description: Neil Hopper was celebrated for continuing to do his job despite the loss of his lower limbs. But what the people he was treating didn’t know was that his injuries were self-inflicted. Now they and their families are asking questions
Author: Jenny Kleeman
Headline: Neil Hopper was celebrated for continuing to do his job despite the loss of his lower limbs. But what the people he was treating didn’t know was that his injuries were self-inflicted. Now they and their families are asking questions
Content: Neil Hopper in a photo from his Instagram page, @bionicsurgeon. Composite: Instagram/ BionicSurgeonNeil Hopper was celebrated for continuing to do his job despite the loss of his lower limbs. But what the people he was treating didn’t know was that his injuries were self-inflicted. Now they and their families are asking questionsWarning: this story contains graphic descriptions of bodily mutilation that some readers may find upsettingByJenny KleemanSat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOf all the things that happened in the fraught days after 72-year-old Liz Spooner had her leg amputated at the RoyalCornwallhospital in Truro in 2022, one memory remains vivid in the mind of her daughter, Faye Harrison. Liz’s surgery had taken much longer than anticipated, Faye remembers, and, delirious after the anaesthetic and morphine, Liz had begun to refuse food and medication. That’s when Faye was ushered into a side room with a consultant surgeon.“He was smiley. He came across as quite charming and caring,” Faye recalls. He ran through a long list of the medications Liz was taking, and began explaining why she needed them. “I remember looking down – you look down at the floor a lot when you have these kinds of conversations – and I noticed he’d got metal sticks coming out of his trouser legs.” Faye blinks in disbelief at the memory. “I thought, blimey, he’s operated on my mum, but he’salsoan amputee.”Neil Hopper was a celebrity in the world of vascular surgery – the specialist field involving veins and arteries, and therefore amputations. He had been a consultant for a decade by the time of Liz’s operation, and had received awards for clinical excellence. But in May 2019, following suspected sepsis, Hopper himself had had to undergo double below-the-knee amputations. When he walked into the surgical theatre on prosthetic legs in January 2020 ready to perform amputations on patients again, a BBC camera crewwas thereto film his heroic comeback. He talked about his experience of sepsis on the sofa ofITV’s This Morning, dressed in shorts that proudly exposed his prosthetics. Using the handle @bionicsurgeon, he had documented his experiences as a disabled doctor on social media. He even applied to the European Space Agency, hoping to be the world’s first astronaut with a disability. He won multiple accolades: named one of thecoolestpeople in Cornwall, and one of thebravestpeople in Britain.View image in fullscreenHopper tells his story on ITV’s This Morning, 6 March 2020.Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockBut Faye chose not to mention his legs during their 15-minute conversation about her mum. Instead, she made some small talk: noting Hopper’s Welsh accent, she declared Cornwall’s beaches to be far better than Wales’s. It was an odd scenario, but there was at least something reassuring about knowing the man caring for her mother was himself an amputee. “I remember thinking, God, he must have amazing empathy.” Coming out of the side room, Faye told her husband about the extraordinary surgeon she’d just met. “It’s awful, really, but I remember saying, ‘He’s got prosthetic legs – and his name’sHopper.’ Because, in times like that, you look for anything that’s going to make you laugh.”It had been a harrowing few days for Liz’s family, but the ordeal had begun a year earlier, when she had fallen on the beach and broken her leg. A people person, Liz was a former nurse who went on to manage a children’s home in Birmingham for 12 years before settling in Cornwall. After her husband’s death in 2009, she filled her days volunteering at the RNLI shop in Rock. It was after a shift there, while walking her dog, that Liz tripped and broke her left femur. It didn’t heal properly and, six months later, she had surgery to insert a metal rod in her leg, which then became infected. In July 2022, Liz was told she needed to make a choice: she could either take antibiotics for the rest of her life, which could stop working, or have her leg amputated. “Get rid of that bloody leg, get rid of the infection, and she’s going to be all right, we thought,” Faye says.double quotation markShe was never my mum again, after that operationView image in fullscreenLiz Spooner (on the right) and her daughter Faye Harrison in Spain in 2017.Photograph: courtesy of Faye HarrisonThey were expecting the procedure to take five or six hours, but Faye tells me it took 11 or 12. Recovering on the high-dependency unit, Liz became paranoid and delusional. She told Faye there were ghosts in her room; that people were out to get her; that she was being secretly filmed. “The nurses and doctors were saying this was normal after a very big anaesthetic and all the morphine. But she was never really out of that state. She was never my mum again, after that operation.” Liz contracted hospital-acquired pneumonia and, nine days after her surgery, she died.Faye says that no one ever explained why her mum’s procedure had taken so much longer than anticipated. If it had been shorter, she wondered, then perhaps Liz wouldn’t have been so delirious afterwards, or she might not have been in hospital for long enough to contract the pneumonia that killed her. But Liz had always believed in theNHS, and so does Faye – she works as an NHS speech and language therapist. She assumed her mum had just been very unlucky. “No reason to doubt anything,” she shrugs.NHS surgeon who had his legs removed to satisfy sexual interest is jailed for fraudRead moreThen, three years after her mother’s death, in September 2025, Faye was listening to the news on her drive into work, and heard Neil Hopper’s name. He had beenjailed after pleading guilty to two counts of fraud by false representation and three counts of possession of extreme pornography. The fraud conviction related to claims he had made on his health insurance after the amputation of his legs. Hopper had not had sepsis, after all – the injuries that caused his legs to be amputated were self-inflicted. He had deliberately harmed himself, because he had an amputation fetish.Faye felt as if she was going to vomit. “Oh my God, I felt sick that he was evennearmy mum.”Royal Cornwall hospitals NHS trustissued a statementon the day Hopper was convicted. “We want to reassure the public that our exhaustive investigations have found no evidence whatsoever to indicate any risk or harm to patients at our hospitals,” it said. But Faye was not reassured.“Who gets their own legs amputated when there’s nothing wrong with them? And then to think that he’d been adoctor.And then – even worse – a doctor who does amputations on other people.” Questions swirled around her head. “My mum was in that operating room a very, very long time. Was something going on?”Across Cornwall and beyond, Hopper’s former patients and their families were asking similar questions. Here was a surgeon prepared to lie for years to his colleagues, his patients, the wider public and his closest family about the nature of his injuries – a man who, on the basis of the extreme pornography he was convicted of possessing,revelled in seeing people in excruciating pain. How could anyone be sure he never posed any risk to patients?Hopper was resolutely silent after his arrest in March 2023. He replied “No comment” in his two police interviews; he did not speak in court. Perhaps the greatest insight into his mindset and character comes from comparing his Bionic Surgeon persona with the truth that emerged during his criminal trial and his fitness to practise tribunal. The contrast lays bare the questions that remain for Hopper’s former patients – and his former employers.On the surface, at least, Hopper seemed to live a very conventional life before he lost his legs. The son of two nurses, he grew up in Aberystwyth and Swansea, and attended a private boarding school. He studied at University of Wales College of Medicine in Cardiff, earning a first-class degree in anatomical sciences and an honours degree in medicine. He met his future wife at medical school, they had a son and a daughter, and the family went to Australia for a year, where Hopper worked as a vascular surgeon in Sydney, before returning to the UK in 2013 to be a consultant surgeon, both at the Royal Cornwall hospital and at the Duchy, Cornwall’s only private hospital. “I developed a keen interest in vascular surgery mainly because it was reconstructive, no two operations were the same, and having to operate on all parts of the body provided the variety to keep my interest,” Hoppertoldthe Western Mail in 2021.In April 2019, so his story went, Hopper and his daughter became unwell during a family camping trip. “My daughter got better but I didn’t, so my family abandoned me at home thinking I had a stomach bug. I started feeling a bit achy so took some paracetamol and went to bed,” hetoldCornwall Live in February 2020. Later, Hopper’s wife and children were away visiting his in-laws; when his wife rang him and he “spoke gibberish” on the phone to her she called a friend, who went around to check on him, found the front door open, and called an ambulance. “The next thing I remember is being in intensive care,” Hopper continued. “I remember my feet hurting a lot.”double quotation markIn the chatrooms and on the message boards, members who had undergone verified castration, amputation or genital removal were given special badges of honourHopper told doctors he’d been vomiting and had diarrhoea. He underwent extensive testing, with medical staff bewildered by the cause of his condition. In the end, they suspected sepsis. “I could see my toes had gone blue so at that point I knew where I was sort of headed,” he latertold the BBC; blue skin on the soles of the feet is a recognisedsign of sepsis. For two weeks, his medical colleagues tried to improve the blood supply to his legs. He was transferred from the Royal Cornwall hospital to Derriford, a specialist training hospital, for hyperbaric oxygen therapy. But it was in vain. Once amputation began to look inevitable, he said to the BBC, he “couldn’t help but imagine the mechanics” of what it would entail. “The thought of power tools being used on me was icky.” Hopper’s toes were removed on 10 May, and, when that wasn’t deemed enough, he opted to have both his lower legs removed on 17 May.“I’m now a bilateral below-knee amputee, which is quite ironic, given my job,” Hopper declared in thefirst videouploaded to his YouTube channel, six months after his surgery; he had already started calling himself the Bionic Surgeon by then. In another video, uploaded to mark his first year as an amputee, heboastedabout getting an all-expenses paid trip to Salford to be on BBC Breakfast. In early 2022, he revealed he was undergoing assessments in Hamburg with the European Space Agency, in a bid to become the world’s first para‑astronaut; he got down to the final 27 candidates. “When I was ill, somebody told me that I’d end up doing Ted Talks and all sorts, and I said absolutely not, this was never going to be a big part of my life, and I’ve completely fallen into that trap,” he chuckled onBBC Radio Cornwall. He knew his injuries had opened up a particular kind of opportunity for him. “My life is more interesting because of what’s happened to me,” hetold a Welsh BBC documentary crew, just before his arrest.But Hopper’s journey to becoming the Bionic Surgeon actually began the year before he lost his legs, with a very different set of videos. It was revealed during his criminal trial that, in August 2018, Hopper used the email address adecentguyincornwall@gmail.com to set up the profile “AdmiroDoc” on eunuchmaker.com, a pay-per-view fetish website featuring videos of men and boys either maiming themselves or allowing others to mutilate them on camera.Marius Gustavson, the Norwegian man living in London who ran the site, had had his own penis, nipple and left leg removed. Gustavson is currently serving a life sentence for multiple offences, including causing grievous bodily harm with intent.‘Ican see how Neil Hopper got into it,” says the man who was known as “Michael” during Gustavson’s trial. “I don’t think he just got it into his head one day to type in ‘Eunuch Maker’ – I think he was on various fetish sites looking for more and more extreme stuff and found his way on there. A little bit of passing interest, and then as soon as you’re on that site, it becomes an echo chamber.”Michael was the first person to report Gustavson to the police, after Gustavson had castrated him on video and branded him with the initials “EM”. Michael had been in a vulnerable mental state and was using drugs when Gustavson mutilated him; he went to the police when he was in recovery a year later, and realised he’d been the victim of what the judge in Gustavson’s trial would call “little more thanhuman butchery”. “The thing with that website is, it made all of this seem absolutely normal,” Michael says.The site operated between 14 January 2018 and 1 March 2021, during which time Gustavsonearnedalmost £300,000 from more than 22,800 paying users from across the globe. (The victims who appeared in the videos were promised money from the revenue; Michael says his castration earned him £60, which didn’t even cover the cost of his travel.) In the chatrooms and on the message boards, members who had undergone verified castration, amputation or genital removal were given special badges of honour. “It was a community. Very supportive, very welcoming and very enthusiastic,” Michael tells me.“There were always rumours of, oh, there’s anactualsurgeon here, there’s anactualnurse,” he continues. Therewasa nurse, it transpired: Nathan Arnold, whoreceived a suspended sentenceafter he was found guilty of GBH for removing Gustavson’s nipple. And there was Hopper. “It’s absolutely horrifying to learn that a consultant surgeon in the NHS really was there.”I am loath to describe the videos Hopper was watching – which I learned about when I attended his criminal court hearing via video link – but the broad details are relevant to his patients. Hopper was performing surgery on them in his professional life while watching people writhing in agony in his private life; this was pornography so sadistic and extreme that possession of it added 10 months to the 22-month prison sentence he received for insurance fraud.The first video cost Hopper £10; it shows Gustavson castrating another man. The second, costing £35, features a man tied to a bed while Gustavson rolls dice to decide which body parts to remove; the man ended up losing his penis and testicles, and bled so much that Gustavson called an ambulance, all with the camera still rolling. In a third video, also costing Hopper £35, a man cuts off his own penis and holds it up to the camera.double quotation markHopper does not regret the facts of the amputations – he had wanted it for 20 years – but he regrets the dishonesty and falsehood“I’ve watched them thousands of times,” Hopper enthusiastically messaged Gustavson on WhatsApp, singling out the video where paramedics had to be called for particular praise.Hopper was paying for these videos a few months after operating on a woman I’ll call Joan. We meet in a cafe in west London; she doesn’t want me to say where she lives or use her real name. Joan had booked into the private Duchy hospital to have a varicose vein removed in advance of her daughter’s wedding. “He was the vein man at the Duchy,” she tells me. “He seemed very nice, really easy-going. He’s a sort of cuddly man – slightly overweight and jolly-looking. I warmed to him.” She thought it was going to be straightforward. “My mother and one of my sisters had had veins removed before, and neither of them had ever had any problems.”Throughout the 30-minute procedure, Hopper was in charge of removing Joan’s vein and administering the anaesthetic. “I hurta lot,” she says, fixing me with her gaze. At first, she didn’t want to make a fuss. “I’m not a baby, I’m not a coward. I thought, I’ll just put up with it until it’s over. But it got to the point where Icouldn’tput up with it. I had to say, this really, really hurts.” Hopper could see her squirming, and hear her pleading for him to stop. He said he’d give her more anaesthetic, but it made no difference. “It still hurt just as much. It felt like he waspullinga vein out of my leg without any anaesthetic at all.”After the operation, Hopper refused to let Joan pay for it. “It was a few hundred pounds, and he let me off the bill. Private doctors don’t do that – they just don’t.” She shakes her head. “At the time I thought, what a nice man – that’s so reasonable of him, because he had hurt me a lot.”Joan was alarmed to read about Hopper’s conviction in the newspaper. “It was unnerving.” She hadn’t followed the details of the case, and didn’t know about the videos Hopper had been watching, until I told her about them in the broadest possible terms. “It makes me feel physically sick. It’s beyond belief,” she says. “But I’m glad I know, actually: I thought I was imagining it. It felt like he hadn’t used anaesthetic, when I had been told he had. But I no longer know for sure that he did.” She shakes her head. “He was obviously deranged, and I’d been at his mercy.”RamsayHealthCare UK, the parent company behind the Duchy hospital, said it was unable to comment on any individual episodes of patient care. “During his period of holding practising privileges with Ramsay Health Care UK, no significant concerns were raised regarding Mr Hopper’s clinical practice or any risk to patient safety,” a spokesperson said in a statement. “We want to reassure our patients, partners and the wider community that we remain fully committed to the highest standards of professional conduct and clinical governance.”double quotation markThere’s going to be more people discovered through this – are we going to have a police officer next? A politician?Towards the end of 2018, Hopper messaged Gustavson asking him to fix a fault that meant he could no longer watch the videos he’d bought. “Don’t worry,” Hopper eventually wrote, “my tastes are more exotic these days.”Gustavsoncausedhis own left leg to be amputated in February 2019. He had placed his foot in a bucket of dry ice for eight hours (uploading a short video of the process to his website) before going to hospital where his leg was ultimately removed below the knee.By April, Hopper was asking for advice on how he could do the same. Gustavson sent him a digital document with instructions, equipment lists and diagrams, telling Hopper where to order the dry ice and how to access the dark web to buy opiates for pain relief. The prosecution in Hopper’s trial argued that Hopper was not groomed: he was an equal and willing participant. “Wow,” Hopper messaged Gustavson, “I’ve dreamed of this for 20 years.”With his wife and children away at his in-laws and both feet submerged in dry ice, Hopper sent Gustavson periodic WhatsApp updates. “It’s going to be awesome being a double amputee,” he wrote. Then, he sent Gustavson a photograph of his erect penis. He continued messaging Gustavson from his hospital bed after the amputation, thanking him for making it all possible, and sending a photo of his bandaged stumps, saying how “sexy” it was. “It feels so cool. No feet!”Gustavson was arrested in 2021. The police investigation into his devices and communications ultimately led them to Hopper, who was first interviewed in March 2023, and alsoa web of others in positions of authority in British society who derived sexual gratification from mutilation. Three days before Hopper’s court hearing, former vicar Geoffrey Baulcomb wassentencedto three years in prison for GBH after maiming another man’s genitals on camera. Michael, the man who first reported Gustavson, is convinced there are going to be more arrests. “There’s going to be more people discovered through this,” he says. “Are we going to have a police officer next? A lawyer? A politician?”It wasn’t Hopper’s fetish that led to his downfall – it was his lies. Before submitting fraudulent health insurance claims to Aviva and Old Mutual Wealth (now Quilter), Hopper had consulted friends and family – people who had no idea his injuries were self-inflicted – about whether he should make the applications. “I sort of feel like I should milk this for as much as possible,” he texted a friend. In a message to his father, he wrote, “If it’s hundreds of thousands, I’ll cash it in. If it’s tens of thousands, I’ll leave it.” His total insurance payout was £466,653.81. He also claimed around £44,000 in disability benefits.The insurance claims had both been paid by July 2019; the same month, Hopper commissioned an architect to design an extension to his home. He spent £15,000 on a hot tub, £3,000 on audio equipment and £22,000 on a luxury camping trailer. He posted pictures of his new kitchen and hot tub on Instagram, then a month later he posted a picture of the family Christmas tree with the comment “Life ain’t bad!”. By November 2022, all the insurance money had been spent.During Hopper’s trial, the prosecution accepted that Hopper had neither taken out health insurance with the intention of making fraudulent claims nor frozen his feet in order to enrich himself; he had made the claims becausenotclaiming might look suspicious. His motivation for harming himself, they argued, was sexual, not financial.Hopper’s defence team presented a different explanation. His defence barrister told the court that Hopper had suffered from lifelong gender dysphoria, as well as body dysmorphia, which manifested in a loathing for his feet. “They felt like an unwelcome extra.” He had tried to fill his life with family and work, but could not quiet the “constant noise” and “persisting, never-ending discomfort” caused by the idea of his feet. (Gustavson’s legal team had made similar arguments at Gustavson’s trial: that he had body integrity disorder and had simply been offering a service to others like him.) But the sexual content, both in the videos Hopper watched and in the communication he sent Gustavson while he was harming himself, are undeniable. Hopper was aroused by what he saw, and what he did.double quotation markDavid remembers waking up during surgery and being roughly pushed back down on to the operating table“He does not regret the facts of the amputations – he had wanted it for 20 years – but he regrets the dishonesty and falsehood,” his barrister continued. Appealing to the judge before sentencing, the barrister informed the court that Hopper’s wife had left him. He asked for a suspended sentence, noting that Hopper would be forever recognisable, but would no longer garner any public sympathy. He read out a statement from Hopper: “My thoughts and behaviours have not had any effect on my job,” it read. “I worked very hard and always tried my best for my patients.”After Hopper received his sentence – 32 months in prison plus a 10-year sexual harm prevention order – the Royal Cornwall hospitals trust said their investigations had revealed “no evidence whatsoever to indicate any risk” to Hopper’s patients. But when Hopper’s fitness to practise was assessed at aMedical Practitioners Tribunal Service (MPTS) hearingin May this year, which looked at whether Hopper should be allowed to continue as a doctor, the tribunal found “an extremely high level of seriousness and risk in this case, and that Dr Hopper has not demonstrated any meaningful insight or remediation into the impact of his behaviour on public protection”. Recommending that he be struck off the medical register, Robert Dudley, on behalf of the GMC, said: “The doctor’s professional life cannot be separated from his personal behaviours.”The tribunal took place virtually, over Microsoft Teams, with Hopper representing himself. He rang in from prison, his place in the hearing marked by a redacted phone number on a grey rectangle. When he gave his final statement, his voice was thin, reedy and full of self-pity.“I’m finding this rather difficult,” he began. “I am currently in prison for these crimes, and I have never denied responsibility or guilt for them.” (He did, however, say “No comment” in his police interviews; he could have done considerably more to help ensure that justice was done.) “I attended this tribunal in order to prove that I understood the seriousness of the allegations and to face them. I had the opportunity to hide away, but, regardless of what people might think of me, I have principles.” He said he was “a person of deep reflection and conscience” and that it had “taken me ages to come to terms with what I’ve done”. Not once did he mention his former patients, or the profound distress he might have caused them. He was struck off on 29 May.‘Not a surprise,” says Mike Bird, partner and specialist in medical claims at Enable Law, when I speak to him a few days after the tribunal gave its verdict. “What worries me is that there’s a huge discrepancy between the perception of how serious this was by the trust where he worked, on the one hand, and the regulator of the profession, on the other. The trust concluded there was no risk to the public – and they said thatafterhe’d been convicted – whereas the MPTS and the GMC said there were extremely high levels of risk.”Bird says his firm has had about 20 serious inquiries from Hopper’s former patients. “There hasn’t been a long line of people saying, ‘I’ve had my limb amputated and I believe it was inappropriately done,’” he tells me; a significant proportion of amputees are elderly, and many of Hopper’s former patients may have already died. “Of those who’ve contacted us, some have felt a sense of betrayal or even a feeling of assault because of what they now think was going on in his mind when he was treating them. They are questioning whether the decisions he made about their treatment were appropriate, whether they were motivated by his own sexual gratification rather than clinical need.” It’s much harder to claim damages for psychological trauma compared with physical injuries. “The law doesn’t always follow reality,” Bird says.In response to a freedom of information request, the Royal Cornwall hospitals trust has released the report it commissioned on Hopper’s caseload, an investigation the trustdescribedin the statement it gave to the press on the day of Hopper’s convictionas “exhaustive”, “comprehensive” and conducted by “an independent clinical expert”. “It’s done by someone who’s not an expert in the field, someone who is not independent of the trust. He’s not talked to other colleagues, other staff or any patients: he’s looked at the medical records of 30 patients,” Bird says. The focus was on procedures that took place between 1 August 2018 and 31 October 2020, years before Faye’s mother, Liz, had her surgery.View image in fullscreenMike Bird, the lawyer representing Hopper’s patients.Photograph: Max Searl/The Guardian“It’s a very brief, very superficial reactive response to a crisis situation – and it’s not enough,” Bird continues. “When I’ve spoken to patients who subsequently contacted us, they have said, ‘Is this not the trust marking its own homework?’ Where’s the independence? Where’s the rigour? When something like this happens, why did the trust not immediately go to NHS England or the Royal College of Surgeons and say, ‘Please help us work out what’s happened’?”“Our priority from the beginning has been to investigate Mr Hopper’s actions so that we can reassure patients there is no evidence of risk or harm to them,” a spokesperson for the Royal Cornwall hospitals NHS trust said in response to this article. “RCHT carried out clinical reviews of all amputation surgery carried out by Mr Hopper at our hospitals over a two‑year period specified by police investigators. These formed part of the police investigation process. Our investigations found no evidence to indicate any risk or harm to patients.”The RCHT added that complex vascular surgery is always managed by a team of healthcare professionals, and is never the decision of one surgeon. “We have received reassurance on vascular surgical outcomes between 2013 and 2023 from the National Vascular Registry, who analysed our data for that period, and said further analysis would not add value to this case.”David Parker was one of the first patients Hopper operated on after he came back to work on prosthetic legs. He was clearly still getting used to them: David says when they first met for his consultation, Hopper “fell in the doorway and fell into his chair”. But it was winter, and Hopper was wearing long trousers instead of shorts, so David had no idea his surgeon was an amputee. He only realised a year or so later, when he saw a documentary on regional television. “It was saying what a hero he was, still doing his job after having his legs removed.”By that time, David didn’t consider Hopper to be a hero. He’d had a procedure to unblock an artery in his neck; Hopper had assured him it would be straightforward and shouldn’t take more than one or two hours, but it ended up taking an entire day. David remembers waking up during surgery and being roughly pushed back down on to the operating table. Ever since he came out of theatre six years ago, he has suffered debilitating nerve pain. He has spent all his retirement savings on private physiotherapy, to little avail.View image in fullscreen‘Something happened in the surgery that day, which I’m still living with’: David Parker, one of Hopper’s patients.Photograph: Max Searl/The Guardian“The day after the surgery, Mr Hopper came and sat on the side of my bed. The first thing he said to me was, ‘Do you remember anything from yesterday?’ And I said, ‘Well, I remember waking up.’ He said, ‘No, no, that didn’t happen. That’s probably just the anaesthetic playing tricks on your mind.’ I never saw him again.”David says he has since had it confirmed by other staff present during the procedure at the Royal Cornwall hospital that hedidwake up during surgery. He has been trying to work out how he came to be injured ever since, with years of emails and follow up meetings. Once the news of Hopper’s conviction broke, David says, “My case made a lot more sense. Something happened in the surgery that day, which I’m still living with.” The nerve damage could have occurred during the procedure on his vein or when he was pushed down on to the operating table. David accepts he may never be able to find out.He doesn’t believe the trust’s assertion that Hopper never posed any risk to patients. “I can’t imagine a man with so many psychological problems being able to do a surgery and put all his personal life to one side. It just wouldn’t happen, would it?” He sighs.“Professionals can talk about his professional life – I’ll talk about his private life,” Michael says when I put this to him. “At the time that I was on that website, it was constantly there in my mind. It colours everything. It takes years to get it out of your system. If you’re looking at that sort of stuff, and it’s the same stuff you’re doing at work day-to-day – I’d find it very difficult to compartmentalise. I don’t think it’d be possible.”It is the never knowing – the lifelong, gnawing doubt – that is the source of ongoing trauma for Hopper’s former patients and their families. They know one thing for sure: they had a doctor who was consistently, and criminally, dishonest.double quotation markI just refuse to believe that there weren’t ulterior motives behind the operations he carried outThe name of the surgeon who operated on Faye’s mother was not revealed in the inquest into her death. Even though she had a consultation with him after Liz’s operation, Faye had never been certain that Hopper had performed the amputation. When she recently contacted the Royal Cornwall hospital for confirmation, she was told that, despite her vivid memories of her consultation with him, there was “… no record of Mr Hopper being involved at any stage” in Liz’s care.In response to inquiries from the Guardian, the Royal Cornwall hospitals NHS trust says Liz’s medical records show that Hopper was not in theatre for the amputation of her leg, and that procedure only took three and a half hours, not the 11 or 12 that Faye claims it did.Faye has text messages she sent to family members during her mum’s surgery informing them that the procedure was taking far longer than the five hours they had originally anticipated. She says she clearly remembers repeatedly ringing the hospital during the surgery to ask why her mother still hadn’t come out of it, and being told by staff that her mother’s delirious state was due to her having such a lengthy procedure.“I just don’t seem to be getting anything back from the hospital that’s correct,” Faye sighs. “Things happened that I know for a fact happened. I know I met Neil Hopper. I know he was involved in my mum’s care. I don’t know whether he’s just lied and covered his tracks, and therefore the hospital is going by what they’ve got.”“He may well have been involved – he just may not have made notes,” says Bird. “He lied to his medical professional colleagues. The medical records he did make – why would they be right? They were written by a proven liar.” It’s another reason, Bird says, that any review into Hopper’s work that’s based on medical notes alone is inadequate.Hopper was told he must serve at least 40% of his sentence, so he will be eligible for release from prison within the next few months. The criminal trial focused only on the charges he could be prosecuted with – fraud and possession of extreme pornography – and not the deception of colleagues, patients, and his wife and children, nor the psychological harm he has caused to the people who put their lives and bodies in his hands. While these things are profoundly wrong, they are not necessarily crimes.“He hasn’t been punished for what he’s done to patients,” says Faye. “I just refuse to believe that there weren’t ulterior motives behind the operations he carried out.” The ongoing doubts have made it harder for her to grieve, she says. She wants to have her mother’s pictures on the walls, but can’t face the prospect of going through Liz’s old photographs, which remain in a box in Faye’s loft.Faye wants the trust to commission an independent inquiry into Hopper, investigating not only whether amputations he performed were needlessly done, but also his conduct during his operations – whether his procedures were prolonged, drawn out or otherwise inappropriately carried out. “It’s horrific that there hasn’t been an independent audit from NHS England or the Royal College of Surgeons. Why hasn’t there been a full independent inquiry?”When we first met, Faye had been in two minds about whether or not to speak out about what happened to her mother. She had feared that, if Liz’s wider family and many friends read about her connection to Hopper, they would be horrified. “I don’t want them to go through what I’ve been through,” she’d said. But then she thought about what Liz would want. “She cared about fairness and justice, and making sure people faced up to things. If she were alive today, I know what she would say. She’d say, ‘Go get that effing bastard.’”Explore more on these topicsCrimeUK criminal justiceCornwallDoctorsHealthNHSfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The idealism of the Esperanto movement, a plague of flies and a clinic in a deep salt mine |  | The Guardian
description: Need something brilliant to read this weekend? Here are six of our favourite pieces from the last seven days
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Need something brilliant to read this weekend? Here are six of our favourite pieces from the last seven days
Content: Composite: Nicci Dhamu/Guardian Design/Getty Images/Alamy; Courtesy of Nicci DhamuView image in fullscreenComposite: Nicci Dhamu/Guardian Design/Getty Images/Alamy; Courtesy of Nicci DhamuSix great readsThe idealism of the Esperanto movement, a plague of flies and a clinic in a deep salt mineNeed something brilliant to read this weekend? Here are six of our favourite pieces from the last seven daysSat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1.‘I thought, I’ve tried everything else, why not give AI a shot?’: the long-lost family reunited by ChatGPTView image in fullscreen‘There is a human touch to AI.’Composite: Nicci Dhamu/Guardian Designdouble quotation markWho would have thought that life would unfold in this way? That ChatGPT would find an article that would lead to an email that would lead to all of this? Technology seems to be in alignment, in the same way that stars can be sometimes. There is a human touch to AI – look what happened.Avtar spent decades wondering what happened to the mother he never got to know. Thousands of miles away, Nicci was haunted by the story of a half-brother given away before she was born. Jenny Kleeman wrote a remarkable story about how a chatbot brought them together.Read more2.Nudists, peaceniks and freeloading travellers: the people keeping the Esperanto dream aliveView image in fullscreenUniversal language.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/AlamyFor a satirist or a cynic, Esperantists are easy fodder. Many of its enthusiasts are undeniably eccentric. But Esperanto was once a force in global politics. Before facing heavy persecution during the second world war, it gained serious traction in international labour, anticolonial and anarchist movements. Katie Thornton wrote an illuminating long read about the idealistic movement and the vibrancy of its annual congress. She explored why today’s adherents – many of whom are no strangers to global conflict – still believe that the widespread adoption of a century-and-a-half-old invented language may yet overpower the world’s divisions.Read more3.‘It makes you feel you’ve got a really dirty house’: what’s behind the UK’s plagues of flies?View image in fullscreenSwatting season.Photograph: cookelma/Getty Images/iStockphotoIf just one fly buzzing around your head is annoying, imagine what it’s like to be surrounded by clouds of them, week after week. Lucy Knight visited one of Britain’s most insect-plagued neighbourhoods for this fascinating story, which also poses the question: although flies are regarded as disgusting, could they be due a rebrand?Read more4.Deep breathing: the asthma clinic buried 250 metres into an Armenian salt mineView image in fullscreenGoing underground.Photograph: Sofia Maria Bergmann/The Guardiandouble quotation markFor most people, spending hours deep underground in darkness would seem an odd prescription for better health. Yet every morning, a handful of Armenians descend 250 metres beneath the earth into an active salt mine where they spend six hours in cavernous chambers carved from rock salt, hoping the air below ground will help them breathe more easily.Pjotr Sauer visited one of the world’s only hospitals in a deep salt mine. The underground clinic’s fate now hangs in the balance after Armenia withdrew state funding, raising broader questions about its role in supporting alternative medicine.Read more5.‘I never mentioned it for 25 years. I didn’t want to be a victim of the bomb’: Hiroshima survivor Koko Kondo on horror, anger and forgivenessView image in fullscreenPeace activist Koko Kondo.Photograph: Aya Fujioka/The GuardianOn that fateful day in 1945, Kondo was just a baby in her mother’s arms. She talked to Simon Hattenstone about her father’s newly discovered eye-witness account of the aftermath, and why she decided to continue his work as a peace campaigner determined that Hiroshima and Nagasaki will never be repeated. “I don’t want to see any child go through that. That’s why I do not want to see any war in this world. Thisbeautifulworld.”Read more6.Just when you thought it was safe … the shark movie is back for moreView image in fullscreenShark Week.Photograph: Discovery Channel/APShark thrillers are often positioned as something akin to an all-natural slasher: horror movies that expand just slightly beyond the bounds of the world we know and into heightened but not completely outlandish territory. They’re the water equivalent of the masked killer stalking around the woods.Jesse Hassenger wrote about Shark Week, which arrives in an overstuffed period for the film genre – even if nothing will ever rival the greatest of them all.Read moreExplore more on these topicsSix great readsnewsShareReuse this content

title: From Spider-Man: Brand New Day to Ariana Grande: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead  | Culture | The Guardian
description: Your friendly neighbourhood superhero spins a new web of adventures, and the singer returns from Oz with her hopeful eighth album
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Your friendly neighbourhood superhero spins a new web of adventures, and the singer returns from Oz with her hopeful eighth album
Content: Worldwide web … Spider-Man Brand New Day.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyView image in fullscreenWorldwide web … Spider-Man Brand New Day.Photograph: FlixPix/AlamyGoing out, staying inCultureFrom Spider-Man: Brand New Day to Ariana Grande: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadYour friendly neighbourhood superhero spins a new web of adventures, and the singer returns from Oz with her hopeful eighth albumSat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaSpider-Man: Brand New DayOut nowThe – sequel to No Way Home maintains the focus on what’s now Spidey’s day job: protecting the city. New characters include crime boss Tombstone, played by Marvin Jones III who, like his character, is an African American with albinism.IshOut nowArtist and director Imran Perretta’s own childhood experiences with the police inform his beautiful black-and-white debut feature film about two 12-year-olds in Luton, which won a prize at Venice’s critics week. The two leads are played by non-professional actors Farhan Hasnat and Yahya Kitana, real-life friends themselves.Wham! 10 Days in ChinaOut nowIn 1985, Wham! were the first western band permitted to play communist China. Lindsay Anderson, who made If….,was invited to shoot the experience but fell out with the group, who released their version of the film shortly after. Now comes a new feature-length take with archive footage and interviews.No Strings Attached: Puppets on FilmBFI Southbank & Imax, London, to 31 AugustPuppets! Need we say more? This puppets-on-film season from the BFI features a variety of marionettes, dummies, dolls and figurines, in films including The Empire Strikes Back, The Dark Crystal and The Muppets Take Manhattan.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenGet over it … Summer Walker.Photograph: Rahul BhattSummer WalkerThe O2, London,1 & 2 AugustAtlanta’s R&B star brings her trilogy of breakup albums – 2019’s Over It, 2021’s Still Over It and last year’s Finally Over It – to London’s O2 arena. Fingers crossed she is definitely over it, but if she’s not then there will be plenty of emotional catharsis to work through across these two shows.Michael CraggBrecon jazz festivalVarious venues,mid Wales,6to 9 AugustSaxophonist Courtney Pine, a liberating cultural force in UK jazz for 40 years, headlines Brecon’s celebrated jazz weekender (6 August), alongside trumpeter Tomos Williams’s jazz/ambient take on Welsh folk music, and rootsy singer-pianist Liane Carroll (both 7 August). Jazz from many fresh perspectives follows through the weekend.John FordhamBoardmastersNewquay,5to 9 AugustPromising music, wellness and surfing on the Cornish coast, Boardmasters offers a unique take on the traditional festival. In terms of the musical lineup, it’s a mix of the usual – Kasabian, Fatboy Slim, Example – and newer acts including Rose Gray, Jacob Alon and Joy Crookes. MCMahler’s First By HeartRoyal Albert Hall, London,1 & 2 AugustAurora Orchestra’s BBC Proms appearances pair a dramatised exploration of a major symphonic work with a performance played entirely from memory. This year, Mahler’s Symphony No 1 gets the Aurora treatment as Nicholas Collon conducts.Flora WillsonGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenYou’ve come a long way, baby … an untitled photograph by Chardchakaj Waikawee.Photograph: Chardchakaj Waikawee/Graces MewsChardchakaj WaikaweeGraces Mews, London,to 19 SeptemberAnalogue, hand-printed photographs of people living on the margins of Bangkok’s society by this Thai artist. The result is a portrait of youth shot through with poverty, struggle and endurance.Gwen JohnScottish National Gallery of Modern Art, Edinburgh,1 Augustto 4 JanuaryBeautiful, quiet, austere, minimal portraiture by arguably Wales’s most important painter. This retrospective is full of works inspired equally by her religious beliefs and love of early French modernism.Reflections: Sangat and the SelfThe Whitworth, Manchester,to 29 August 2027Artists Jasmir Creed and Roo Dhissou pair up for this participatory exhibition rooted in Sikh philosophy, which also features work from the Whitworth’s collection. This is a show all about community, healing, care and spiritual practice.Kawaii Art & CultureWolverhampton Arts Centre,to 9 AugustJapanesekawaiiculture is a global phenomenon, and now it’s coming to Wolverhampton, in a show curated by artist Tamla Pearce all about how kawaii art, fashion, toys, animation, food and design travelled the world.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenTheatre with bite … Mollie Gallagher as Clarice Starling in The Silence of the Lambs..Photograph: Marc BrennerThe Silence of the LambsCurve theatre, Leicester,1to 15 AugustTV writer and playwright Gina Gionfriddo adapts Thomas Harris’s chilling thriller for the stage. The play will pull the audience into the warped relationship between FBI trainee Clarice Starling and infamous murderer Hannibal Lecter, played by John Partridge of EastEnders fame.Miriam GillinsonCatsRegent’s Park Open Air theatre, to 19SeptemberWith Jesus Christ Superstar and Starlight Express staged in London, Andrew Lloyd Webber is having another moment. Now comes choreographer and director Drew McOnie’s production of Cats at the outdoor theatre where musicals seem to glow with a special kind of magic.MGFreddie MeredithPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh,5to 30 AugustForget all the podcasters and panel show-famous standups: niche character comedy is the real point of the Edinburgh fringe. This year, few will do it better than Meredith (Such Brave Girls, Make That Movie), whose debut hour Need a Light? revolves round his smoking-area-philosopher alter ego.Rachel AroestiCarlos Acosta: Myths and Modern MastersRoyal Opera House, London,5to 9 AugustThe ever charismatic Carlos Acosta just can’t give up dancing – and why should he, he was made for it? The now 53-year-old has had more farewell tours than the Rolling Stones – in fact, he’s dancing to the Stones in one of the pieces in this gala show, Christopher Bruce’s Rooster – yet he can still impress.Lyndsey Winshipskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine.
