title: There can be no letup. Humiliated Infantino must stand down at Fifa or be removed | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: Uefa’s decisive call for a boycott and declaration of no confidence must be the opening salvos in a concerted push to dethrone the game’s global leader
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Uefa’s decisive call for a boycott and declaration of no confidence must be the opening salvos in a concerted push to dethrone the game’s global leader
Content: ‘Every day Gianni Infantino remains in power is a fresh stain on an institution whose reputation is on the floor’Photograph: Manu Fernández/APView image in fullscreen‘Every day Gianni Infantino remains in power is a fresh stain on an institution whose reputation is on the floor’Photograph: Manu Fernández/APGianni InfantinoThere can be no letup. Humiliated Infantino must stand down at Fifa or be removedNick AmesUefa’s call for a boycott and declaration of no-confidence must be the opening salvos in push to dethrone game’s global leaderSat 1 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 11.03 EDTShareThere is no time to dance around the subject.Gianni Infantinomust stand down as Fifa president or otherwise be legally removed. No fresh chances can be made available for an official who has demolished trust in football’s integrity and governance, trashing all remaining credibility of the body that oversees the world’s most-cherished sport.Infantino wasforced into a humiliating climbdownon Saturday morning when he accepted the failure of his plan to sell off portions of the World Cup to private investment. He resolved to resume dialogue about football’s growth “in the spirit of shared interest in our game”. But such a naked attempt to save his own skin cannot hold. Every day Infantino remains in power is a fresh stain on an institution whose reputation is on the floor.Gianni Infantino ‘has lost Uefa’s confidence’ after Fifa chief scraps World Cup sell-off planRead moreThe overreach involved in unilaterally launching theFifaForward Enterprise (FFE) scheme – with its vision to place huge influence on football’s future in the palms of venture capitalists – would be enough to bring down most leaders. But Infantino’s rap sheet goes far beyond that. He has routinely made a mockery of Fifa’s own statutes and governance regulations, so nobody should be surprised that patience has finally snapped in corridors of power globally. Fifa’s “football unites the world” slogan has never looked more empty.Article 10.3 of those regulations, which specifically pertains to the presidency, requires the incumbent to ensure “Fifa’s objectives, mission, strategic direction, policies and values are sustainably pursued, protected and implemented, and that a positive image of Fifa is fostered”. It stipulates “promoting friendly and peaceful relations within Fifa”, which is a nonsense given the degree to which federations and senior personnel have distanced themselves from Infantino in recent days.The rules give no green light to the pursuit of multiple private projects that, most recently in lockstep with the current US administration or its tributaries, have been tabled with scant appetite for oversight or explanation.Where to begin?The Folarin Balogun sagatipped many leading figures in football, particularly in Europe, towards the edge. There had already been widespread bafflement and disgust atInfantino’s presentation of the new Fifa peace prizeto Donald Trump in December, with little background given about the process and highly contestable information provided about the US president’s qualifying achievements. Stakeholders were frustrated by a lack of consultation aboutthe introduction of “hydration breaks”, which fundamentally toyed with the fabric of matches at this summer’s World Cup.View image in fullscreenThe saga involving Folarin Balogun after his ban for a red card was suspended tipped many leading figures in football towards the edge.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersThe bizarre expedited bidding process for the 2034 tournament, which resulted in Saudi Arabia’s candidature beingwaved through in December 2024, also brought widespread criticism. This list only covers the past 20 months of controversies inflicted by Infantino, capped on Friday by revelations thatplans for a 64-team World Cup are in full swing.When ascathing statement from Uefa on Saturdaycalled for an end to “secret schemes on fast track timescales, cooked up by faceless individuals and of dubious benefit to the game”, it was not only referring to the FFE project and its casual sidelining of other decision makers within Fifa.A critical mass has been reached. Uefa took a decisive lead in following more than a year of harsh words with strong, united action inpledging to boycott future Fifa tournamentsif Infantino did not withdraw his plan. It undoubtedly influenced the outcome and the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, secured an achievement that may define his own reign. But it will mean nothing if Infantino, who is understood to have deployed a major consultancy to smooth relations with federations in recent days, is given the oxygen to dangle fresh promises and turn heads back towards the status quo.View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino’s rap sheet goes far beyond attempting to launch the Fifa Forward Enterprise unilaterally.Photograph: Claudio Thoma/EPAThere is an acknowledgment within Uefa and beyond that the pace must not let up. Senior figures are adamant Infantino must not survive the current scandal. Some insiders feel a crucial next step will be for member associations, the overwhelming majority of whom had formally pledged their support for Infantino’s re-election next March, to recall those letters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDoing so requires a request to Fifa but could, in sufficient numbers, be a de factovote of no confidencein Infantino. Fifa had lobbied aggressively for those submissions but many FAs would now be red faced if their expression of fealty towards Infantino was more widely publicised.Member associations have a duty not to shrink in staving off existential threats to their sport otherwise they, like Infantino, are doing it an egregious disservice. Backing away now would mean leaving the job half done at best.Uefa have pledged to devise a new method for distributing Fifa’s wealth, delving into its multibillion cash reserves without “selling the family silver”. Behind the scenes it continues to work with other confederations in an effort to find credible candidates for Infantino’s replacement, with a view to running in the election should the Swiss hold on until then. The present crisis can be used to reshape football for the better but only if Infantino is not in situ to impose the final say.The alternative is that Fifa, and by extension the game, continue lurching from one disaster to the next. It is no laughing matter when the public conversation around football centres on one man, his ego and brazen ventures.In December Zvonimir Boban, a former sidekick to Infantino as Fifa’s deputy secretary general,told the Guardian that “the way is lost”after the peace prize award to Trump. Fifa will not find a route back until Infantino plays no further part in its operation.Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaWorld Cup 2026World CupFootball politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Games are the opposite of fun, and I’d ban them for anyone over 12 | Emily Watkins | The Guardian
description: Get your balls, pucks, Scrabble boards and packs of cards away from me – all I want is space to be together, ideally with a coffee or a glass of wine, says writer Emily Watkins
Author: Emily Watkins
Headline: Get your balls, pucks, Scrabble boards and packs of cards away from me – all I want is space to be together, ideally with a coffee or a glass of wine, says writer Emily Watkins
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/2024 Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/2024 Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onBoard gamesThe hill I will die on: Games are the opposite of fun, and I’d ban them for anyone over 12Emily WatkinsGet your balls, pucks, Scrabble boards and packs of cards away from me – all I want is space to be together, ideally with a coffee or a glass of wineSat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.06 EDTShareThe other day, I met a friend at the park for a catch-up. After 45 minutes of blissful note-swapping – my newtabi shoes, his new boyfriend – he pulled out a pair of ping-pong paddles and indicated a nearby table. “Fancy a quick game?” We are no longer speaking.I’m joking, but only sort of. As far as I’m concerned, games of any sort ought to be illegal once everyone present is over the age of 12. I will make grudging exceptions for professional athletes, because apparently they’re earning a living, and realistically there is very little chance of me being asked to join in with, say, the Wimbledon final. But when it comes to anything less formal, the risk of being corralled is just too high: bat those balls, pucks, packs of cards, spinning bottles and Scrabble boards away from me, please.Truly, there is no social situation made better by adding a game. In a setting with people I know and love, it feels like a cruel and unusual punishment to have organic conversation curtailed by something ghastly likeArticulate!And although structured activities are often wheeled out for groups of strangers, that’s even worse – because now not only am I playing a game, but doing so with a bunch of people I don’t know, and I want to die.Let’s go round the office and introduce ourselves with two truths and a lie! Let’s get each of the hens to write down their favourite thing about Milly and she can guess who wrote what! Let’s stick pins in our eyes!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Radio 4’s Today programme has become really annoying since I left | John HumphrysRead moreIn axing games, I’m not advocating for anything to replace them. On the contrary, all I want is space to be together, ideally while clutching either a coffee or a glass of wine, depending on the time of day. Don’t start thinking that activities that bridge that divide – pub quizzes, for instance – are an exception to my furious veto, either; they’re actually the most dire of all, the Uncanny Valley of organised fun. All the cues – friends, booze – are there for a lovely time, then suddenly,shhhhhh!, it’s the music round and Ollie takes this onevery seriously.Speaking of which, I’m fully aware that there exists a whole cohort who feel just as strongly as I, only in the opposite direction. I have encountered them in the wild – frothing at the mouth as they chastise you for putting your card on the left instead of the right or whatever – and frankly, they frighten me. Maybe I envy their strength of feeling. I’m not sure I’ve ever felt that righteous about anything, but it looks energising.Am I pathologically uncompetitive? Has my lack of interest in games birthed a unique ineptitude at almost every single one? Yes and yes! Nonetheless, my years on the sidelines have made one thing abundantly clear: the real fun begins as soon as the games stop. As I said to my friend at the park: put the paddles down and get me a glass of pinot, please.Emily Watkins is a freelance writer based in LondonDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsBoard gamesThe hill I will die onQuiz and trivia gamesTable tenniscommentShareReuse this content

title: Biohacker Bryan Johnson is keeping his girlfriend’s menstrual blood in his freezer | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The longevity influencer and his girlfriend, Kate Tolo, say they’re studying women’s health – a worthy goal, but perhaps some skepticism is in order
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The longevity influencer and his girlfriend, Kate Tolo, say they’re studying women’s health – a worthy goal, but perhaps some skepticism is in order
Content: ‘It’s important to remember that Tolo (who has a background in fashion) and Johnson (whose background is in tech) are not exactly highly credentialled medical researchers.’Photograph: Bridget Bennett/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s important to remember that Tolo (who has a background in fashion) and Johnson (whose background is in tech) are not exactly highly credentialled medical researchers.’Photograph: Bridget Bennett/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesThe Week in PatriarchyHealthBiohacker Bryan Johnson is keeping his girlfriend’s menstrual blood in his freezerArwa MahdawiThe longevity influencer and his girlfriend, Kate Tolo, say they’re studying women’s health – a worthy goal, but perhaps some skepticism is in orderSat 1 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTShareThe tech entrepreneurBryan Johnsonhas devoted his life tododging death. The 48-year-old is obsessed with becoming thehealthiest person in the worldand is on a quixotic quest to reverse his biological age and live forever. As such, Johnson is disciplined about what he eats, takes dozens of supplements a day, and measures every single biomarker possible, boasting that he is “certainly the most biologically measured person ever”.In short: good luck finding any ice cream in his freezer. But you know what you will find? His girlfriend’s menstrual blood. On Thursday, Johnson, a chronic oversharer, posted a photo of his 30-year-old girlfriend, Kate Tolo, on Xwith the caption: “Kate’s period blood is in my -80 °C freezer. Around 10 mL.”This isn’t the first time Johnson has collected a loved one’s bodily fluids: a few years ago he boasted about infusing himself with a liter of his “blood boy’s” plasma. What in God’s name is a blood boy? Oh, that’s just what Johnsoncalls hisson Talmage, who was 17 at the time. Johnson also donated a liter of his own blood to his own father.This also isn’t the first time Johnson has taken it upon himself to share personal information about his loved ones on the internet. Last year, he posted data comparing his and his teenage son’s nocturnal erection metrics. “Nighttime erection data from my 19-year-old son ... and me,”he wrote on X, tagging Talmage. “His duration is two minutes longer than mine. Raise children to stand tall, be firm, and be upright.”Once we’ve all taken a moment to recover from that, we can move on to the menstrual blood in the freezer. What is Johnson planning to do with it? Study it, apparently. “Menstrual blood is valuable and underutilized … It’s a non-invasive look into the uterus,” Johnsonexplained on X. Tolo and Johnson intend to examine the blood for everything from endocrine disruptors to microplastics. “I like that Kate is a science experiment with me,” he added.OK. But doesshelike it? Well, she hasn’t said she doesn’t. Rather shereplied to his postwith a message saying: “Thanks for looking after me bby.”Tolo hasn’t just given a one-off blood sample. Johnson has said that she is collecting “14 million data points on her menstrual cycle”,which he touts asa “world first for female health”. Her protocol involves “100+ tasks a day” and “50+ devices”, all of which is being monitored by a “12 person medical team”. Tolo has to take regular urine samples, swallow a temperature pill, and blow into a metabolism tracker. At exactly 9.42 pm, he writes, she has to “insert techno tampon device”. When theIndependentasked for more information about the techno tampon, Johnson said: “We will be sharing more on that soon.”Tolo has done some sharing of her own. In mid-July, she was featured in aWall Street Journal piecetitled: “Bryan Johnson’s girlfriend wants to share her body with the world,” where she explained that she’s doing all this data-tracking for the good of womankind. “I’m really doing it because I think that this is our path toward women being understood in the world and being seen,” Tolo told the Journal. On a personal level, Tolo has said she has polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, and is hoping to find treatments that might help her symptoms. Helping her out with that is the famous techno tampon: the Journal’s piece features a photo of Tolo looking very intently at a small tampon-shaped device which will track her blood-flow variations.As Johnsonhas said: “Women are not well understood medically.” It wasn’tuntil 1993, when US Congress passed a law requiring that women and minorities be included in clinical research, that we began to be properly represented in medical trials. Menstruation has also beenunderstudied. Indeed, until 2023 there hadn’t been a published study testing period products like tamponsusing human blood. They’d used saline solution instead. This sort of “medical misogyny” hasimpactedthe quality of care that women get, and resulted in women’s pain not beingtaken as seriouslyas men’s.In many ways, then, Johnson and Tolo’s new women’s health initiative is to be applauded. It’s helping break down thestigmaattached to menstruation, and it’s raising awareness about women’s health.All that said, I think a smidgen of skepticism is warranted. It’s important to remember that Tolo (who has a background in fashion) and Johnson (whose background is in tech) are not exactly highly credentialled medical researchers. They own a company called Immortals that sells supplements. And guess what?According to the Journal: “The company is on the verge of launching products for women.” Which makes all of this feel a lot like a marketing campaign. I don’t know if the techno tampon will end up being a giant step forward for womankind, but it might well provide a healthy boost to the Immortals balance sheet.Elon Musk’s xAI is challenging Minnesota over its ban on ‘nudification’ technologyMinnesota is implementing a first-in-the-nationlawto ban apps and software that allow someone to “nudify” an image or video. Guess who isn’t excited about this? Musk’s AI company. xAIsuedto block the new law on Monday, arguing that its definition of “intimate part” is too broadand the statute“imposes an overbroad, content-based ban on free speech”. A good time to remember that Musk is theworld’s biggest free speech hypocriteand only seems to care about free speech when it enriches him.We are entering a terrifying new era of genocide-as-a-business-modelThe genocide scholar Omer Bartov has a powerful piece in theNew York Timesabout how: “If the plans that are being elaborated for Gaza go forward, genocide may come to be seen by some nations as the legitimate and lucrative extension of politics by other means.”Majority of Maga voters would support GOP candidate accused of sexual assaultPer a Politico poll: “Two-thirds of self-identified MAGA Trump voters say they would continue supporting a GOP candidate accused of sexual assault” by a former partner. That’s “13 percentage points higher than the share of Trump 2024 voters writ large, which include those who do not identify as MAGA”. These numbers don’t really make sense considering that 100% of Trump voters voted for a manaccused of sexual misconductby multiple women, and found liable for abuse in theE Jean Carrollcase.Republican congressman Max Miller accused by ex-wife and ex-girlfriend of abuseSeems like a verycommon themein the party of family values! As for whether this will impact Miller’s career, see the poll above.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUS government map of Africa mislabels every country at global conferenceThe map wasapparently made with OpenAI tools.Schools are adding pepper-spraying drones to help combat active shootersPerthe Washington Post, at least nine schools in three states (Florida, Georgia, Colorado) have bought drones “that can zoom through halls, smash windows and pepper-spray active shooters if teachers report a threat”.Nearly 400,000 studentshave experienced gun violence at school since the 1999 attack at Colorado’s Columbine High School. Instead of sparking gun reform, it’s spawned a multibillion-dollar security industry focused on campus shootings.Senate unanimously passes resolution opposing pardon for Ghislaine MaxwellResolutions like this arelargely symbolic, so a possible pardon isn’t completely out of the question.Matt Damon’s stunt double in The Odyssey is a 4ft 6in woman called Devyn DaltonDalton is getting a lot of buzz after an interviewer congratulated Damon on his biceps in the Odyssey and the actorexplainedthat his double was a female stunt performer who had “the greatest arms I have ever seen”. I have investigated further and can confirm they are elite arms.The week in pawtriarchyThe Trump administration has slashed environmental research funding, meaning cash-strapped scientists are having to get creative. Enter an OnlyFans account calledOnlyMarms, promising “unfiltered yellow-bellied marmot content from the Rockies!” While OnlyFans is known for risqué content, you’ll be glad to hear this is G-rated. “We’re not trying to sexualize marmots,” the marmot researcherDaniel Blumstein said. “Although I was just at an international conference and three people came up to me and said: ‘Oh, you have to have more pictures of Marmot feet.’” So far the site has only raised about $3,000, but let’s hope it builds marmentum.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHealthThe Week in PatriarchyWomen's healthcommentShareReuse this content

title: In the battle of Elon Musk v the press, we can’t let truth be the loser | Jane Martinson | The Guardian
description: The trillionaire Tesla owner has called the editor of the Economist a ‘traitor to the west’ after a clash-filled interview. How should the media respond? asks Guardian columnist Jane Martinson
Author: Jane Martinson
Headline: The trillionaire Tesla owner has called the editor of the Economist a ‘traitor to the west’ after a clash-filled interview. How should the media respond? asks Guardian columnist Jane Martinson
Content: A screen in Times Square, New York City, shows an image of Elon Musk, 12 June 2026Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA screen in Times Square, New York City, shows an image of Elon Musk, 12 June 2026Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockOpinionElon MuskIn the battle of Elon Musk v the press, we can’t let truth be the loserJane MartinsonThe trillionaire Tesla owner has called the editor of the Economist a ‘traitor to the west’ after a clash-filled interview. How should the media respond?Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.31 EDTShareElon Musk’slong interview with the editor of the Economistis as good a representation as any of the current clash between two worlds. In one corner, the editor of an 182-year-old news organisation which promotes economic liberalism and freedom. In the other, the world’s first trillionaire, who spreads misinformation to his hundreds of millions of followers on his own social media platform. The bout is a masterclass in the challenges journalists face in a new world of AI, fact avoidance and online aggression.The flash points in Zanny Minton Beddoes’ conversation with Musk start with definitions. Musk says that the people Minton Beddoes calls “far-right” and “fringe” (she mentions Germany’s AfD party) are in fact just “normal people”. They clash over whether the speed of his cuts to USAID led to unnecessary deaths in developing countries – she believes his claim that it didn’t defies not only statistics but the evidence from her reporters on the ground. Asked if he is racist, he cites the fact he has four children with a woman who is “half Indian”. In an awkward exchange, when asked by Minton Beddoes whether he is anti-Muslim, Musk says he is against “people coming to a country with antithetical views … I’m against rape and murder.”The tone shifts when Minton Beddoes accuses Musk of spreading misinformation about Europe and particularly her home town, London, telling him that the statistics show that it is a safer place to live than most large US cities. She appears genuinely irritated that he rejects all evidence that violent crime is far lower than he says and grooming gangs are not terrorising the streets. After she asks if he understands why this makes people loathe him, it becomes a playground spat. Musk points out that with so many followers on X, he must be popular. Besides, “they hate you far more than they hate me”. She admits to the media losing trust.The exchange says a lot, not just about both participants and what they believe in, but also the state of our current media ecosystem. To use the metaphor of the summer, if the interviewwere a Homeric quest, the editor would be trying to get back to a place of truth and safety while Musk would be the angry sea god unleashing violent storms and monsters after the challenge was seemingly over.That dynamic was mirrored in the response. The interview appears to end with the two agreeing to disagree; they even continue to chat while Musk has his photo taken. When Minton Beddoes promoted the interview on X, Musk then reposted it, adding “zany interview with Zanny”. She liked this so much she reposted his repost. After some of his followers posted rude things about the media he piled in on “the reality distortion nightmare mirror that is the legacy mainstream press”. By the weekend, hewas calling her a “traitor to the west”. On Thursday, she confessed to being “bemused” but not scared by the “more and more aggressive” response. She has learned not to look at online comments,she told Radio 4’s Media Show. “If you scroll through them and read hundreds of things saying how awful you are, it’s not very pleasant, so don’t do it.”View image in fullscreenZanny Minton Beddoes, the Economist’s editor-in-chief.Photograph: Felix Clay/The GuardianIt seems particularly timely to see what lessons can be learned from all this, given the latestgovernment-backed investigation into the safety of journalistsfound that many admitted to self-censoring reports on contentious issues such as rightwing protest for fear of being attacked. Throwaway vitriolic comments about journalists are directly linked to increased aggression online and off, the report found. Female journalists bear the brunt of this aggression.The shift to online and video journalism, the increasing celebritification if you will, has made more journalists identifiable, and therefore afraid for their safety. Again, Minton Beddoes is a great example of this given that the Economist, famous for the anonymity of its writers, has recently moved into far more video content. The Insider – the platform on which she interviewed Musk – is a weekly interviewlaunched last September; guests have included Benjamin Netanyahu and Tucker Carlson, so Minton Beddoes is no stranger to combative subjects.Musk’s view of truth is the reason the exchange feels more important than similar confrontations. Asking powerful people questions and continuing to try to find the answers even when they react badly is the essence of what journalism is. In her short response to newsletter subscribers this week, Minton Beddoes promised to double down on the issues raised in the interview. She told them to look forward to new reports examining the facts surrounding the impact of shutting down USAID, the number of victims of grooming gangs in Britain and the amount of violent crime in European cities – all topics she had clashed with Musk over.The news business has not always behaved as ethically as it should andtrust levels are at an all-time lowand falling across the developed world. But data and on-the-ground reporting are the only ways to beat misinformation. You can claim that it’s just too dangerous to walk around in Britain,as Musk did– despite having not visited for several years – or you can find the data which suggests that homicide rates in general and even knife violence crimes are far lower than in major US cities, as the Economistdid in a social videoliked 73,000 times.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOwnership of his own platform and infinite riches may give Musk a loudspeaker, but this old-fashioned reporting is the kind of public service the world needs. Especially if Musk really is the Cassandra he says he is and artificial intelligence is going to best humans within a decade, making it even harder to keep a firm hold on reality.Jane Martinson is a Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group. As the Marjorie Deane professor of financial journalism at City St George’s, University of London, she has a connection through a charitable foundation to Zanny Minton Beddoes, who is chair of trustees. She writes in a personal capacityDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: If you think kids will respect a robot teacher, you have never met a kid | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: A New York school district has paused plans to bring an android into the classroom. Is this our educational future?
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: A New York school district has paused plans to bring an android into the classroom. Is this our educational future?
Content: ‘As bad as this idea was, at least it didn’t involve a robot disciplinarian issuing hall passes and assigning detention to unruly students.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘As bad as this idea was, at least it didn’t involve a robot disciplinarian issuing hall passes and assigning detention to unruly students.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionRobotsIf you think kids will respect a robot teacher, you have never met a kidDave SchillingA New York school district has paused plans to bring an android into the classroom. Is this our educational future?Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.43 EDTShareWhat’s more harrowing than sending your child to school? Maybegetting stuck on a city busthat can’t drop below 55 miles per hour or it will explode, but that’s about it. Once your kid hits school age, you have to decide (if you’re lucky) between public and private education, vet the teachers, and neurotically worry about whether they’re learning enough and are socializing effectively. For seven hours a day, someone who’s practically a stranger is responsible for the wellbeing of one of the most important people in your life.It’s a stressful situation, but maybe it would be less so if your kid’s teacher was a humanoid robot.Or not. Upstate New York’s Salamanca city central school districtrecently pauseda $60,000 program to install an android teacher’s aide from the company Realbotix, named Sally, to assist their actual instructors. Sally was to have specifically been deployed into high school classrooms for students studying technology and robotics. As thesuperintendent of Salamanca school district said: “The robot also provides opportunities for students to learn how the robot is maintained, how it is updated with new approved content, and how to troubleshoot issues.” As you can imagine, Sally was chosen by the students of Salamanca to be a perky brunette rather than other options, like “bald middle-aged man” or “aspiring author struggling to finish their novel during lunch break”. I shudder to think what crude jokes teenage boys would come up with regarding their artificial teacher.Fortunately, public outcry caused the district (which boasts a municipal population of only 6,000 people) to pause their dystopian plans. As bad as this idea was, at least it didn’t involve a robot disciplinarian issuing hall passes and assigning detention to unruly students. All we need is RoboCop chucking kidsthrough a plate-glass windowfor being tardy to third period. Sally was programmed with working arms and hands, but not legs, which would prevent any random acts of violent retribution.I wish any of this made sense. The superintendent said Sally would give a small town, rural student body a chance to interact with high-level technology they’d otherwise have to“travel 1-2 hours” to see. Students could ask it questions about pertinent topics related to their classes. You know, like they could with the smartphones they probably have in their pockets with access to the internet – repository of all information known to humanity. But see, the difference is, this smartphone is shaped like a pretty lady.Teenagers are already skeptical or even outright annoyed by their teachers, with their pedantic rules and insistence that learning is fundamental. Teaching can be a thankless job, because of lack of resources, even in large metropolitan areas, let alone small towns. Public school teachers areoften underpaid, making it harder to earn a decent living in a taxing profession. Why not take that $60,000 for a robot and divide it up amongst your instructors? Or just buy every student a laptop? Is having an uncanny valley android gesticulating aboutArduino boardsgoing to change anyone’s lives besides the upper management at Realbotix? No teenager is going to take this thing seriously or do anything except throw erasers at it while their real teacher isn’t looking.Big tech has transformed the classroom – and parents are right to be worried | Velislava HillmanRead moreAnd anyway, if society is going to thoughtlessly usher in an age of synthetic learning through artificial intelligence, why go with a generic humanoid? We should at least make our robots something kids would like. We could start with aself-aware Super Mario. I’d absolutely stop whatever I was doing to talk to a robo-Mario if I could, and I’m sure teens would do the same.Why is silicon the best material for building microprocessors? How does cloud storage work? What’s the easiest way to beat the Rainbow Ride level in Super Mario 64? Are Princess Peach and Princess Daisy sisters or just good friends?It doesn’t have to be just Mario. What about a robot Pikachu? Could Salamanca school district license the likeness of Logan Paul or MrBeast to teach algebra? We could have androidBlippisrunning preschools, holographic Robin Williamses from Dead Poets Society in universities, and fake Sydney Sweeneys teaching acting. What if the Paw Patrol could work as crossing guards?Once again, the people we’ve put in charge of raising our children show a lack of understanding of actual children. Kids don’t want nondescript robots answering questions a search engine could do just as fast. They want to play Roblox and drink Mountain Dew. And maybe, just maybe, a real, flesh-and-blood human being could inspire them to want more than that. We’ll never find out if we try to outsource education to tech companies.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsRobotsOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)US educationNew YorkcommentShareReuse this content

title: Like Burnham, I was an altar boy. His Catholic upbringing is shaping the way he governs | Julian Coman | The Guardian
description: With a prime minister raised in a tradition that emphasises our mutual dependency, we may finally have a leader who can address the anomie gripping our country, says Guardian associate editor Julian Coman
Author: Julian Coman
Headline: With a prime minister raised in a tradition that emphasises our mutual dependency, we may finally have a leader who can address the anomie gripping our country, says Guardian associate editor Julian Coman
Content: Liverpool Metropolitan Cathedral.Photograph: Ian Dagnall/AlamyView image in fullscreenLiverpool Metropolitan Cathedral.Photograph: Ian Dagnall/AlamyOpinionAndy BurnhamLike Burnham, I was an altar boy. His Catholic upbringing is shaping the way he governsJulian ComanWith a prime minister raised in a tradition that emphasises our mutual dependency, we may finally have a leader who can address the anomie gripping our countrySat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.05 EDTShareLike Andy Burnham, I was once an enthusiastic altar boy, although I don’t recall competing to be at the front with the communion plate as the prime ministerapparently did. Much of my motivation had little to do with piety. The tips received for serving at weddings were often very generous and I got on well with Father Jerome, an engagingly worldly monk from Ampleforth who shared my passion for Manchester United.I’m five years older than Burnham, but the atmosphere of the small-town northern Catholicism we grew up with will have been much the same.The second Vatican council’s reforms, responding to the social changes under way since the 1960s, were “democratising” the tone and style of worship, and traditionalists were mourning the sidelining of the old Latin mass. The huge success of Pope John Paul II’s groundbreakingvisit to Britainin 1982 – the first by a reigning pontiff – had made the faith seem more mainstream and less rarefied. Politically, most Catholics voted Labour, and the large number of Celtic surnames in parish registers testified to a demographic significantly different from Anglican congregations, which were both more English andmore Tory.Burnham is the first British prime minister to have been raised in this kind of environment, and he has been explicit about its influence upon him. To which the response of many secular well-wishers may well be polite indifference. Catholicism gets abetter press among progressivesthese days, as Rome takes a stand against the cruelties and excesses of Maga-style xenophobia and nationalism. But most liberals would be wary of any Catholic proselytising in areas beyond migration and human rights.They should look deeper. Like Burnham, I lapsed – in my case when I went to university and started looking for different kinds of truths in western Marxism and leftwing social theory. But unlike Burnham, I went back to the church in my 30s. So I have watched with some fascination as the significance of the new prime minister’s cradleCatholicismhas been pondered beyond the confines of the religious press.Two weeks into Burnham’s premiership, it is already clear that something important is at stake here that meshes with Burnham’s conventionallypolitical critiqueof “40 years of neoliberalism”. He himself talks of “a direct read-across between what I was learning at … church and Labour values”, which might sound a bit broad brush and a bit obvious, in a “be kind” type of way. In fact it is anything but, and it matters that the church was a Catholic one.During the 1980s – the decade Burnham has pledged to “roll back” – Margaret Thatcher did not attempt to disguise thetheological rootsof a political vision that emphasised self-reliance and theProtestant work ethicas primary virtues. The Methodist worldview she inherited from her lay-preacher fathertranslatedinto a strident individualism, and a contempt for the collectivist institutions and ethos of the postwar welfare society. As Thatcherassertedin the first phase of her premiership: “Economics are the method; the object is to change the soul.”As she evangelised, the surplice-clad Burnham wasimmersed in the Catholic resistance to this harsh new social doctrine, digesting and disseminating the sermons of the archbishop of Liverpool, Derek Worlock. Based on the social teaching of papal encyclicals, Worlock’s politics (and those of his Anglican counterpart, David Sheppard) emphasised fraternity, solidarity and mutual obligation. “I am my brother’s keeper,” he observed in 1990. “And he’s sleeping pretty rough these days.”Cut to Burnham’s first bigpolicy announcement, when he vowed to use his premiership to end rough sleeping across the country. Commentary, understandably enough, has focused on the practical difficulties he encountered in delivering a similar pledge in Greater Manchester as mayor. But just as important is the message it sent about priorities: in the early morning of his first day in the country’s highest office of state, Burnham made a point of going to talk to homeless people on the streets of central London.The Catholic church would call this the “preferential option for the poor”, a way of systematising the gospel idea that the last should be first. In the ethical architecture ofCatholic social teaching, it is accompanied by other pillars designed to protect people from both an overmighty technocratic state and the moral indifference of the market. Subsidiarity, the idea that power should not be hoarded at the top but devolved downwards, is clearly at the heart of nascent Burnhamism. The dignity of work, elaborated upon in papal encyclicals such as John Paul II’sLaborem Exercens, has been at the core of our angst-ridden debates about the legacy of deindustrialisation and the future of AI.The clue is in the word “social”. Thatcher’sassertionthat “there is no such thing” as society channelled a Protestant emphasis on individual responsibility. It revealed a perspective with a lineage going back to post-Reformation distrust of a Catholicism that, with its smells, bells and rituals, inserted its clerics between the believer and their Bible. Burnham’s much-quoted naming of his chief influences as “Everton FC, the Labour party and the Catholic church” indicates a quite different sensibility; one which finds meaning and truth in relationships and social institutions, and is at heart convivial. His determination to present the crisis in social care as an issue to becollectively faced and resolvedcomes from the same source.One could go on. Burnham’slove of Philip Larkin, a (self-described “agnostic”) poet who captured the pathos and sadness – but also the beauty – in ordinary lives, is of a piece with an understanding of the world that is not obsessed with individual achievement and material wealth. It was Labour’s grievous error in the 90s and 00s to succumb to the meritocratic, aspirational creed, alienating vast swathes of its traditional support that looked to the party for different, associational values.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham’s Catholic upbringing appears to have provided him with convictions that allowed him to emerge relatively intact from that heretical turn. The intriguing possibility is that as a result, the country finally has a prime minister able to understand the deeper origins of the anomie gripping a country in which former sources of social solidarity are under threat, or have already disappeared. The nation’s discontents are of course eminently practical, with the cost of living and the degradation of public services taking their place at the top of the list. But they can also be attributed to a sense that the common good – another concept of Catholic social teaching – has been chronically neglected in many ways, in an unbalanced, unequal society.That is a moral issue about the way we live now, as much as it is a technical policy challenge. If Burnham’s stint as an ambitious altar boy can help him resolve it, it will be good news for a largely secular nation.Julian Coman is a Guardian associate editorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The US war on Iran is spinning out of control | Mohamad Bazzi | The Guardian
description: Trump’s conflict keeps escalating, with Saudi Arabia joining airstrikes in Iraq and reportedly planning an attack on the Houthis. A recession could follow
Author: Mohamad Bazzi
Headline: Trump’s conflict keeps escalating, with Saudi Arabia joining airstrikes in Iraq and reportedly planning an attack on the Houthis. A recession could follow
Content: ‘Saudi Arabia announced it had joined the US in carrying out a series of airstrikes inside Iraq.’Photograph: Thaier Al-Sudani/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Saudi Arabia announced it had joined the US in carrying out a series of airstrikes inside Iraq.’Photograph: Thaier Al-Sudani/ReutersOpinionUS-Israel war on IranThe US war on Iran is spinning out of controlMohamad BazziTrump’s conflict keeps escalating, with Saudi Arabia joining airstrikes in Iraq and reportedly planning an attack on the Houthis. A recession could followSat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTShareThe US war against Iran is spiraling out of control. Over the past week, the conflict has expandedacross the Middle East, with attacks and counterattacks in at least five other countries. Instead of a quick war that sought to topple Iran’s regime, Donald Trump has started a regional conflict that risks severely disrupting energy supplies and prices – and triggering a global recession.After a few days of relative calm, the conflict resumed with the Pentagon carrying out almost nightly strikes against Iran, and Tehran retaliating against US military bases in the region. The conflict also extended to attacks inSaudi Arabia, Iraq, Yemen, Jordan and Egypt. And there’s little sign that peace negotiations between the US and Iran, which are being brokered by Pakistan and Qatar, are making much progress.The most serious escalation took place on Wednesday, when Saudi Arabia announced it hadjoined the USin carrying out a series of airstrikes inside Iraq, against the Iranian-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), killing at least 20 fighters. Saudi officialshad blamedthe Iraqi-based militias for launching drone attacks against Saudi oil facilities on 27 July, and warned that the kingdom would retaliate if the Iraqi government did not restrain the groups. The PMF is a network of mostly Shia Muslim militias that was created, with Tehran’s support, in 2014 to fight the Islamic State terror group that had taken control of large parts of Iraq.The Guardian view on a US-Saudi nuclear agreement: an offer that further erodes international safeguards | EditorialRead moreTrump said the US and Saudi militaries coordinated with the Iraqi government before carrying out airstrikes, but Iraqi leadersquickly deniedhaving any prior knowledge. That denial highlighted the fact that many regional leaders don’t want to be associated with Trump’s expanding regional war. And the attacks threatened to undermine a fragile power balance within Iraq, which has struggled to stop the US-Iran war from spilling over its borders and to maintain a good relationship with both sides.After the US invadedIraqin 2003, it ousted Tehran’s enemy, Saddam Hussein, and his Sunni-dominated regime from power. Washington then helped install a Shia-led government for the first time in Iraq’s modern history, opening the door for Iran to extend its influence over its neighbor and cultivate powerful Shia militias. Iran’s efforts were largely overseen by Qassem Suleimani, a general who headed the foreign operations wing of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Suleimani was assassinated by a US drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020, on Trump’s orders – an attack that helped set the stage for the current war and fueled further animosity between the US and Iraq’s PMF coalition, whose deputy chief, Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, was killed alongside Suleimani.Beyond drawing Iraq’s Shia militias further into the regional conflict, the US and Saudi Arabia risk expanding the war in even more dangerous directions. The kingdom is reportedly planning for amajor military offensiveagainst the Houthi militia, another Iranian ally, which controls large areas of Yemen.After Trump launched his war in late February, Iran effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquid gas supplies passed each day. As a result, some oil producers, especially Saudi Arabia, shifted their exports to the Red Sea. But the Houthis are able to disrupt international shipping through the Red Sea, as they did after Israel’s invasion of Gaza in 2023, when the Yemeni militia began firing missiles and drones at ships near the Bab el-Mandab strait. That caused insurance premiums to soar and forced companies to reroute vessels around Africa, adding weeks to a typical journey and increasing the cost of goods in Europe and elsewhere.So far, the Houthis have not tried to disrupt ships passing through the Red Sea on a large scale, via the Bab el-Mandab chokepoint, which comes closest to Yemeni territory. But on 20 July, the militia declared a blockade on Saudi vessels transiting the Red Sea, claiming it was in retaliation for an air and naval blockade that the kingdom had imposed years ago against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. The Houthis have since attacked several ships in the Red Sea, forcingSaudi Arabia to reroutenearly half of its oil exports through a longer and more expensive journey around the southern tip of Africa. On 25 July, the Houthis claimed tohave struck“sensitive” oil infrastructure sites inside Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones, disrupting the kingdom’s Red Sea export hub of Yanbu. The Saudis have retaliated with air strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.Like Iran’s other neighbors in the Persian Gulf, the Saudi economy has been hit hard by the war, especially Tehran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz and its attacks against energy infrastructure in the Gulf. Saudi Arabia’s GDP decreasedby nearly 5%in the second quarter of 2026, compared with the same period last year.Has Trump dragged the US into a forever war in Iran? | Mohamad BazziRead moreSaudi leaders are blaming Iran for thelatest Houthi escalation, and they’ve vowed to establish an international maritime coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea. On Thursday, the Saudi defense ministry announced that 14 states – including Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Sudan – had agreed so far to join the coalition. But it’s unclear how this new Saudi-led effort would differ from an existing naval protection mission, organized by the European Union and known asOperation Aspides, which is focused on the Red Sea.While Saudi Arabia’s crown prince and de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman, has tried to steer clear of a direct confrontation with Iran, his latest conflict with the Houthis risks reopening a painful chapter in recent Saudi history. In 2015, Saudi Arabia, with US weapons and political support, led a coalition of Sunni Arab states to intervene in Yemen’s long-running civil war. The Saudis tried to dislodge the Houthis from Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, and restore the country’s internationally recognized government to power. By the end of 2021, the United Nations estimated that the conflicthad killed377,000 people in Yemen, nearly 60% of whom did not die from direct warfare. Rather, they died from food shortages, cholera outbreaks and destruction of Yemen’s healthcare system.Despite thousands of airstrikes over seven years, the Houthis remained in control of the capital and the two sides agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022. But negotiations over a permanent peace deal, which would recognize Houthi control over parts of Yemen and provide some form of Saudi reparations, stalled after the militia started attacking ships in the Red Sea in 2023.Today, Saudi Arabia’s tenuous ceasefire with the Houthis is in danger of collapsing – yet another casualty of Trump’s disastrous war againstIran.Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York UniversityExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranOpinionIranIraqSaudi ArabiaYemenMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Jamaica stun Australia as England miss out on Commonwealth Games netball final | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jamaica reached the Commonwealth netball final after defeating defending champions Australia in one of the biggest surprises in the sport’s history
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Jamaica reached the Commonwealth netball final after defeating defending champions Australia in one of the biggest surprises in the sport’s history
Content: Jamaica celebrate their stunning upset victory against Australia.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenJamaica celebrate their stunning upset victory against Australia.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPCommonwealth Games 2026Jamaica stun Australia as England miss out on Commonwealth Games netball finalRoses beaten by New Zealand 61-54 in semi-finalEngland to face Australia for bronze medalSean Inglein GlasgowSat 1 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 06.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJamaica are through to theCommonwealth Gamesnetball final after defeating defending champions Australia in one of the biggest surprises in the sport’s history.In the best game of the tournament by far, Australia scored three goals to reduce Jamaica’s lead to one with 36 seconds remaining.Boxer secures Tuvalu’s first Commonwealth Games medal without winning a boutRead moreBut in front of a near-capacity crowd at the Hydro that included William and Kate, the Prince and Princess of Wales, Sophie Dwyer missed a three-foot shot to level for Australia after the siren.It meant the Sunshine Girls clung on for a shock 46-45 win. And that Australia had failed to reach the final for the first time since netball was introduced to the Games in 1998.Earlier England’s hopes of gold were dashed in a 61-54 defeat by New Zealand that was far more comprehensive than the scoreline suggests.The Silver Ferns went into the semi-final without defender Catherine Hall, who ruptured an anterior cruciate ligament in her knee against Wales. However, their influential goal attack Georgia Heffernan, who suffered an ankle injury against Wales, was able to play through the pain.And while she scored nine goals from 10 attempts and provided 15 goal assists, it was the Silver Ferns’ Grace Nweke who dominated the match. England simply had no answer to the 6ft 4in goal shooter, who finished with 52 goals from 57 attempts.View image in fullscreenGrace Nweke dominated the match to steer New Zealand into the final with victory against England.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PANew Zealand will now play Jamaica in Sunday’s final. England will face Australia in the bronze medal match.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEleanor Cardwell, who was part of the England team that lost the bronze medal match to the Silver Ferns in 2022, stressed the importance of refocusing on Sunday’s match against Australia.“I don’t want that feeling again,” said Cardwell. “I think that’s going to add extra fuel to the fire. We need to really want it tomorrow, and I know we really want it, we want to come away with a medal.“Obviously, the bronze isn’t all we wanted, but that’s the one that we are going to fight for now. We’ve got to go back, recover well and have the conversation about what we’re going to do tomorrow.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026England netball teamNew Zealand netball teamDiamondsNetballCommonwealth GamesAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content
