title: Boxer secures Tuvalu’s first Commonwealth Games medal without winning a bout  | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Boxer Tarona Taafaki made history for ⁠Tuvalu by winning the Pacific island nation’s first Commonwealth ⁠Games medal without winning a single fight
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Boxer Tarona Taafaki made history for ⁠Tuvalu by winning the Pacific island nation’s first Commonwealth ⁠Games medal without winning a single fight
Content: Tuvalu’s Tarona Taafaki (right) goes toe to toe with Lovlina Borgohain of India in the women’s 75kg semi-final.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenTuvalu’s Tarona Taafaki (right) goes toe to toe with Lovlina Borgohain of India in the women’s 75kg semi-final.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPCommonwealth Games 2026Boxer secures Tuvalu’s first Commonwealth Games medal without winning a boutTarona Taafaki makes history in women’s 75kg categoryAll boxers eliminated in semis receive bronze medalsSean Inglein GlasgowSat 1 Aug 2026 06.07 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA boxer has made history for ⁠Tuvalu by winning the tiny Pacific island nation’s first Commonwealth ⁠Games medal without winning a single fight.Twenty-year-old Tarona Taafaki, ⁠one of five entrants in the women’s 75kg category, received a bye to the semi-finals where she lost on an unanimous points decision to India’s Lovlina Borgohain on Friday. AtCommonwealth Games, all boxers eliminated in the semis receive bronze medals.Commonwealth Games 2026 medal tableRead more“I’m very proud and very glad to be able to represent my country on this big stage,” said Taafaki, one of only eight athletes and paraathletes from her country in Glasgow. “Probably 95% of the audience don’t know where my country is, so I feel very privileged to represent Tuvalu.”Badi Taafaki, her coach and father, said the medal would be celebrated by the 10,000 population of the 10 sq mile nation – the world’s fourth smallest – and serve to highlight a climate emergency.“For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything,” he said. “We’re one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it’s a stepping stone.”Athletes often train on the island’s airport runway as it is its most stable land mass. However, with sea levels rising, climate experts predict half of the nation’s capital, Funafuti, could be submerged by 2050. “Yes, we train on the runway,” said Taafaki. “When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.”However, Tarona and her brother Pasoni, who also boxed in the Commonwealth Games, are based in New Zealand where the facilities are better. “When I was growing up, boxing barely existed in Tuvalu,” said Badi. “We didn’t have gloves, so we were forced to fight bare-knuckle, and hit bags filled with sand. My children are very fortunate. They have opportunities and facilities that I never had.Boxingis our whole life. Strength is in our bloodline. It’s where our genealogy comes from.“If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change. It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can’t sleep if there’s a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes.”Taafaki is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight. Australia’sTaylah Robertson picked up a bronzein the women’s flyweight category on the Gold Coast in 2018 despite losing her first bout to England’s Lisa Whiteside.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026TuvaluCommonwealth GamesBoxingAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Faster, faster: Iraola in a rush to plug Liverpool gaps before Premier League starts | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: New head coach needs to use the transfer market with defensive cover vital as injuries hamper their US pre-season tour
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: New head coach needs to use the transfer market with defensive cover vital as injuries hamper their US pre-season tour
Content: Liverpool will complete their Chicago pre-season tour with a friendly against Leeds on Sunday.Photograph: Nikki Dyer/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLiverpool will complete their Chicago pre-season tour with a friendly against Leeds on Sunday.Photograph: Nikki Dyer/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesLiverpoolFaster, faster: Iraola in a rush to plug Liverpool gaps before Premier League startsNew head coach needs to use the transfer market with defensive cover vital as injuries hamper US pre-season tourAndy Hunterin ChicagoSat 1 Aug 2026 11.25 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Faster, faster,” bellowedAndoni Iraolathroughout the open training session Liverpool held in Chicago on Friday. His first pre-season tour as Liverpool head coach ends at the city’s famous Soldier Field Stadium on Sunday, with a friendly against Leeds, and “faster, faster” could apply to all aspects of the club’s preparations for a new Premier League campaign that begins in three weeks’ time.Iraola was in his element as he immersed himself at the centre of every training drill that Liverpool performed at Chicago Fire’s Endeavor Health Performance Center, their base for the past two weeks in the US. “Faster, faster” was the new head coach’s instruction to his players as three teams of seven worked on their pressing games. He also shouted it when they walked over to a different pitch, recently vacated by Robert Lewandowski and his newChicago Fireteammates, to work on offensive and defensive set-piece routines. Sprints were demanded following every rondo.Inter make new approach to Liverpool for Curtis Jones with £30m offer likelyRead moreThere is an urgency to Iraola’s situation atLiverpoolas he works towards his first season in charge, not only to his style of football. Post World-Cup holidays have deprived him of eight first-team players so far, injuries of a further six.It was telling that, after Liverpool’s open training session had ended, many of the fans invited headed to the gym for a look through its glass windows. Jérémy Jacquet, Liverpool’s £60m recruit from Rennes, was inside working on his recovery from a shoulder problem.He was joined by Giovanni Leoni, who is rehabilitating from an anterior cruciate ligament rupture and appears to have doubled in chest size since sustaining the injury on his Liverpool debut last September. Nearby was Joe Gomez, who pulled up with a muscle injury eight minutes into the first friendly of the tour. All central defenders, all out.The concentration of problems in one particular area was a recurring theme under Arne Slot last season and has not eased yet. Two 18-year-olds, Mor Talla Ndiaye and Ifeanyi Ndukwe, have impressed in their absence but Liverpool are looking to loan out the latter next season having been unable to secure a work permit.Among the observers on Friday was Mike Gordon, the president of Liverpool’s owners, Fenway Sports Group, who has returned to a more hands-on role at the club afterthe departure of Michael Edwardsas FSG’s chief executive of football.View image in fullscreenTeenage defender Ifeanyi Ndukwe is likely to be loaned out by Liverppool.Photograph: Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesGordon is expected to be in attendance at Soldier Field on Sunday when Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak should feature for the first time in pre-season. FSG will not be the only ones at Liverpool looking for a return on their combined £241m investment in the pair.“We need a very good version of Florian,” Iraola said this week, when confirming he intends to play the Germany international “in that position behind the striker” rather than on the left, where he operated without reward at the World Cup, or in the variety of roles that Slot tried without success.Wirtz supplying Isak and/or Hugo Ekitiké was always the intended plan of attack for Liverpool last season. The trio ultimately played only 119 minutes together as injuries struck. That stat was never lost on Slot as hewas ushered to the exitafter a turbulent and toxic campaign.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLiverpool need a very good version of Isak, too. The excuse of playing catch-up having missed pre-season, or almost four months of the season due to a fractured ankle and fibula, no longer washes for a striker who featured in all four games of Sweden’s World Cup. Isak has looked sharp in pre-season training. He not only has to sustain that sharpness next season but convince he is a suitable fit for this Liverpool team.View image in fullscreenFlorian Wirtz will be used behind the striker this season under Andoni Iraola for Liverpool.Photograph: Becky Oliver/LFC/Liverpool FC/Getty ImagesIraola’s options and vision for Liverpool will improve as senior names return but he undoubtedly requires more help through the transfer market. Work is under way ona move for Bradley Barcola, who is open to leaving Paris Saint-Germain for Anfield, but a deal for a winger who the European champions value at £145m is yet to be struck.A lack of defensive cover cost Liverpool last season and remains a glaring issue, and there are doubts over the futures of Curtis Jones, Federico Chiesa and Harvey Elliott, among others.Liverpool’s head coach has admitted he “hates this month of August” because of the uncertainty that surrounds players while the season starts. “It’s difficult to build a proper team with a lot of question marks,” he added. Between Soldier Field on Sunday and St James’ Park on 23 August, the building work must accelerate.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolAndoni IraolaLeeds UnitedChicago FirefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Transfer news: Welbeck joins Chelsea, Brentford complete record Sangaré deal | Transfer window | The Guardian
description: Chelsea signed Brighton’s veteran striker Danny Welbeck in a deal worth a reported £5m
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Chelsea signed Brighton’s veteran striker Danny Welbeck in a deal worth a reported £5m
Content: Danny Welbeck, 35, has signed a two-year deal at Chelsea.Photograph: Chris Lee/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDanny Welbeck, 35, has signed a two-year deal at Chelsea.Photograph: Chris Lee/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesTransfer windowTransfer news: Welbeck joins Chelsea, Brentford complete record Sangaré deal35-year-old Brighton striker Welbeck seals £5m moveMali international Sangaré joins Bees for reported £39mAgenciesSat 1 Aug 2026 12.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChelsea have signed Brighton’s veteran striker Danny Welbeck in a deal worth a reported £5m. Welbeck has agreed a two-year contract and will link up with Xabi Alonso’s squad on their pre-season tour.The 35-year-old’s move to Stamford Bridge is a break from Chelsea’s policy of signing younger players with the potential to be developed. It is the first time they have paid a transfer fee for a player over the age of 26 since they signed Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang from Barcelona in 2022 when the striker was 33.Chelsea fined £10m and given suspended transfer ban by FA over agent breachesRead more“When you hear of interest from Chelsea, it’s something that fills you with such immense pride. Knowing the history of Chelsea, it’s a club that wants to win trophies and is pushing to do that every single season,” Welbeck said.“I’m really honoured to come to a club of this stature at what feels like a really exciting time. I know a few of the boys already and I’ve had fantastic conversations with the manager and already feel that connection. I’ve got that fire in my belly and I’m ready to give it everything for this club to make everyone at Chelsea, and the supporters, proud.”Alonso was keen to add experience to his squad after last season’s disappointing 10th-place finish in the Premier League. He opted for Welbeck after the former Manchester United and Arsenal forward enjoyed a memorable campaign with Brighton.Welbeck, who has 42 caps for England, scored 13 goals in 37 Premier League games last term after netting 10 times in 2024-25.Welbeck’s arrival in west London will raise questions about the future of Chelsea striker Liam Delap, who signed from Ipswich last season, as well as fellow forwards Nicolas Jackson and Marc Guiu.Welbeck is the latest player to move from Brighton to Chelsea in recent years after João Pedro, Moisés Caicedo, Robert Sánchez and Marc Cucurella, whojoined Real Madridearlier this summer.Chelsea spent a British record £117m to sign the England forward Morgan Rogers, 24, from Aston Villa in July. They also securedthe France defender Maxence Lacroix, 26, from Crystal Palace for £52m earlier this week and signed Atalanta defender Marco Palestra, 21, for £43m.Brentford seal record Sangaré dealBrentfordhave signed the Mali international Mamadou Sangaré from ⁠Lens for a club-record fee, reported to be £39m. Sangaré, 24, joinsBrentfordon a five-year contract, with ⁠the option to extend for another year.“Mamadou ​is someone ‌that we’ve tracked ‌for quite some time. He’s been on ‌our radar and was a player we were really keen to bring in,” the Brentford head coach Keith Andrews said. “He’s a humble young man, but he’s equally as ⁠determined to succeed in his career. He ​fits ​everything we want from ​a Brentford player, on and ​off the ‌pitch.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSangaré left Austria’s Rapid Vienna to ‌joinLenslast year, and featured prominently as they won the ​French Cup for the first time and finished second in Ligue 1.View image in fullscreenMamadou Sangaré has swapped RC Lens for Brentford in a £39m move.Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/ReutersBournemouthhave announced the signing of António Silva from Benfica for a fee believed to be in the region of £25m. The 22-year-old defender becomes new manager Marco Rose’s second signing of the summer after the arrival of Álvaro Rodríguez earlier this week.Silva made 235 senior appearances forBenficaand collected six major honours during his time in Portugal. He told the club website: “I am very happy to be here. It’s a pleasure to play for Bournemouth and in the Premier League.“The mentality is always to win. I will try my best, and I will play for the fans. We have everything here that helps us perform on the pitch, and I can’t wait to get started.”Explore more on these topicsTransfer windowChelseaBrighton & Hove AlbionBrentfordLensBournemouthBenficanewsShareReuse this content

title: Yealimi Noh leads Women’s Open by three shots after Ryu Hae-ran stumbles | Women's Open | The Guardian
description: Ryu’s bid for a third consecutive major win is in doubt, while England’s Lottie Woad and Charley Hull remain in contention at Royal Lytham and St Annes
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Ryu’s bid for a third consecutive major win is in doubt, while England’s Lottie Woad and Charley Hull remain in contention at Royal Lytham and St Annes
Content: Yealimi Noh leads Ryu Hae-ran, Jeeno Thitikul, Lucy Li, Esther Henseleit and Shiho Kuwaki by four shots on seven under par.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAView image in fullscreenYealimi Noh leads Ryu Hae-ran, Jeeno Thitikul, Lucy Li, Esther Henseleit and Shiho Kuwaki by four shots on seven under par.Photograph: Peter Byrne/PAWomen's OpenYealimi Noh leads Women’s Open by three shots after Ryu Hae-ran stumblesRyu’s bid for third consecutive major win in doubtEngland’s Lottie Woad and Charley Hull in contentionEwan Murrayat Royal Lytham & St AnnesSat 1 Aug 2026 14.38 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 15.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRyu Hae-ran has 18 holes to recover from events in the third round of the Women’s Open. Her stumble at Royal Lytham and St Annes would have counted as one of the most remarkable in recent major championship memory had it taken place a day later. Saturday proved it is never, ever over on terrain such as this. Adam Scott can verify that, such was his horrible capitulation here as Ernie Els claimed the Open of 2012. There must be something about Lytham.Ryu is looking to set an extraordinary record of three major wins in as many starts. Early in the third round, she looked firmly on course for that. The South Korean marched to a four-shot lead after four. Her advantage was the same on the 7th tee. By the time she walked from the 18th green, Ryu was three adrift of Yealimi Noh. Quite the turnaround. How damaging? That remains to be seen.Charley Hull doubles down on caddie prank after strong start to Women’s OpenRead moreRyu joined Jeeno Thitikul, Lucy Li, Esther Henseleit and Shiho Kuwaki on an aggregate of four under par. That group is the closest to Noh.Lytham provides a fiendishly difficult test. Ryu looked unflappable until the 7th, where she cracked a drive right, towards the railway line between Blackpool South and Preston. After a penalty drop, a bogey hardly seemed disastrous. Yet it triggered a horrible run. Ryu made bogey on the 8th, 10th, 12th and 14th after finding a series of bunkers. Her lead, one at the turn, had evaporated by the 10th when she found herself level with Kuwaki.As Ryu was faltering, Noh delivered a links masterclass. Her 69 included an inward half of 33. Noh’s prominence here is a surprise, given her overall major record is not particularly impressive. “It was a little bit of a rocky start,” said Noh, who was three over through six. “But my putting was solid after that and my shots too. I just settled into a better routine and focused on my tempo on the back nine.“It’s just another round of golf out there tomorrow and I’m going to enjoy it. I’m just happy to be in this position and ready to go again.”Nelly Korda birdied the 17th to move to one under par. The world No 1 could have been considered in the mix at that point but a horrible double bogey at the last followed, which surely ended her Women’s Open dream. The eight-shot gap is not the only problem for Korda, instead the number of strong players between her and Noh. Lydia Ko is one of them and feels notable at minus one.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Home hope remains alive. Lottie Woad’s 70 means she is very much in touch at three under.Charley Hull is just a stroke further backafter her 71. Hull claimed she played like a 10-handicap amateur in the early stages of her round. The vagaries of Lytham mean any player within sight of the lead going into the final day has a legitimate hope of glory. Woad’s unflustered nature is an advantage here while Hull is long overdue major success.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The more times you’re in that position the more comfortable you get,” said Woad. “I know I can play well in this tournament and I have done the last two years and had that experience of being in the mix. And even this year, obviously a few weeks ago I was leading at the Evian Championship, so I can kind of use that experience as well. The more times you put the yourself in that position is obviously a good thing.“It’s always great when the fans are pulling for you. I mean, it’s not all going to be on me tomorrow. Charley is playing great too, so people going to be supporting both of us.” Indeed they are. As Ryu already knows, she is firmly up against it in her bid to make history.Explore more on these topicsWomen's OpenGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: Wiebes outsprints Le Court and Vollering to win Tour de France Femmes opening stage | Tour de France Femmes | The Guardian
description: Lorena Wiebes took the first yellow jersey of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes after outsprinting the race favourites Kim Le Court and Demi Vollering
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: Lorena Wiebes took the first yellow jersey of the 2026 Tour de France Femmes after outsprinting the race favourites Kim Le Court and Demi Vollering
Content: Lorena Wiebes enjoys her win on the first stage of the Tour de France Femmes in Lausanne.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersView image in fullscreenLorena Wiebes enjoys her win on the first stage of the Tour de France Femmes in Lausanne.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersTour de France FemmesWiebes outsprints Le Court and Vollering to win Tour de France Femmes opening stageWiebes’ turn of speed too much for 2023 winner Vollering‘It was a long sprint, but I’m super happy’Jeremy Whittlein LausanneSat 1 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLorena Wiebes took the first yellow jersey of the 2026Tour de France Femmesafter climbing the Côte Saint-François and outsprinting race favourites Kim Le Court and 2023 champion, Demi Vollering.“The team worked super hard today,” Wiebes said. “When Demi attacked, I knew I had to follow. It was a long sprint, but I’m super happy.”Tour de France Femmes 2026: Lorena Wiebes powers to stage one win in Lausanne – liveRead moreIt was the Dutch rider’s sixth stage win in the Tour de France Femmes. The 27-year-old also won the opening stage of the 2026 women’s Giro d’Italia in May but was disqualified because her bike had an illegal weight, an outcome which left her team considering legal action against cycling’s governing body, the UCI.“I’m really happy with the support I have had from the team and the staff,” she said. “They fully believed in me, when even I had some doubts.”Wiebes, of SD Worx-Protime, leads the race overall by four seconds from Le Court and six seconds from Vollering. The defending champion, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, finished eighth and is 10 seconds behind the race leader.The final outcome of the race is likely to be decided by minutes, although Lars Boom, sports director to Vollering, who lost the 2024 race by just four seconds, valued the time gain.“That’s always nice,” Boom said. “You never know what’s going to happen with wildfires in France, so in the end it’s always better to get seconds than to have to gain seconds.”The high temperatures and rolling roads split the field after 83km, on the third category Côte de Villars-le-Comte, where numerous riders lost contact with the peloton and one of the day’s four breakaways, French rider Océane Mahé of the lowly Ma Petite Entreprise team, took the lead in the Queen of the Mountains classification.But with 50km left to race the quartet’s advantage began to dwindle and they were finally swallowed up with 6km remaining, on the lakeside approach to Lausanne’s uphill finish.View image in fullscreenLorena Wiebes wears the yellow jersey on the podium.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersVollering, buoyed by the announcement that Red Bull has become her FDJ United–Suezteam’s latest sponsorship partner, led into the final 600m, but Wiebes’ turn of speed was too much for her compatriot, who was surprisingly overtaken by Le Court in the closing metres.Wiebes came to the Tour Femmes looking for vindication after the Giro controversy in late May. Her win was wiped out by disqualification after her bike weighed in at slightly under the regulation 6.8kg. Wiebes also lost the pink race leader’s jersey and a bitter dispute ensued between the team and the UCI over the methods used to measure the bike’s weight.“I would have been perfectly fine with it if the scale had consistently shown the same weight,” Wiebes said. “But having the bike’s weight vary during the weighing process – that was the most frustrating part for me.”Her SD Worx-Protime team manager, Danny Stam, said that a legal case against the UCI was now pending.“Our team’s lawyers are working on it,” he told De Telegraaf. “We’ve received feedback but it’s going to be a long process. Still, justice needs to be served.“I just find it unacceptable that a decision with such a huge impact on a rider is made when a bike is hanging from a tent that’s nearly blowing away. Can’t we operate a bit more professionally in this day and age? Can’t we just weigh a bike inside an enclosed truck, away from the wind? Instead of: ‘Now it weighs this, now it weighs that.’”Tomorrow’s second stage begins in nearby Aigle, ironically on the doorstep of the UCI headquarters, where Wiebes will take to the start line in the yellow jersey. Five more climbs and high temperatures may make it another tough stage, but the flat finish on Geneva’s Quai du Mont-Blanc looks well-suited to the Dutch rider.Explore more on these topicsTour de France FemmesCyclingUCI (Union Cycliste Internationale)newsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pretty much the downfall of society’: Adam Ramsay-Peaty on press intrusion, forgiveness and going all in for LA 2028 | Adam Ramsay-Peaty | The Guardian
description: After a rollercoaster week at the Commonwealth Games, the double Olympic champion tells Donald McRae he will never stop believing what he can achieve
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: After a rollercoaster week at the Commonwealth Games, the double Olympic champion tells Donald McRae he will never stop believing what he can achieve
Content: Adam Ramsay-Peaty has had a tricky few years since his eight-year winning streak ended in 2022.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAdam Ramsay-Peaty has had a tricky few years since his eight-year winning streak ended in 2022.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAdam Ramsay-PeatyInterview‘Pretty much the downfall of society’: Adam Ramsay-Peaty on press intrusion, forgiveness and going all in for LA 2028Donald McRaeAfter a rollercoaster week at the Commonwealth Games, the double Olympic champion says he will never stop believing what he can achieveSat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Icouldn’t switch off because it’s been a real rollercoaster of a week,” Adam Ramsay-Peaty says with a weary smile on a quiet Thursday morning in Glasgow. He has just endured a rough night in which, after winning his third medal of theCommonwealth Games, he managed less than three hours of sleep. The medals consist of bronzein the 100mand50m breaststrokeand a silver in themen’s 4x100m medley. For most swimmers this would constitute success and satisfaction, but Ramsay-Peaty is different.The fact that none of his three medals are gold, or attached to anything remotely like the kind of supreme performance that Ramsay-Peaty churned out with an aura of invincibility for eight years, has taken a chunk out of the double Olympic champion. There have beentears of frustrationand an admission that “nothing makes sense this week”.Ramsay-Peaty also sent out afiery message to his tormentorsin the tabloid press, and on social media, to stress that “you can’t hurt me” before urging an end to the excessive intrusion into his private life: “It has to stop. How many athletes have to go through this until the media learn their lesson?”Now, in a small room on the outskirts of the city, Ramsay-Peaty admits that “decompressing last night was hard”. The European championships, which begin in Paris on 10 August, will see him gather himself for the next chapter in a tumultuous career, which he hopes will peakat the LA Olympicsin 2028.View image in fullscreenRamsay-Peaty won the first of his three Olympic gold medals in Rio in 2016.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian“I’ve experienced a lot in this sport,” Ramsay-Peaty, now 31 years old, says intently. “I’m never going to stop believing what I can do. I just need to get to that peak once more.”Ramsay‑Peaty did not lose a single race in the 100m breaststroke from 2014 to 2022. Apart from winning three Olympic golds and eight world titles, by 2021 he had swum the20 fastest times in the history of the discipline– and the 10 fastest in the history of the 50m.Afterfinally losing a 100m race,in the 2022 Commonwealth Games, Ramsay-Peaty suffered a breakdown a year later, quit swimming and lost himself in a haze of drink and depression. It was an epic feat todrag himself back from the brinkand, in the 2024 Olympic final,miss gold by two-hundredths of a secondwhile swimming with anundiagnosed case of Covid.“After those Commonwealths in Birmingham,” Ramsay-Peaty says of his shock defeat four years ago, “I went on the attack and turned myself into scorched earth. I gave too much and that led to the burnout zone in 2023. I know not to do that now. I’ve got to find that peace and consolidation and realise we couldn’t have done anything more.“We’ve trained extremely hard. I’ve only been 12 weeks in London with a new coach and a new programme. That takes time to reach fruition. Once you prune the tree, you grow more fruit in the end.”After losing the 100m last Saturday, having swum almost three seconds slower than his world record, Ramsay-Peaty said: “I’m not crying because it’s a bronze instead of a gold. I’m crying because I know that the swim could have been better, and I worked way better than that.”Another bronze in the 50m was accepted more philosophically by Ramsay-Peaty: “When I was undefeated for eight years, it was athlete first, then human. Now it’s human first.”View image in fullscreenRamsay-Peaty’s return was one of the major draws of this year’s Commonwealth Games.Photograph: Quinn Rooney/Getty ImagesThis is a healthy alternative to the raging obsession that once consumed him. “It’s a natural progression from putting absolutely everything into the sport, which came at a huge cost,” he says. “You realise now that if you’re second you’re not going to die. You just have to learn from it. So there is a new approach because to do what I did you have to go to a place of anger, almost a place of hate, and I don’t want to be in that place. It’s a huge emotional cost that isn’t sustainable. I know I can win with a newer mindset and without the dark stuff.”Ramsay-Peaty remains a fierce competitor and, looking ahead to the Europeans, the old fire crackles: “I’ve still got to burn the boats. I’ve still got to go all in, and believe I can win. If I don’t have that mentality I’m never going to get close. I know the Europeans are going to be fast in the heats. But I’m going to be good.”After a dozen years at the summit, it sounds as if the more human side of Ramsay-Peaty is winning: “Every athlete has their own version of success. Of course, mine is still tied to quantifiable things like medals and times. But if I enjoy this journey and know I’ve given my best, and I touch that scoreboard in LA, that’s already success. That’s not defeatist. I’m still going to be a warrior. I’m still going to fight and give my absolute best.”I tell Ramsay-Peaty about a column in which my colleague Barney Ronaycompared him and his monumental achievements to other ageing sporting greatssuch as Lionel Messi. Ramsay-Peaty grins; he watched the 39-year‑old Messi stroll around so many World Cup pitches this summerbefore bursting into flaming geniuswhen his grinding teammates needed him.“Team sports have the benefit of being able to carry special players. But as a swimmer, when you’re older, it’s harder to race in the heats, and then the semis and finals. There’s nowhere to hide. When I’m going through that last 25 metres, it’s not like I can pass the ball and say: ‘You take this bit for me.’ Believe me, I probably would. But on the other side, with the success I had when I was younger, I wouldn’t have wanted to be in a team sport because my values and work ethic are so high I don’t think anyone could have kept up.”View image in fullscreenRamsay-Peaty has been striving to find a better balance between his professional ambitions and his personal and mental health.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianHas he made sense yet of what went wrong in Glasgow especially as, a few months ago, he won the nationals in a time that would have clinched gold in the 100m Commonwealth final? “I was probably in a better block of work then, as we have to constantly balance our aerobic and anaerobic capacities. Maybe this past week was one of adaptation and, with a week of rest going into the Euros, I’ll be stronger. I worked the hardest I’ve worked in a very long time these last 12 weeks but maybe it wasn’t enough time for me to adapt. You also have to be race‑fit, and that’s a very different skill set. It still doesn’t make sense but tomorrow we have a debrief with my coach, Lisa Bates.”Ramsay-Peaty adds: “We overthink a lot in this sport and we can look at all the data variables and rip up what is actually a lot of good work. Sometimes we just have a bad day, and that’s OK. But it’s not OK if it keeps happening.”Bates replaced the great Mel Marshall, who had coached Ramsay-Peaty for his entire career until the 2024 Olympics. Marshall now works in Australia. “I’ve known Lisa for a long time,” Ramsay-Peaty says, “and Mel’s very close friends with her. It came with the decision to move to London because my wife [Holly] is pregnant so we needed her family. We’re having a little girl in December.”Holly’s father is Gordon Ramsay, and the combination of a celebrity chef’s family in London and an Olympic champion’s working-class family from Uttoxeter has been catnip for the tabloids. Personal problems between the swimmer and his parents have been the source of feverish gossip and adding his wife’s name since their marriage has fuelled wild speculation.Has it had a serious impact on him? “I wouldn’t say on me because I’ve got a thick skin. But I care about my wife, I care about my son [from his previous relationship]. I care about the relationships that people think I have with my son, and my own family, but that’s my private life. I have incredible relationships with some people in the media, like the one with you, which is built on trust over time. The ones that don’t go well are with the tabloids selling these stories for advertising. It’s pretty much the downfall of society when we’re exploiting people’s private lives to sell. Will it get better? Probably not. Will the truth come out one day? Absolutely.”View image in fullscreenRamsey-Peaty says tabloid intrusion into his personal life has had a much greater impact on his  family than on him.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianHis mother, Caroline, posted a statement on social media this week about the rift. Is he hopeful there can be a reconciliation? “For me, as a Christian, there has to be forgiveness. It doesn’t mean you have to forget, but forgiveness takes time. I’m not saying that it won’t get better but it has to come from a place where I feel like they’ve improved as people, in a sense, and opened that communication up. I haven’t told one thing to the media. I haven’t done one story over the last eight months and more.”We return to the sense of invincibility that Ramsay-Peaty carried for so many years. I read him a quote thathe gave me in 2015, after he had won three gold medals at the world championships. Aged 20, he sounded remarkably mature as he said: “I feel no pressure. I enjoy racing. What’s the worst that could happen? You’re going to come second or lose? It’s not like someone has got a gun to your head.”Eleven years on, he says : “There’s a part of me which screams that you want that risk [of hating defeat]. That’s the athlete. The human knows that isn’t the right path. That isn’t going to make me the best husband, the best father, the best friend. That athlete is incredibly selfish, and will ruin any form of relationship. I guarantee that because I’ve been there. But I still haven’t found that healthy medium.“In training I don’t struggle one bit with that [athlete’s] mentality. I can switch it off when I leave training. It’s more about the exhaustion of training twice a day, going for it every single day. It’s now about finding what is optimal and sustainable in LA.”If Ramsay-Peaty is preparing for the 100m he needs to swim around 9,000m on a training day. But if he concentrates purely on the 50m it would be “way less, probably 3,000m a day. You’d only have to do 12k a week, but I’m doing 40k for an extra 50 metres.”Is he thinking of giving up the 100m and aiming only for the 50? “Not yet, no. I know I can be so strong in the 100. We’ve got to keep it in perspective. This is my first championships in two years. It’s been a bad week and we need to be better.”Does he believe he will finally unearth the elusive balance of compulsion and decency and, in 2028, complete his journey in the most meaningful way, whatever the colour of any medals he might win?Ramsay-Peaty pauses and then his face cracks open in a big, gleaming smile: “Yes. I’ve got a good armoury. I’ve just to get the polishing cloth out now.”Explore more on these topicsAdam Ramsay-PeatySwimmingOlympic GamesCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: EU to hold urgent meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday over Ceuta crisis | Spain | The Guardian
description: Divisions remain in the bloc over mass crossing of migrants into Spanish territory in north Africa
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Divisions remain in the bloc over mass crossing of migrants into Spanish territory in north Africa
Content: Police officers and Spanish soldiers escorting people in Ceuta to the border with Morocco on Saturday morning.Photograph: Jon Nazca/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice officers and Spanish soldiers escorting people in Ceuta to the border with Morocco on Saturday morning.Photograph: Jon Nazca/ReutersSpainEU to hold urgent meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday over Ceuta crisisDivisions remain in the bloc over mass crossing of migrants into Spanish territory in north AfricaLisa O’Carrollin London andSam Jonesin MadridSat 1 Aug 2026 15.03 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 06.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU is to hold an urgent meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday amid continued divisions in the bloc over the arrival of more than 50,000 migrants in the Spanish territory of Ceuta in northAfrica.The decision was taken by officials representing EU member states and Frontex border agency experts at what was described as a “sobering” meeting on Saturday.Spain confirmed at least 67 people had died in the attempted crossing. Some drowned, while others were crushed as they tried to cross a breakwater barrier.The decision to call a summit of ministers was unanimous as EU leaders seek to heal divisions in the bloc and restore a unified approach to migration.Spain said migrant crossings into Ceuta had stopped overnight, as police began installing a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier off its border ‌withMorocco.Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, said on Saturday: “I have been in touch with the Spanish prime minister and [we are] providing what help we can.”Italy and Denmark, with some support from Poland and Sweden, used the meeting on Saturday to criticise Spain for what had happened.In a furious letter on Saturday, Spain’s prime ministerPedro Sánchezhit out against “fake news” and “disinformation”, pointing out that “virtually all” migrants had been returned to Morocco after the army intervened on Friday, “preventing any unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe”.It is understood suspected Russian attempts to spread disinformation to sow dissent within the EU was also discussed at the meeting on Saturday.There is frustration in Spain that previous incidents of this scale, such as mass arrival of migrants on the border of Belarus and Poland or Russia and Finland, were labelled as “hybrid attacks” , and met with solidarity from the rest of the EU.Although more than 48,000 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday, the influx triggered a political crisis for the Madrid government and led some fellow EU countries to call for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.Juan Jesús Vivas, the president of Ceuta, said that while many people had returned to Morocco, not all those who had crossed into the city had left.“We’re not back to normal because there are several thousand people who need to be returned, and there is still an atmosphere marked by unease and concern,” he said. He also called for “all the security measures deployed” in Ceuta to remain in place to guarantee the safety of the population.Sánchez asked for the meeting after what appeared to be a breakdown of EU unity on external border policy, with Italy attacking Spain.Italy announced on Friday evening that it would suspend its Schengen arrangements with Spain for a month, even though Ceuta – and Spain’s other north African territory, Melilla – are subject to special Schengen rules that prevent onward movement within the zone.Map showing location of Ceuta in Mediterranean region, and another showing location of Tarajal breakwater on border between Ceuta and MoroccoItaly’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now-closed schemeto regularise the statusof more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”.Sánchez was forthright in a letter sent to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Council president, António Costa, and Micheál Martin, the prime minister of Ireland, which holds the EU presidency.View image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez speaking at a press conference in Ceuta on Friday.Photograph: Borja Puig de la Bellacasa/Moncloa handout/EPASánchez said that while most EU countries had expressed support and solidarity over events in Ceuta, others had chosen to attack Spain.“Such an attitude – driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest – is … contrary to European law, humanitarian law and the principles of solidarity that bind us together,” he said.In a pointed rebuke to Italy, he noted that Spain was “according to Frontex, one of the least porous external borders of theEuropean Union, with a number of irregular entries that is half that recorded, for example, in Italy in recent years (2021–26)”.Senior EU officials met on Saturday in a “political crisis response team” convened by Ireland’s presidency.3:37Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - videoIreland’s prime minister, Micheál Martin, said on Saturday that, as the holders of the EU presidency, “Ireland will convene a meeting on Tuesday of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council, chaired by Jim O’Callaghan [justice minister], to discuss developments in Ceuta.“We remain in close contact with all member states and the institutions and continue to monitor the situation,” he said in a social media post.O’Callaghan, who is leading the meetings on behalf of the EU, said he had been in touch with Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, to express his solidarity and support.In remarks that appeared to respond to Sánchez’s criticisms, von der Leyen said she welcomed his suggestion of a video conference “to take stock of what has happened”, adding: “Fighting illegal migration requires solidarity and a united European response.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrance’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said his country would not be seeking Spain’s suspension from Schengen rules.“It’s absolutely not on the table,” he said on Saturday. “We have great cooperation with Spain.”Many of the remaining people who crossed into Ceuta returned to Morocco on Saturday morning amid a reinforced Spanish police and military presence.“We hope to go to Europe to work and earn a living – that’s it,” Souleil Boyan, a 19-year-old from Senegal, told Agence France-Presse outside a migrant centre in Ceuta where dozens of other people from sub-Saharan Africa were waiting for officials.“We all know that in Africa there isn’t much opportunity,” he added.The Spanish government said in a statement on Saturday that the situation in Ceuta remained calm and quiet.It said containment barriers were being installed at the Tarajal beach breakwater, including a 500-metre-long inflatable barrier and a line of anchored buoys.View image in fullscreenSpanish soldiers in Ceuta on Saturday.Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/ReutersThis week’s mass crossing dwarfs the last similar event in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over two days.That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed the territory to Morocco and Mauritania.That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara, a move that caused a rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group.Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreSánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria.The Spanish government has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla could not be summarily returned under special rules.But some migration experts have expressed doubts about that explanation. Mauricio Valiente, the director general of the Spanish Refugee Aid Commission, said the route into Ceuta was very different from theAtlantic route from Africa to the Canary Islands, which is often operated by people smugglers.“Unlike what happens in the Canary Islands, these aren’t people who have to get into a small boat,”he told elDiario.es. “This is a matter of being just metres from a land border, jumping into the sea and trying to get around a breakwater, which makes it much easier to do, even with all the risks.”Valiente said there had been a steady increase in arrivals to Ceuta this year, even before the supreme court ruling.“The causes are complex, and there are surely many reasons,” he said. “But to simplify it by referencing the court ruling or organised crime – to say there’s a direct cause-and-effect relationship – is completely unfounded.”Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, visited Ceuta on Saturday and said he had spoken to migrants there.“I have spoken to a number of them who made it quite clear they intend to make it to Britain,” he said.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropeEuropean UnionMoroccoMigrationPedro SánchezAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Top mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead after 11 hit by avalanche in Pakistan  | Mountaineering | The Guardian
description: Other members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak have also died, climbing company says
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Other members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak have also died, climbing company says
Content: Nirmal Purja pictured in 2021 after his return from leading the first team to summit K2 in winter.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APView image in fullscreenNirmal Purja pictured in 2021 after his return from leading the first team to summit K2 in winter.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APMountaineeringTop mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead after 11 hit by avalanche in PakistanOther members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak also died, climbing company saysGeneva AbdulSat 1 Aug 2026 09.41 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA world-renowned Nepali mountaineer and former UK Special Forces member has died after being among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak.Nirmal Purja was killed leading an expedition of 10 other people on the world’s 12th-highest mountain when an avalanche struck at around noon on Thursday.Elite Exped, the company Purja co-founded, said in a statement: “Today it is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak.”“We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive,” it said, without further detail.Purjamade history in 2019 after climbing all 14 of the world’s peaks over 8,000 metresin just over six months. He later led the first team to summit K2, the world’s second-highest mountain, in winter.1:52Nirmal Purja climbs world’s 14 highest peaks in record-breaking 189 days – video report“Records are made to be broken,” the former Gurkha and UKSF membertold the Guardian in 2019. “Someone one day will come along and be stronger. People are only limited by their imagination. If you don’t dream, then you won’t do it. Human beings are capable of doing amazing things.”The expedition included five Nepali climbers, as well as US, Pakistani, Omani and Chinese nationals. Another foreign climber was also part of the group, said Karrar Haidri, the vice-president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan.Elite Exped also confirmed the deaths of other expedition members, including his climbing partners and guides, Pur Bahadur Gurung (Yukta), a Nepali citizen, and Nima Sherpa.“Our deepest thoughts, prayers and heartfelt condolences are with their families, friends and loved ones,” the Elite Exped statement said. “No words can erase the pain of this unimaginable loss, and we ask that everyone respects their privacy as they grieve.”Map of Broad PeakOn Friday, rescuers had said thatfour bodies had been foundand efforts were under way to retrieve them despite the harsh weather. Among the victims were Nadhira Alharthy, the first Omani to climb Everest, and a US climber, Mallory Geis.View image in fullscreenNadhira Alharthy, the first Omani to climb Everest, was also among the victims.Photograph: instagram/alharthynoorTrackers carried by the climbers showed a rapid loss of altitude, suggesting the team had been caught in an avalanche. Purja’s tracker, however, shifted location after the initial rapid descent. The GPS data suggested the avalanche occurred close to 9am local time at 6,579 metres (21,585ft), between camps two and three on the west ridge of the 8,047-metre mountain, the most popular ascent route.View image in fullscreenBroad Peak is the 12th highest mountain in the world at 8,051 metres.Photograph: Naveed Hussain/AlamyThe British adventurer Bear Grylls said the news of Purja’s death was “heartbreaking for so many climbers around the world who had a relationship with this remarkable and unique man”.In the 2023 documentary Finding Michael, Purja and Grylls were enlisted to recover the body ofMichael Matthews, the youngest Briton to climb Everest, who disappeared on the mountain in 1999.Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of them in the special forces. In 2018, he was awarded an MBE by the queen for his achievements in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.He also drew plaudits for twice risking his life to help others. The first time was while descending from Annapurna, when he led a rescue of fellow climber Chin Wui Kin, who had been separated from an accompanying expedition and left without food, water or oxygen for 40 hours. He later died in hospital.Less than a month later, Purja and his team rescued two climbers from a height of 8,400 metres, sacrificing their own supplementary oxygen to the climbers in need.“For me it’s not about ego,” he previously told the Guardian. “It’s about principles. You can’t call yourself a climber and not help in that situation.”The Prince of Wales said he was “truly saddened to hear of the tragic death” of Purja, adding that he “served with distinction” before “becoming one of the world’s greatest mountaineers”.Explore more on these topicsMountaineeringPakistanSouth and central AsiaAvalanchesNepalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dozens injured as earthquake hits near Naples in seismic swarm | Earthquakes | The Guardian
description: At least five taken to hospital and about 300 evacuated in strongest quake to hit southern Italian region in 40 years
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: At least five taken to hospital and about 300 evacuated in strongest quake to hit southern Italian region in 40 years
Content: People inspecting damaged buildings in Pozzuoli after the earthquake.Photograph: Felice de Martino/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople inspecting damaged buildings in Pozzuoli after the earthquake.Photograph: Felice de Martino/EPAEarthquakesDozens injured as earthquake hits near Naples in seismic swarmAt least five taken to hospital and about 300 evacuated in strongest quake to hit southern Italian region in 40 yearsDonna Fergusonand agenciesSat 1 Aug 2026 09.49 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 06.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 26 people have been injured after a 4.7-magnitude earthquake rocked a region near Naples, in southernItaly.The quake, which occurred at 7.46pm on Friday night, caused power outages, disrupted public transport and damaged a pier in Campi Flegrei, the site of Europe’s largest volcanic crater.It is the strongest tremor to hit the region in the past 40 years and caused part of a cliff and several unoccupied buildings to collapse.At least five of those injured were taken to hospital and about 300 people were evacuated from their homes in the city of Pozzuoli, near the epicentre of the quake, after it triggered landslides.Many residents spent the night on the streets, afraid their buildings would be damaged or collapse.One person was only “alive by a miracle”, a rescuer told Reuters, as Italy’s civil protection minister, Nello Musumeci, urged caution and warned that the volcanic activity was not yet over.The quake – which had a depth of 3km and was felt across Naples and the island of Ischia, and as far away as the Sorrento peninsula – was part of an ongoing seismic swarm, Italy’s national institute of geophysics and volcanology said.After it struck, seismographs registered about 60 more tremors, with one 3.1-magnitude quake at 5.47am being felt by residents of Bacoli and Pozzuoli as well as Naples.View image in fullscreenA woman walking through a closed street in Pozzuoli the day after the earthquake.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images“There is a risk that the mountain could continue to collapse, so it is dangerous,” the rescuer said. “What makes us angry is that this situation was foreseeable, because there had already been problems with the mountain for a year and a half … The municipality knew about the situation and did nothing – perhaps if they had acted sooner, this could have been avoided.”The heaviest damage was reported in Pozzuoli, where a building partly collapsed and large chunks of rubble crushed parked cars but did not cause any injuries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA car sits crushed under rocks that fell from a ridge near the Solfatara volcanic crater in Campi Flegrei.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesNine buildings have been deemed unsafe as buildings inspections continue.“We were afraid,” one resident said. “We all ran out of our homes because it was impossible to stay inside. It lasted a long time and was very powerful, and we no longer know what we are supposed to do. We have been left here in the middle of the street, and no one has come to check on us or tell us what to do. We are here with very young children.”Firefighters said they received reports of lifts being stuck and of a high-voltage pylon supplying electricity to the Agnano area of Naples having partly collapsed, causing disruption for 100,000 households.The port authority said the Pozzuoli pier was unusable, and ferry and hydrofoil services to the islands had been suspended. High-speed train passengers were experiencing delays of up to six hours, with some being rerouted.Explore more on these topicsEarthquakesItalyEuropeNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘MPs have had their stomachs pumped’: concerns over ‘alcohol-soaked’ culture in Westminster | Politics | The Guardian
description: Alcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report finds
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Alcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report finds
Content: MPs socialise on the terrace outside the House of Commons. Politicians have described how alcohol is readily available throughout the day, including at daytime lobbying events.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/In Pictures/GettyView image in fullscreenMPs socialise on the terrace outside the House of Commons. Politicians have described how alcohol is readily available throughout the day, including at daytime lobbying events.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/In Pictures/GettyPolitics‘MPs have had their stomachs pumped’: concerns over ‘alcohol-soaked’ culture in WestminsterAlcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report findsDenis CampbellSat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParliament is “Britain’s last alcohol-soaked workplace” where MPs are offered free drinks as early as midday despite alcohol-related scandals, areport has revealed.Drinking is commonplace and some MPs have had their stomachs pumped after consuming so much alcohol that they ended up in hospital, one disclosed.Alcohol is “embedded” in how Westminster works, driven by loneliness among MPs, socialising in order to meet ministers, and drinks being served at daytime and evening events.View image in fullscreenThe Churchill Room bar on the terrace of the House of Commons.Photograph: Lisa Ryder/AlamyThose are the findings of a survey of 190 MPs and their staff which shows that Westminster’s drinking culture endures, despite rising concern and a string of incidents, including an MP’s researcherallegedly having had her drink spikedin Strangers’ bar in parliament and the revelation that the Labour MP Neil Coyle was at one timedrinking up to 200 units of alcohol a week– the equivalent of 10 pints a night. The spiking led to a police investigation and the temporary closure of Strangers’ bar.The report, by the Institute of Alcohol Studies (IAS) thinktank, said: “The findings suggest that Westminster remains a highly unusual workplace where alcohol is embedded in professional life, networking, lobbying and socialising in ways that would be exceptional in most other UK workplaces.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, visit a pub during a trip to Essex. The report found alcohol was embedded in networking, lobbying and socialising for those working in Westminster.Photograph: Richard Pohle/Pool Times Media Ltd/AP“Participants described alcohol as being available throughout the working day, frequently provided for free, and often intertwined with career advancement.”Twenty-four MPs, 58 Westminster staff and 108 constituency office personnel shared their experiences and views. One MP, describing how readily available alcohol was at Westminster, said: “Going to a meeting at noon and alcohol’s available. Of course, I’m not used to that in my old job.”The free alcohol at events on the parliamentary estate, which organisations arrange to help them lobby MPs, emerged as a particular issue.Another MP said: “Where else in a work environment would you go, unless it was the works Christmas do, and there was free alcohol there for you? It just wouldn’t happen in real life.”A third said: “You can start drinking here from 12 o’clock onwards and go around and consume large amounts of alcohol, and it’s relatively freely available.”A fourth described events as a “legitimised opportunity to drink alcohol”, while a fifth said this routine provision of alcohol helps to create a “casual attitude to drinking”.Hannah Spencer, the Green party MP elected at the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, received a mixed reaction from MPs when in April she labelled Westminster’s drinking culture“unprofessional and worrying”and said it led to cases of “questionable and dangerous behaviour”. She remarked that “you can smell the alcohol when people are in between votes”.View image in fullscreenHannah Spencer said she found Westminster’s drinking culture ‘unprofessional and worrying’ after being elected as an MP this year.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe IAS report also found that:42% of the MPs interviewed had been offered an alcoholic drink at a work meeting or event on a weekly basis during the previous six months; 13% said that occurred daily.22% had concerns about a colleague’s drinking.Parliament’s long and unusual working hours, the loneliness many MPs experience being away from home, the pressures of the job and socialising in order to advance their careers can all act as catalysts for drinking.The report added: “The availability of alcohol was seen to encourage unhealthy behaviour in general, from affecting colleagues’ sleep and stress levels to potentially normalising high-risk drinking, with one MP referring to colleagues having had their stomachs pumped in hospital and going back into Westminster the following day.”Some MPs said the findings should prompt Westminster to rethink its attitude to alcohol. The Labour MP Cat Smith said: “We wouldn’t accept a surgeon operating after a drink or a driver getting behind the wheel – so why should we accept legislators voting on the laws of the land after one?“If we’re serious about being a professional workplace, we have to ask hard questions about practices like late night votes that sit alongside on-tap bars.”Beccy Cooper, who was a public health consultant before entering parliament as a Labour MP in 2024, said the report was a wake-up call. In a foreword to the report, she suggested that parliament should draw up its first formal workplace policy on alcohol.She added: “Two findings stood out to me. Almost one in 10 respondents reported a negative experience because of someone else’s drinking at work and 70% either didn’t know, or weren’t sure, how to raise a concern about a colleague’s drinking.“That combination – real, measurable harm and no clear route to address it – is exactly the kind of gap we need to address.”View image in fullscreenSome MPs said Westminster should rethink its attitude to alcohol and parts of the job such as late night votes that sit alongside bars on-site.Photograph: House of Commons/PAKatherine Severi, the IAS’s chief executive, said Westminster should limit the provision of free alcohol to evening events as part of a renewed drive to make it a more modern workplace, which many MPs and staff support. “Very few professions these days would allow free alcohol from midday, or regularly host outside organisations sponsoring events where drinking is the norm during working hours,” she added.The report also said that the commercialisation of parliament as an events venue contributed to MPs’ drinking.In 2023, parliament’s independent complaints and grievance scheme saidalcohol was a “frequent factor” in its investigationsinto alleged misconduct at Westminster. In its findings of 30 investigations it undertook between 2021 and 2022, it added that drinking in parliament’s array of bars was “leading to intimidating behaviour like shouting and swearing”.In July 2023, Daniel Greenberg, the parliamentary standards commissioner, said alcohol had led to “behaviour problems” at Westminster and suggested the sale of alcohol on the state be kept under review.A parliament spokesperson said everyone working there had been reminded to use alcohol responsibly, but hinted that immediate changes were unlikely. “Any changes to parliament’s provision of alcohol would ultimately be a matter for members to decide on. The estate is a unique working environment that includes public access and events,” they said.“Parliament’s behaviour code makes clear that everyone should be treated with respect at all times, and those who choose to drink alcohol on the estate must do so responsibly.”Westminster’s efforts to promote more responsible drinking include greater provision of no- and low-alcohol products and venue staff’s right to refuse to serve anyone who is, or looks likely to become, intoxicated.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsPoliticsAlcoholHouse of CommonsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Worst we’ve known’: UK turns to imports as drought and heat hit vegetable crops | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: Growers in dismay after scorching weather and lack of rain affect yields, sending wholesale prices rocketing
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Growers in dismay after scorching weather and lack of rain affect yields, sending wholesale prices rocketing
Content: Carrot grower Rodger Hobson says this year has ‘heartbreaking and wallet-breaking’.Photograph: suppliedView image in fullscreenCarrot grower Rodger Hobson says this year has ‘heartbreaking and wallet-breaking’.Photograph: suppliedFood & drink industry‘Worst we’ve known’: UK turns to imports as drought and heat hit vegetable cropsGrowers in dismay after scorching weather and lack of rain affect yields, sending wholesale prices rocketingSarah ButlerandJoanna PartridgeSat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePubs, restaurants and supermarkets are having to buy lettuce and broccoli from Spain at what should be the height of UK growing season, as drought and extreme heat hit crops.The wholesale price of tomatoes is up by more than 60%, iceberg lettuce by 90% and potatoes by more than 40% as a number of farmers struggle to grow in consistently high temperatures. Even those with irrigation systems and reservoirs on their farms say water is running low.Broccoli growers say their yield has halved. “We are having to put two heads of broccoli together to make the weight the pack is sold in,” said David Simmons from Riviera Produce. He grows a variety of vegetables on his family’s farm in Cornwall and is also on the board of the Brassica Growers’ Association, a trade body.View image in fullscreenDavid Simmons and his son Tom tend to one of their brassica crops in Cornwall. Simmons said their broccoli yields had halved.Photograph: Riviera Produce“The UK is very short [of broccoli] at the moment, so it’s being imported from Spain and Holland to try to cover the orders,” Simmons said. “Cauliflowers could go short in the next couple of weeks, we can see that being the next issue.”The English pea harvest is down by a third, according to Stephen Francis from Fen Peas, a group of 60 Lincolnshire farmers. Growers in Scotland, which accounts for about a fifth of UK pea production, are thought to be expecting an average harvest.Growers are looking at different varieties, such as those used in southern Europe and better suited to higher temperatures, said Francis, although farmers will also need help to invest in more water storage to help them cope in future.Meanwhile, thebosses of Britain’s biggest supermarketshave written to Andy Burnham to say wildfires and extreme weather pose a threat to Britain’s food security. More than 100 organisations – including Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Waitrose and Aldi, as well as food manufacturers and wholesalers – called on the government to make the food system a national priority and reduce reliance on food imports.View image in fullscreenDavid Simmons, left, said cauliflowers could be in short supply in the next couple of weeks.Photograph: Riviera ProduceA year of exceptionally hot and dry weather has also led to the earliest UK cereals harvest in at least 20 years, according to the Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board.Across Europe, crops ranging from wheat and potatoes to tomatoes and olives are being hit by drought, fires and extreme heat.Tim O’Malley, the chair of Nationwide Produce, a wholesaler that supplies restaurants and catering companies, said: “It is worse than the public realise. We are running out of water.”He added that field crops such as leafy green vegetables, broccoli and iceberg lettuce were the worst affected. From May, June and throughout the summer these are usually sourced from the UK. But “last week we did something very unusual and went back to Spain”, O’Malley said. “They have got hot weather but they are more used to farming in these conditions.”Production of tomatoes, most of which are imported from the Netherlands and Belgium to the UK at this time of year, is also starting to be hit by sustained high temperatures, which is resulting in smaller and damaged fruit.Rodger Hobson, a carrot grower in Yorkshire, said this year had been the “worst we’ve ever known”.“It’s heartbreaking and wallet-breaking,” he said, adding that crops were “wilting on their feet”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHobson usually produces about 30,000 tonnes of carrots annually, equivalent to approximately 4% of the UK crop. Britain produces almost all (97%) of the carrots it consumes, despite being only grown in few regions that have the sandy soils the root vegetable requires.“Any [temperature] over 25C and it goes into shutdown, anything over 30C and it pretty much starts to die. All we can do is keep pouring water on,” Hobson said.View image in fullscreenCarrot plants wilting on Rodger Hobson’s farm. He says his crop ‘pretty much starts to die’ at any temperatures over 30C.Photograph: Rodger HobsonThe main carrot crop, which would usually harvested from September onwards, will suffer this year unless there is significant rainfall soon. The situation means domestically produced carrots could run out a couple of months early in the spring, requiring imports to be found to make up for the shortfall.New potatoes grown in the UK are already on supermarket shelves, while main-crop potatoes will be harvested in September or October.“We are not expecting as much as we have had in recent years,” said Scott Walker, the chief executive of the industry body GB Potatoes. “Given Europe is having the same heatwave, that will also have a impact on the amount of crop there.”He added that consumers might have to get used to “more variation in sizes of potatoes” sold in supermarkets later this year.Growers are calling on the government to do more to help them build reservoirs, so they can store winter and spring rain for watering their crops in summer. Farmers, many of whom operate on very tight margins, if they manage to make a profit at all, say building water storage is costly and such projects often require planning permission, which can take a long time to be granted.Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryVegetablesFoodFarmingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ECB official warns climate crisis poses growing threat to ‘core financial stability’ | Economics | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: As wildfires rage across Europe, Frank Elderson tells the Guardian nature loss poses a growing risk to the global economy
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Exclusive: As wildfires rage across Europe, Frank Elderson tells the Guardian nature loss poses a growing risk to the global economy
Content: A man inspects damage to his property in an area scorched by a wildfire near Vila Vella, Spain.Photograph: Damian Torres/APView image in fullscreenA man inspects damage to his property in an area scorched by a wildfire near Vila Vella, Spain.Photograph: Damian Torres/APEconomicsECB official warns climate crisis poses growing threat to ‘core financial stability’Exclusive: As wildfires rage, Frank Elderson says more work needed to assess risk from collapse of ecosystem servicesRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentSat 1 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 11.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior policymaker at theEuropean Central Bankhas said the climate emergency and the breakdown of nature poses a dramatically growing risk to the global economy.Frank Elderson, a member of the ECB’s executive board, said the eurozone lender of last resort was stepping up its monitoring of the financial risks linked to the destruction of “ecosystem services”, which are nature-related processes or assets that support human activity.“These services are not stable but they are in rapid decline. That’s why we talk about the climate and nature crises,” he said. “So knowing that dependency, and knowing those exposures by the banks, we come to the conclusion that this is relevant.”Across France and Spain,wildfires have raged amid record-breaking temperatures, torching land, businesses and homes, in an emergency that will carry a heavy economic cost beside the direct human toll.In an interview with the Guardian before the current devastation acrossEurope, Elderson said it was clear the rising frequency of natural disasters linked to global heating posed a threat to financial stability.He said more work needed to be done to assess the risk from the collapse of ecosystem services, as reliance on nature was more complicated to map than the impact of a single extreme weather event.Ecosystem services are defined as any benefit that can be drawn from a natural structure or process – for example, water can be used as a raw material, an energy source through hydropower, or for transportation. It is also a habitat for marine life critical for food production, and a basis for recreational services.“Nature-related risks can pose material economic and financial risks, including through their impacts on credit risk, growth, inflation and – over the long-term – potential financial instability,” Elderson said.“I did interviews [previously] saying, you know, if you destroy nature, you destroy the core on which our economies depend. And that got people’s attention. This is not some kind of a flower-power, tree-hugging exercise. This is core economics. This is core financial stability, core price stability.”As the supervisor responsible for Europe’s largest banks, the ECB has launched a programme of work to assess how the escalating damage to ecosystem services could expose the financial system to risk.The central bank plans to publish analysis later this year investigating how “ecosystem degradation pathways” could translate into credit loss dynamics for the eurozone’s banks.A Dutch lawyer and central banker, Elderson was instrumental in the creation of theNetwork for Greening the Financial System(NGFS) in 2017, alongside Mark Carney and François Villeroy de Galhau, the then chiefs of the Bank of England and Banque de France. He served as founding chair of the group of 114 global central banks and financial supervisors pushing to develop climate risk management.The green agenda in financial services has faced pushback under the US presidency of Donald Trump, as some businesses battle to remain engaged in the fossil-fuel economy.Trump pulled the US out of the NGFS last year, leaving Europe to take the lead on climate-related risks without the involvement of the world’s most powerful economy.Elderson said the banking industry remained convinced that climate and nature-related risks had to be addressed.“I would think it’s very difficult to find a bank in Europe that will honestly tell you that they think this is not relevant,” he said. “I think that timehas passed.”Explore more on these topicsEconomicsGlobal economyEuropean Central BankClimate crisisWildfiresEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: Pity the poor limpets – must the summer holidays mean they get smashed by a child? | Coastlines | The Guardian
description: Lyme Regis, Dorset: Busy beaches can be bad news for shellfish. If curious children don’t know they are live creatures, then let’s educate them
Author: Sara Hudston
Headline: Lyme Regis, Dorset: Busy beaches can be bad news for shellfish. If curious children don’t know they are live creatures, then let’s educate them
Content: Limpets on East Cliff beach.Photograph: Sara HudstonView image in fullscreenLimpets on East Cliff beach.Photograph: Sara HudstonCountry diaryCoastlinesCountry diary: Pity the poor limpets – must the summer holidays mean they get smashed by a child?Lyme Regis, Dorset:Busy beaches can be bad news for shellfish. If curious children don’t know they are live creatures, then let’s educate themSara HudstonSat 1 Aug 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 00.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy favourite beach at Lyme Regis is the capricious East Cliff, visible only at low tide. The best way to reach it is down a 114-step walkway.The path drops through rough scrub, a feral mix of wild plants and garden escapes, sizzling with grasshoppers. Buddleia flourishes next to sallow bushes, hazel and gorse. Sour blackberries are already reddening among the brambles and somewhere in the tangle, a stonechat calls. The sound, like two dry pebbles clicked together, echoes the faint tap of fossil hammers audible from the beach below.You emerge on the sea wall, a wide, curving promenade edged with metal railings that gives the feel of being on the deck of a ship.
