Lyme Bay spreads before you, spangle-sparkling in the sun all the way to the Isle of Portland on the distant horizon.Immediately below the wall lies a tidal stretch of flat rock, thickly colonised by periwinkles, limpets and barnacles. It’s a lovely place for a paddle, and when I went there last week there were lots of families enjoying the gentle slosh of the turning tide.As I walked, I passed a small child banging away with her fossiling hammer. Her mother caught my eye and smiled. At the exact moment I was about to smile back, I realised that the child was not bashing a rock as I had supposed, but a large limpet. Before I could think, I said: “She’s hammering a limpet, which is a live creature.” “Oh,” said the mother, at a loss how to respond. The child continued to smash. I walked on.This was the second time in a few weeks I have seen kids killing limpets with the knowledge of nearby adults, who do nothing. The first occasion (ironically given the name of the place) was at Battery Rocks in Penzance, where a couple sat watching a boy eviscerating one of these molluscs. Noticing a stranger looming near, the man said to his partner: “Is that a vegan coming to protest?”Does this matter? I think so. As adults it’s up to us to guide kids’ natural curiosity so it becomes care for the living world.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsCoastlinesCountry diaryRural affairsMarine lifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Turn failing water firms into not-for-profit cooperatives, MPs and mayors tell PM | Water industry | The Guardian
description: Labour politicians say mutualised model puts public in control without adding debt to government’s balance sheet
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Labour politicians say mutualised model puts public in control without adding debt to government’s balance sheet
Content: A union flag floats downstream from a polluted tributary of the River Deben, near a storm overflow at Wickham Market, Suffolk.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenA union flag floats downstream from a polluted tributary of the River Deben, near a storm overflow at Wickham Market, Suffolk.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersWater industryTurn failing water firms into not-for-profit cooperatives, MPs and mayors tell PMLabour politicians say mutualised model puts public in control without adding debt to government’s balance sheetHelena HortonSat 1 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMPs and mayors close to Andy Burnham have told the prime minister there is a “third way” to gain more control of failing companies, as the row over whether or not to nationaliseThames Waterrumbles on.Burnham is said to be concerned about the increase in government debt that Treasury projections show could be a result of nationalising water companies.He has previouslycalled for “public control”of the companies, which have pumped sewage into England’s waterways while hiking bills and failing to invest in infrastructure.ButLabourMPs and regional mayors say a mutualised model, where water companies are transformed to not-for-profit entities run by local people, could remove the debt risk while allowing for public control.Their intervention comes with the release of a report published by the Good Growth Foundation on water cooperatives. Burnham has generally been supportiveof these kinds of models.The Labour MP Helena Dollimore said Burnham should “end the era of extraction” in the water industry, as she launched the plans for the mutualised model, with the support of Surfers Against Sewage, the mayor of West Yorkshire, Tracy Brabin, the mayor of South Yorkshire, Oliver Coppard, the mayor of York and North Yorkshire, David Skaith, and the Co-operative party general secretary, Joe Fortune.They say the model could be tested first with ThamesWater, which is close to financial collapse and in talks with the government over a potential rescue deal for its creditors. This deal would let the company off fines and environmental obligations. If it fails to be agreed, the company will be put under temporary government control, known as a special administration regime (SAR).According to the report’s recommendations, the rest of the sector would be “put on notice”, with every company facing tougher regulation, including enhanced monitoring, tighter restrictions on executive pay, and a ban on dividends unless a company meets performance targets.Any company that fails under these conditions would be forced into SAR and then into a cooperative model.View image in fullscreenThames Water is on the verge of financial collapse.Photograph: Chris Batson/AlamyMPs and mayors say Burnham should introduce a “bail-in” mechanism for the SAR, similar to the one used by the Bank of England for failing banks, so that shareholders and creditors bear the cost of failure rather than the taxpayer.Companies that come out of a SAR would be required to do so as not-for-profit cooperatives, rather than being sold to the highest bidder, which is the case at the moment.Coppard said: “Water is an essential utility that simply should not be farmed out to the private sector – that’s a lesson we’ve learned the hard way. A cooperative model would put control back in the hands of people, help keep bills as low as possible, and allow us to finally intervene in the inexorable dumping of sewage in our rivers.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWater bosses’ pay rises despite bonus ban and public fury over bills and pollutionRead moreThe prime minister is looking at options for how water could be brought under public control. Downing Street sourceshave saidthat there is no prospect of immediate nationalisation of Thames Water. Thecompany’s creditorshave also been gearing up to take the government to court if the deal fails.Brabin said: “The people of West Yorkshire have paid the price for Yorkshire Water’s failings for far too long, with repeated pollution failings and hiking bills repeatedly during a cost of living crisis. Greater public control of water companies is the only way to protect our communities and environment for future generations.”This plan would mean water company debts would not end up on the government’s balance sheet, and would give customers more control of how the businesses were run, the report’s authors said.Praful Nargund, the director of the Good Growth Foundation,said: “Mutualisation offers a different route … It delivers the public control and long-term investment we need without handing taxpayers the bill for decades of failure.”Dollimore, who is the MP for Hastings and Rye, said: “Our failing water infrastructure is a huge problem that must be a top priority for our Labour government. From pollution to outages to flooding, the people we represent experience the impact every day of this failure while paying more for the privilege.“We have already taken important steps to ramp up regulation but we must now go further to protect this vital national infrastructure, while always being fiscally responsible.”Explore more on these topicsWater industryAndy BurnhamThames WaterWaterLabourWater billsUtilitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Local media needs support if devolution push is to succeed, publishers say | Devolution | The Guardian
description: Shift from Westminster risks weakening scrutiny as regional titles battle hostility, big tech and ‘news deserts’
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Shift from Westminster risks weakening scrutiny as regional titles battle hostility, big tech and ‘news deserts’
Content: Andy Burnham with the mayor of South Yorkshire, Oliver Coppard, during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield on Friday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham with the mayor of South Yorkshire, Oliver Coppard, during a visit to a family centre in Sheffield on Friday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PADevolutionLocal media needs support if devolution push is to succeed, publishers sayShift from Westminster risks weakening scrutiny as regional titles battle hostility, big tech and ‘news deserts’Ben QuinnPolitical CorrespondentSat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGreater support for local media is needed to hold mayors and councils to account underAndy Burnham’s plans for devolution, which would involve a massive transfer of power into local government, publishers have said.A range of figures involved with local news broadly welcomed new plans unveiled by the prime minister, but said that monetising content, barriers erected by populist politicians and the roles of big tech and the BBC were among the challenges they faced.Theo Bamber, the chief executive of the News Media Association, the trade body representing UK national, regional and local news publishers, said that any moves to give people greater control would be an illusion unless the decisions affecting their lives could be scrutinised by trusted and professional local journalists.“We were interested that the government’s announcements about greater devolution have not mentioned press or media policy,” he said.“We believe that is a mistake because the two should not be siloed and, ultimately, the success of devolution is dependent on scrutiny.”Bamber said that 46 million people a month were consuming local media and that this was proof of the resilience of the sector. He also said it was a counter to the proliferation of misinformation amid unrest in Southampton and Belfast recently.However, as No 10 moved to devolve more power from Westminster to regions, there was also concern that these plans came as some journalists found their access to meetings was being limited, or were being sidelined as policymakers cut down on press conferences or chose to use social media instead.AReform UKcouncil leader’s decisionto ban his councillorsfrom engaging with a prominent local newspaper was condemned last year as a “massive attack on local democracy” and a sign of things to come should the party form the next government.There has also been unease that Keir Starmer’s administration appeared to embrace influencers, and that Burnham has been relatively slow to make himself available to face questions.The National Union of Journalists (NUJ) warned that a lack of a strong local news sector would threaten any devolution agenda and that support could not be left to the “vagaries of the market”.“Access to trusted local news is essential for democracy to thrive. However, millions across the UK now live in news deserts and the industry has faced decades of decline,” said Laura Davison, the NUJ general secretary, who noted large-scale job losses and the fact that about 300 local papers had closed since 2005.”John McDonnell, the veteran Labour MP and secretary of the NUJ’s parliamentary group, said: “If power is to be devolved on any scale then there is an even greater need for securing the role of local media to report on and hold local decision makers to account. This needs resourcing to make effective.”Under a scheme announced earlier this year, the government will provide up to £12m of funding over two years to support local news outlets as it tries to fill so-called “news deserts”. Local media outlets in print, online, radio or TV can bid for grants to support their financial sustainability and transition to digital business models under the new fund.However, there are calls for additional support, including from those involved in startups seeking to make up for the lack of an established news outlet in some areas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMike Harris, the publisher ofthe Lead,an independent progressive digital newspaper, said: “We’ve launched the first new local titles in many of the communities in the UK most at threat from the far right, but it’s unbelievably challenging making the business model work.“People in working-class communities do donate and subscribe to our local newspapers but it’s hard to make the model work in comparison with launching in wealthier cities with lots of middle-class professionals. The Local News Fund is a great start but with the spread of extremist online content, often seeded by foreign dictatorships or far-right grifters, we risk losing the battle for truth unless news, which is expensive to do well, is supported.”The Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it | EditorialRead moreThe plans by the Burnham government are seen as an opportunity by those with a record of working at the regional news coalface.Sarah Lester, the editor of the Manchester Evening News, said she hoped the devolution plans would also lead to a “devolution of media”.“The scale of devolution being proposed and the fact local money will be spent locally is something that is really good and of course must be scrutinised,” said Lester, whose publication is regarded as a role model for how local media has been able to adapt and prosper, with award winning investigations such as the one which led toAwaab’s Law, which requires social housing landlords in England to address serious health and safety hazards.“Of course not all areas will get as much media attention as Manchester. There is a need for scrutiny and that becomes even more important as decision making is devolved. My hope is that this will raise the profile of some of the challenges local and regional media face. While we appreciate what the government has done to date when it comes to initiatives such as the news fund, this falls short in dealing with issues such as the way in which local news is downgraded on big tech platforms. Ultimately, we don’t want hand outs. We want a level playing field.”Explore more on these topicsDevolutionRegional & local newspapersAndy BurnhamNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Ozempic to eye creams: demand for bathroom mini fridges is heating up | Skincare | The Guardian
description: Sales soar as consumers seek maximum convenience, though experts say most products don’t need to be kept cool
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Sales soar as consumers seek maximum convenience, though experts say most products don’t need to be kept cool
Content: Mini fridges are being installed in en suite bathrooms and walk-in wardrobes.Photograph: Liudmila Chernetska/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenMini fridges are being installed in en suite bathrooms and walk-in wardrobes.Photograph: Liudmila Chernetska/Getty Images/iStockphotoSkincareFrom Ozempic to eye creams: demand for bathroom mini fridges is heating upSales soar as consumers seek maximum convenience, though experts say most products don’t need to be kept coolChloe Mac DonnellSat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 05.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen it comes to essential fixtures and fittings for bathrooms, the most common are tubs and taps. But now there is a new must-have emerging: a mini fridge.Used to store everything from beauty products to GLP-1 medication, the growing demand reflects a wider trend in how the wellness industry andweight-loss drugsare reshaping homes.Emma Lewis, the marketing manager for Sub-Zero & Wolf, a luxury cooling appliance manufacturer in Essex, said the company had seen a tenfold increase in demand for mini fridges over the past two years.Clients have requested they be installed everywhere from en suites to walk-in wardrobes to home offices.Lewis described mini fridges as “beverage centres”, noting they were originally used to chill drinks in at-home bars and gyms. But she said nowadays they were more likely to house face creams, jars of supplements, gut health shots and injectables.“It is more convenient to have products to hand in say a bathroom rather than having to walk to a kitchen fridge,” Lewis said. “That sense of ease is really what people want.”At Sub-Zero & Wolf, prices start from a whopping £5,000, but the trend is not limited to high-end spenders. On the secondhand retail site Gumtree, where the average mini fridge costs £45, searches rose by 85% from January to June.Smeg sells a 38-litre compact version of its trademark retro style for £899, while online marketplaces are peppered with colourful versions and even mirrored options for less than £30.View image in fullscreenSmeg’s mini fridge.Photograph: SmegGumtree’s chief executive, Nav Dhillon, says mini fridges were “moving beyond student halls and hotel rooms to become a lifestyle purchase” with warmer weather further driving demand.However, Dr Ariel Haus, a dermatologist and the founder of the London-based clinic Dr Haus Dermatology, said the amount ofskincareproducts that require refrigeration was limited.“A mini fridge is a nice-to-have for a handful of actives, and a gimmick for almost everything else,” he said.He said vitamin C serums and retinoids – vitamin A derivatives including retinol and tretinoin – were examples of products that should be refrigerated.“Active forms of vitamin C, like L-ascorbic acid, are highly unstable and oxidise quickly when exposed to heat, light and air,” he said. “Once a vitamin C serum oxidises, it turns yellow or brown and loses potency, so keeping it cool genuinely extends shelf life.”Skincare staple or expensive gimmick: do you really need an LED face mask?Read moreRetinoids behaved similarly, Haus said, degrading faster in warm conditionsWhen it comes to weight-loss drugs, storage depends on the type. Online NHS guidelines advise that semaglutides that come in injection form, including Ozempic, and tirzepatides should be stored in a fridge between 2-8C before their first use. After that they can be stored at room temperature below 30C.As for the need for “supplement fridges”, some probiotics and liquid omega 3s require chilling but if so it should be stated clearly on the packaging.According to the Global Wellness Institute, the UK’s wellness industry is worth more than £160bn. Last year, theBritish Beauty Council’s value of beauty reportfound that for the first time, Britons were spending more on beauty than on attending football matches and going to the gym combined. Homes have begun to mirror these findings with at-home saunas, sleep trackers, LED face masks and now mini fridges becoming regular rather than rare fixtures.Some like to fridge-flex with standalone styles. Other fridges are built into undercounter units and bathroom vanities or concealed behind panelling. Lewis said “very subtle” refrigerated drawers were also popular among clients.However, it is not a trend that will easily work for your typical three-piece bathroom. Under UK electrical regulations, plug sockets must be placed at least 3 metres away from a source of water such as a bath. Only sockets with residual current device protection – a safety switch which protects people from electric shocks – are allowed and must be installed by a qualified electrician.A fridge no matter the size also requires space around it to cool and minimise fire risk. As a result, Lewis said fridges were not advisable for “wet room”, but were more suited to much larger bathrooms or dressing rooms.As for what need not go in the fridge, Haus said eye creams and sheet masks were regularly misunderstood. “A chilled eye cream will temporarily constrict blood vessels and reduce puffiness. That’s a real effect, but it’s cosmetic and short-lived,” he said.Sheet face masks were “single-use, sealed, and typically formulated with stable ingredients designed to sit on shop shelves at room temperature for months,” Haus said. “Chilling one doesn’t improve what’s in the serum, it just makes it feel nice on the skin for 30 seconds, which is sensation, not skincare.”Explore more on these topicsSkincareBeautynewsShareReuse this content

title: EU relations, climate crisis and Gaza: why Ed Miliband is fired up by Foreign Office challenges | Ed Miliband | The Guardian
description: Labour veteran is said to relish role that requires careful negotiation of Trump and impending G20 leadership
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Labour veteran is said to relish role that requires careful negotiation of Trump and impending G20 leadership
Content: Ed Miliband was appointed to the Foreign Office in Andy Burnham’s first cabinet as PM last month.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreenEd Miliband was appointed to the Foreign Office in Andy Burnham’s first cabinet as PM last month.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersEd MilibandAnalysisEU relations, climate crisis and Gaza: why Ed Miliband is fired up by Foreign Office challengesPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorLabour veteran is said to relish role that requires careful negotiation of Trump and impending G20 leadershipSat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTShareExtraordinarily, given the importance of geopolitics, the office of foreign secretary has sometimes appeared a consolation prize in British politics, perhaps reflecting the transfer of responsibility to Downing Street or the Cabinet Office.That is not howEd Milibandviews the job. His allies say suggestions that he nurses resentment after he was deprived of the chance to be chancellor misunderstand his grasp of the policy challenges ahead. “Ed has an immense appetite to get things done and is relishing being in this job,” one says. “Ed will be a policy-driven foreign secretary.”To that end, he is preparing a distinct agenda on relations with the EU over the next decade, Britain’s chairing of theG20next year and the climate crisis. Miliband is also determined to contribute to some of the big debates about shaping the international order of the future – debates that may take him into difficult territory given the volatility of the US alliance.Palestine may take longer to address, partly owing to the Israeli elections and the sudden glimmer of progress overHamas disarmament, but his instincts are clear. In 2014, as Labour leader, he urged his MPs to vote to recognise Palestine.View image in fullscreenThe UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, speaks with his French counterpart, Jean-Noël Barrot, during a visit to the Quai d’Orsay in Paris last week.Photograph: Leon Neal/ReutersAcutely conscious that he is the tenth foreign secretary since William Hague stood aside in 2014, Miliband also arrives without a Foreign Office permanent secretary after thesacking of Olly Robbins, and with some staff on a rolling strike over the large job cuts that Robbins had announced he would impose.But Miliband, working with the newEuropeminister based in the Foreign Office, Hamish Falconer, intends to be closely involved in talks on the UK’s relations with the EU since he regards a successful solution to that relationship as the single biggest question facing the UK. His personal involvement will give the Foreign Office greater influence in the Europe debate than under Keir Starmer’s leadership, when the Cabinet Office was the sole proprietors of negotiations with the EU.Miliband represents a Eurosceptic constituency and remains bound by Labour’s manifesto red lines not to enter the single market or customs union in this parliament. But that does not prevent him from seeking to influence Andy Burnham’s longer-term thinking about where the UK’s relationship with the EU should be in 10 or 15 years. Burnham, Miliband’s aides argue, has shown an openness to ideas on social care and the same openness may apply to issues such as European defence.“Having a closer relationship with Europe is a key foreign policy priority to protect our national security and grow our economy,” an ally said. “Ed will be working in lockstep with No 10 and Hamish Falconer to make this happen. He sees Europe as at the heart of this agenda.”View image in fullscreenHamish Falconer was made minister for intergovernmental relationsandEuropean relations by Andy Burnham.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersFriends also said Miliband wants to find a way to revive the ailing G20, a largely economic multilateral body that has been steadily declining in influence since 2008, when the UKplayed a major role coordinating the response to the financial crashduring Gordon Brown’s premiership.In the latter days of his own tenure at No 10, Starmer appointed Brown to act as his special envoy on global finance and cooperation in advance of the G20, and Brown will retain the role, working alongside Miliband who was one of his advisers while chancellor. Lord Wood, who acted as a foreign policy adviser during the Brown premiership, has also been appointed to the Foreign Office as a minister in the Lords, and will bring experience and intellect to the role.With the UK due to chair the postponed illicit finance summit in December in advance of taking over the G20, ideas such as a global wealth tax and greater transparency in overseas financial holdings areall being promoted. But the secrecy of Britain’s overseas territories has for a decade been a millstone in the UK’s call to combat corruption.Kirsty McNeill, the new international development minister and a former executive director at Save the Children, has been asked to wrestle with the impact of massive aid cuts. She has previously said the UK will not regain credibility on aid unless it sets out a path for returning aid spending to 0.7% of GDP. Aidwill fall to 0.3% next yearandBurnham’s £2 bus fare capis being funded by a raid on the aid budget. The G20 at least provides a creative way for her to build alliances to tackle unjust debts and illicit financial flows.Aglobal wealth tax was proposedduring the Brazilian presidency of the G20 in 2024 after a study commissioned from the French economist Gabriel Zucman. “There is overwhelming public support for this idea,” Zucman said at the report’s launch. “Ten years ago, nobody believed 130 countries would support a minimum tax on multinationals. It was thought of as utopian.”The report said billionaires were paying an average of 0.3% tax on their wealth – less than the rates paid by workers. Zucman said the average wealth of the top 0.0001% of individuals had grown by 7.1% a year on average between 1987 and 2024, increasing the share of global wealth held by billionaires from 3% to 14%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion26:57Why it is so hard to tax the super-rich – videoTrump’s own G20 summit is due in Miami in December, by which time he could be diminished by a reverse in the midterm congressional elections. There has been a slow drop-off in world leaders attending the G20 partly owing to geopolitical rifts overUkraineand questions over its value, but by next year the economic fallout from the war in Iran may require economic and political coordination.Miliband is not, meanwhile, expected to act quickly on Burnham’s admission thatLabourneeded to “do better” on Gaza. Burnham suggested action on trade with illegal Israeli settlements was on his agenda, but Foreign Office diplomats have questioned the enforceability of such a ban.A debate is under way as to whether European states would best help the political parties opposed to the Israeli prime minister in the October elections by imposing fresh sanctions, underlining Benjamin Netanyahu’s diplomatic isolation, or whether he would use international disapproval to his domestic advantage.From Ukraine and Sudan to Gaza: why have hospitals become a target of war?Read moreThe pressure from the Labour backbenches for a more robust policy that treats international law with the same seriousness in the Middle East as the UK does in Ukraine is intense. A letter from 80 parliamentarians coordinated by the MP Kim Johnson called on Burnham to impose comprehensive sanctions on Israel and recognise the findings of the UN commission of inquiry thatIsrael is committing genocide. Burnham has said it is for the international courts to make such determinations.But a consequential question will be how Miliband retains his progressive credibility and yet remains on good terms with the US state department under Trump. Wood, a sceptic about past UK foreign military interventions, strongly opposed the US military attack on Iran.But the need to retain a modicum of US support for Ukraine has, ever since Trump’s election, been seen as an essential UK foreign policy priority, one that has required compromises and often involved working with the recently deceased Republican senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine. That is unlikely to change in the short term.Explore more on these topicsEd MilibandForeign, Commonwealth and Development OfficeUkraineEuropeDonald TrumpAndy BurnhamBenjamin NetanyahuanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv missile attack kills at least 10 as Zelenskyy seeks attack role for Starlink | Russia | The Guardian
description: Donald Trump retreats further from commitment to let Ukraine manufacture its own Patriot missiles. What we know on day 1,620
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Donald Trump retreats further from commitment to let Ukraine manufacture its own Patriot missiles. What we know on day 1,620
Content: Firefighters in Kyiv put out a blaze at an apartment building hit by a Russian missile strike early on Saturday.Photograph: Gleb Garanich/ReutersView image in fullscreenFirefighters in Kyiv put out a blaze at an apartment building hit by a Russian missile strike early on Saturday.Photograph: Gleb Garanich/ReutersRussia-Ukraine war at a glanceRussiaExplainerUkraine war briefing: Kyiv missile attack kills at least 10 as Zelenskyy seeks attack role for StarlinkDonald Trump retreats further from commitment to let Ukraine manufacture its own Patriot missiles. What we know on day 1,620Guardian staff and agenciesFri 31 Jul 2026 23.55 EDTFirst published on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKyiv was once again under attack by ballistic missiles early on Saturdaywith at least 10 people killed, according to Reuters. “Fires and destruction occurred in five districts of the capital,” the state emergency service posted. Twenty-two people were reportedly also injured in the attack. It came asDonald Trump retreated further from a promiseto letUkrainemanufacture its ownPatriot air defence interceptors, which it desperately needs to shoot down Russian missiles. More than a ‌dozenexplosions reverberated through Kyiv, and residents were warned to stay in shelters.In Kyiv’s Darnytsky district, the attacks damaged multiple buildings and vehicles, with authorities reportingseven people killed and 14 woundedin the area.Two people were killed and eight others were woundedin Solomiansky district, where strikes damaged a five-storey residential building. “Everything was smashed, the windows, everything,” 75-year-old resident Kateryna Kravchenko told AFP of her apartment. “I can barely stand. I don’t know how I’m going to get through all this.” The emergency service said on Saturday morning that105 people in Kyiv had been rescuedfrom impacted areas.Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday urged Trump and other US officials to help Ukraine gain permission from Elon Musk touse satellite internet service Starlink for guiding strikes inside Russia. Zelenskyy made the request directly to Trump during an Oval Office meeting this week, according to one person familiar with the matter. He also reportedly told lawmakers later on Capitol Hill that he wanted Starlink’s help. Trump did not commit to Zelenskyy’s request. Musk allows Starlink use within Ukraine, including Russian-occupied areas, but restricts it inside Russia.During acabinet meetingat Camp David, Trump told reporters that handing over the underlying Patriot technology was “a hard thing” to do. Ukraine’s Zelensky had met Trump earlier this week and said Trump had agreed to license the production of Patriot missiles to Ukraine. Asked whether he was ready to grant Kyiv a licence to build Patriots domestically –something he had suggestedat a Nato summit in Turkey just this month – Trump said: “We have not agreed to that. We’re talking about it, but it’s a hard thing to give away that kind of technology.” Giving away the weapons carried its own risks, he added: “People that you give that technology [to], they can some day turn on you. You know that is possible.”Several thousand Ukrainians rallied in central Kyiv on Friday, angry about Zelenskyy’s decision to ⁠oust the defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov.Fedorov is ​widely credited with driving military innovation during Ukraine’s war with Russia. But having taken charge of the wartime ministry in January, he was dismissed in a surprise government reshuffle ⁠in mid-July. Since then, Ukrainians have been gathering next to the presidential office, pushing for Fedorov to be reinstated as he refused to accept another government post.Russia’s main grain lobby group warned on Friday that Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian ships and ports could shut down grain exports via the Black Sea,pushing up ⁠prices and causing hunger in ⁠Africa and the Middle East. Russia, the ​world’s largest wheat exporter, and Ukraine, also a large agricultural exporter, have been attacking each other’s facilities and vessels in the Black Sea area in recent weeks, driving wheat prices higher. The disruption to shipping in the Black Sea ⁠caused by Ukrainian attacks “poses a direct threat to global food security”, Russia’s Union of Grain Exporters and Producers told Reuters.Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian online retailer Wildberriesamount to “acts ⁠of terrorism” against civilians, affecting millions of people in Russia and other countries, the company’s founder ⁠and CEO, Tatyana ⁠Kim, ​complained on Friday. Ukraine has attacked more than a dozen Wildberries sites since 18 July in ⁠a bid to disrupt the operations of the company, avendor to the Russian war effortand linchpin of Russia’s consumer economy.Explore more on these topicsRussiaRussia-Ukraine war at a glanceUkraineEuropeDonald TrumpexplainersShareReuse this content

title: D4vd hearing details high hopes and brutal end of girl at heart of murder case | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: Texts reveal that singer and Celeste Rivas Hernandez had been in touch stretching back to when she was 11 years old
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Texts reveal that singer and Celeste Rivas Hernandez had been in touch stretching back to when she was 11 years old
Content: A makeshift memorial for Celeste Rivas Hernandez outside her home in Lake Elsinore, California, on 21 April 2026.Photograph: Damian Dovarganes/APView image in fullscreenA makeshift memorial for Celeste Rivas Hernandez outside her home in Lake Elsinore, California, on 21 April 2026.Photograph: Damian Dovarganes/APLos AngelesD4vd hearing details high hopes and brutal end of girl at heart of murder caseTexts reveal that singer and Celeste Rivas Hernandez had been in touch stretching back to when she was 11 years oldUwa Ede-Osifoin Los AngelesSat 1 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rising pop singerD4vdand 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez were in the throes of a clandestine relationship months before her mangled and decomposing bodyturnedup last September stuffed in an impounded car registered to the musician.D4vd, born David Anthony Burke, is set tostand trialfor murder, child sexual abuse and mutilation of human remains in connection to the teenager’s death.Los Angeles county prosecutors accuse Burke of stabbing Celeste to death and subsequently severing her limbs as he sought to prevent her from revealing their sexual relationship, which began when he was 18 and she was 13 in November 2023.Singer D4vd had impregnated teenager he is accused of fatally stabbingRead moreBurke has pleaded not guilty to the charges.The ghastly discovery of Celeste’s remains sent social media sleuths, particularly those in corners of Discord where Burke had carved a niche as an online gamer before pivoting to music, racing through the singer’s past videos and content for any clues concerning his ties to Celeste.The clearest picture yet of a rocky, off-on relationship emerged during a recent preliminary evidentiary hearing, where prosecutors presented text messages that the two exchanged stretchingback to 2022, when Celeste was 11.At times, Burke regaled the girl with dreams of an idyllic future: her moving into his home, getting married in Italy and having children together.The fact that she was a minor and had been reported missing by her family, however, cast a shadow over those plans.“i can’t wait to move in tg without the cops bitching baby,” Burke allegedly wrote in June 2024 to her, Courthouse Newsreported. Months prior, in February, police officers visited him at a residence in West Hollywood after finding his number in the teenager’s phone log as they sought her whereabouts. When police informed Burke of her age, he shared she told him she was 18.Texts indicate that he wanted the sexual nature of their relationship to be a secret. She had asked him in July 2024 if anyone knew they had intercourse. “Nope and I would like to keep it that way before we get married,” Burke replied.Their relationship hit a few rough patches. The teenager expressed a desire for a more serious connection. “All we do is have sex and just hang out man i want more than that for myself,” shereportedlysaid.In January 2024, after Celeste had become pregnant with Burke’s child, she had an abortion, which she later regretted. “I don’t like talking about it because it gets me really upset, but I’d do anything to have it back,” shereportedlywrote to Burke in August 2024.“Let’s end that there,” hereplied. “I don’t like talking to u when you’re upset,” adding later that while the abortion “saddened” him, he did not “dwell on it”.The night before prosecutors say Burke killed Celeste in April 2025, they had a heated argument over text about his relationship with another woman. The teenager allegedly threatened to end his career.Prosecutors had also presented evidence of Burke having a cushy recording label deal, which they suggested gave him motive to allegedly silence Celeste.“What was presented by our office over the course of the last week is a small but illustrative fraction of the evidence investigators have accumulated that proves defendant Burke is guilty beyond a reasonable doubt of the brutal murder of Celeste Rivas Hernandez,” the Los Angeles county district attorney, Nathan J Hochman, said in a statement. “This has been a parent’s worst nightmare, hearing the ghoulish details of how their child was killed, dismembered and left as trash.”It remains unclear what strategy Burke’s attorneys will employ at trial. They did not reply to a request for comment on the case proceeding forward.During the preliminary hearing, the defense team cast doubt on a medical examiner ruling Celeste’s death to be a homicide.Defense attorney Marilyn Bednarski asked Grant Ho, a doctor who performed Celeste’s autopsy, if his report could rule out that the teenager could have been holding an instrument that caused her stab wounds.Ho said he could not, but that the teenager’s autopsy did not indicate self-harm.Prosecutors presented forensic testing that found blood probably originating from Celeste in Burke’s former residence.A second defense attorney, Blair Berk, questioned a Los Angeles police criminalist about why other items in the house were not tested for DNA, noting that multiple people lived in the home.Burke, who remains in custody without bail, will be arraigned in court on 31 August. His trial date has not been announced.Hochman said in a Thursday appearance on NewsNation he will confer with Celeste’s family as well as Burke’s lawyers before deciding whether to pursue the death penalty.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsLos AngelesUS crimeCaliforniaWest CoastfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin Wall | Germany | The Guardian
description: Supporters fear structure could be torn down as safety hazard and want it to become memorial to postwar foreign labourers in honour of its Turkish creator
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Supporters fear structure could be torn down as safety hazard and want it to become memorial to postwar foreign labourers in honour of its Turkish creator
Content: ‘Perhaps he wasn’t the perfect artist, but he created something artistic,’ one supporter said of Osman Kalin’s treehouse.Photograph: Gordon Welters/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Perhaps he wasn’t the perfect artist, but he created something artistic,’ one supporter said of Osman Kalin’s treehouse.Photograph: Gordon Welters/The GuardianGermany‘A symbol of resistance’: the fight to save treehouse built on no man’s land next to Berlin WallSupporters fear structure could be torn down as safety hazard and want it to become memorial to postwar foreign labourers in honour of its Turkish creatorDeborah Colein BerlinSat 1 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 05.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes the currents of history converge in a single spot. In Berlin, one of the most intriguing of those places is a small traffic island with a lovingly tended garden and a ramshackle two-storey structure called the Treehouse at the Wall.In 1983, Osman Kalin, a Turkish “guest worker”, was looking in his corner of the city cleaved by theBerlin Wallfor a patch of earth in which to plant his onions, garlic and cucumbers. Virtually on his doorstep in the Kreuzberg district was a slice of no man’s land next to the concrete barrier and barbed wire. Although it sat in West Berlin, cold war logic meant the lot officially belonged to the communist East.The east-west border cut a sharp angle near a curved street called Bethaniendamm. The wall was built to slice straight across the road, which left a triangle-shaped scrap of land on the wrong side. Neither side could use it and so nearby residents commandeered it as a dump – until Kalin came along.View image in fullscreenOsman Kalin at the treehouse in 2016.Photograph: Eden Breitz/AlamyPerhaps it took an outsider such as Kalin to see the potential in the postage stamp of fertile soil beneath the orphaned furniture and discarded drug paraphernalia. And it required a certain audacity to build something abutting the wall patrolled by East German soldiers withshoot-to-kill orders.Over the decades, the “guerrilla garden” came to symbolise a rebel spirit in dark times, the ingenuity of immigrants who were often made to feel unwelcome, and the tragedy and absurdity of great-power confrontation in a city where citizens on both sides just wanted to breathe free.That’s a lot of mythology for one place to hold, and four decades of upheaval have left their mark. Now supporters of the Treehouse at the Wall fear it could be demolished by city authorities as a public safety hazard and are rallying to save it.Kalin, one of the first generation of so-calledGastarbeiterbrought by WestGermanyto plug a labour shortage, was “a remarkable figure”, said Suat Özkan, the general secretary of a Turkish community group in Berlin. “Perhaps he wasn’t a master of language, perhaps he wasn’t the perfect architect, perhaps he wasn’t the perfect artist, but he created something artistic – something that became totally unique.”View image in fullscreenPictures inside the treehouse show Kalin and his son Mehmet.Photograph: Gordon Welters/The GuardianKalin, who was born in 1925 in Anatolia, arrived in West Germany in the late 1960s as a manual labourer. Under the programme, about 14 million guest workers came to the country between 1955 and 1973. Despite the temporary nature of the scheme, many stayed on. Nearly 3 million people of Turkish origin now live in Germany, about 200,000 of them in Berlin.Kalin at first squatted the land with his flower and vegetable garden and a small improvised shed. Then, eventually, against the odds, he won permission from the East German authorities to stay, so long as whatever he built there would not be taller than the wall.In time he replaced the shed with the larger “treehouse”, which despite the name is not up in the branches but built around a mature trunk that was on the site.After the city reunited in 1990, Kalin faced eviction orders but found an unlikely ally in the neighbouring St Thomas church, which located 18th-century papers showing it was the rightful owner of the land and allowed him to stay.Since Kalin’s death as a local hero in 2018, his son Mehmet has tended to the property and his father’s legacy.“Right when two global political systems were facing off,” Özkan said, Osman Kalin carried out an “act of defiance against the GDR regime, against the system, to show that it is possible to stand up and carry out a kind of revolution”.He added: “It’s a symbol of resistance as well as a symbol against racism, discrimination and hostility.”View image in fullscreenTongue-in-cheek Nato and Soviet flags whip from erected poles outside the treehouse.Photograph: Gordon Welters/The GuardianÖzkan said that more than six decades after West Germany established the guest worker programme, it was long past time for the reunited nation to pay tribute to its waves of immigrants.“We still haven’t managed to construct a central memorial,” he said, to the foreign labourers who helped build the postwareconomic miracle. “This house should serve as a kind of memorial.”Stefan Zeppenfeld, a historian who publisheda book in 2021about Turkish labourers in West Berlin during the cold war, said it took decades for Germany to acknowledge its transformation into a “country of immigration”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe noted that migrant labourers like Kalin were relegated to neighbourhoods close to the wall, such as Kreuzberg, that became prime real estate after the wall’s fall in 1989.Zeppenfeld said the treehouse crystallised many aspects of what made up Berlin and its people. “The history of German division or theiron curtainis still absolutely crucial and defining for Berlin, for Berlin’s sense of identity,” he said. “And I find it absolutely fascinating that this building is still standing – it’s one of the few tangible legacies where we can actually see agency by Turkish guest workers as a real part of the cityscape.”View image in fullscreenSuat Özkan: ‘This house should serve as a kind of memorial.’Photograph: Gordon Welters/The GuardianAs a first step, Özkan is planning an open-air exhibition on the chain-link fence surrounding the structure, complete with archival pictures and Kalin’s extraordinary life story.The tension with city authorities ahead of aBerlin election in Septemberis that supporters of the treehouse want to maintain its scruffy authenticity while safety and legal concerns have forced a conversation about its structural integrity.Outside, the wooden facade is made up of listing, mismatched planks. Tongue-in-cheek Nato and Soviet flags whip from erected poles while plum and apple trees mark the seasons. Inside, a jumble of black-and-white photographs and construction tools point to the Kalin family’s past and future in their garden idyll. A donated chandelier lends an unexpected touch of elegance.Florian Schmidt, a Kreuzberg district councillor, said his office was working closely with the Turkish community and Kalin’s son Mehmet, who has done extensive repairs on the house, to “grant the necessary permits” for it to remain.“Due to the unusual situation – the site being a no man’s land and the lack of planning permission – use of the treehouse was initially prohibited,” Schmidt said in an emailed statement, noting that Mehmet had been granted a temporary exemption to do work there. “Issues relating to ownership rights are also being clarified.”View image in fullscreenOfficials are working to ‘grant the necessary permits’ for the structure to remain.Photograph: Gordon Welters/The GuardianAdrian Sampson, of Alternative Berlin Tours, which spotlights the city’s subculture and street art, was leading a group of visitors past the treehouse on a hot July day as he explained Kalin’s legacy.“His story is about three things: resistance, community spirit and multiculture all together there. And that’s what Kreuzberg is about,” said Sampson, who is originally from Melbourne.Asked about speculation that the site’s days could be numbered, he said: “I think it’d be an absolute shame, like really a pity for the city, because it just makes a lot of people happy.”Explore more on these topicsGermanyBerlin WallEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: New York City’s Flatiron building enters new era with $58.5m apartments | New York | The Guardian
description: Manhattan’s triangular building will open this fall to wealthy residents, with 36 apartments exposing Flatiron’s ‘steel skeleton’
Author: Adam Gabbatt
Headline: Manhattan’s triangular building will open this fall to wealthy residents, with 36 apartments exposing Flatiron’s ‘steel skeleton’
Content: The Flatiron building in New YorkPhotograph: Adrian GautView image in fullscreenThe Flatiron building in New YorkPhotograph: Adrian GautNew YorkNew York City’s Flatiron building enters new era with $58.5m apartmentsManhattan’s triangular building will open this fall to wealthy residents, with 36 apartments exposing Flatiron’s ‘steel skeleton’Adam Gabbattin New YorkSat 1 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNew YorkCity’s Flatiron building has had many lives: as a structure seen as a deathtrap; as a nuisance which created a deadly, petticoat-lifting, wind current and, mainly, as a commercial space.Now, the triangular building, a favorite of tourists and locals alike, is entering a new era: as a residential building, where apartments cost up to $58.5m.Completed in 1902, the Flatiron was once derided as a folly, but the Beaux-Arts building is now one of New York’s most admired buildings. Named Flatiron for its resemblance, from above, to a clothes iron, the building’s ornamental brick and terracotta exterior has been hidden behind scaffolding for the best part of seven years.Now, the reimagined Flatiron will open to very wealthy residents later this fall. There are 36 apartments in the building, including some which span entire floors: there’s a double-height lobby, too, a pool, and a games room which will apparently have a billiards table.But for all the shared amenities, the real allure will be the apartments themselves. They have been styled by a venerated New York design firm, which stripped back the interior, exposing some of the Flatiron’s interior “steel skeleton”, the building’s interior steel frame which was cutting edge technology at the time.Images shared with the Guardian show one of the four bedroom, four bathroom apartments in the Flatiron, which features a curved sofa in what the press materials describe as the building’s “prow” – the sharpest angle of the structure. Photos show that there has been a generous application of marble in the bathroom, and equally liberal use of brushed steel in the kitchen.View image in fullscreenA residential room in the Flatiron building.Photograph: Adrian GautAccording to the realtor Corcoran’s website, 14 of the apartments in the Flatiron are already in contract. The cheapest, on the third floor, appears to have been bought for $10,950,000: the buyer will get a three bedroom, three bathroom apartment with anot-largeopen plan kitchen and “great room”. There are also two dressing rooms.The flagship apartment, however, is the one which occupies the entirety of the top floor. In contract for $58.5m,the floorplanof the five bedroom, five bathroom apartment depicts a sauna, two dressing rooms, a dining roomanda breakfast room, and a 72ft “great room”. It is unclear who has bid on the apartment.“There’s always hesitation taking on a landmark building like this. But there’s also an advantage. It has an incredibly special character that makes it worth the pain,” Daniel Brodsky, the managing partner of the Brodsky Organization, which owns the building, told theFinancial Timesin an interview.Brodsky told the Times that Jeff Bezos, the billionaire Amazon founder, had spent more than $100m buying several properties three blocks north of the Flatiron.“There’s a group of wealthy people who want to be in a convenient place; good transportation, the best restaurants in the city, the park … it’s a very easy place to live. You’re surrounded by coolness,” Brodsky said, in what was possibly the first time Bezos’ name has been associated with the term “coolness”.The Flatiron was designed by Daniel Burnham, arguably the hottest architect of its age, and was initially called the Fuller Building. That failed to take off, and ‘Flatiron’ stuck, although pedants might point out that the floorplan of the building is actually a scalene triangle, whereas an actual flatiron would typically be an isosceles.One of New York’s tallest buildings when it was completed, the Flatiron’s terra-cotta and limestone façade, featuring lion heads and eagles, has been renovated for the reopening, with a specialist employed, the BBC reported, to replicate and restore “thousands of terra-cotta pieces from the facade, reinstalling each by hand”.While the Flatiron might be fondly regarded now, it wasn’t universally popular on its completion, amid fears that the building was so narrow it could fall over. It also didn’t help people warm to the building when it emerged that the design had inadvertently created a “Flatiron breeze” – a powerful, localised wind caused by the building’s shape. According to the author Alice Alexiou, the breeze “blew total strangers into each other’s arms, causing much embarrassment”, and in a tragic incident, blew a 14-year-old messenger boy called John McTaggert into middle of Fifth Avenue, where he was run over by a car and later died.“It was long common knowledge that if you walked by the Flatiron on a windy day, at the very least your skirts were going to end up over your head, and your legs exposed. It was now all the rage for groups of men of a certain character to loiter at the foot of the Flatiron, expressly to catch a glimpse of feminine flesh,” Alexiou wrote inThe Flatiron: The New York Landmark and the Incomparable City That Arose with It.Despite the chaos it was causing at street level, the Flatiron defied predictions that it would topple over. “During a 60-mile-an-hour windstorm that battered the city one morning soon after the first tenants moved in, you couldn’t feel the slightest vibration in the building,” Alexiou wrote.It was built to last, in other words, and this latest iteration will continue its legacy – even if its price means it is far beyond the reach of the majority of New Yorkers.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: China’s tech advances are causing chaos from Silicon Valley to the White House | Technology | The Guardian
description: New AI models, advanced robots and specialty computer chips are unsettling markets and the US tech industry.
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: New AI models, advanced robots and specialty computer chips are unsettling markets and the US tech industry.
Content: The Moonshot AI stand at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai in July.Photograph: Héctor Retamal/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Moonshot AI stand at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai in July.Photograph: Héctor Retamal/AFP/Getty ImagesTechnologyChina’s tech advances are causing chaos from Silicon Valley to the White HouseNew AI models, advanced robots and specialty computer chips are unsettling markets and the US tech industryNick Robins-EarlySat 1 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the past month, a series of advancements in China’s artificial intelligence, chip manufacturing and robotics technologies have rattled financial markets, caused divisions among US tech moguls and left theTrump administrationscrambling to respond.Silicon Valley has long pointed to China’s tech industry as a competitive threat and used its growth as rationale for why US firms should not face regulatory oversight that could slow them down. In recent weeks, however, China’s progress has pushed US tech CEOs past vague warnings and into open disagreement over how to address Chinese-made products upending their industry.The most immediate threat to Silicon Valley’s status quo has come from a series of Chinese-made open-source, open-weight AI models that are free to download and use. The models, such as Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, are powerful enough to compete in some applications with proprietary and comparatively expensive AI products from OpenAI and Anthropic.The emergence of China’s open-source AI alternatives has caused divisions in both the White House and US tech industry over whether to oppose or embrace these new models. On one side are chip manufacturers who see revenue opportunities from increased AI usage and tech companies concerned about OpenAI and Anthropic’s growing dominance in the AI industry. On the other is Anthropic and OpenAI, which face profit pressures from open source models and argue that Chinese-made modelspose security risks.The White House is similarly divided, historically hawkish on China’s tech industry but wary of blocking low-cost AI models that American businesses have come to rely on. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent suggested in recent weeks that the US could sanction Chinese AI firms over alleged intellectual property theft from American companies, while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick hasreceived letters from tech-startup foundersasking him not to cut off access to open models.Amid reports that the Trump administration was considering banning or limiting the use of China’s open source models, a swath of prominent big tech companies including Microsoft, Nvidia, Palantir and Meta also recently published a letter urging lawmakers to refrain from putting restrictions on open models. Additionally, Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huangwent to Capitol Hill on Tuesdayto meet with Democratic and Republican party leaders to lobby in support of open models.While facing heat fromChinaand other tech companies, OpenAI and Anthropic revealed in recent weeks that their AI models went rogue during cybersecurity tests and hacked into outside organizations. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman visited lawmakers and administration officials this week to discuss controls on AI following the incident. That forced Donald Trump to field questions about whether he would put more safety restrictions on AI development.“We have to be careful in both ways. We don’t want to restrict them when all of a sudden we come in second to China,” Trump said, adding: “I know many of these people. I don’t want to restrict them from doing great work.”While the Trump administration debates potential safety controls and limits on Chinese-made AI models, it took tangible action this week against China’s increasingly prominent robotics industry. The Federal Communications Commission announced on Tuesday aban on humanoid robotsfrom China over what it alleged was an unacceptable national security risk.China’s humanoid robots from companies such as Unitree have been the subject of numerous viral videos this year, showcasing their ability to dance or interact with people when programmed to do so. The FCC alleged that the robots could also steal data or surveil US citizens, as well as threaten US manufacturing and supply chains.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe FCC’s decision further escalates the US competition with China over emerging technologies and comes as fears over China’s tech have shifted financial markets. A reportfrom the Informationthis week stating that China had begun mass production of specialty chips key to the AI boom spurred a stock selloff thaterased $1tn in market valuefrom other chip manufacturers.As Chinese-made tech advancements increasingly begin to rival their US counterparts, Silicon Valley’s divisions could intensify, markets could become more skittish and the Trump administration could face more pressure over how to counter China’s influence.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)Silicon ValleyTrump administrationUS foreign policyChinaUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Proteinmaxxing’ could lead to higher prices for infant formula, say experts | Food & drink industry | The Guardian
description: Whey protein, a key infant formula ingredient, is in growing demand, partly linked to rising use of weight-loss drugs
Author: Sarah Marsh
Headline: Whey protein, a key infant formula ingredient, is in growing demand, partly linked to rising use of weight-loss drugs
Content: Whey protein powder is a key ingredient in infant formula, where it is used to mimic human breast milk by adjusting the protein ratio and making it easier to digest.Photograph: TheToidi/AlamyView image in fullscreenWhey protein powder is a key ingredient in infant formula, where it is used to mimic human breast milk by adjusting the protein ratio and making it easier to digest.Photograph: TheToidi/AlamyFood & drink industry‘Proteinmaxxing’ could lead to higher prices for infant formula, say expertsWhey protein, a key infant formula ingredient, is in growing demand, partly linked to rising use of weight-loss drugsSarah MarshConsumer affairs correspondentSat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rise of “proteinmaxxing” – a trend in which consumers try to eat as much protein as possible – could lead to higher prices for infant formula, experts warn.Whey protein, a key ingredient in infant formula, has surged in popularity over the past year as health professionals emphasise the benefits of protein.The growing use of GLP-1 weight-loss medications, which suppress appetite, has also boosted demand for concentrated whey protein – often found in protein shakes and bars – as users seek to preserve muscle mass while losing weight.As demand rises, so do prices. Expana, a global market intelligence platform, said whey protein concentrate 80, with 80% pure protein, cost €11,733 (£10,050) per metric tonne in July 2025 and was now at €25,875.Whey protein is a vital ingredient in infant formula where it is used to mimic human breast milk by adjusting the protein ratio and making it easier to digest. High-whey formulas are designed specifically for newborns and babies under one year old.Industry insiders warn that rising demand could soon be felt by consumers as infant formula manufacturers struggle to absorb higher ingredient costs. Office for National Statistics data shows the average price of baby formula has already increased by 4.8% over the past year with a 750g box now costing £12.11, up from £11.55 a year earlier.Dr Vicky Sibson, the director of the First Steps Nutrition Trust, an independent UK public health nutrition charity, said: “Whey is a major ingredient in infant formula, so significant increases in its price risk increasing the price of formula itself.”She added: “We know from the Competition and Markets Authority’s [CMA] report that infant formula manufacturers have passed any rise in input costs on to consumers, including during the cost of living crisis.”Sibson said it was “hugely concerning” because of “mounting evidence that many families using formula to feed their babies find it unaffordable, and the coping strategies they use – like watering down feeds – may be harmful”.She said a solution the CMA had proposed was for the government to impose a mandatory price or profit cap. “There is precedent for this from other countries including Greece and it’s warranted because the CMA’s work exposed high profit margins of between 50% and 75%. Companies should not be allowed to protect their margins at the expense of the wellbeing of mothers and babies,” she said.Jose Saiz, who covers the European dairy market at Expana, said: “Overall, higher ingredient costs have already led to higher consumer prices across many dairy and nutrition products, although the extent of cost pass-through varies by market and brand.”He said some infant formula manufacturers were reformulating products to use more D90 demineralised whey powder. D90, which has 90% of its minerals removed, helps manufacturers achieve the required whey-to-casein ratio while supplying both whey proteins and lactose. As more producers switch to the ingredient, demand has risen sharply, pushing up D90 prices as well.Saiz said: “Over the past six months, many manufacturers have reformulated their recipes in response to rising ingredient costs. One of the main responses has been to increase the use of demineralised whey powder 90 (D90), an ingredient used primarily in infant formula.”He added: “Infant formula manufacturers report that current high whey protein prices are becoming economically unsustainable at existing retail price levels. Many believe further consumer price increases will eventually be necessary unless raw material costs ease.”Explore more on these topicsFood & drink industryConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A towering piece of monoculture’: how The Odyssey discourse has dominated this summer | The Odyssey | The Guardian
description: Christopher Nolan’s smash hit epic has continued to excite and enrage everyone from rightwingers to academics, an old-fashioned throwback to a uniting big-screen event
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Christopher Nolan’s smash hit epic has continued to excite and enrage everyone from rightwingers to academics, an old-fashioned throwback to a uniting big-screen event
Content: Matt Damon in The Odyssey.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenMatt Damon in The Odyssey.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyThe Odyssey‘A towering piece of monoculture’: how The Odyssey discourse has dominated this summerChristopher Nolan’s smash hit epic has continued to excite and enrage everyone from rightwingers to academics, an old-fashioned throwback to a uniting big-screen eventPeter Bradshaw reviews The OdysseyThe Odyssey: jaw-dropping action, dark magic and dolphin cameos – discuss with spoilersGo woke, get rich: why rightwing hate campaigns don’t affect the box officeJesse HassengerSat 1 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf a high-profile academic isreviewing a movie for the London Review of Books, that movie in question must be making some kind of mark on some kind of culture. And if people are actually reading a movie review in the London Review of Books, and writing thinkpieces in disagreement or favor of said movie or its review, that movie may actually be a cultural phenomenon.The Odyssey: jaw-dropping action, dark magic and dolphin cameos – discuss with spoilersRead moreNormally, volume of discourse about a movie should not be mistaken for a sign that people are actually seeing it. Sometimes online factions just have a bored fixation not shared by the rest of the world. ButChristopher Nolan’sThe Odysseyhas some major receiptsat the box office, too: the movie has already outgrossed Oppenheimer, Nolan’s last movie, itself a shockingly popular movie for adults. Though The Odyssey’s audience skewed male in its first weekend, by its second its gender split wascloser to 50/50, suggesting reach beyond the stereotypically male-driven action-adventures. It’s also reaching out to older moviegoers, an endangered demographic in a summer where under-25s have driven the success ofObsessionandBackrooms. Three-quarters of The Odyssey’s audience has been over 25, while memes inspired by the movie (most popular:Matt Damon’s anguished face portraying Odysseus listening to the sirens’ song andRobert Pattinson’s slimy suitor demanding that “someone get these BEGGARS out of here!”) have indicated that younger people are paying attention too.All told, The Odyssey fast closing in on a billion dollars worldwide, and the number of movies that have done this without superheroes, sequel hype or a whole lot of animation is vanishingly small. This is the strange, rarified air that Nolan’s film now occupies. Meanwhile, exactly those other types of movies traditionally aiming for that territory – superhero movies such asSupergirl, remakes includingMasters of the UniverseorMoana, animation films likeToy Story 5andMinions & Monsters– have failed to catch on more broadly. Some have bombed, some have underperformed and some have become seemingly frictionless billion-dollarsmashes, but none feel like true events. Though an incoming mega-smash featuringSpider-Manreinforces that sometimes audiences will still rush out for the right familiar superhero, Nolan’s movie still stands outin a summerthat may have seen tides turn against IP.Of course, The Odyssey is also, in its way, a form of IP;it’s a storythat almost everyone purports to at least kinda-sorta know, even if the specifics are lost somewhere in the halls of high school. Nolan’s big-budget adaptation of the Homeric epic has emerged as a towering piece of monoculture that throws back to pre-fragmentation days. Or, at very least, back to less preordained smashes including Barbie or Top Gun: Maverick, IP projects that seem to dig deeper into audiences’ psyche than other, more preordained blockbusters.Go woke, get rich: why rightwing hate campaigns don’t affect the box officeRead moreSpecifically, these kinds of monocultural events stand in opposition to so many 21st-century box office hits that manage to make tons of money while still feeling like a niche. This waspioneeredbytheTwilight movies, which would make $700m worldwide like clockwork without ever feeling like an all-demographics smash, but there are plenty of hit superhero movies that also qualify: movies that a lot of people who like that sort of thing saw, without convincing infrequent moviegoers (whose infrequency has seemingly only grown post-pandemic) to show up. Even aless expectedsmash such asA Minecraft Movieisn’t exactly a unifying force across demographics. Call it the difference between Avatar (massive worldwide phenom that seemed to reach across demographics) andAvatar 3(big hit for the not-insubstantial group of people who have been watching every Avatar movie, but nothing your grandparents likely went out for).It’s tempting to classify The Odyssey’s cultural success as reminiscent of a pre-internet time, and in some ways it is, befitting its connections to old-fashioned sword-and-sandal epics of the 1950s. Yet it’s really a convergence of old-fashioned monoculture and more newfangled discourse explosion. Rather than a superhero movie generating endless rewritings of the same nerd-to-normie translations (who was that character and are they going to be in the next superhero thing?) and glorified spoilers (is there a post-credits scene? And while we’re at it, can you describe it for me?), here is an R-rated movie, based on an epic poem, aimed at adults, prompting essays from film critics, academics and amateur Nolan scholars. It’s movie discourse fit for a 200-student freshman seminar, writ even larger.View image in fullscreenTom Holland, Matt Damon and Christopher Nolan attend The Odyssey premiere in Mumbai.Photograph: Prodip Guha/Getty ImagesThat might sound dismissive in its own way. But as tediously rancorous as the Very Online versions of these discussions can be, fueled by sometimes-insufferable Nolan acolytes and their equally disagreeable opponents, with the bonus unwelcome intrusion of afailed pre-release rightwing culture war, there’s at least a trackable rationality to a lot of post-release Odyssey discourse. Is it even something like ... healthy cultural-studies debate?! At first, the classicist and, most crucially, Odyssey translator Emily Wilson seemed to be forming a surprise backlash (given that Nolan had cited her translation’s opening line as inspiring his work) with her London Review of Books piece, focusing on the director’sdeviationsfrom the text, what she sees as thematic inconsistencies and simplifications, and some potential blind spots in race and gender. This then turned into an internet-fueled critique of an academic’s analysis of film, which some felt included some misreadings of certain characters, scenes and ideas.Some of the exchanges feel like a turf war between classics and film – are academics not encouraged to weigh in on movies using a different framework? Are mainstream film critics not encouraged to defend their sometimes (often) less rigorous discipline from those who feel confident dipping into it because of the subject matter? Other discussions have emerged (or re-emerged) from within the film community, reviving questions about whether the most popular name-brand writer-director in the world gives the short shrift to his female characters.Anne Hathaway’s Penelope joins her two other Nolan characters, from The Dark Knight Rises and Interstellar, as some of the strongest in his filmography. But it’s undeniable that Nolan tends to characterize hisfemale leadsas wives or wife figures, and some haveopinedthat the new movie’s wealth of women feel marginalized in ways they aren’t in the millennia-old original text.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOdyssey debates have touched exhibition, too: is Nolan’s film, shot entirely on IMAX cameras but only available to be shown in that native format in a few dozen theaters worldwide, placing undue emphasis on a more elitist form of spectacle? Or is he simply providing a level of showmanship that causes demand to outstrip a symbolically meager supply?View image in fullscreenAnne Hathaway and Tom Holland in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/APThe sheer volume of back-and-forth can be wearying – even (especially?) for pop-culture writers who make their living generating reviews, essays, thinkpieces and follow-ups off of the biggest hits of the day. Here’s a bummer stat from my own experience: since the beginning of this year’s summer movie season, there have been at least half a dozen discussion-worthy movies I haven’t written about in any great detail, because of middling-to-low demand. On the other hand,I’vewrittenaboutThe Odyssey and Obsession, this summer’s other major cultural phenom, close to a dozen times put together. I’m grateful for the work – and for the existence of popular movies that can withstand more robust and varied discussion than a 700-word, thumbs-up-or-down review. On the other hand, a new genuine monoculture threatens to simply refine which handful of movies generates 90% of coverage. (At least the “ending explained” industrial complex will have a chance to examine endings that might actually bear analysis, as The Odyssey in particular does.)‘An intermission is a must’: why Greek cinemas are adding a loo break to The OdysseyRead moreWhat’s most striking about the Odyssey discourse, however, is that even amid some built-in rancor or disdain, people actually seem excited to engage in it, rather than listlessly scrolling through it on their way to the next tempest in a teapot. That hybridization of old-school monoculture and more technologically enhanced saturation – unlike those 1950s epics and realImax availabilitynotwithstanding, both the movie and discussion of it feels nearly as accessible as a streaming series du jour, and probably more rewarding – doesn’t feel like astroturfing, but an actual post-release excitement that’s rarer and more fun than pre-release hype. (You have to be truly excited to successfully wring memes from the carefully controlled images of a Nolan film.) Even that ginned-up faux-outrage about the movie’s diversity became amusingly sporting with the gradual and merry realization that most people trulydo not care about what infuriates Elon Musk. The movie that a vocal minority insisted was bringing about the destruction of the west, or whatever they were prattling on about, has turned out to be a great unifier – not necessarily of opinion, but towards a reminder that going to the movies and talking about them after, rather than casting about for what else is on, can still feel like a vital part of living in the world.Explore more on these topicsThe OdysseyChristopher NolanAction and adventure filmsHomerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best theatre to stream this month: Self Esteem dazzles with Teeth ’n’ Smiles | Stage | The Guardian
description: Rebecca Lucy Taylor leads David Hare’s rock’n’roll drama, Michaela Coel tells us Chewing Gum Dreams and Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo stars in a murder mystery
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Rebecca Lucy Taylor leads David Hare’s rock’n’roll drama, Michaela Coel tells us Chewing Gum Dreams and Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo stars in a murder mystery
Content: Rock revival … Rebecca Lucy Taylor in Teeth ’n’ Smiles.Photograph: Jono WhiteView image in fullscreenRock revival … Rebecca Lucy Taylor in Teeth ’n’ Smiles.Photograph: Jono WhiteThe best theatre to stream this monthStageThe best theatre to stream this month: Self Esteem dazzles with Teeth ’n’ SmilesRebecca Lucy Taylor leads David Hare’s rock’n’roll drama, Michaela Coel tells us Chewing Gum Dreams and Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo stars in a murder mysteryChris WiegandSat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeeth ’n’ SmilesLike a time capsule crowbarred open, its fug filling the auditorium, this year’s 50th anniversary production of David Hare’s dramaabout a 60s rock band’s unravellingmade for a fascinating evening. The tunes by brothers Nick and Tony Bicât – plus Rebecca Lucy Taylor AKA Self Esteem’s new number,Maggie’s Song, which expertly matches their milieu – have been collected on acast recordingbest played on repeat. Altogether now: “Don’t let the bastards come near you. They just want to prove you’re sane.”Chewing Gum DreamsIn September, London’sTheatre503 and tiata fahodziwill revive Michaela Coel’s sparky, name-making monologueChewing Gum Dreams. OnNT at Homeyou can see Coel herself perform this whirlwind tour of a 14-year-old girl’s world, from the top deck of the 67 bus to nightclubs, chemists and the classroom.Romeo and JulietAfter 14 years at the helm, Antoni Cimolino steps down as artistic director of Canada’sStratford Festivalthis season (Jonathan Church takes up the role in the autumn).
