Cimolino began as an actor and the archive ofStratfest@Homeincludes his 1992 Romeo, opposite Megan Porter Follows from Anne of Green Gables.Marco da Silva Ferreira: F*cking FutureOur critic Lyndsey Winship detected “a somewhat 3am vibe” to Portuguese choreographer Marco da Silva Ferreira’s “subtly intoxicating” protest dance piece when it visited Sadler’s Wells East in June. Available onArte.tv, captured at the Lyon Dance Biennale in 2025.View image in fullscreenBlockbuster … from left: Joe Bolland as Guildenstern, Hiran Abeysekera as Hamlet and Hari Mackinnon as Rosencrantz in Hamlet at the National Theatre.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHamletHiran Abeysekera’s irreverent Prince of Denmark wears a Blockbuster Video sweater and now you can rent his performance with aNational Theatre at Home subscription. Filmed at the Lyttelton theatre, Robert Hastie’s production was part of Indhu Rubasingham’s opening programme, with Francesca Mills’s Ophelia roundly praised.The Pansy CrazeMason Alexander Park hosts an epic series celebrating queer performers through the ages – not just theeponymous 1930s partiesbut also the Elizabethan era – in what is billed as blending “the dazzle of a cabaret with the intimacy of a piano bar”. Laverne Cox, Jesse Tyler Ferguson and Sasha Velour also star. FromAudible.Murder at the GatesStranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo – who makes his West End debut in Rent in September – can be heard onthis new musical concept albumby Steven Sater and James Bourne. It revolves around an heiress’s murder mystery party that goes spectacularly wrong.HumoRafaela Carrasco’s flamenco ballet is the story of 19th-centurycigarreras– the women who made and sold cigars – unfolding in both factories and at fiestas, exploring their fight for emancipation. On a stage dressed with just a few flowers and chairs, it’s richly atmospheric with the ensemble sometimes puffing away. title: Alley Cats: Ricky Gervais is back with a boorish, sweary comedy – and I didn’t laugh once | Television | The Guardian
description: Animated cats banter tediously in a show that’s determined to shock, but which leaves you checking your watch to see how long is left. It’s lazy, dated and far too pleased with itself
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: Animated cats banter tediously in a show that’s determined to shock, but which leaves you checking your watch to see how long is left. It’s lazy, dated and far too pleased with itself
Content: From left: Jo Hartley as Kitten, Diane Morgan as Olive, Ricky Gervias as Gus, Andrew Brooke as Fang and Tom Basden as Ponce in Alley Cats.Photograph: NetflixView image in fullscreenFrom left: Jo Hartley as Kitten, Diane Morgan as Olive, Ricky Gervias as Gus, Andrew Brooke as Fang and Tom Basden as Ponce in Alley Cats.Photograph: NetflixThe watcherTelevisionAlley Cats: Ricky Gervais is back with a boorish, sweary comedy – and I didn’t laugh onceAnimated cats banter tediously in a show that’s determined to shock, but which leaves you checking your watch to see how long is left. It’s lazy, dated and far too pleased with itselfRhik SamadderSat 1 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAccording to multiverse theory, there are parallel realities in which news of a newRicky Gervaisproject instils a feeling other than dread. But we don’t live in them. Having seen his new series, Alley Cats (Netflix, from Friday 7 August), a boorish banter-vehicle in which animated cats shoot the breeze like a bunch of pub bores, I’m not sure what there is to report – other than the fact that I didn’t laugh once. Considering what a fan I once was, I find this remarkable. What happened?Woke happened, is what his diehard fans would say. Gervais has paid the price of a shifting Overton window on jokes about dwarves and disabled people and trans people. You can’t say anything any more, they lament, while defending a wealthy, highly platformed man who proves the opposite. They’re not wrong, though – politics plays a part. While writing this, I stepped outside to say hello to a queer friend who was, naturally, buying a bicycle in the street. I asked her what she made of Ricky Gervais.“He’s defunct. We don’t need him any more,” she said, as if describing DVDs by post. His work didn’t make her laugh now, she said, but added that this was a relief. If he was both problematic and she found him funny, she’d have to suffer a contradiction within herself. He’d let her off the hook; but a comedian’s politics and their craft are still different things.I like contradictions and dislike safe comedy. I actually agree that swathes of our culture are risk-averse and boring. Nothing makes me laugh harder than a good transgressive joke. Humour is often about dissolving dogma, acting as a safety valve for our collective id. The darker meats, close to the bone, have the juiciest flavour. But “good” is as important as “transgressive”. Alley Cats leans on one at the expense of the other. That’s why it limps.The series follows a gang of stray cats, who mostly spend their time watching TV on a sofa in a derelict house. Gus, voiced by Ricky Gervais, is a fat ginger tom, who bellows ignorant or misanthropic opinions over everyone else. Ponce, voiced byTom Basden, is a pampered, middle-class pedigree who talks sense but is fatally undermined because he has no balls, lol. Then there’s Puke (David Earl), a mangy pervert with a penchant for inter-species sex who says things such as “I gave a hedgehog anal once”.Jokes like this, about having weird sex with animals, come up every episode. There are jokes about fat people, blind cats, intellectual disabilities. Gus swears in every line, the way some Brits do, with a habitual fondness for the worst swear word, the one that gives Americans conniptions. The show is lazy and pleased with itself. The more it was determined to shock, the more I checked my watch. The episodes are 15 minutes long – but feel much longer.The weight-bearing comic idea here, that cats are arseholes, feels about 30 years old at a minimum. Animal sex, bum stuff, the ambient sense that gay is funny – these are all jokes I remember people making at school. I didn’t find them funny then either. They have aged like milk, but the main point is that they have aged. They’re predictable. Humour relies on surprise, and there are none here. The lad banter does give way to sentiment, predictably every episode, with the finesse of a chop shop. And then Cat Stevens plays.Every beer-slopping geezer I know has borrowed Gervais’s comic rhythms. Biting their lower lip with guitar-hero sensuality, dominating conversations with glib comebacks that expose a squirrelly self-loathing. I’d still argue he’s only a rung below Tony Hancock, Monty Python and Richard Curtis in terms of importance to British comedy.The OfficeandExtraswere, respectively, the most influential and funniest sitcoms of the 00s. His podcast helped define the medium. He’s done sophisticated character work, written love and friendship stories that made my heart bigger. Now it’s contracting again, like a universe imploding on itself. We’re a long way from Slough, and this alley feels like a dead end.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherRicky GervaisTV comedyAnimation on TVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A forgotten Victorian children’s book helped me grieve my father | Culture | The Guardian
description: The stories in Mrs Leicester’s School, written by a woman who killed her own mother, were suffused with grief, and finally triggered mine as I was teaching a class of students
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The stories in Mrs Leicester’s School, written by a woman who killed her own mother, were suffused with grief, and finally triggered mine as I was teaching a class of students
Content: Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningCultureA forgotten Victorian children’s book helped me grieve my fatherThe stories in Mrs Leicester’s School, written by a woman who killed her own mother, were suffused with grief, and finally triggered mine as I was teaching a class of studentsChris TownsendSat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen my dad went into hospital for what would be the final time, shortly before Christmas last year, I had been finishing up a lecture series on early children’s literature for the university where I teach. My dad had had a drinking problem practically my whole life, but his alcoholism had worsened across decades. Then suddenly, after years of poor health, his liver just gave up on him. He was dead within days.Shortly after his death I was due to lecture on a relatively forgotten book of stories for children called Mrs Leicester’s School, mostly written by the English writer Mary Lamb but with parts by her more famous brother, Charles. I was not prepared for how moved I would be by the simple message of one of the stories. That often bizarre and sometimes grim collection of tales for pre-Victorian boys and girls changed the way that I, an almost 40-year-old man, think about grief.My lecture began with the Lamb siblings themselves, who were reasonably successful writers in their time; any branch of Waterstones will still carry their Tales from Shakespeare. But Mary is better known today because she killed her own mother with a knife in 1796, during a breakdown. Charles intervened, but their mother couldn’t be saved. Mary was spared imprisonment because Charles pledged to become her legal guardian. They took up writing children’s books.The fact that Mary killed her own parent coloured my first encounter with Mrs Leicester’s School, which is far more emotionally intense than any kids’ book ought to be. Many of the children who act as the narrators of the stories have lost parents; several of the stories directly concern their experiences of loss.I was especially struck by the story of Elizabeth Villiers, or The Sailor Uncle, which I focused on for my lecture, delivered to two dozen 20-year-olds in a dusty theatre. It begins after the young Elizabeth’s mother has died. She doesn’t think of her death as a cause for tears, as she has never seen her father cry; he mostly locks himself in his study.double quotation markI started talking about it in a lecture to my students. At one point, I realised I was cryingThat changes when her “sailor Uncle” returns from sea, and Elizabeth takes him to his sister’s grave, where he is struck by an “agony of grief”. This in turn sets off Elizabeth’s father. The “very first day I ever saw my father weep”, she tells us, became the day she “first learned my mother’s death was a heavy affliction”. Elizabeth, upset, blames her uncle for bringing painful feelings into her home. Nevertheless, he is kind to her and when he eventually heads back to sea, Elizabeth realises that she will miss him terribly.It was this part of Lamb’s story that really got to me when I narrated it to my students that morning. Elizabeth’s father sits her down, dries away the tears she’s shed for her uncle, and says to her: “Let it be a lesson to you to be as kind as possible to those you love; and remember, when they are gone from you, you will never think you had been kind enough.”At this point in my lecture, I realised I was crying, and had been for some time. My students were aware, but, rather than laughing with embarrassment, they were rapt. One girl, who also had cheeks shining with tears, looked straight at me and simply nodded, slowly.Lamb doesn’t spell it out, but the father is finally working through his grief. He has exited the locked study of his repressed emotions. Grief is a complicated thing, and always distinct in its complications, but what we shared in that lecture theatre was a recognition of the power of literature to make grief shareable, and somehow bearable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe sense of loss we feel for those we love, Lamb’s little book tells us, reminds us that there are many kinds of love that make life worth living in the first place. When my dad died, my grief was complicated by the fact that I long ago felt I’d lost him; I’d been grieving for years, and I wasn’t sure I had any tears left. Mrs Leicester’s School helped me see that I did.Did a cultural moment prompt you to make a major life change? title: ​The Guide #254: Artist anonymity ​i​s a radical act in ​our cultural obsess​ion with visibility | Culture | The Guardian
description: ​H​idden creators ​reveal how invisibility can be a shield and spotlight in an era of relentless self‑exposure
Author: Gabrielle Schwarz
Headline: ​H​idden creators ​reveal how invisibility can be a shield and spotlight in an era of relentless self‑exposure
Content: Who are they? Two Guerrilla Girls pose for the camera.Photograph: Guerrilla Girls/Art Night/PAView image in fullscreenWho are they? Two Guerrilla Girls pose for the camera.Photograph: Guerrilla Girls/Art Night/PAThe Guide newsletterCulture​The Guide #254: Artist anonymity ​i​s a radical act in ​our cultural obsess​ion with visibilityIn this week’s newsletter: ​H​idden creators ​reveal how invisibility can be a shield and spotlight in an era of relentless self‑exposureDon’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGabrielle SchwarzSat 1 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1985, an anonymous group of women disguised in gorilla masks burst on to the art scene in New York. At night, the Guerrilla Girls, as they named themselves, fly-posted around the city: funny, eye-catching posters highlighting gender and racial biases in museums and galleries. (“Do women have to be naked to get into the Met. Museum?” read one now-famous poster.) “Of course, we were afraid that if we blew the whistle on some of [the art world’s] most powerful people, we could kiss off our art careers,” a founding memberexplainedin an interview for their 1995 book. “But mainly, we wanted the focus to be on the issues, not on our personalities or our own work.”The collective is still active; 55 members have come and gone over the years. When giving interviews, they use pseudonyms borrowed from dead women artists: Frida Kahlo, Lee Krasner, Käthe Kollwitz. Only a handful of their true identities have been revealed over the years, mostly after their deaths or due to lawsuits. But this week, a Guerrilla Girl made headlines when she chose to unmask herself on her own terms. “I’d had a pact with another Girl that whoever died first, the survivor would bring her out,”saidthe 83-year-old artist Joyce Kozloff (codename: Liubov Popova). “But I suddenly realised that if I were dead, I couldn’t tell the story my way.”Anonymity isn’t a straightforward route for artists. This is especially true now, in a media culture that is increasingly ruled by the twin cults of celebrity and personal identity. If you want attention in the 21st century, nothing matters more than making strangers on the internet feel as if they reallyknowyou. And yet there are still those – visual artists, writers, musicians, film-makers – who have opted for the cloak of anonymity.Often, there’s an element of self-protection. Just as the Guerrilla Girls were anxious about jeopardising their professional opportunities via their activism, the anonymous author known as the Secret Barrister – who started blogging in 2015 in order to shed light on the legal system – has explained that their hidden identity keeps them safe. “Put simply, anonymity buys me the ability to speak plainly, frankly and without fear or favour about the problems that I see in the criminal justice system,” theywrotein one post. When Banksy first picked up the spray paints in the early 1990s, he was just another Bristol street artist using an alias to avoid getting into legal trouble. These days, his acts of vandalism are unlikely to be prosecuted, given that an original Banksy is far more valuable than any property it may have defaced.View image in fullscreenFaceless … Daft Punk.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOthers just want to focus on the work. ForElena Ferrante, the bestselling novelist behind the “Neapolitan quartet”, using a nom-de-plume was initially a way to deal with shyness but evolved into a crucial dimension of her practice. “Anonymity lets me concentrate exclusively on my writing,” she has said. The French electronic duo Daft Punk never hid their names – Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo – but they did conceal their appearances with robot costumes (or, in some early instances,a cloth bag over their heads) for performances and press. “One thing I like about the masks is that I don’t have people constantly coming up to me and reminding me what I do,” Bangalteronce said. “It’s nice to be able to forget, but there are occasional downsides. Several years ago in Ibiza some guy ran up exorbitant bar tabs at clubs while claiming to be me.”Some have more niche motivations for staying under the radar. In 1968, the Directors Guild of America introduced the pseudonym “Alan Smithee” as an alternative credit for any director that wished to disown one of their own films. This was usually because the artist felt that others had meddled to the extent that they did not have creative control over the final product (though then the pseudonym itself became too notorious, and has since been officiallyretired). A few high-profile authors including JK Rowling and Stephen King have published books under a different name in an attempt to avoid market oversaturation, or to see whether their success is just down to hype. In Rowling’s case, she would have already been used to having a pen name. The initials “JK” were suggested by her Harry Potter publishers – she doesn’t actually have a middle name – because they feared young boys wouldn’t knowingly buy a fantasy book by a woman writer.Then, there’s the aura of mystery. It may seem counterintuitive, but anonymity can be a useful strategy to get everybody talking about you, particularly in this age of oversharing and content overload. People become desperate to figure out who you are. On a practical level, it’s nearly impossible to conduct your business nowadays without sharing personal data – unless you’re willing to be paid only in crypto. More than once, I’ve been told by someone in a given industry that of course they know who XYZ is. A decade ago, an investigative journalist put forward a convincing, though unconfirmed, case identifying Ferrante as literary translator Anita Raja. Earlier this year an in-depth Reuters investigation seemed to definitively confirm past reports that Banksy is a 50-something-year-old man called Robin Gunningham.Celebrities’ pseudonyms also rarely survive for long. The debut novel in the Cormoran Strike series by “Robert Galbraith” had barely sold 1,500 copies when Rowling’s authorship was leaked by a lawyer. Perhaps that settles the “talent or hype” question.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt was people’s incessant curiosity that in 1990 inspired the Guerrilla Girls to put out a new poster with the headline “GUERRILLA GIRLS’ IDENTITIES EXPOSED!”The workfeatured 10 columns with over 500 names of women involved in the art world at the time, concluding with the line “AND MANY MORE……..” This was obviously a joke, as it would have been impossible for so many to be involved (although each of the since confirmed members are on there). But what a clever way to live up to the group’s original raison-d’être: by calling attention to the countless under-recognised women who have, in fact, wanted to make a name for themselves.To read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Rhys Nicholson: ‘Get a hobby – don’t become a full-blown racist’ | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The comedian and Drag Race Down Under judge on Harry Styles, not having the legs for short shorts, and why sleep is the most expensive beauty product
Author: Emma Joyce
Headline: The comedian and Drag Race Down Under judge on Harry Styles, not having the legs for short shorts, and why sleep is the most expensive beauty product
Content: ‘There are very few people I’m comfortable with queerbaiting, but Harry Styles, I’m fine for you to keep queerbaiting’ … Australian comedian Rhys Nicholson.Photograph: StanView image in fullscreen‘There are very few people I’m comfortable with queerbaiting, but Harry Styles, I’m fine for you to keep queerbaiting’ … Australian comedian Rhys Nicholson.Photograph: Stan10 Chaotic QuestionsTelevision & radioRhys Nicholson: ‘Get a hobby – don’t become a full-blown racist’The comedian and Drag Race Down Under judge on Harry Styles, not having the legs for short shorts, and why sleep is the most expensive beauty productEmma JoyceSat 1 Aug 2026 18.22 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’re back on the judging panel of Drag Race Down Under vs The World. What do you think gives Australian queens the edge?I think our drag tends not to focus as much on female impersonation. It’s about building a character. People like Lazy Susan, who’s on the judging panel this year, is one of my favourites because there’s no illusion about this being a man in women’s clothing, but there’s creativity to it. I think Australian drag is about creating art, as opposed to creating a woman.You’re also on The Traitors Australia soon. Is there a reality TV show you haven’t been on that you’d like to?Doing Traitors actually taught me that I don’t think I want to be a contestant again, because I’m used to knowing what’s going on. In Drag Race, I know what’s going on all the time and I’m in on everything, but being on Traitors was likeOh my god!What would I do? Maybe that UK show Hunted – where you’re on the run. I’d just go to Daylesford and hang out in a house for a few weeks. Put on a wig or something.You wear a lot of fabulous suits. How many do you own?I have a new suit for every episode [of Drag Race], so it’s in constant rotation. Some I’m lent, and my stylist and I put them together, but I have about 40. I do a big clear-out every year and last year I took about 10 or 15 of them to this op-shop at the top of my street in Melbourne. I dropped them at the door and a few days later I walked past and the windows had becomeall the suits. It looked like a memorial for me.Anna Friel: ‘I go to every location with a bag full of lightbulbs. Lighting really affects how one thinks’Read moreSpeaking of … is there a song you’d want played at your funeral?Baby I’m Burnin’by Dolly Parton … What I actually want for my funeral – and this is true and my husband told me to keep telling people this so they don’t think he’s a monster – is a natural burial, where they put you in a cotton shroud and plant a tree on top of you. But I want to goinwith athud. That’s important to me. It’s like the last time someone will go “Jesus, Rhys.” Maybe they could put a bit of water in the bottom so it squelches – I want that splat noise. Then maybe Baby I’m Burnin’ would play after that.If you had to lip-sync for your life, or for the world, what song would you pick?Imagine if I did Both Sides Now by Joni Mitchell.[Sound of disgust]A ballad! It would probably be something like Barbra Streisand’s Don’t Rain on My Parade, or something from the 60s, because if I was a drag queen it would be that era of drag that’s 50s and 60s-inspired. I wanna look like Joan from Mad Men.What would your drag name be?Dina Hunger.I really hope that’s not how you go!No! I want to get very fat so I go in with that good thud.View image in fullscreen‘I think Australian drag is about creating art as opposed to creating a woman’ … Rhys Nicholson with Lazy Susan, Michelle Visage and guest judge Beks on the first episode of Drag Race Down Under vs the World.Photograph: StanIs there an ideal length for men’s shorts?What Harry Styles is doing is fine by me. There are very few people I’m comfortable with queerbaiting, but Harry Styles, I’m fine for you to keep queerbaiting.But I reckon if you’re gonna go above the knee, it needs to be short shorts. And you can be any size or shape to wear short shorts – it’s a confidence thing. I don’t really have the legs for them. But, as a hard rule, never three-quarters.What’s your biggest beauty tip?Sleep! The amount of time and energy and substances I used in my 20s to not sleep and now all I want to do is sleep … and I’m not against botox or anything. I use my face too much in standup. But I think sleep is the most expensive beauty product I own.What do you do when you can’tget to sleep?I smoke pot. It’s legal; I have a prescription for it. I don’t like sleeping pills. I don’t even like the feeling of being stoned that much, but I have a little vape pen and it helps because I used to have really bad insomnia. For years I slept like three or four hours a night and was going insane.What’s your most controversial pop culture take?This isn’t controversial, I guess, but I think you can leave a major news organisation without having to activate a hard-right base. It’s possible. To all these men, it’s totally possible to start a podcast about your interests. Cooking? Maybe do one about cooking. You don’t need to go full hard-right. Get a hobby; don’t become a full-blown racist.Finally, who is the most famous person in your phone contacts?ProbablyMichelle Visage. Don’t have RuPaul’s number – never got that.Ronny Chieng? James Acaster? Ronny Chieng is the most famous person I know, and I’ve just filmed a special and he and James Acaster produced it. What’s funny to me is, because we all started around the same time and they’ve obviously [makes a skyrocketing motion with their hands], people freak out about them and it’s like, I showed Ronny how to use the curtain at the Sydney Comedy Store. Now he’s in The Devil Wears Prada 2!Drag Race Down Under vs The World is now streaming onStan. New episodes drop weekly. The Traitors Australia season 3 premieres on 4 August on Network 10Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radio10 Chaotic QuestionsAustralian televisionStanTelevisionRuPaulfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gregg Araki on sex, film and queer resistance: ‘All the terrible shit in the world is because of sexual repression’ | Gregg Araki | The Guardian
description: As his 12th feature film, I Want Your Sex, hits theaters, the cult gay film-maker is as fired up as ever
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: As his 12th feature film, I Want Your Sex, hits theaters, the cult gay film-maker is as fired up as ever
Content: Gregg Araki at the Los Angeles premiere of I Want Your Sex on Tuesday.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APView image in fullscreenGregg Araki at the Los Angeles premiere of I Want Your Sex on Tuesday.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APGregg ArakiInterviewGregg Araki on sex, film and queer resistance: ‘All the terrible shit in the world is because of sexual repression’Owen MyersAs his 12th feature film, I Want Your Sex, hits theaters, the cult gay film-maker is as fired up as everSat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs straight sex the most perverse sex of all?Gregg Araki’s new film makes a convincing case. Titled I Want Your Sex, the movie is a deliriously fun and often hilarious study of desire, power and art that features bondage, full-frontal and a vagina made out of pink chewed-up bubble gum. “For me, it is a very queer story,” the director says, speaking the week of the film’s release in a video call from his Los Angeles home. “It’s a take on kink and alternate sexuality that goes right across the straight-queer spectrum.”While it is not the first heterosexual movie by Gregg Araki – that honor goes to his 1995 acid trip of a road movieThe Doom Generation– it features the new queer cinema pioneer’s starriest cast in years, perhaps in a sign that Hollywood at large has caught up to the cult director’s anarchic vision. Forty years into his career, we still want Araki’s sex: the film is set to reach the director’s biggest audience to date, opening to 700 US screens this week, a stunning figure for an independent film and a wider opening than recent films by indie veterans likeNicolas Winding RefnandJim Jarmusch.Today, the director is in a buoyant mood; he wears a striped tank top and looks at least two decades younger than his age of 66. “The world’s so fucked up right now with wars andICEand fucking genocides that I want to put a little queer joy and positivity into the world,” he says.The film follows Elliot (Cooper Hoffman), a puppyish 23-year-old college graduate whose ambitions in life amount to a vague goal to start a podcast. After he starts working as an assistant for the brash, sexually carnivorous artist Erika (a turbo-chargedOlivia Wilde), he instantly falls under her spell, leading to a polymorphous parade of sexual epiphanies as he becomes, as he says of one of Erika’s artworks, “a slave to this vagina”.‘Beautiful and terrifying’: the best American LGBTQ+ books, chosen by Samuel R Delany, Kaveh Akbar, Eileen Myles and moreRead moreThere’s an infectious sense of mischief to I Want Your Sex, helped by an ensemble cast that includesCharli xcxas Elliot’s dorky girlfriend, whose idea of a good time between the bedsheets is poring over a neurology textbook, as well asJohnny KnoxvilleandMargaret Choas detectives who interrogate Elliot after a body is discovered floating face-first in a swimming pool. My favorite might be Zap, played by Mason Gooding, who cuts down Elliot’s claim of being “queer adjacent” by retorting: “Have you ever sucked a dick?” Araki has a soft spot for the character too. “He’s very much my snarky sensibility,” the director says.The film was initially scheduled to shoot after Araki wrapped promotion forWhite Bird in a Blizzard, a 2014 drama starringShailene WoodleyandEva Green. Back then, the script was something like “a comic50 Shades of Grey”, he says, with a female intern seduced by her male boss. But after initial funding fell through, the project was put on ice, and when Araki revisited the script after making 2019’s teen TV comedyNow Apocalypse, he worried it felt tone-deaf in the wake of#MeToo. “I started to feel uncomfortable with the [script’s] image of a woman getting dragged around by the hair, even in a consensual situation,” he says. “I don’t want to kink-shame anybody, but as a man, I didn’t really want to put that image out there.“That’s when I got the idea to flip the sex roles and make it a male sub and a female dom,” he says. “I’ve always been a very hardcore feminist from the time I was in film school in the late 70s, so the Erika Tracy character became much more interesting to me.” The script further crystallized in the wake of a 2022studythat found that gen Z were having less sex than previous generations. “When Erika says [to Elliot]: ‘Your generation’s all about Fomo and you’re missing out on the sexual part,’ that was kind of my reaction to that article,” he says.View image in fullscreenOlivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman in I Want Your Sex.Photograph: Courtesy of Magnolia PicturesThe day before our interview, the Hollywood trade magazine Varietytweetedan Araki quote predicting that gen Z will inevitably “regret” not having sex out of fear of getting hurt. While some readers got defensive, others seemed to take it as a metaphorical kick up the butt. “He’s so right let me start fucking for real,” wrote one young cinephile.When I mention the reaction, Araki seems thrilled about getting people talking. “That is one of the most exciting things about the movie to me,” the director says. “I don’t want to lecture anybody, but I want to open up a conversation.“I don’t want to sayallof gen Z, but a certain number of gen Z live a sheltered life and don’t go out much,” he continues. “It’s like [they have] a fear of making a mistake, or being uncomfortable or of having an experience that’s not wonderful. A lot of those experiences arenotwonderful! The first time you ever get your heart broken or someone cheats on you, it really rocks your world. I just can’t imagine going through life without that experience.”Araki thinks that sex is missing in movies, even the ones that are ostensibly all about it. “There’s this whole talk about [cinema’s] sexual renaissance withBabygirlandPillion,” he says. “But I didn’t find Babygirl sex-positive at all. The way that the Nicole Kidman character gets punished for exploring her own desires made me a little uncomfortable.”The hockey-themed gay TV showHeated Rivalryhas also been accused of sanitizing sex for the female gaze. “Uh huh,” Araki says with a slight frown. I’m surprised to learn that he is a big fan, but he doesn’t seem to mind a little debate. “I thought the sex scenes were well-handled and not really watered down,” he says. “It’s kind of what a lot of my sex scenes are: ‘R-rated HBO’. You don’t see genitalia but it’s as explicit as you can be without crossing the line into adult entertainment.”View image in fullscreenAraki and the cast of I Want Your Sex at the film’s  LA premiere.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersAmid its fiesta of raunch, there’s a sly sweetness to I Want YourSex. Despite Elliot’s initial reservations, it seems that Erika unlocks the young man’s unexplored desire to fulfill orders. At times, the pair’s rapport is surprisingly touching, even if there are signs this won’t end well. “I kind of like being your toy,” he tells her moonily over lunch as she nonchalantly drags on a cigarette.‘I feel both thrilled and ruined by this’: Olivia Wilde and Edward Norton on making sex comedy The InviteRead more“I based Cooper’s character on myself when I was in my early 20s and trying to figure out what my sexual identity was,” Araki says. (The director now identifies as gay but was in a public relationship with actor Kathleen Robertson in the late 90s.) Meanwhile, Erika is partly inspired by post-fame Araki, with much of her dialogue culled from the director’s own past interviews. Before shooting began, he told Wilde that there was no room for nerviness on his set. “I was like: ‘Whoever plays this part needs to be completely fearless and not give a fuck about what people think,’” he says. “She was like: ‘That’s what I want to do.’” (Between this andThe Invite, Wilde has emerged as one of the most fun actors to watch this summer.)The director has always taken audiences out of their comfort zones. Araki’s breakout feature The Living End featured a then unprecedented sex scene between the film’s HIV-positive gay lead characters, while 2004’s Mysterious Skin unflinchingly examined the after-effects of childhood sexual abuse in a film anchored by career-best performances from a youngJoseph Gordon-Levittand future Oscar-nominated directorBrady Corbet. He says that the key to his relationships with actors is trust: “I’m not a director that is like: ‘OK, here’s how you’re going to act this scene.’ Once I find the right person and they’re in front of the camera, I just let them have at it.”View image in fullscreenAraki’s 2005 film Mysterious Skin starred Joseph Gordon-Levitt.Photograph: Courtesy of TLA ReleasingWhile Wilde and Hoffman’s chemistry is both explosive and often outrageously funny, I Want Your Sex is just as cutting in its satire of the commercial art world. Erika’s art is frankly hideous, with her gallery space full of garish pop-feminist sculptures and photography that would be bought by a finance bro trying to impress his co-workers with his hip bona fides. Araki, perhaps a little generously, describes the character as a cross betweenRobert Mapplethorpeand the “pure provocation” of Madonna circa Sex, the 1992 top-shelf publication that caused much pearl-clutching for its graphic content. Has society gotten any more open-minded about sex, 34 years later?‘Coming out in the 90s? You might as well say ‘I love cock!’’ Nathan Lane on gay life, Broadway and defying stereotypesRead more“In America, things are worse than they’ve ever been,” Araki says. “The level of puritanical tyranny, repression and cancelling of trans people … it is awful right now. That’s why the movie ends with the Jessie Ware songFree Yourself. I’m old school in a sense: I absolutely believe in ‘make love, not war.’“So much of the hatred, the misery and the aggression and the violence and all the fucking terrible shit in the world right now is from this weird sexual repression,” he goes on. “My movie is my version of Free Yourself, you know what I mean? The sentiment of the song is very positive, inclusive and progressive – the opposite of this culture of oppression and fascism with the dictatorship of our current administration.”He feels fundamentally hopeful about the next generation, despite wishing they would get laid more. “Whenever we do screenings in New York, [the audience is] all these Letterboxd kids,” he says, referring to the social platform for movie fans. “And they’re very sophisticated cinephiles –Charli xcxis one of them! They have very discerning taste in auteurs. It really gives me hope that this younger generation seeks out films that are not your standard popcorn multiplex movies.”View image in fullscreenCharli xcx and Hoffman in I Want Your Sex.Photograph: Courtesy of Magnolia PicturesWhile a recentGlaad reportfound that LGBTQ+ inclusion is at a three-year low in films from the 10 largest distributors, Araki says that queer cinema is in great shape if you know where to look. “At Cannes this year, it was like abonanzaofqueermovies,” he says. “It’s amazing that that is the state of where we are at. That’s kind of where the queer new wave came from in the first place, way back in the early 90s where all of us – Todd [Haynes] and Gus [Van Sant] and I – were just kids.”Araki says that he can see some similarities between LGBTQ+ life today and that of the early 90s. He leaves me with this slightly grim but necessary thought. “Because of the Aids crisis, queer people were kind of being exterminated, so there was a need for expression,” he says. “I think that exists today as well. Queer film-makers that can see the writing on the wall, and that the right wing in this country are not going to stop at trans people. We’re not safe.“It’s very important to be able to have a queer voice and be unfiltered about it,” he says. “That’s where almost all my movies come from. You know, that’s the magic.”I Want Your Sex is out now in the US, on 27 August in Australia and on 28 August in the UKExplore more on these topicsGregg ArakiComedy filmsComedyLGBTQ+ rightsOlivia WildeHeated RivalryCharli xcxinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The machine turned into a lonely character gazing at an empty beach’: Alon Goldsmith’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: On his daily bike ride, the LA-based photographer stumbled upon the perfect subject for this black-and-white portrait
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: On his daily bike ride, the LA-based photographer stumbled upon the perfect subject for this black-and-white portrait
Content: Eye Spy, 2026, shot on iPhone 16 Pro Max.Photograph: Alon GoldsmithView image in fullscreenEye Spy, 2026, shot on iPhone 16 Pro Max.Photograph: Alon GoldsmithSmart shotPhotography‘The machine turned into a lonely character gazing at an empty beach’: Alon Goldsmith’s best phone pictureOn his daily bike ride, the LA-based photographer stumbled upon the perfect subject for this black-and-white portraitGrace HollidaySat 1 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn New Year’s Day 2026, Alon Goldsmith began what he calls a “365-day project, which involves taking and posting a photo every day for a year. On some days, it’s a struggle to find something worthy of being included and on others it’s a challenge to make a choice,” he says.This image was taken on day 111. Johannesburg-born, LA-based Goldsmith was on his daily bike ride, which usually takes him through Venice and around Santa Monica Pier, areas he describes as containing a “cornucopia of curiosities”.‘‘It’s difficult for children to avoid the temptation of screens’: Soumayan Biswas’s best phone pictureRead more“I spend a lot of rides hunting for photos,” he says. “Looking at the world from this vantage point allows me to slow down and notice what’s around me in a different way. When I’m not rushing, the world reveals itself more fully.”This Hi-Spy Viewing Machine is situated on the pier, looking over the beach. Goldsmith decided to translate what he captured into black and white during editing.“I think the change emphasises the graphic and cinematic nature of the composition,” he says. “The drama of the clouds in black and white adds sculptural weight, and the bird helps to anthropomorphise the machine, turning it into a lonely character gazing out at an empty beach.”Tidying up, or erasing elements, like the swooping seagull or smudge of heaped sand, was out of the question, however: “The ethics of street photography forbid altering an image in that way.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Notes from a nursing home: ‘Our books told of who we were. The story of us. Then the movers came and asked what should go’ | Books | The Guardian
description: Pencil marks in the margins of books gathered over a lifetime was proof of a life lived. So when it came time for Andrew McKean to move into aged care, leaving his books behind made the self thinner
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pencil marks in the margins of books gathered over a lifetime was proof of a life lived. So when it came time for Andrew McKean to move into aged care, leaving his books behind made the self thinner
Content: ‘Leaving the books was leaving the rooms where we had been younger.’Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen‘Leaving the books was leaving the rooms where we had been younger.’Composite: Guardian DesignBooksNotes from a nursing home: ‘Our books told of who we were. The story of us. Then the movers came and asked what should go’Pencil marks in the margins of books gathered over a lifetime was proof of a life lived. So when it came time forAndrew McKeanto move into aged care, leaving his books behind made the self thinnerAndrew McKeanSat 1 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 21.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy wife, Patricia, and I came to our nursing home with little more than clothes, a few photographs and some books we could still carry. The shelves we left behind still stand in the emptied rooms of the house we called home for 30 years. Those shelves once groaned under the weight of books we had gathered, page by page, year by year.Notes from a nursing home: ‘We don’t speak of sadness here’Read moreOur books told ofwho we were, or who we thought we might become. There were the novels Patricia read in the long evenings after the children slept, their spines cracked from her hands. There were the histories I brought home from the library sales, dusty volumes of wars and voyages that filled the quiet hours when rain beat on the roof. Poetry too, slim books with thin paper, marked where a line struck true. We kept them not only for the stories printed inside but for the story they made of us.The day came when the movers stood in the doorway and asked what should go. We had known it would come. The nursing home allows only a small cabinet beside the bed. Four or five volumes at most. The rest must be given away or sold or simply left for strangers to claim. Patricia sat in the armchair and looked at the ranks of titles as though they were faces she would not see again. I walked the length of the shelves and touched the backs of books I had not opened in decades.What struck hardest were the notes in the margins. In one novel of mine a pencil mark still shows where I disagreed with the hero’s choice. In Patricia’s copy of a memoir, she had written a single word beside a paragraph about loss. That word was “yes”. Elsewhere a date appears in the corner of a page, the day we first read it together by the fire. Those marks were private conversations with the print, small proofs that we had lived inside those pages. To give the books away was to give away the proof.We packed a few to keep. One slim volume of poems for Patricia, the one she could recite without looking. One fat history for me, its maps still folded at the end, and a precious paperback of James Joyce, Dubliners, where in Araby the unnamed adult narrator describes the former tenant of Joyce’s childhood home, a priest, who died there, and left behind a few paper-covered books, the pages of which were curled and damp: The Abbot, by Walter Scott, The Devout Communicant, and The Memoirs of Vidocq. The rest of our books went into boxes. I remember the sound of the tape sealing those boxes. It was a dry, final sound. Patricia did not cry, but her hands stayed on the last shelf longer than they needed to.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeet the members of the Dull Men’s Club: ‘Some of them would bore the ears off you’Read moreLeaving the books was leaving the rooms where we had been younger. The chairs by the window, the lamp that threw a circle of light on the open page, the habit of reaching for a particular volume when the day turned sour. Those habits formed a kind of self. Without the shelves the self felt thinner. Who was the man who once knew the order of every title? That man stayed behind with the books. The man who walks the corridor of the nursing home is a smaller edition, abridged. Yet here, though our room holds so little space for our own, the common rooms carry shelves stacked high with books left by those who came before us. Volumes of every kind lean together, novels and histories and poems, their pages turned by many hands. Anyone may take them, read them, return them. They are not ours, and the margins hold no marks of ours, yet they stand open for the days that remain.I can still close my eyes and see the blue spine of the travel book we bought the year we thought we might cross the sea. I can hear Patricia’s voice reading aloud from the novel she loved best. The margins we marked are gone, but the memory of marking them is not. In this narrow room the few books we kept lean against each other on the cabinet. When I open one I find the old pencil lines still speaking of the hours we spent with them. The print is the same. Only the room has changed, and the man who holds the book.Andrew McKean is a writer and a resident of an aged care facility in New South Wales, AustraliaExplore more on these topicsBooksAged careAgeingAustralian lifestylefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We didn’t feel safe’: Booking.com users face battle to get money back | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: From melted electric sockets to shabby alternatives, readers tell of dealings with platform when things go wrong
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: From melted electric sockets to shabby alternatives, readers tell of dealings with platform when things go wrong
Content: One family ‘were forced to find and pay for alternative accommodation for the remaining four nights at a further cost of £334’ during a trip to Batumi, Georgia.Photograph: Sergey Alimov/GettyView image in fullscreenOne family ‘were forced to find and pay for alternative accommodation for the remaining four nights at a further cost of £334’ during a trip to Batumi, Georgia.Photograph: Sergey Alimov/GettyConsumer affairs‘We didn’t feel safe’: Booking.com users face battle to get money backFrom melted electric sockets to shabby alternatives, readers tell of dealings with platform when things go wrongShane HickeySat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJane Ripley* spent some time researching the best apartment to stay in for her family’s trip to Batumi in Georgia, eventually settling on one with an “exceptional” rating on Booking.com.But when the Ripleys arrived at 11pm on the first day, they were directed to another property that was shabby and had stains on the furniture and ceiling.“The host was unfriendly … We had genuine concerns about raising complaints directly. We were forced to find and pay for alternative accommodation for the remaining four nights at a further cost of £334,” she says.Ripley made a series of complaints, starting the day after they arrived at the property. She says the property has since been removed from the site, but despite asking for a full refund of £570 for the original booking and the replacement accommodation, she has been offered only £36 in credits.She is one of a number of readers who have contacted Guardian Money with stories of trying to get their money back after booking with the travel platform.Millions of people use accommodation platforms such as Booking.com, Airbnb and Vrbo each year without a hitch, butwhen things go wrong, the sites’ terms and conditions suggest the companies have no liability for compensating people.This remains a grey area in law – and holidaymakers are ending up out of pocket as a result.T&CsIf you have difficulties with your hotel when you book a package deal, you will be covered financially and legally by the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018, which means the holiday operator is responsible for sorting out any problems – from disruption caused by wildfires to the hotel not being up to scratch.But if you book accommodation through Booking.com, the terms state that the contract is between you and the host. “When you make (or request) a booking, it’s directly with the service provider – we’re not a ‘contractual party’,” say the terms and conditions.View image in fullscreenReaders have been frustrated by Booking.com’s inability to force hosts to refund them.Photograph: Mateusz Słodkowski/SOPA Images/ShutterstockAs a result, getting compensation or your money back is not as clearcut.It is a similar story when booking with Airbnb, according to itsterms and conditions. And also Vrbo, which says agreements are between guests and the travel providers. “We are not a party to any such agreements,” it says.The consumer campaigner Martyn James says that by stating they are not part of the contract, these companies can argue they are only acting as a conduit and are not responsible for the supply of goods or services.“This hasn’t really been tested in law massively, but I’d be willing to bet that the courts would take a dim view of the businesses operating in these grey areas,” he saysComplaintsTravellers who have contacted Guardian Money have been frustrated by Booking.com’s inability to force hosts to pay up.Before arriving at a hotel he had booked in Mongolia, John Taylor* was charged £1,177 – £120 more than the agreed price. When he cancelled, there was no refund, he says, even though free cancellation was part of the booking.After “rounds of chasing” and giving Booking.com evidence of the payment, he was told by the website he was entitled to a refund but that the hotel had not engaged with Booking.com. He had still not received a refund when he contacted the Guardian in April. It eventually arrived in the middle of June.View image in fullscreenOne reader faced accommodation problems during a weekend break in Paris last summer.Photograph: Tom Nicholson/ReutersAnother reader, Kate Worthing*, booked a Parisian apartment for a weekend last summer. It was described as having an “elegant and refined” location. But the apartment building was in the middle of a refurbishment, with uncovered electrical wires in the communal hallway, and there were automatic lights that did not function. The rental itself contained worn fixtures and fittings and a melted electrical socket, she says.“The main reason we left was because we didn’t feel safe. The electrical faults and wooden staircase, with no discernible fire escape, were not an option, and we were not prepared to put our family at risk,” she says. When she managed to contact the host, she was refused a refund of the £1,700 she had paid, as they claimed it was safe.Booking.com told her that it “facilitates reservations between guests and accommodation partners, and in refund matters we are bound by the property’s policies and their final decision on waiving fees”.It said it could not issue a full refund but offered £417 in travel credits as compensation.Guardian Money contacted Booking.com about these and other cases. It said the hotel or apartment owner is responsible for providing refunds if something goes awry.“We’d expect our accommodation partners to be on hand for guests during their stay, but if there is an issue at check-in, customers should contact us as soon as possible,” it said.“As well as relocations, we can also advocate on their behalf and raise issues directly with the accommodation provider, and work to reach a resolution. If there are repeated issues with a property, we can and will address these with the accommodation owner to ensure future guests have a good experience.”For travellers worried about being caught in the gap between a platform and a host, James says people should try to book directly with the provider, but use caution.“I use these [aggregator] sites to compare and contrast, then look into booking direct,” he says. “If you call the hotel, you might even get a discount from them for doing so. Watch out for private apartments, though. This is where fakes have lurked, and any firm that asks you to pay by bank transfer knows that you can’t recall the money if things go wrong.”* Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsConsumer affairsTravel & leisureConsumer rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Intense, salty, foul’: the best (and worst) supermarket anchovies, tasted and rated | Food | The Guardian
description: We put 10 tinned and jarred varieties to the test to see which anchovies are the best catch for your cash
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: We put 10 tinned and jarred varieties to the test to see which anchovies are the best catch for your cash
Content: Ready, salted: all the anchovies were eaten straight from the tins or jars.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreenReady, salted: all the anchovies were eaten straight from the tins or jars.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.The FilterFoodReview‘Intense, salty, foul’: the best (and worst) supermarket anchovies, tasted and ratedWe put 10 tinned and jarred varieties to the test to see which anchovies are the best catch for your cashThe best supermarket tinned sardinesTom HuntSat 1 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.To taste these anchovies, I invited a friend, the food journalist and author Sudi Pigott, to join me. Arriving with a packet of Pujadó Solano anchovies and her new book, Consider the Anchovy, in hand, she and I tasted 10 brands of anchovies straight from the tin or jar with sparkling water and cucumber to cleanse the palate. According to Pigott, the best anchovies are “juicy, plump and velvety, with a sweet, nutty taste of jamón!”The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The anchovy supply chain has been heavily affected by El Niño, which caused abnormal weather events in Peru, where the most economical anchovies in our test were fished. But premium anchovies sourced from the Bay of Biscay (the Cantabrian Sea) have also faced external pressures. A lack of supply, among other factors, has increased prices and left some supermarket shelves bare.We scored anchovies on appearance, texture (including pin bones), flavour and value. I was shocked at the variation in quality in this category from minnow-sized, stubbly and tough brown fillets that were unbelievably salty to the most remarkably flavoured, tender, rose-coloured fillets that reminded us of serrano ham.The best supermarket anchoviesBest overall:Waitrose No 1 Cantabrian anchovy fillets in extra-virgin olive oilView image in fullscreen£1.75 for 50g at Waitrose (£3.50/100g)★★★★☆Small, dusky-pink fillets. Seductively sweet, smooth and salty but well balanced in flavour. Creamy and soft in texture, with a few hairy bones. Caught in the north-east Atlantic. MSC certified.Best bargain:Tesco Finest Cantabrian anchovy fillets in oilView image in fullscreen£2.95 for 100g at Tesco (£2.95/100g)★★★☆☆Medium-large, broad and even-coloured rosy-pink fillets. Smooth and rich, with a complex umami flavour, though still a little salty and some bones left in. Cured for a minimum of 12 months. MSC certified and caught in the Cantabrian Sea.And the rest …Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Cantabrian anchovy filletsView image in fullscreen£2.50 for 74g at Sainsbury’s (£3.38/100g)★★★★☆A wide, flat tin of beautifully presented, large, broad, rosy-pink fillets. Very salty, but with a creamy, melt-in-the-mouth texture and a well-rounded flavour, plus a lovely nutty, cured note of jamón serrano. Caught in the north-east Atlantic, packed in Spain. MSC certified.Ortiz anchovies in olive oilView image in fullscreen£7.15 for 47.5g at Ocado (£15.05/100g)£8.80 for 47.5g at the Fish Society (£18.53/100g)★★★★☆Medium-size fillets with a sweet, perfumed aroma. A milder salt content than most, which leads to a more balanced flavour: still sharp but complex, hammy, nutty and sweet. Ortiz was established in 1891 and is often seen as the benchmark for high-quality artisanal anchovies. Fished in the Cantabrian Sea, packed in Spain.M&S Collection Cantabrian anchovy fillets in extra-virgin olive oilView image in fullscreen£1.75 for 30g at Ocado (£5.83/100g)★★★☆☆Narrow, slightly bony fillets, with a varied brown-pink colour. An inviting floral, perfumed aroma. Sweet and nutty, with an intense flavour. Matured for six months. Fished in the Cantabrian Sea, packed in Morocco.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEpicure anchovy fillets in extra-virgin olive oilView image in fullscreen£2.55 for 50g at Ocado (£5.10/100g)£2.60 for 50g at Ocado (£5.20/100g)★☆☆☆☆Small, hairy fillets, with a sweet but very salty and intense flavour. Packed in Spain. Fishing location not stated.Aldi the Fishmonger anchovy fillets in extra virgin olive oilView image in fullscreen79p for 50g at Aldi (£1.58/100g), in store only★☆☆☆☆A tin of small, ragged fillets with a dark brown centre and pale edge (indicating a lack of freshness or heat damage). A fishy cat-food aroma, a very firm bite, and an intense, salty, sharp flavour. Caught in the south-east Pacific and packed in Peru.Asda Exceptional Cantabrian anchovy fillets in extra-virgin olive oilView image in fullscreen£2.90 for 100g at Asda (£2.90/100g)★☆☆☆☆Small, bristly, almost hairy fillets packed in a jar of extra-virgin olive oil. A sharp, intense and very salty flavour. OK for cooking, but rather one-dimensional. Fished in the north-east Atlantic, Bay of Biscay. Packed in Spain. MSC certified.Morrisons anchovy fillets in olive oilView image in fullscreen£1 for 50g at Morrisons (£2/100g)☆☆☆☆☆A tin of small, varied and thin fillets, with a dark, broad blood line and strong fishy aroma. Super-intense, deep but harsh flavour and unyielding, tough fillets. Caught in the south-east Pacific.John West anchovy fillets in olive oilView image in fullscreen£3.20 for 95g at Tesco (£3.37/100g)£3.20 for 95g at Sainsbury’s (£3.37/100g)☆☆☆☆☆Small fillets packed in sunflower oil with just 4.7% extra-virgin olive oil! Surprising, considering it is named on the label. Very intense, salty, foul and loose texture. Overpriced, full of pin bones, and made with preservative sodium benzoate. Caught in the south-east Pacific, produced in Peru.For more, read thebest (and worst) supermarket sushiandthe best supermarket vine tomatoesExplore more on these topicsFoodThe FilterFishSeafoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why generations swear by hot caldo – ‘a Mexican Gatorade’ – in summer | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Across Latin American households in the US, the steaming broth nourishes while keeping family traditions alive
Author: Melissa Hellmann
Headline: Across Latin American households in the US, the steaming broth nourishes while keeping family traditions alive
Content: ‘It’s a dish that evokes memories for Puerto Ricans and brings out many emotions,’ chef Natalia Vallejo says.Photograph: Rafael Ruiz Medero/Discover Puerto RicoView image in fullscreen‘It’s a dish that evokes memories for Puerto Ricans and brings out many emotions,’ chef Natalia Vallejo says.Photograph: Rafael Ruiz Medero/Discover Puerto RicoUS immigrationWhy generations swear by hot caldo – ‘a Mexican Gatorade’ – in summerAcross Latin American households in the US, the steaming broth nourishes while keeping family traditions aliveMelissa HellmannSat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Patty Rodriguez hears the wordcaldonow, she thinks fondly of home. But as a child growing up in southernCalifornia, she despised eating the piping-hot soup-like meal during the summers. Rodriguez would swirl around the chunks of fish with her spoon and imagine that she was performing a magic trick where the dish disappeared. She would roll her eyes as she asked her family why they served the dish more often when it was hot outside. “This is not a hotel,” Rodriguez recalled her mother and aunts saying. “You don’t choose what you want to eat. You’re going to eat what we make.”As an adult, Rodriguez realizes thatcaldo, which translates to broth in Spanish, was an inexpensive meal that could feed her Mexican American household for several days. It provided the nourishment and hydration needed during the hot summer months.A common dish served throughout Latin America,caldoboastsregional variationsin places including Mexico, Puerto Rico and El Salvador. The broth often features whole pieces of meat and chunks of vegetables such as carrots, potatoes and corn on the cob. While the hot meal is served year round, in some cultures it is paradoxically more popular during the summer months. For first- and second-generation Latin Americans,caldois more than just a meal; it’s a cultural touchstone that connects them to their heritage and helps them honor their families.“Now it’s love,” Rodriguez said as she choked back tears. She’s now the co-founder ofLil’ Libros, a children’s bilingual media company. While working as a radio producer for 20 years, Rodriguez was often the only Latina in her workplace; she yearned to share her culture with her teammates and the audience. Her relationship withcaldoevolved as she learned to accept her Mexican American culture. “I was rejecting not just the food,” said Rodriguez, “but I was rejecting my identity.”In recent years, Rodriguez is elated whenever her mother calls to share that she’s madecaldo de pollo, which includes pieces of chicken. “I get the kids in the car and I drive to my mom’s house,” Rodriguez said. “I want my children to experience this with her.”View image in fullscreenAcaldo de albóndigas, or meatball broth, that Patty Guzman made for her two sons.Photograph: Courtesy of Patty RodriguezRamon Guzman, a 33-year-old creative director at the Crazy Gorilla and Vezcos Media, still has ambivalent feelings towardscaldo. He makescomedy skitson YouTube about Mexican American culture and has poked fun at the dish in several videos over the past decade. In a2021 video, Guzman imitated a Mexican mother who refused to let her son turn on the air conditioning and forced him to eatcaldoas he profusely sweated through his shirt.The skit reflected his childhood growing up as a first-generation Mexican American in San Bernardino,California. “The main emotions were confusion and suffering,” Guzman said, recalling eatingcaldoas a child. “I did not enjoy eatingcaldoin the summer. I’m already sweating, and then eating thecaldomakes me sweat even more.”Guzman now realizes that the dish provided comfort to his mother, whose family made it for her as a child growing up in Mexico. The dish has followed Guzman into his adulthood; his girlfriend, who is also Mexican American, serves it to him more often during the summer, when she says that she craves it the most.Caldo’s salt and nutrients make it tantamount to “a Mexican Gatorade”, he said.Guzman sees the dish as a tool to teach pain tolerance that has been passed down through generations. He described eating the meal during the summer as “layers and layers of a little pain” that helps people learn to weather the vicissitudes of life. “I will try to dabble in it and make my own version of it whenever I have kids,” Guzman said. “It makes you a bit stronger and more resilient … I’m sure I’m going to be thinking of my mom when I feed it to my future kids.”Caldo is also popular in Puerto Rico. At the San Juan restaurant Cocina al Fondo, chef Natalia Vallejo said thatcaldo de gallina– a stew that features hen meat, plantains and herbs – is requested by diners more often during the summer. “This dish is deeply connected to my childhood,” she said. “The recipe is inspired by acaldomy paternal grandfather used to make. He cooked it over a wood fire. It’s a dish that evokes memories for Puerto Ricans and brings out many emotions.”Vallejo, who won theJames Beard Best Chef: Southaward in 2023, viewscaldoas a portal into her past. Her family would usecaldofor other recipes. “My favorite memory is that we used the broth to make wood-fired chicken and rice, which was wrapped in banana leaves,” Vallejo said. “It was delicious.”In Aelen Trujillo’s family,caldoserved a practical purpose on the hottest days when they wanted to minimize active cooking time. As the dish simmered on the stove, her Mexican grandmother would step away from the warm kitchen so that she wouldn’t overheat. Trujillo, a 24-year-old content creator and stay-at-home mom, now cookscaldofor her family during the summer because it reminds her of her grandmother.She ensures that her young children eat recipes from each of their Mexican and Central American heritages so that they remember their origins. “My grandparents once they came here they had to assimilate and they didn’t have a lot of things. A lot of the culture or the tradition that they had growing up you never really celebrated,” said Trujillo, who is a first-generation Mexican and Honduran American. “Food was the only way that I was able to connect with my culture and feel more Mexican or to touch those roots.”Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationCaliforniaMexican food and drinkFoodWest CoastAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for oyster mushroom burgers with five-spice slaw | Burgers | The Guardian
description: These roasted oyster mushrooms are meaty, savoury and chewy, made even more satisfying in a south-east Asian-style dressing
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: These roasted oyster mushrooms are meaty, savoury and chewy, made even more satisfying in a south-east Asian-style dressing
Content: Meera Sodha's oyster mushroom burgers with five spice cabbage.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha's oyster mushroom burgers with five spice cabbage.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.Meera Sodha recipesBurgersMeera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for oyster mushroom burgers with five-spice slawThese roasted oyster mushrooms are meaty, savoury and chewy, made even more satisfying in a south-east Asian-style dressingMeera SodhaSat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot every plant makes a great burger filling. You might think pulses or potatoes for heft, but the lack of texture and propensity to mush can be unsatisfying. This is where mushrooms excel; they trade in satisfaction. Roasting them brings out their natural umami and removes water content, leaving them chewy, caramelised and occasionally crisp. They can also make friends with the most unlikely of ingredients, like they have here with peanut butter, soy, agave and sesame.Oyster mushroom burgers with five-spice cabbageWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appNow, two types of agave syrup are available in the supermarkets: dark is richer, more caramelly; lighter is simpler and more neutral. If you only have or can find light, use that. These mushrooms can be cooked on skewers on a barbecue, but do so over indirect heat under a watchful eye.Prep10 minCook30 minServes4For the mushrooms600g oyster mushrooms60g smooth peanut butter2 tbsp toasted sesame oil1 tbsp dark agave syrup2 tbsp red or brownmiso1½ tbsp light soy sauce1 tbsp apple cider vinegar3 garlic cloves, peeled and mincedFor the five-spice cabbage200g white cabbage, finely shredded5 spring onions, trimmed, greens and whites finely shredded½ tsp fine sea salt½ tsp ground five-spice1½ tbsp apple cider vinegar15g coriander leaves, finely chopped1 tbsp mayonnaise, plus extra to serve4 brioche burger buns, to serveHeat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9, and line two trays with baking paper.If your mushrooms are in big clumps, break them gently into individual mushrooms and put them in a large bowl. Put the peanut butter, sesame oil, agave, miso, soy sauce, vinegar and garlic in a small bowl, stir until you have a smooth sauce, then pour this over the mushrooms.Using your hands like claws in an arcade machine, carefully toss to cover all the mushrooms in the sauce. Spread the mushrooms over the two trays, then bake for 12-15 minutes, until all the liquid has dried out and the edges are charred, then remove from the oven.While the mushrooms are cooking, make the slaw. Put the cabbage and spring onions in a big bowl, sprinkle over the salt and scrunch with (clean) hands. Mix through all the other salad ingredients.To assemble the burgers, split and toast the brioche buns – one minute in a toaster works well. Spread one cut side of each bun with mayo, pile on a quarter of the mushrooms, then top with some slaw. Repeat with the other burgers, clap on the lids and serve.Explore more on these topicsBurgersMeera Sodha recipesFoodVegetablesMain courseVegetarian food and drinkNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘I joked we should join the young people for a club night. We didn’t’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Richard, 63, a communications consultant, meets Katrina, 60, a GP
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Richard, 63, a communications consultant, meets Katrina, 60, a GP
Content:
Composite: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘I joked we should join the young people for a club night. We didn’t’Richard, 63, a communications consultant, meets Katrina, 60, a GPSat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenRichard on KatrinaWhat were you hoping for?Easy conversation with someone interesting, smart and relaxed.First impressions?Katrina arrived and my blind date trepidation vanished. She looked good, was warm, and the conversation flowed straight away.What did you talk about?Our grownup kids. Running. Travel. Our devotion to our coffee machines.Most awkward moment?I thought Katrina was still working her way through her post-meal mint tea, so was taken aback when she said, “Shall we call it a night?”Good table manners?Impeccable.Best thing about Katrina?She is great company.Would you introduce Katrina to your friends?Yes. I’m sure she gets on really well with most people.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Katrina in three wordsCalm, warm, open.What do you think Katrina made of you?She laughed at a few things I said, and we had quite a few things in common, so I think she felt I was easy company.Did you go on somewhere?As we left the restaurant and saw a queue of young people outside a bar, I joked that we should join them for a club night. We didn’t.And … did you kiss?No.If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be?Nothing. I had a fun evening with a lovely woman and don’t think it could have been improved.Marks out of 10?A strong 8.Would you meet again?I really enjoyed Katrina’s company, we talked and laughed a lot. So of course.View image in fullscreenRichard and Katrina on their date.View image in fullscreenKatrina on RichardWhat were you hoping for?To finally meet “the one”.First impressions?Polite, relaxed and quietly handsome.What did you talk about?Coffee snobbery – our coffee machines (identical), the best beans, our children aspiring to own the same machine.Most awkward moment?Arriving late.Good table manners?Impeccable. Attentive without ever being overbearing.Best thing about Richard?He’s a great conversationalist.Would you introduce Richard to your friends?Of course.Describe Richard in three wordsWarm, genuine, polite.What do you think Richard made of you?I hope he saw me as warm, approachable and engaging.Did you go on somewhere?No. We looked at the club opposite, but agreed that wasn’t going to happen.Blind date: ‘I should have made a move, but I’m not good at that sort of thing’Read moreAnd … did you kiss?No. Just a polite and rather formal goodbye.If you could change one thing about the evening what would it be?Honestly, not much. I really enjoyed the evening, and for a blind date it exceeded my expectations.Marks out of 10?9/10.Would you meet again?Possibly, as friends – I’m not sure there was a romantic spark, but I really enjoyed his company. I’d happily introduce him to the joys of the hill at Ashton Court parkrun.Katrina and Richard ate atMarmo in Bristol. Fancy a blind date?
