title: Jess Cartner-Morley’s August style essentials: lace trims, snazzy knits and one truly beautiful bag | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Whether you’re in full summer mode or quietly planning for autumn, our fashion expert’s monthly picks will carry you stylishly between the two
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Whether you’re in full summer mode or quietly planning for autumn, our fashion expert’s monthly picks will carry you stylishly between the two
Content: View image in fullscreenJess Cartner-Morley‘s editFashionJess Cartner-Morley’s August style essentials: lace trims, snazzy knits and one truly beautiful bagWhether you’re in full summer mode or quietly planning for autumn, our fashion expert’s monthly picks will carry you stylishly between the twoHow to create the perfect women’s holiday capsule wardrobeJess Cartner-MorleySat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.August: do you buy for the holiday you’ll be melting through this month, or the one you’ll be pretending to enjoy in a jumper come October? Answers on a postcard, please! The key to staying (relatively) sane in silly season is to embrace the contradictions.The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Read on for the holiday-coded necklace I’ve fallen in love with and the elegant leather handbag I’m dreaming of when I hang up my straw basket. Plus, a lace camisole and a cosy jumper – and the absolute sweetest grip socks for my pilates girlies.Ballerina-style pilates grip socksH&MBallet socks£8.50£8.50 at H&MView image in fullscreenBallet socks£8.50 at H&MI’ve done reformer pilates for years, and I am a little bit touchy about the stereotype of the pristine blonde, ponytailed pilates princess. We are not all like that! Old black cycling shorts and whatever comes out of the T-shirt drawer works for me. But now that most studios insist on them for safety, I’ve had to buy more grip socks, and when I spotted these on the woman next to me in class, I had to grill her for deets. They are ridiculous but fun. I like to tie the ribbons around my ankles, Noel Streatfeild-style.H&MBallet socks£8.50£8.50 at H&MThe coolest summer necklaceL’Atelier 73Palm Tree pendant necklace£30£30 at L’Atelier 73View image in fullscreenPalm tree pendant necklace£30 at L’Atelier 73L’Atelier 73 is a new-ish London brand that I love for interesting, affordable jewellery. My current crush is these summer pendant necklaces – this one is a palm tree, but there’s alsothe sunor acactus– in colourful, enamel-plated copper. The colourful woven rope braid is adjustable so you can change the length to suit your shirt’s neckline or to complement shorter necklaces.L’Atelier 73Palm Tree pendant necklace£30£30 at L’Atelier 73Your scented ‘candle’ for summerDropletOrange blossom reed diffuser£40£40 at DropletView image in fullscreenOrange blossom reed diffuser£40 at DropletReed diffusers work brilliantly for home fragrance, but most of them look hideous. I don’t want to wait for cosy candle season for my home to smell nice, but I also don’t want my bathroom to look like a cheap Airbnb. The answer? This beautiful hand-blown glass piece with a single reed diffuser, which looks as good in your hallway as a Diptyque candle. It’s from Droplet, a brand launched by siblings Sam and Lucie Beecham with a mission to combine Grasse-level fragrance with elevated London design. Available in several scents; I love the citrus-floral orange blossom, with notes of tuberose and magnolia.For more, read our guide to thebest diffusersDropletOrange blossom reed diffuser£40£40 at DropletMy new favourite hair maskNo98 BeautyHydra Bond hair mask£35£35 at No98 BeautyView image in fullscreenNo98 BeautyHydra Bond hair mask£35 at No98 BeautyFragile hair is a problem for me, so I’m endlessly searching for products that really help, and this does. OK, I admit, it was the extremely chic packaging of No98 Beauty that drew me in to start with – but it was the effectiveness of this, the brand’s bestselling product, that got me hooked from the first time I tried it. You have to put it on damp hair and leave it for 20 minutes before shampooing, which is a bit of a faff, but I run a bath, wet my hair and slather this on, then soak with a book or a podcast for a bit. It works!For more, read our guide to thebest hair masksNo98 BeautyHydra Bond hair mask£35£35 at No98 BeautyHave you looked at Topshop recently?TopshopOrganza shirt in light pinkfrom£38£38 at Topshop£38 at AsosView image in fullscreenOrganza shirt in light pink£38 at Topshop£38 at AsosThere has been a notable uptick in the number of Topshop pieces being worn on the fashion desk. There is good stuff in there again – and, as deputy fashion editor Chloe Mac Donnell pointed out, isn’t it nice to be able to buy Topshop and know the money isn’t going to Philip Green? I am very into thismonochrome lace column panel white maxi skirt, £45, but my top pick is this organza shirt. It’s such an elevated and charming eveningwear option over a colourful contrast bra or camisole.TopshopOrganza shirt in light pinkfrom£38£38 at Topshop£38 at AsosExcellent summer trousers from the posh bit of ZaraZara SrplsIvory cotton cargo trousers.£69.99£69.99 at Zara SrplsView image in fullscreenIvory cotton cargo trousers£69.99 at Zara SrplsI am pretty wary of ordering high-street fashion online – the fabric is so often disappointing – but I make an exception for Zara Srpls, which is a limited-edition seasonal collection. It’s described as “premium”, but the prices aren’t wildly higher than regular Zara. These perforated-cotton cargo trousers feel breezy and summery – tailored black trousers kill the vibe at this time of year – but they’re still dressy. I might swap out the matching fabric belt for a tan leather one when I want to sharpen things up.Zara SrplsIvory cotton cargo trousers.£69.99£69.99 at Zara SrplsHills I will die on: snazzy jumpers are an undercelebrated wardrobe categoryEssentiel AntwerpNavy, red and pink fine-knit cardigan£260£260 at Essentiel AntwerpView image in fullscreenNavy, red and pink fine-knit cardigan£260 at Essentiel AntwerpSeriously. There are so many occasions – from late night at a festival when it gets chilly to a restaurant dinner when you want to feel cosy but look snazzy – when a glam jumper is a wardrobe life-saver. In anticipation of the return of one of our most beloved designers, Christopher Kane, when he relaunches Mulberry at London fashion week next month, I’ve been stalking his classic knits on eBay – thisfringed hot pink number, new with tags, is £413.68, while thispreloved diamante-trim rollneckwent for£135.90. Of the newbies out there, my fave is this delicious Essentiel Antwerp cardigan-cum-autumn-jacket. The lace-trim collar! Strawberry buttons! Irresistible.Essentiel AntwerpNavy, red and pink fine-knit cardigan£260£260 at Essentiel AntwerpA truly beautiful handbagLongchampSmart L totefrom£730£730 at Longchamp£730 at FarfetchView image in fullscreenLe Smart L tote£730 at Longchamp£730 at FarfetchLongchamp’sLe Pliagebags, a timeless classic for every British teenager who likes to think of herself as half-Sorbonne, are very popular among gen Z right now. (They’re now recycled canvas; I think they used to be nylon.)The Le Pliagestarts at about £115, but Longchamp’s real hero products are the beautiful leather bags, crafted in the brand’s five ateliers in the Loire and Normandy. Le Smart L tote Bag is made from the most luxurious topstitched, grained cowhide leather, with a Hermès-adjacent threaded closure strap, internal snap fastening and subtle gold hardware. £730, but what price true love?LongchampSmart L totefrom£730£730 at Longchamp£730 at FarfetchKeep your feet free a while longerReissMabel woven flat denim sandalsfrom£158£158 at Reiss£158 at John LewisView image in fullscreenMabel woven flat denim sandals£158 at Reiss£158 at John LewisClosed-toe shoe season will come for us all, but it is not here yet. A simple flat mule is the most elegant style of sandal. More grownup than a flip-flop or ahiking sandal, it is smart enough for work or to wear with a dress for dinner. These Reiss sandals are made from comfortable knotted open weave, with a padded sole and a cute 2cm heel. Perfect with white jeans, a linen button-down and shades.ReissMabel woven flat denim sandalsfrom£158£158 at Reiss£158 at John LewisUnderwear as outerwearM&SContrast lace trim cami top£36£36 at M&SView image in fullscreenContrast lace trim cami top£36 at M&SThis has been the year of bras visible under sheer layers, nighties on the beach. A lace camisole is the classic, and this one is a beauty: the colour is timeless, the eyelash lace looks swanky, the straps are adjustable.M&SContrast lace trim cami top£36£36 at M&SExplore more on these topicsFashionJess Cartner-Morley‘s editWomen's hairWomen's jewelleryHandbagsHair careWomen's topsSkirtsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: No apologies, no freebies: the man who makes Andy Burnham’s jackets on how to weather a storm | Men's fashion | The Guardian
description: Private White VC’s James Eden says PM should not be criticised for wearing a high-quality British-made brand
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Private White VC’s James Eden says PM should not be criticised for wearing a high-quality British-made brand
Content: James Eden (left) says he ‘remains apolitical’, even though the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, is now his company’s most high-profile client.Photograph: Private White VCView image in fullscreenJames Eden (left) says he ‘remains apolitical’, even though the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, is now his company’s most high-profile client.Photograph: Private White VCMen's fashionInterviewNo apologies, no freebies: the man who makes Andy Burnham’s jackets on how to weather a stormChloe Mac DonnellPrivate White VC’s James Eden says PM should not be criticised for wearing a high-quality British-made brandSat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 09.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has not yet been two weeks since James Eden, the founder of the Manchester men’s clothier Private White VC, saw one of his best-known customers move in to No 10 Downing Street.In any sane world the man who makes the prime minister’s jackets would be popping open the champagne. His garments have been seen by millions of people and described by journalists all over the world writing about Burnham’s buttoned-down style.Instead, Eden, a proud advocate of British manufacturing, has found himself defending his company in the face of a media onslaught.“‘Man of the people’ Andy Burnham’s down-to-earth outfits are all actually designer – including an £80 T-shirt … that’s more than he cut electricity bills by,” said the Daily Mail in a front-page story.A slew of online hate followed, with commentators accusing the PM of being a hypocrite for wearing expensive clothes when voters’ personal finances are stretched.Eden’s clothes are not cheap, a fact he is proud of. And, perhaps typically for a man whose company was founded by his Victoria Cross-winning great-grandfather Jack, he is not going to take the “outrageous” criticism lying down.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham is a loyal customer of Private White VC. Other high-profile clients include David Beckham and Liam Gallagher.Photograph: Private White VC“There should be no cynicism or criticism about a British PM promoting British goods,” he says. “There’s nothing to debate. He is the premier spokesperson of British trade and industry. Of course he should be wearing British-made stuff.”Eden is speaking to the Guardian from the 173-year-old Manchester mill where every piece of the brand’s clothing is designed, cut and stitched together. He describes Burnham as “down-to-earth” and a “proud Mancunian”, saying the PM first started buying from the brand about three years ago.Burnham’s dress sense is just one of many points of difference between “the king in the north” and his stuffier predecessor, Keir Starmer. The former Manchester mayor’s look is rooted in the casual style of north-west England.It is here that Eden, a former investment banker, runs the clothing manufacturing business his great-grandfather established in the 1940s.While Jack White’s company focused on raincoats, Eden’s label includes ready-to-wear alongside bespoke tailoring. Employing about 100 people, 90% of its products are made in the mill that overlooks the River Irwell, while the other 10% come from small independent suppliers, including cashmere from Scotland.Such a focus on handcrafted items made by local craftspeople comes with a high price tag. Burnham’s waterproof Harrington jacket costs £695, his ‘ “marine” jeans £295 and a zipped polo shirt £195.Eden does not shy away from these prices. In fact, as one of the last survivors of Britain’s once-thriving manufacturing industry, he is keen to talk about numbers.“I don’t believe we are expensive at all,” he says. “We offer a world-class product. We don’t compromise on quality. We work with the best of the best, including the best weavers and the best finishers.” On average, Eden pays his workers £20 per hour, “not the €2 you’d get in a factory in eastern Europe or 20 pence in the far east”. His longest-serving employee has been working for the family’s companies nearly 60 years.Due to the widespread impact of fast fashion, super-low prices and a throwaway culture around clothing have become normalised, especially in the UK.View image in fullscreenBurnham’s purchase of Private White VC clothing has prompted criticism from the rightwing tabloids, but the company’s founder says 99% of its proceeds stay within the local community and the UK.Photograph: Paul Groom/Private White VC“I understand there is an affordability issue with many of the items we sell,” he says. “[But] if you spend £10 or even £50 on a piece of clothing and it collapses after one wash, that suddenly becomes a very expensive piece of clothing,” he says.On Instagram, Eden has posted videos where he breaks down where a customer’s money goes when they buy an item from the brand. He estimates that 99% of an £850 jacket stays in the UK economy.“Sourcing things from local suppliers and employing people locally, all those proceeds stay within the local community and within the UK,” he says. The person who maintains the mill’s boiler started as an apprentice in the 1980s, his full-time customer service team all live locally, and every photographer, stylist and makeup artist for its shoots is Manchester-based.It is bright news in an industry that over the past decade has found itself in a fight for survival. According to the British Retail Consortium there have been more than 400,000 retail jobs lost since 2016 whileseveral British brandshave closed or been sold off.While Burnham has been quick to cut business rates forthe hospitality industry, Eden says an easy win for the fashion industry is to allocate a proportion of defence and NHS apparel-making to UK manufacturers, the bulk of which are made in Bangladesh and China.During the pandemic, Eden’s factory was awarded a PPE contract. He hired dozens of extra staff to make millions of medical-grade gowns and face masks. He has since repurposed the specialist equipment to make jersey collections, meaning he was able to retain many of those extra workers.“If the Ministry of Defence or the NHS were to establish a supply chain here, the country could employ thousands of people,” he says. “At face value, the prices might not be cheaper than abroad, but that money and tax will stay in the towns where the factories are.”Eden says he is aware of some factories in the UK paying workers cash in hand and treating them unfairly. By contrast he compares his factory to “an open kitchen” where anyone is welcome to have a tour. Photos of Burnham doing just that sparked debate in the brand’s comment section, leading Eden to write on LinkedIn: “I knew posting about Andy Burnham was going to divide the city, the country.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham is ‘the premier spokesperson of British trade and industry’, says James Eden. ‘Of course, he should be wearing British-made stuff.’Photograph: Private White VCEden says he “remains apolitical”, stressing that he will support anyone who advocates for British-made products and local businesses.David Beckham and Liam Gallagher have also visited the mill, while other high-profile customers include Eddie Redmayne, Tom Hardy, Pierce Brosnan, the Eagles, Daniel Craig and Robert De Niro. The brand has never given anything to anyone for free.He suspects Burnham originally discovered the brand via word of mouth. “Our customers are incredibly loyal,” he says. “They wear our pieces because they absolutely love them. And then they end up talking to others about the story behind those pieces.”Eden has found that praise from the men that buy his clothing has much more impact than a paid influencer ever could. And his rule about no complimentary pieces applies even to the prime minister. “We wouldn’t consider anyone that is after a freebie,” says Eden. “It shows that they are not respecting the time, the labour, the tradition and all the hard bloody work that’s gone into what we do. They are not for us.”This article was amended on 1 August 2026 to describe James Eden as a former investment banker, rather than a former venture capitalist.Explore more on these topicsMen's fashionAndy BurnhamfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Exploring Rabat, Morocco – this year’s Unesco World Book Capital | Morocco holidays | The Guardian
description: Rabat is a gorgeous seaside city with great food and culture, but for book lovers there’s an added incentive to go this year
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rabat is a gorgeous seaside city with great food and culture, but for book lovers there’s an added incentive to go this year
Content: The Kasbah of the Oudayas in Rabat boasts tremendous views.Photograph: Sergio Formoso/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Kasbah of the Oudayas in Rabat boasts tremendous views.Photograph: Sergio Formoso/AlamyMorocco holidaysExploring Rabat, Morocco – this year’s Unesco World Book CapitalRabat is a gorgeous seaside city with great food and culture, but for book lovers there’s an added incentive to go this yearBen AitkenSat 1 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first book I read willingly was Bridget Jones’s Diary. I was 19. Up to that point, I hadn’t been much of a reader. I’d been more into football, or Baywatch, or Robin Budd in the year above – anything really. Given the choice between reading a book and staring at a wall, I would have plumped for the latter.After finishing my A-levels, I worked in a barbecue restaurant in Portsmouth – which is where I found Bridget Jones. The book was lying around in the staffroom. I picked it up and read a few pages, and then a few more, and then a few more. It felt exciting. Like I’d met someone. Like I was suddenly in a relationship. Over the next few days, I remember cancelling nights out so I could go to bed and read. My mum thought I was depressed.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsIt hardly matters what book gets you going. For Jeanette Winterson, it was the Book of Deuteronomy.For David Nicholls, it was Tales from Moominvalley. What matters is that a book gets you going. Throughout my 20s, I worked as a carer, but I was always reading and scribbling on the side. I became a published author seven years ago. It’s not an overstatement to say that Bridget Jones changed my life. That books did.So when I learned that 2026 wasNational Year of Reading(a UK-wide campaign intended to promote the importance and joy of reading) and that Rabat was to be this year’sUnesco World Book Capital(a rotating designation intended to promote the importance and joy of reading), I packed a few volumes and set off for Morocco’s capital. I was hoping for a cultural adventure, and perhaps a tagine, in this ancient seaside city perched scenically between Casablanca and Tangier.View image in fullscreenBen Aitken in Rabat, Morocco.Rabat was made the capital of Morocco in 1912, at the beginning of the turbulent 44-year period when the country found itself under the thumb of the French. The first thing I saw of the city was the New Town, or Ville Nouvelle, which was laid out in the 1920sà la française, meaning it looks nothing like the huge medieval medina that’s just up the road.From the central train station, I proceeded to the solar-poweredMohammed VI Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, where the permanent exhibition – Shifting Horizon(s) – does exactly what it says on the tin. Highlights include the abstract paintings ofMohamed Melehiand a provocative photograph byLalla Essaydi. Part of a series calledBullet Revisited, the latter shows a woman covered head to toe in gold bullets, and is a powerful indictment of the violence women suffer.I walked north to the medina, an irregular network of narrow streets lined with small shops flogging mint, slippers, strawberries andsabon beldi, a black soap made from the flesh and oil of olives. The medina was busy but calm. Not once was I asked to consider a carpet or sample a sardine. Indeed, I felt rather invisible. In this respect, the customer service was uncannily French.I followed my nose to the Kasbah of the Oudayas, an enchanting district of low whitewashed houses. Built on high ground in view of the ocean, this former royal citadel was ideally placed to spot visitors on the horizon, and greet them appropriately.After checking into a riad on Rue Bazou, I descended a flight of stone steps to the beach, a modest curve of sand where scores of people were playing football and volleyball. I crossed the cooling sand and climbed on to the breakwater to better observe a neon sun sink slowly seaward, as a lone surfer, way out in the offing, sought inch-perfect swell.View image in fullscreenEnticing streets in the Kasbah of the Oudayas.Photograph: Adam Smigielski/Getty Images/iStockphotoI took a pew at the beachsideRelais Marinrestaurant. I didn’t deliberate over the menu. Like casserole and paella, tagine is a dish in two senses; both the cooking vessel and the meal, on this occasion a confusion of lamb, almonds and prunes in a delicious gravy that, with time, had reduced to a bold, flavourful pesto, which I mopped up with chunks ofkhobz(Moroccan flatbread). I could have eaten another.The next morning I went to the Cafe des Oudayas. Situated next to the Andalusian Gardens – a wonderful place full of orange and pomegranate trees – this alfresco cafe offers three things: mint tea, biscuits and an excellent vantage point.As I eked out the tea, I watched a boy poised on the edge of a towering rock, 30 metres above the Bou Regreg river. Goaded by his friends, he meant to jump, but he hesitated for minutes in the intensifying sun. His dive, when it finally came, was a thing of beauty – a wide and graceful arc, shapely, immaculate, somewhat divine, almost unreal. The gallery held its breath until he re-emerged – to be met with disingenuous disdain.“La poule a attendu une éternité!”(The chicken waited for ever!) Lads, eh?View image in fullscreenA bookseller presides over his stock.Photograph: Nur Photo/Getty ImagesOn a whim, I boarded an electric tuk-tuk, one of 60 in the city. I asked the driver to take me directly to theChellah, a medieval necropolis that also houses what’s left of the Roman city of Sala Colonia, but, knowing best, the driver instead went out of his way to show off his home town, swinging by St Peter’s cathedral and a nightclub calledAmnesia, where Morocco’s king is said to have boogied back when merely a prince.The Chellah – when I finally got there – did not disappoint. After doing a round of the picturesque ruins, I climbed to a gorgeous onsite cafe and ordered the couscous. Befitting tradition, the dish comprised a pyramid of seven vegetables, a moat of couscous, a jug of broth and some meaty treasure hidden within the veg. It was unmistakablybon.If one requires beer in Rabat, one heads toLe Dhow, a bar and restaurant on a boat moored in the shadow of the kasbah. Sitting on the upper deck, I savoured an ice-cold pint while chatting with a British undergraduate studying at theUniversité Internationale de Rabat. I asked if she felt comfortable in the city. “It’s been fine,” she said. “Some men have said hello. One asked for a photo. To be honest, I’ve experienced a lot worse in Worcester.”I’m just going to come out and say this – don’t go to Rabat because it’s this year’s World Book Capital. Despite my best efforts, the exact nature of the 300-plus events the city is purportedly going to run during its year as WBC remain a mystery to me. Instead, go to Rabat because it’s an excellent city.C’est simple.On my final evening, I chanced on a humble bookshop in the medina – Bouquiniste El Azizi. Of the hundreds of preloved books assembled in the diminutive space, a dozen or so were in English. Among them was Bridget Jones’s Diary. I picked it up and read a few pages – and then left it for someone else to stumble on, and perhaps break their duck with.On leaving the shop, I noticed a sign:Les livres prennent soin de nous. Books take care of us. The sentiment strikes me as the right note to finish on.Ben Aitkenis the author of Shitty Breaks: A Celebration of Unsung Cities, £9.99. title: Fiona Allen: ‘The closest I’ve come to death? A trip in a black cab with John Worboys. I had a lucky escape’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The actor and comedian on her hatred of selfishness, her unhappy resting face, and why she dropped her agent
Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: The actor and comedian on her hatred of selfishness, her unhappy resting face, and why she dropped her agent
Content: Fiona Allen: ‘Last night I dreamed that I was Boudicca driving a chariot into Waitrose car park.’Photograph: Natasha PszenickiView image in fullscreenFiona Allen: ‘Last night I dreamed that I was Boudicca driving a chariot into Waitrose car park.’Photograph: Natasha PszenickiThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewFiona Allen: ‘The closest I’ve come to death? A trip in a black cab with John Worboys. I had a lucky escape’Rosanna GreenstreetThe actor and comedian on her hatred of selfishness, her unhappy resting face, and why she dropped her agentSat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in Lancashire, Fiona Allen, 61, went to drama school in Salford. From 1999, she co-wrote and starred in the Emmy-winning and Bafta-nominated TV sketch show Smack the Pony. She had roles in Shameless, Skins, Waterloo Road and EastEnders, and her films include 24 Hour Party People, Fat Slags, Gladiatress and Finding Emily. In 2023, she took her show On the Run to the Edinburgh festival fringe and later toured the UK. This year, she performs White Lies at Edinburgh’sGilded Balloon Teviotfrom 5 to 29 August. She is married with three children and lives in Berkshire.What is your greatest fear?My kids navigating the world as it is today – and daddy longlegs.What is your earliest memory?Nursery. I must have been about three. This little boy and me got these trikes and we went round and round, laughing. And then he went down the slide headfirst and I thought: “My hero.” We had a blast, but then they split us up and we weren’t allowed to play with each other.What is the trait you most deplore in others?Coldness, selfishness.Aside from a property, what’s the most expensive thing you’vebought?A sports car. I was in my 20s; I’d fallen out with my boyfriend, so to cheer myself up I got myself a little silver and black Mazda and a matching jumper and jacket. And do you know what, it worked. I saw him do a double take.What is your most treasured possession?A little dibber from my dad that was from his grandad, a jewellery box from my mum, and my olive trees.Describe yourself in three wordsPassionate, gobby, flabby.What do you most dislike about your appearance?My resting face, because people say: “Don’t worry, it might never happen.” And I think: “What? I’m really happy.”What is your most unappealing habit?I’m like an excitable puppy when I’m chatting, and I butt in.What is the worst thing anyone’ssaid to you?The second agent I had said: “The thing is, you look like something but then you open your mouth.” So I got myself a sketch show and left, and she lost out.What do you owe your parents?So many apologies.What did you dream about last night?I was Boudicca driving a chariot into Waitrose car park.If not yourself, who would you most like to be?My cockapoo, Herbert. He has a great, carefree life and tremendous eyelashes.What or who is the greatest love of your life?My dog – sorry, my family.Tuppence Middleton: ‘My guiltiest pleasure? Watching Naked Attraction when my partner is out’Read moreWhich living person do you most despise, and why?Amoral tech bros.What is the closest you’vecome to death?I think I had a close shave with the taxi driver John Worboys. I was in Soho and going back to Chiswick where I lived, and I got a black cab. This guy wouldn’t stop talking and he offered me champagne, and I said: “I don’t like champagne.” It went a bit quiet and I thought I’d offended him. Then I remember going: “Hang on a minute, you shouldn’t be drinking champagne if you’re driving.” And he said: “I’ve just won the lottery and I’m finished after this.” I had a lucky escape.What do you consider your greatest achievement?Growing three brains.How would you like to be remembered?She was surprisingly good at the harpsichord.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Q&ATV comedyComedyTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: can I conquer my wife’s book club? I can certainly divide it  | Family | The Guardian
description: She says I’m not allowed to select books as I’m the only man and not a full member. But how could they not love Death Comes for the Archbishop?
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: She says I’m not allowed to select books as I’m the only man and not a full member. But how could they not love Death Comes for the Archbishop?
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: can I conquer my wife’s book club? I can certainly divide itShe says I’m not allowed to select books as I’m the only man and not a full member. But how could they not love Death Comes for the Archbishop?Tim DowlingSat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 12.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy wife would have everyone in our book club believe that the First Rule of Book Club is: Tim Is Never Allowed to Pick the Book. Having failed in herseveral attempts to have me removed from book club, she has settled for imposing restrictions on my participation to make my membership seem second tier.“You’re not allowed to pick because you’re not really even in book club,” she says to me before every meeting. “You’re like a mascot.”“What are you talking about?” I always say. “I’m the beating heart of book club.”In truth, there is no First Rule of Book Club. There is, however, a longstanding protocol under which my suggestions are given less weight than anyone else’s. This is partly because I’m the only man and my opinions sometimes go against the grain of majority taste, and partly because the only time I did get to pick the book everyone loathed it, including me.But more than a year has passed since then, and on a night when my wife and I are hosting book club in our kitchen, I feel ready to try again.double quotation markI wake to find my wife staring at me over the top of her Kindle, as if I have done something terrible. ‘I hate this book,’ she saysLast year I started keeping a list of the books I’ve read on my phone, because I could never remember the names of any of them, even the most recent ones. This list is where I went for inspiration when I needed a solid, unassailable choice.“What about a classic?” I say casually, when the time to choose arrives toward the close of the evening. Tonight’s book has been universally popular, and everyone is in a mood to see the point of book club.“Yeah, I’m ready for a classic,” says Nicola.The book I have in mind – from midway through my list – is indeed a classic, a century old and a recognised masterpiece, but also obscure enough that I can be fairly certain no one else has read it. My oldest son recommended it to me, and I in turn recommended it to his brother. We were all in agreement: a banger.“Death Comes for the Archbishop?” says Emma, with transparent scepticism.“Trust me,” I say. “It’s a banger.”“What’s it about?” says Nicola.“It’s about an archbishop, who dies,” I say.“Spoiler alert,” my wife says.“But really it’s about everything,” I say.“Let’s do it,” says Sash.Three weeks later I wake early in the morning to find my wife staring at me over the top of her Kindle as if I have done something terrible. Searching my memory for recent crimes, I find myself blameless. But she is still staring.“What?” I say.“I hate this book,” she says.“Death Comes for the Archbishop?” I say.“Stupid priests riding around on donkeys everywhere,” she says. “Is it like this all the way through?”“I mean, that’s the premise, more or less,” I say.Two afternoons later, while I’m sitting in my office shed, I develop an eerie sense that somewhere nearby I am being discussed. I cross the garden to find my wife talking to the middle one in the kitchen.“Whatever it’s called,” she is saying. “Death Comes for the Fucking Archbishop.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You didn’t like it?” the middle one says.“I haven’t finished it,” she says. “Because I hate it.”“I read it last year,” he says.“An absolute banger, right?” I say.“Banger is maybe not the word I would choose,” he says. “It’s quite slow, and not much happens.”“We agreed,” I say. “A banger.”double quotation markMy wife raises her objection to the many journeys by donkey. Suzy, with a cry of affection, lists all the donkeys by nameThe following Thursday we arrive at Emma’s house for the next instalment of book club. Often the early part of the evening is taken up with preliminary topics: local gossip, domestic mishaps, recent holidays. Not this time.“I hated the book,” my wife says.“I loved the book!” says Suzy.“I also hated it,” says Emma.My wife raises her objection to the many journeys by donkey. Suzy, with a cry of affection, lists all the donkeys by name.“Huh,” I say. “I had forgotten the names of the donkeys.”The discussion becomes animated. Death Comes for the Archbishop has split book club opinion down the middle. But as certain key episodes are recounted in detail, I fall silent. Fran turns to me and suggests that, given the intensity of feeling, I might care to defend my choice.“I can’t,” I say. “I don’t remember anything. I read it, like, a year and a half ago.”“You mean you didn’t re-read it?” she says.“Why would I?” I say. “The whole point of being the chooser is so you get a freebie.”“You see?” my wife says. “This is why he’s never allowed to pick the book.”Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Who could have done this?’ Mystery over Briton found dead in a suitcase in Athens | Greece | The Guardian
description: Greek police throw entire homicide division at trying to explain fate of 38-year-old Elizabeth-Jane Ross
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Greek police throw entire homicide division at trying to explain fate of 38-year-old Elizabeth-Jane Ross
Content: Elisabeth-Jane Ross arrived in Greece almost three weeks before her mysterious death in Athens.View image in fullscreenElisabeth-Jane Ross arrived in Greece almost three weeks before her mysterious death in Athens.Greece‘Who could have done this?’ Mystery over Briton found dead in a suitcase in AthensGreek police throw entire homicide division at trying to explain fate of 38-year-old Elisabeth-Jane RossHelena Smithin AthensSat 1 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo worlds separated by sheets of corrugated iron: one, a tree-lined road, bordered by a park and the home of Greece’s oldest sports club; the other a wasteland of derelict buildings and graffiti-covered walls in what was once a car park.It is here, on the wrong side of the divide, in Kypseli, a neighbourhood in central Athens, that the body of Elisabeth-Jane Ross was found, inside a suitcase last month.The 38-year-old who had longtime connections to the country – she reportedly worked in the charity sector – had arrived in the Greek capital on holiday almost three weeks earlier. “She was an angel,” a friend in her native Edinburgh told the Guardian. “Wherever she went, she did good. Who could possibly have done this?”The homeless man who made the grim discovery was among the few who ventured into the abandoned lot, located between an apartment block and design school on Evelpidon Street. It was midday on 18 July.What he did next – alerting authorities to the find – would shake up police forces in Greece andScotland. “We’ve had the entire homicide division of the Greek FBI working night and day on the case,” said the police spokesperson Konstantina Dimoglidou. “We’re in contact with other police forces. We’re going to solve this.”View image in fullscreenThe abandoned building in Athens where the body of Ross, 38, was found in a suitcase.Photograph: Louiza Vradi/ReutersBut four days after Ross was publicly identified, with Greek authorities announcing the body was that of a Briton based on fingerprints that matched biometric data in the US, mystery continues to shroud the case.Initial examination of her remains proved inconclusive although pathologists deemed she had probably been dead for several days before the discovery. There were no evident injuries or sign of struggle on her body, raising further questions as to how she had died.On Friday, as local people left flowers at the site, police said investigators were intensifying their search of CCTV footage after it emerged that DNA analysis of the suitcase had not produced any evidence that could be linked to a suspect.“Whenever I pass by I think of that poor woman,” said Manos Andreou, a fashion designer who walks his dog each day along Evelpidon. “Until the area was closed off, I used to go in there and let her run around it, so it’s all been a bit of a shock. They say they’re looking at camera footage, they say they’re making progress, but can you see any cameras anywhere on this street?”The daughter of a lawyer, Ross, who had lived and worked in the US, flew into Athens from Edinburgh on 26 June. Until 15 July she had stayed with the son of a Greek friend in Keratsini, a working-class suburb close to the port of Piraeus. Before moving on, she had told him she would be spending a few days with friends from the US in Kypseli.Detectives, now desperately trying to reconstruct her movements, have expressed frustration at their inability to trace the Americans. Other members of the Briton’s social network in Athens have been interviewed at length, giving testimony that has been described as “incredibly helpful”. None are considered suspects.“July 15 was the last day she had contact with any of her friends,” said the police spokesperson. “Our investigations are focused on the intervening days and whom she may have met and where she stayed. The Americans have not been identified or found.”Police remain confident the suitcase was not at the crime scene more than 48 hours before its discovery on 18 July. They are also convinced that Ross died nearby in Kypseli although have stopped short of describing her death as a murder.“There is always the possibility that she died and then for some reason was hidden,” added Dimoglidou. “Our priority is to get to the bottom of who left the suitcase. Whoever they were was careful not to leave any fingerprints or DNA.”Adding to the mystery, it emerged that the Briton’s mobile phone was in operation and being used days after her death. Ross’s distraught father is reported to have told police he received text messages from his daughter, believing she was alive and well, until her body was identified, publicly, on Wednesday.Messages spoke of her “need to be alone”. Authorities, who have yet to retrieve the device, believe they were deliberately sent so that she would not be declared missing and “to buy time”. Investigators have located the phone’s digital footprint to Athens.One source said: “We have to presume that the person who had her phone and then sent these messages, days after pathologists believe she probably died, is connected to the crime and we cannot rule out that they knew Ms Ross.”More than 60 people in the Greek police department’s homicide division have been assigned to the case. Urgency is such that investigators have also requested that laboratory tests be fast-tracked to determine the cause of death.“At such times, when there is advanced decay because of heat or the conditions in which a body is kept, only toxicological tests and in-depth examination of [vital organ] tissues can determine, exactly, how a person died,” said Grigoris Leon, who heads the Hellenic Society of Forensic Medicine.There would be answers, he said, that would unearth the truth.“I have no doubt they will come but it won’t be easy and it will take time.”Explore more on these topicsGreeceCrimeScotlandEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We stared into an abyss’: the men and women battling France’s megafire | France | The Guardian
description: Exhausted firefighters, foresters and volunteers wage ‘war of attrition’ against blaze that forced 200,000 people from their homes
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Exhausted firefighters, foresters and volunteers wage ‘war of attrition’ against blaze that forced 200,000 people from their homes
Content: Residents of Le Porge, near Bordeaux, watch as the massive wildfire threatens their homes. Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty ImagesExhausted firefighters, foresters and volunteers wage ‘war of attrition’ against blaze that forced 200,000 people from their homesByJason Burkein Le PorgeSat 1 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy noon it is time for a break. The temperature is about 35C, the smell of ash, cinders and burnt wood hang acrid in the air. At tables laid out in the shrinking shade on the desiccated grass and sand outside the sports centre in Le Porge, 200 men and a handful of women have gathered. Firefighters, soldiers, police, gendarmes, officials, first aid teams, foresters and volunteers sit elbow to elbow, plates of sausages, steak and potatoes in front of them.The village was evacuated just over 14 hours after the “megafire” – as it has become known inFrance– broke out 6km away last week. The blaze has consumed 42,000 hectares (104,000 acres) of mainly forestland west of Bordeaux. Though finally contained, there are outbreaks every day, pushing to the limit emergency services and the hundreds of amateurs who have come to their aid.“We’ve turned a corner but we are very, very tired. We have gone beyond what we thought possible,” said a senior firefighter at Le Porge, downing a litre of water in less than a minute. “We stared into an abyss.”Overhead, three planes carrying huge tanks of water and retardant flew low towards new fires. A drone buzzed nearby, sent up by the fire brigade to detect with thermal cameras the creeping underground blaze – described by local media as a “zombie fire” – that threatens fresh chaos in the coming days, weeks and months.View image in fullscreenFirefighters continue to battle flare-ups caused by smouldering peat in Le Porge.Photograph: Catalina Martin-Chico/Panos/The GuardianAround the village, roads run straight through a smouldering, smoking and deserted landscape of charred but upright trees. In places, the forest is intact, the tall pines in their serried green ranks. In others, chosen at apparent random by the racing flames, it has been reduced to ash and cinders as far as the eye can see.“Now we are all running on adrenaline, but the crisis is going to pass and that’s when it will be really hard. That’s when we will weep,” said Remy Bossion, 46, whose home was damaged in the fire and who is now spending his days helping cut 200-metre-wide firebreaks through the remaining forest to slow any future outbreaks.This weekend, fires elsewhere in France are bringing similar, if less extensive, devastation. In the Var region,George and Amal Clooneywere forced to evacuate their home as a wildfire burned nearby. In the famous forests of Fontainebleau outside Paris, in Corsica and near Dijon, the flames still threaten.View image in fullscreenA smouldering landscape of charred trees in Le Porge.Photograph: Catalina Martin-Chico/Panos/The GuardianAcross Europe, emergency services are struggling. In the UK, 120 firefighters have been tackling a blaze in Suffolk for three days. In Spain, the cumulative number of fires in 2026 has set a new record for this time of year. In Greece, three firefighters diedin Creteand thousands of tourists were evacuated from resorts.The fire weather across the EU has broken records for this time of year, newdatashows. Scientists say models of climate change have long predicted such extreme weather, though some disasters appear to be striking earlier and with more strength than expected.Will brutal wildfires force French leaders to take climate crisis seriously?Read more“We still have a month or more of summer to go. We need rain, a lot of rain,” said the senior firefighter in Le Porge, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he did not have authorisation to talk to the media.Leaders in France have been seeking to reassure worried communities – and avert a political crisis. “We are gradually getting back to normal,” said Sophie Brocas, the prefect of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region and the Gironde department, which includes Le Porge, on Thursday night. President Emmanuel Macron said last week it was not the time to analyse lessons to be learned while France was still in “full battle”.No one doubts the scale of the megafire, which at one pointreached the suburbs of Bordeaux itself,but the question of its origins and the availability of resources necessary to fight it is bitterly contested.View image in fullscreenNicolas Di Domenico and his brother François survey the ruined houses.Photograph: Catalina Martin-Chico/Panos/The GuardianAmong the residents of Le Porge eating at the makeshift canteen was Nicolas Di Domenico, a local public works contractor who learned of the blaze when his electricians working near the village of Saumos called to say a spark from a faulty machine being used by workers cleaning a high-tension cable had just ignited a fierce blaze.‘It felt like being in a disaster movie’: uncertainty after evacuation from France’s Gironde wildfireRead moreDi Domenico, 46, said: “It was a short circuit or something of that nature and immediately everything went up because it’s all so dry. The guys there tried to use a fire extinguisher but it was too intense. My guys basically ran for their lives and by the time the fire brigade turned up it was huge.”The blaze initially overwhelmed firefighters, who had difficulty accessing the deeper forest where it was spreading. Within six hours, it had travelled 6km (3.7 miles) to reach the outskirts of Le Porge. Very early the next morning, residents were in the streets, burning cinders were falling from a red sky and a decision was made to evacuate.“The authorities should have stopped all work in the forest. Someone got their priorities wrong,” Di Domenico said.Many in Le Porge and elsewhere in the region accuse the local administration of being “asleep at the wheel” before the fire, and then failing to commit sufficient resources fast enough. Many have asked why France’s ageing fleet of firefighting planes had not be replaced or sufficiently reinforced.“We feared this for a long time, and were warning about the planes specifically since 2017,” said Sebastien Delavoux, head of the firefighting section of the CGT union. “This summer has shown we have reached the extreme limit of what is possible for France’s firefighters.”View image in fullscreenA burnt-out house in Le Porge. The mayor said the fire was impossible to predict and ‘beyond anything we’ve seen before’.Photograph: Catalina Martin-Chico/Panos/The GuardianThe mayor of Le Porge, which lost 20% of its homes and only “by a miracle” escaped further devastation, described an event that was impossible to predict, despite multiple warnings over the years.“The conditions this year are totally exceptional. We’ve never seen anything like this,” Martial Zaninetti said. “You can always say it’s not enough, we’ve not got adequate resources, enough planes, or of whatever, but the scale is completely beyond anything we’ve seen before.”On Wednesday evening, at a base on the edge of the zone worst hit by the fire, senior firefighters gathered around a map taped to the side of a fire engine for a briefing. Burnt red by the sun and with notebooks in hand, grizzled sector commanders stood to receive missions for the night, when lower temperatures and higher humidity make it easier to fight a blaze. Younger team members, still in their fire retardant overalls and covered in soot, watched as their superiors greeted each other with black humour and bags of Haribo sweets.View image in fullscreenLe Porge has lost 20% of its homes and only ‘by a miracle’ escaped further devastation.Photograph: Catalina Martin-Chico/Panos/The Guardian“All right, my little chicken? Ready for another night of work? Not too much for you,” joked one officer to his replacement as he finished his 12-hour shift. “Are you planning your holidays already?” came the response.One said the struggle with the megafire was now shifting from a dynamic and dangerous “war of manoeuvre” to a long, slow and hard “war of attrition”.“We were on the defensive at the beginning but now it’s not spreading any more. There are still lots of individual outbreaks that have us running around and when everyone is exhausted, that is hard. So the mobilisation remains total,” he added.Instead of the usual summer tourist traffic on the long straight roads through the pines of the Landes, there are now long convoys of fire trucks, ambulances, police cars and a motley collection of agricultural water tankers, lorries rigged with plastic containers and pickups carrying jerry cans connected to garden hoses. Some ferry water to the fire engines, allowing the crew to remain at an outbreak without leaving to replenish their tanks. Others spray roadsides or the new firebreaks which leave wide, white scars through the forest.View image in fullscreenA couple on Moutchic beach in Lacanau as the wildfire rages.Photograph: Maximilien Lamy/AFP/Getty ImagesIn the small resort town of Lacanau, just to the north of the worst-hit zones, volunteers refilled containers at a makeshift pumping station set up by volunteers at the sailing club.Armand Fargeas, 51, who runs pleasure trips for tourists on Lacanau’s inland lake, said: “We’ve got 600 people in our WhatsApp group, which for a community like ours is a huge number. What’s really great is that you have every generation getting involved. We might not agree on politics, but the spirit of solidarity is amazing.”Now the hotels and camping sites are empty – all evacuated – and the bistros shut. Rows of sailing boats and paddleboards were drawn up on the shore.“We hope the tourists come back. It’s a catastrophe,” said Anne-Marie Nardou, 74, as she brought fruit and drinks to Fargeas and his friends.Some of the roughly 200,000 people forced to leave their homes by the fire are now being allowed home. On Friday, an exhibition hall in Bordeaux, the regional capital, began to empty of hundreds of evacuees, though many still awaited permission. Tens of thousands of others remained with friends, relatives or in hotels.Frédéric Farrugia, a 55-year-old financial adviser who lives in the coastal village of Lège, watched on his home’s security cameras as the fire brigade fought to save the building. Eventually, the flames were beaten back, though homes 50 metres away were destroyed. Animage of the infernotaken by his wife, Severine, as she escaped with him and their cat after being woken by gendarmes at 2am led to an offer of temporary accommodation from a wellwisher.“We were on the dual carriageway with these flames like a wall along one side. It was a bit like the apocalypse,” Farrugia said. “I think that now the French will realise that the climate is heating up and that we have to react.”View image in fullscreenThe wildfire turns the sky red over Lake Moutchic in Lacanau. The popular tourist destination had to be shut down.Photograph: Sapte Fabrice/Abaca/ShutterstockIn Lacanau as elsewhere, many also talk about the obvious effects of the climate crisis. Anthony Legrand, a carpenter in the village, said he had seen massive change over the decades: tides that reduce the width of the stunning beach, green algae and, of course, repeated fires, including one in 2022 that devastated a swathe of forest not far from his small home.“You’d think that would be a warning but no one paid attention,” he said. “It’ll be the same this time. They’ve got memories like goldfish.”In Le Porge, the mayor said the “worst had passed for now” but risks of a new megafire remained high, now and in coming years.“Right now, we need new shelter, clothes, insurance, legal support, doctors and psychologists,” Zaninetti added. “But this is a problem for the long term. Unless we find another way to live with the forest, this will just happen again.”Explore more on these topicsFranceWildfiresExtreme heatClimate crisisEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: EU to hold urgent meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday over Ceuta crisis | Spain | The Guardian
description: Divisions remain in the bloc over mass crossing of migrants into Spanish territory in north Africa
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Divisions remain in the bloc over mass crossing of migrants into Spanish territory in north Africa
Content: Police officers and Spanish soldiers escorting people in Ceuta to the border with Morocco on Saturday morning.Photograph: Jon Nazca/ReutersView image in fullscreenPolice officers and Spanish soldiers escorting people in Ceuta to the border with Morocco on Saturday morning.Photograph: Jon Nazca/ReutersSpainEU to hold urgent meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday over Ceuta crisisDivisions remain in the bloc over mass crossing of migrants into Spanish territory in north AfricaLisa O’Carrollin London andSam Jonesin MadridSat 1 Aug 2026 15.03 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 06.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU is to hold an urgent meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday amid continued divisions in the bloc over the arrival of more than 50,000 migrants in the Spanish territory of Ceuta in northAfrica.The decision was taken by officials representing EU member states and Frontex border agency experts at what was described as a “sobering” meeting on Saturday.Spain confirmed at least 67 people had died in the attempted crossing. Some drowned, while others were crushed as they tried to cross a breakwater barrier.The decision to call a summit of ministers was unanimous as EU leaders seek to heal divisions in the bloc and restore a unified approach to migration.Spain said migrant crossings into Ceuta had stopped overnight, as police began installing a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier off its border ‌withMorocco.Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, said on Saturday: “I have been in touch with the Spanish prime minister and [we are] providing what help we can.”Italy and Denmark, with some support from Poland and Sweden, used the meeting on Saturday to criticise Spain for what had happened.In a furious letter on Saturday, Spain’s prime ministerPedro Sánchezhit out against “fake news” and “disinformation”, pointing out that “virtually all” migrants had been returned to Morocco after the army intervened on Friday, “preventing any unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe”.It is understood suspected Russian attempts to spread disinformation to sow dissent within the EU was also discussed at the meeting on Saturday.There is frustration in Spain that previous incidents of this scale, such as mass arrival of migrants on the border of Belarus and Poland or Russia and Finland, were labelled as “hybrid attacks” , and met with solidarity from the rest of the EU.Although more than 48,000 people had voluntarily returned to Morocco by 6pm on Friday, the influx triggered a political crisis for the Madrid government and led some fellow EU countries to call for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.Juan Jesús Vivas, the president of Ceuta, said that while many people had returned to Morocco, not all those who had crossed into the city had left.“We’re not back to normal because there are several thousand people who need to be returned, and there is still an atmosphere marked by unease and concern,” he said. He also called for “all the security measures deployed” in Ceuta to remain in place to guarantee the safety of the population.Sánchez asked for the meeting after what appeared to be a breakdown of EU unity on external border policy, with Italy attacking Spain.Italy announced on Friday evening that it would suspend its Schengen arrangements with Spain for a month, even though Ceuta – and Spain’s other north African territory, Melilla – are subject to special Schengen rules that prevent onward movement within the zone.Map showing location of Ceuta in Mediterranean region, and another showing location of Tarajal breakwater on border between Ceuta and MoroccoItaly’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, blamed the situation in Ceuta on the Sánchez government’s decision to offer a now-closed schemeto regularise the statusof more than 1 million undocumented migrants and asylum seekers. He said the programme had incentivised human trafficking and was “profoundly wrong”.Sánchez was forthright in a letter sent to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Council president, António Costa, and Micheál Martin, the prime minister of Ireland, which holds the EU presidency.View image in fullscreenPedro Sánchez speaking at a press conference in Ceuta on Friday.Photograph: Borja Puig de la Bellacasa/Moncloa handout/EPASánchez said that while most EU countries had expressed support and solidarity over events in Ceuta, others had chosen to attack Spain.“Such an attitude – driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest – is … contrary to European law, humanitarian law and the principles of solidarity that bind us together,” he said.In a pointed rebuke to Italy, he noted that Spain was “according to Frontex, one of the least porous external borders of theEuropean Union, with a number of irregular entries that is half that recorded, for example, in Italy in recent years (2021–26)”.Senior EU officials met on Saturday in a “political crisis response team” convened by Ireland’s presidency.3:37Tens of thousands of migrants cross into Spanish enclave Ceuta from Morocco - videoIreland’s prime minister, Micheál Martin, said on Saturday that, as the holders of the EU presidency, “Ireland will convene a meeting on Tuesday of the EU Justice and Home Affairs Council, chaired by Jim O’Callaghan [justice minister], to discuss developments in Ceuta.“We remain in close contact with all member states and the institutions and continue to monitor the situation,” he said in a social media post.O’Callaghan, who is leading the meetings on behalf of the EU, said he had been in touch with Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, to express his solidarity and support.In remarks that appeared to respond to Sánchez’s criticisms, von der Leyen said she welcomed his suggestion of a video conference “to take stock of what has happened”, adding: “Fighting illegal migration requires solidarity and a united European response.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrance’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said his country would not be seeking Spain’s suspension from Schengen rules.“It’s absolutely not on the table,” he said on Saturday. “We have great cooperation with Spain.”Many of the remaining people who crossed into Ceuta returned to Morocco on Saturday morning amid a reinforced Spanish police and military presence.“We hope to go to Europe to work and earn a living – that’s it,” Souleil Boyan, a 19-year-old from Senegal, told Agence France-Presse outside a migrant centre in Ceuta where dozens of other people from sub-Saharan Africa were waiting for officials.“We all know that in Africa there isn’t much opportunity,” he added.The Spanish government said in a statement on Saturday that the situation in Ceuta remained calm and quiet.It said containment barriers were being installed at the Tarajal beach breakwater, including a 500-metre-long inflatable barrier and a line of anchored buoys.View image in fullscreenSpanish soldiers in Ceuta on Saturday.Photograph: Fabian Bimmer/ReutersThis week’s mass crossing dwarfs the last similar event in May 2021, when Morocco loosened its border controls, allowing about 10,000 people to enter the territory over two days.That crossing came amid heightened tensions between Madrid and Rabat over Spain’s decision to allow the leader of the Western Sahara independence movement, the Polisario Front, to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. Morocco and the Polisario Front both lay claim to Western Sahara, which was under Spanish rule until 1975, when colonial authorities handed the territory to Morocco and Mauritania.That diplomatic crisis ended in 2022 when Madrid reversed its longstanding policy of neutrality and backed Morocco’s plan for Western Sahara, a move that caused a rift between Spain and Algeria, which had supported the Polisario group.Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreSánchez visited Algiers on 20 July – the first visit by a Spanish head of government in four years – marking a thaw in relations with Algeria.The Spanish government has attributed the latest influx to “human-trafficking mafias” that have taken advantage of a decision by Spain’s supreme court, which recently ruled that those intercepted at sea while trying to enter Ceuta or Melilla could not be summarily returned under special rules.But some migration experts have expressed doubts about that explanation. Mauricio Valiente, the director general of the Spanish Refugee Aid Commission, said the route into Ceuta was very different from theAtlantic route from Africa to the Canary Islands, which is often operated by people smugglers.“Unlike what happens in the Canary Islands, these aren’t people who have to get into a small boat,”he told elDiario.es. “This is a matter of being just metres from a land border, jumping into the sea and trying to get around a breakwater, which makes it much easier to do, even with all the risks.”Valiente said there had been a steady increase in arrivals to Ceuta this year, even before the supreme court ruling.“The causes are complex, and there are surely many reasons,” he said. “But to simplify it by referencing the court ruling or organised crime – to say there’s a direct cause-and-effect relationship – is completely unfounded.”Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, visited Ceuta on Saturday and said he had spoken to migrants there.“I have spoken to a number of them who made it quite clear they intend to make it to Britain,” he said.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropeEuropean UnionMoroccoMigrationPedro SánchezAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Tourist plane crashes during flight over Peru’s Nazca Lines, killing 13 | Peru | The Guardian
description: Aircraft crashes into field after departing from nearby city of Pisco, according to local authorities
Author: Dan Collyns
Headline: Aircraft crashes into field after departing from nearby city of Pisco, according to local authorities
Content: The Nazca Lines are a group of extensive geoglyphs scraped into the desert in Peru.Photograph: Sebastian Castañeda/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Nazca Lines are a group of extensive geoglyphs scraped into the desert in Peru.Photograph: Sebastian Castañeda/ReutersPeruTourist plane crashes during flight over Peru’s Nazca Lines, killing 13Aircraft crashes into field after departing from nearby city of Pisco, according to local authoritiesDan Collynsin LimaSat 1 Aug 2026 18.31 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice inPerureport that 13 people, among them foreign tourists, have been killed in a plane crash in southern Peru, near the Nazca Lines.Local authorities in Nazca confirmed that 11 tourists and two pilots died when the Cessna Grand Caravan crashed in Pueblo Viejo, approximately 4 miles (6km) from the city of Nazca and roughly 12km from the Nazca Lines site.The passengers were identified as seven Italians, two Germans – believed to be a couple – and two Spanish people. The pilot and copilot were named as Americo Salazar Cuellar and Irenka Del Carpio respectively.The plane had departed the nearby city of Pisco at about 1pm local time (7pm BST) to fly over the Nazca Lines, but minutes later lost contact with the control tower and crashed at 1.20pm, police reported.The cause of the crash is as yet unknown, and the local authorities have launched an investigation.“We have information that 11 passengers and two crew members have died,” Police Major Jorge Andrade told reporters at the crash site.“Given the severity of the accident, there are no survivors. We have recovered four bodies so far,” Andrade added.The Guardian has seen video footage which showed firefighters and police working amid the smouldering wreckage of the plane in the desert. Images appeared to show bodies on the sand.This deadly plane crash is far from the first at the Unesco world heritage site, which attracts hundreds of thousands of tourists every year. Several operators compete to offer overflights of the iconic lines which date to AD200-700, amid serious concerns about the safety and maintenance of the aircraft.In 2022, a small plane crash killed seven people, including two Chileans and three Dutch nationals. In October 2010,four British touristsand two Peruvian crew members were killed when a small plane operated by AirNasca crashed after flying over the lines. Earlier in the same year, three Chileans and four Peruvians died when a Cessna 206 crashed. In April 2008, five French tourists were killed in another crash, but the pilot survived.“The investigation of the accident and the oversight of aviation operations are the responsibility of the competent authorities, who will determine the causes and assign liability in accordance with the law,” the municipality of Nazca said in a statement on Saturday.Peru’s tourism ministry expressed “deep sorrow over the tragic deaths of tourists and crew members” in astatement.Themysterious etchings in the desert,which include vast hummingbird, monkey and whale figures, are only fully visible from the air.Explore more on these topicsPeruPlane crashesAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Boxer secures Tuvalu’s first Commonwealth Games medal without winning a bout  | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Boxer Tarona Taafaki made history for ⁠Tuvalu by winning the Pacific island nation’s first Commonwealth ⁠Games medal without winning a single fight
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Boxer Tarona Taafaki made history for ⁠Tuvalu by winning the Pacific island nation’s first Commonwealth ⁠Games medal without winning a single fight
Content: Tuvalu’s Tarona Taafaki (right) goes toe to toe with Lovlina Borgohain of India in the women’s 75kg semi-final.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenTuvalu’s Tarona Taafaki (right) goes toe to toe with Lovlina Borgohain of India in the women’s 75kg semi-final.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPCommonwealth Games 2026Boxer secures Tuvalu’s first Commonwealth Games medal without winning a boutTarona Taafaki makes history in women’s 75kg categoryAll boxers eliminated in semis receive bronze medalsSean Inglein GlasgowSat 1 Aug 2026 06.07 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 10.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA boxer has made history for ⁠Tuvalu by winning the tiny Pacific island nation’s first Commonwealth ⁠Games medal without winning a single fight.Twenty-year-old Tarona Taafaki, ⁠one of five entrants in the women’s 75kg category, received a bye to the semi-finals where she lost on an unanimous points decision to India’s Lovlina Borgohain on Friday. AtCommonwealth Games, all boxers eliminated in the semis receive bronze medals.Commonwealth Games 2026 medal tableRead more“I’m very proud and very glad to be able to represent my country on this big stage,” said Taafaki, one of only eight athletes and paraathletes from her country in Glasgow. “Probably 95% of the audience don’t know where my country is, so I feel very privileged to represent Tuvalu.”Badi Taafaki, her coach and father, said the medal would be celebrated by the 10,000 population of the 10 sq mile nation – the world’s fourth smallest – and serve to highlight a climate emergency.“For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything,” he said. “We’re one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it’s a stepping stone.”Athletes often train on the island’s airport runway as it is its most stable land mass. However, with sea levels rising, climate experts predict half of the nation’s capital, Funafuti, could be submerged by 2050. “Yes, we train on the runway,” said Taafaki. “When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.”However, Tarona and her brother Pasoni, who also boxed in the Commonwealth Games, are based in New Zealand where the facilities are better. “When I was growing up, boxing barely existed in Tuvalu,” said Badi. “We didn’t have gloves, so we were forced to fight bare-knuckle, and hit bags filled with sand. My children are very fortunate. They have opportunities and facilities that I never had.Boxingis our whole life. Strength is in our bloodline. It’s where our genealogy comes from.“If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change. It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can’t sleep if there’s a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes.”Taafaki is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight. Australia’sTaylah Robertson picked up a bronzein the women’s flyweight category on the Gold Coast in 2018 despite losing her first bout to England’s Lisa Whiteside.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026TuvaluCommonwealth GamesBoxingAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bessent ‘to-do’ list shows proposal for US to buy $5bn-$10bn of Japanese yen | US politics | The Guardian
description: Treasury secretary’s notepad, photographed by Reuters on Friday morning, prompts questions over US plans
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: Treasury secretary’s notepad, photographed by Reuters on Friday morning, prompts questions over US plans
Content: Scott Bessent’s notepad with his proposal to buy Japanese yen.Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersView image in fullscreenScott Bessent’s notepad with his proposal to buy Japanese yen.Photograph: Daniel Heuer/ReutersUS politicsBessent ‘to-do’ list shows proposal for US to buy $5bn-$10bn of Japanese yenTreasury secretary’s notepad, photographed by Reuters on Friday morning, prompts questions over US plansRobert Mackeyand agenciesFri 31 Jul 2026 20.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 21.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring a cabinet meeting at Camp David on Friday, the US treasury secretary Scott Bessent carelessly revealed plans for the US to buy $5bn-$10bn ⁠in Japanese yen in a scribbled “to do” list left visible to a Reuters photographer.The image, taken over Bessent’s shoulder during a portion of the meeting open to journalists, showed a Camp David notepad with the underscored words “To Do” followed by “Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil”.Bessent’s name card on the Camp David conference table is visible and ​positioned immediately above the notepad.The ‌photograph was taken at ‌11.33am local time, Reuters reported. Video of the televised portion of the cabinet meeting showed that the notepad wasstill clearly visiblein front of Bessent when he spoke, to praise the president, 30 minutes later.A treasury spokesperson did not immediately respond to a Reuters request ‌for comment on the contents of the notepad, “or whether the treasury had intervened to help prop up the yen’s value against the dollar on Friday”, the news agency said.The Financial Timesreportedlater that the Federal Reserve Bank of New Yorksold euros to buy yenon behalf of the US treasury department.The depreciation of the yen, which dipped last week to its weakest level since 1986, has been driven by a number of factors, including rising oil prices,according to Bloomberg News.Earlier on Friday, about two hours before the note was seen in front of Bessent, Reuters reported that the treasury department had notified a number of banks that ‌it could intervene in the yen market that day, an unnamed source said.Japanese authorities had stepped in ​to prop up the yen earlier on Friday, triggering a substantial strengthening of the Japanese currency during early trading hours.There appears to have been another sizeable strengthening of the yen against the dollar during the late afternoon on Friday.Data from LSEG shows the dollar dropped from about 158.9 yen at around 4.14 pm ET to about 157.6 yen just before 5pm – a drop of about 0.8%.The US treasury has not intervened to prop up the yen since 2011, when it joined other G7 countries in a coordinated action after a devastating earthquake and tsunami rocked Japan.Explore more on these topicsUS politicsCurrenciesUS foreign policyJapanAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: First Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birds | Bird flu | The Guardian
description: Helicopter surveillance finds dead and dying greater crested terns off South Australian coast as H5 virus spreads
Author: Graham Readfearn
Headline: Helicopter surveillance finds dead and dying greater crested terns off South Australian coast as H5 virus spreads
Content: More than 80 dead and dying greater crested terns have been spotted off the South Australian coast in what is a suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event.Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RFView image in fullscreenMore than 80 dead and dying greater crested terns have been spotted off the South Australian coast in what is a suspected H5N1 bird flu mass mortality event.Photograph: imageBROKER/David & Micha Sheldon/Getty Images/imageBROKER RFBird fluFirst Australian mass mortality event suspected as deadly bird flu virus rapidly escalates among native birdsHelicopter surveillance finds dead and dying greater crested terns off South Australian coast as H5 virus spreadsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastGraham ReadfearnEnvironment and climate correspondentSat 1 Aug 2026 02.12 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 19.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 80 dead and sick birds seen on rocks off the South Australian coast are suspected to be the first mass mortality event from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, only six weeks after the disease arrived in Australia.Authorities reported on Saturday that helicopter surveillance had revealed 49 dead greater crested terns on Baudin Rocks, near Robe, as well as 35 more sick terns.While some of the birds had been collected for testing, South Australia’s chief vet Skye Fruean said it was likely the first mass mortality event from the disease.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailSouth Australia also reported three suspected positive cases in other greater crested terns, including one inland at Monarto, suggesting the disease has begun moving away from the coast. The Monarto area is home to several poultry farms.Three silver gulls were also suspected positive, SA authorities said, adding to the first silver gull found a few days ago and confirmed positive by the CSIRO earlier on Saturday.Kate Millar, the chief executive of conservation charity BirdLife Australia, called it a “very significant escalation of the bird flu situation in Australia, and a very bleak milestone”.“Sadly, we’re at the beginning of a long and challenging battle and birds and wildlife are going to need all the help they can get,” she said.Jack Gough, the chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said it now appeared the disease was “starting to take off” and “mirroring the experience in South America of early detections, then rapid increases in numbers and spread leading to mass mortality events in wildlife.”“We are still at the very early stages of this devastating disease spreading, but the possible first mass mortality coming just days after the virus was declared not eradicable indicates how quickly this could escalate,” he said.Fruean said there was “nothing we can do” to stop the spread of the disease, but that surveillance was working.The news came at the end of a significant week in the development of the disease when numbers jumped by 20 in just a few days to the current total of 53.Australia was the last continent to have the unwelcome arrival of a disease that has killed millions of birds and mammals around the world.Victoria this week confirmed its first cases of the virulent strain in a greater crested tern found in Portland, with the state joining Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland that have all recorded positive cases.On Saturday, Victorian authorities said samples from five crested terns had been sent to the CSIRO laboratory in Geelong, with preliminary testing suggesting more positive results.Five confirmed cases in birds at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island also raised concerns for the welfare of the area’s Australian sea lions – an endangered species.
