Tens of thousands of seals have died worldwide from the disease.But it has been the cases among silver gulls that has experts like Sean Dooley, the national affairs adviser at BirdLife Australia, concerned that the spread of the virus has now reached a critical new stage.“When people think of a seagull, they’re almost always thinking of the silver gull,” said Dooley.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAustralian sea lions, an endangered species, are at risk of contracting H5N1 bird flu.Photograph: Brad Leue/Alamy“They’re very common, and primarily they are coastal, but they do come inland and can turn up in Lake Eyre following floods,” said Dooley.Silver gulls are the second Australian native species to catch the disease, after dozens of detections in greater crested terns.But it is the silver gull’s behaviour and habits that have experts concerned because they scavenge from dead or dying animals, meaning they can easily pick up the disease from other sick birds.They also pick detritus from water bodies – lakes and flooded areas included – and these are known to be breeding grounds for the disease.“There is such a large population of silver gulls, and they move into other habitats. They could be the vector that takes bird flu inland,” says Dooley. “They’re also really successful in urban areas and could bring the disease into those bird populations.”Because Australia has a high concentration of unique birds, the susceptibility of many native species isn’t known. But the fears are there is no reason to think they would manage any better than birds overseas.Birds that flock around water have tended to be the hardest hit. Examples include sandwich terns, black-headed gulls and northern gannets in Europe and, in Peru, pelicans.Dooley said the mood at BirdLife Australia this week had been one of “trying to suppress that sinking, gut-churning feeling”.The winter season for birdwatchers along the coast had been one of the best in 10 years, said Dooley, with rare petrels turning up in numbers along the east coast.“Now that has been heavily tinged because probably among those were birds carrying H5N1.”This article was amended on 2 August 2026 to correct the spelling of Skye Fruean’s name.Explore more on these topicsBird fluWildlifeBirdsMarine lifeAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Petrol prices on track to top $2 a litre as Bowen sounds death knell for fuel excise relief | Petrol prices | The Guardian
description: Petrol now costs more than $1.90 a litre in every capital city, with diesel expected to exceed $2.40 a litre
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: Petrol now costs more than $1.90 a litre in every capital city, with diesel expected to exceed $2.40 a litre
Content: Car owners are likely to see petrol prices above $2 a litre and diesel above $2.40 after the government confirmed the end of the fuel excise discount.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenCar owners are likely to see petrol prices above $2 a litre and diesel above $2.40 after the government confirmed the end of the fuel excise discount.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersPetrol pricesPetrol prices on track to top $2 a litre as Bowen sounds death knell for fuel excise reliefPetrol now costs more than $1.90 a litre in every capital city, with diesel expected to exceed $2.40 a litreGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniFri 31 Jul 2026 22.22 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePetrol prices could surpass $2 a litre and diesel $2.40 in coming days, after the government’s 16-cent discount ends on Sunday.The 32-cent per litre reduction in fuel excise, introduced in March at the peak of the fuel price spike, was halved to 16 cents in July.The excise will return to its normal level on 3 August, adding 16 cents per litre to the wholesale prices paid by service stations.Chris Bowen, the energy minister, told reporters on Saturday the government would not extend the temporary cost-of-living relief.“Obviously we always monitor the situation and take steps as necessary, but our policy decision is clear,” Bowen said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailA 16 cent increase in fuel prices would add $8.80 to the cost of filling up, for a vehicle with a 55-litre tank.Tom Woodlock, a senior market analyst at Argus Media, said service stations typically took four or more days to adjust prices at the pump to match changes in excise or overseas pricing.Retailers have already passed higher wholesale fuel prices on to customers after the US resumed strikes on Iran in mid-July, pushing upoil and import costs.‘Dodged a bullet’: inflation eases to 3.8%, reducing chances of interest rate rise for Australia’s mortgage holdersRead moreUnleaded petrol prices have risen to 205.6 cents per litre in Canberra, 204.4 in Darwin and 200.5 in Hobart, according to MotorMouth data on Saturday.Petrol costs more than 190 cents in every capital city, meaning it would pass 200 cents if the 16-cent increase was passed on in full.Melbourne was facing diesel prices of 242.7 cents per litre on Saturday, up 68 cents from its June low of 173.9 cents, according to Motormouth. Canberra was at 244.4 cents a litre, Darwin at 244.1 and Hobart 241.8.Diesel costs more than 235 cents per litre in every capital city except Perth, meaning it would pass 250 cents if service stations pass on the price hike in full.Petrol price graphThe strait of Hormuz has been almost completely closed to traffic since Iran and the US returned to fighting two weeks ago. Iranstruck two tankers under US escorton Friday after thetwo countries resumed trading strikesthis week.Brent crude oil, the global benchmark, has risen from about US$70 on 2 July to nearly US$90 on Saturday, pushing up import prices in Australia’s region.‘A new trajectory’: EVs now almost quarter of Australia’s new car sales as fuel crisis bitesRead moreSome analysts have predicted oil prices will return to US$100 a barrel if conflict continues. In March, when oil hit that price, and Australia had no fuel excise relief, petrol surpassed 250 cents a litre, and diesel passed 300 cents.Economists have credited the excise discount withsuppressing Australia’s inflation rateand supporting household spending as the economy weakens. Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said in a note on Saturday the loss of the discount could push petrol prices up to 210 cents a litre.“This will push up headline inflation again as well as the cost of the average household’s weekly fuel bill by around $20,” Oliver said.Bowen on Saturday defended the decision to end the discount and the related heavy vehicle road user charge, paid by trucks. He warned against panic buying and repeated the government’s call for motorists to buy only the amount of fuel that they need.“I think Australians have understood … this is a temporary measure,” he said.Bowen said Australia had 43 days’ worth of petrol stocks, 39 days of diesel, and 34 days of jet fuel. As of Saturday, 44 fuel ships were on the way to Australia with 3.1bn litres set to be delivered in the coming month, consistent with previous weeks, he said.Fuel orders were locked in through up to October, and no orders to Australia had been cancelled during the international crisis, Bowen said.Explore more on these topicsPetrol pricesAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Adani to pay no company tax despite $1bn revenue from Queensland coalmine | Adani Group | The Guardian
description: Indian conglomerate offsets earnings from Carmichael mine to report $340.6m loss, after promising billions in taxes and royalties
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: Indian conglomerate offsets earnings from Carmichael mine to report $340.6m loss, after promising billions in taxes and royalties
Content: Adani will pay no tax this financial year despite generating about $1bn in revenue from coal mining in Queensland.Photograph: WikimediaView image in fullscreenAdani will pay no tax this financial year despite generating about $1bn in revenue from coal mining in Queensland.Photograph: WikimediaAdani GroupAdani to pay no company tax despite $1bn revenue from Queensland coalmineIndian conglomerate offsets earnings from Carmichael mine to report $340.6m loss, after promising billions in taxes and royaltiesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettBusiness editorFri 31 Jul 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 31 Jul 2026 22.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndian conglomerate Adani will pay no company tax despite generating almost $1bn in revenue from coal mining in Queensland over the past year.Financial accounts show the Carmichael thermal coal operations used large costs – including production and related party logistics expenses – to offset its $963.5m revenue in the 12 months to 31 March. This resulted in a recorded $340.6m loss for the year, erasing its tax bill.Guardian Australia analysis of company accounts shows the mining project has never paid corporate tax after opening in 2021,despite past pledges by Adanithat the operations would plough billions of dollars in taxes and royalties into the economy.Adani donated $600,000 to Liberal National party before 2024 state election using federal ‘loophole’Read moreAdani Mining’s accounts show that it paid $58m in royalties in the 12-month period. Royalties are payments made to governments to extract state-owned minerals. Adani also paid a $33.1m royalty to a related party.Tim Buckley, a former investment banker and the director of Climate Energy Finance, said the company was structured so that it wouldn’t pay corporate tax in Australia.“This is a perfect example of why Australia needs new rules that ensure foreign entities have a sensible capital structure,” said Buckley, who advocates for changes that would limit the amount of deductions a business can make to reduce tax.Adani’s project approval in central Queensland’s Galilee Basin wasfiercely contested, opening a new jurisdiction of thermal coal extraction that raised environmental concerns.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailIndustry groups supporting the conglomerate had claimed Adani’s project would fund schools, hospitals and other infrastructure for “almost a century” through mining taxes and royalties.A spokesperson for Adani Mining said the project provided direct jobs for more than 1,400 Queenslanders last financial year.“We comply fully with our state and commonwealth taxation and royalty obligations and our statutory profit and tax outcomes are determined in accordance with Australian accounting standards and the corporations act,” the spokesperson said.The Carmichael operations opened during a prosperous time for coalminers. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine sent global energy prices soaring in 2022.Coalprices are now also being supported by energy supply constraints caused by conflict in the Middle East.The Adani-controlled Abbot Point port business, named North Queensland Export Terminal, also did not pay any company tax over the most recent 12-month reporting period, despite earning $356.6m.Various operating expenses lead to a $6.8m loss, with no tax payable.The terminal business’s chief executive, Mark Smith, said accounts were prepared in accordance with Australian accounting standards and reflect the capital-intensive nature of owning and operating major export infrastructure.“The terminal plays an important role in supporting Queensland trade and we remain focused on delivering safe, reliable, and efficient export services for our customers,” Smith said.Explore more on these topicsAdani GroupBusinessMiningCoalTaxClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU offered Spain support ‘from first moment’ of Ceuta crisis, says von der Leyen, after Sánchez hits out – Europe live | Europe | The Guardian
description: ‘Not a single person reached mainland Spain or rest of EU,’ says European Commission president, after Spanish PM condemned ‘selfish, polarising’ reaction of some countries
Author: Taz Ali
Headline: ‘Not a single person reached mainland Spain or rest of EU,’ says European Commission president, after Spanish PM condemned ‘selfish, polarising’ reaction of some countries
Content: 10.08 EDTVon der Leyen: 'Not a single person reached mainland Spain or rest of EU'The European Commission president,Ursula von der Leyen, said she welcomed calls from leaders for a meeting to“take stock of what has happened”in Ceuta, but maintained that the EU had offered help to Spain“from the first moment”.Her remarks were likely a response to criticism from the Spanish prime minister, who accused Europe of providing “little support” in dealing with the border crisis and called for an emergency meeting of EU interior ministers to address the situation.In a post on X, Von der Leyen said:double quotation markThe good news is that the vast majority of those who arrived illegally have returned to Morocco, due to the effective work of Spanish and Moroccan law enforcement.Not a single person reached mainland Spain or the rest of the EU.This shows why the control of our European borders matters. We have a strong system in place. But it needs to be further strengthened.”Share

title: Dozens injured as earthquake hits near Naples in seismic swarm | Earthquakes | The Guardian
description: At least five taken to hospital and about 300 evacuated in strongest quake to hit southern Italian region in 40 years
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: At least five taken to hospital and about 300 evacuated in strongest quake to hit southern Italian region in 40 years
Content: People inspecting damaged buildings in Pozzuoli after the earthquake.Photograph: Felice de Martino/EPAView image in fullscreenPeople inspecting damaged buildings in Pozzuoli after the earthquake.Photograph: Felice de Martino/EPAEarthquakesDozens injured as earthquake hits near Naples in seismic swarmAt least five taken to hospital and about 300 evacuated in strongest quake to hit southern Italian region in 40 yearsDonna Fergusonand agenciesSat 1 Aug 2026 09.49 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 06.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least 26 people have been injured after a 4.7-magnitude earthquake rocked a region near Naples, in southernItaly.The quake, which occurred at 7.46pm on Friday night, caused power outages, disrupted public transport and damaged a pier in Campi Flegrei, the site of Europe’s largest volcanic crater.It is the strongest tremor to hit the region in the past 40 years and caused part of a cliff and several unoccupied buildings to collapse.At least five of those injured were taken to hospital and about 300 people were evacuated from their homes in the city of Pozzuoli, near the epicentre of the quake, after it triggered landslides.Many residents spent the night on the streets, afraid their buildings would be damaged or collapse.One person was only “alive by a miracle”, a rescuer told Reuters, as Italy’s civil protection minister, Nello Musumeci, urged caution and warned that the volcanic activity was not yet over.The quake – which had a depth of 3km and was felt across Naples and the island of Ischia, and as far away as the Sorrento peninsula – was part of an ongoing seismic swarm, Italy’s national institute of geophysics and volcanology said.After it struck, seismographs registered about 60 more tremors, with one 3.1-magnitude quake at 5.47am being felt by residents of Bacoli and Pozzuoli as well as Naples.View image in fullscreenA woman walking through a closed street in Pozzuoli the day after the earthquake.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images“There is a risk that the mountain could continue to collapse, so it is dangerous,” the rescuer said. “What makes us angry is that this situation was foreseeable, because there had already been problems with the mountain for a year and a half … The municipality knew about the situation and did nothing – perhaps if they had acted sooner, this could have been avoided.”The heaviest damage was reported in Pozzuoli, where a building partly collapsed and large chunks of rubble crushed parked cars but did not cause any injuries.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA car sits crushed under rocks that fell from a ridge near the Solfatara volcanic crater in Campi Flegrei.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesNine buildings have been deemed unsafe as buildings inspections continue.“We were afraid,” one resident said. “We all ran out of our homes because it was impossible to stay inside. It lasted a long time and was very powerful, and we no longer know what we are supposed to do. We have been left here in the middle of the street, and no one has come to check on us or tell us what to do. We are here with very young children.”Firefighters said they received reports of lifts being stuck and of a high-voltage pylon supplying electricity to the Agnano area of Naples having partly collapsed, causing disruption for 100,000 households.The port authority said the Pozzuoli pier was unusable, and ferry and hydrofoil services to the islands had been suspended. High-speed train passengers were experiencing delays of up to six hours, with some being rerouted.Explore more on these topicsEarthquakesItalyEuropeNatural disastersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Italy says it’s temporarily suspending EU Schengen arrangement with Spain after 60,000 migrants reach Ceuta – as it happened | Spain | The Guardian
description: The measure will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: The measure will impact people travelling by plane or boat between the two countries
Content: 13.27 EDTClosing summaryJakub KrupaAnd, on that note,we will be closing the blog for today.At least 57 people have died trying to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after as many as 60,000 migrants entered the tiny territory from Morocco(17:33).At least 57 people die as tens of thousands cross to Spanish enclave of Ceuta from MoroccoRead moreSpain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, called it a “a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity”(12:51) and blamed on misleading narratives spread by human traffickers (12:54,13:17).In response,Italy has moved to suspend its free-travel Schengen arrangements with Spain by sea and air(18:26), claiming it was necessary to safeguard the security of its citizens (19:02,19:07). It is understoodit will amount to “targeted, selective checks” on third-country nationals arriving from Spain(19:19).But by Friday afternoon,the Spanish authorities claimed that a vast majority of the migrants have voluntarily returned to Morocco(16:41,18:20), with hundreds more going back by the hour as there was no onwards migration route to mainland Spain or the EU (14:02,15:04).Map of CeutaThe huge influx, which took place over the course of just 24 hours,overwhelmed the city of 85,000 people,triggered a political crisisfor Madrid and led to a barrage of criticism from the US (15:25,15:29,18:02) and other EU countries,includingbroader calls to suspend Spain’s membership of the Schengen area(9:42,10:21,12:10,13:52,14:52,16:59,17:38).Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco?Read moreIf you haveany tips, comments or suggestions,email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.I am also on Bluesky at@jakubkrupa.bsky.socialand on X at@jakubkrupa.Share

title: EU relations, climate crisis and Gaza: why Ed Miliband is fired up by Foreign Office challenges | Ed Miliband | The Guardian
description: Labour veteran is said to relish role that requires careful negotiation of Trump and impending G20 leadership
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Labour veteran is said to relish role that requires careful negotiation of Trump and impending G20 leadership
Content: Ed Miliband was appointed to the Foreign Office in Andy Burnham’s first cabinet as PM last month.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersView image in fullscreenEd Miliband was appointed to the Foreign Office in Andy Burnham’s first cabinet as PM last month.Photograph: Jack Taylor/ReutersEd MilibandAnalysisEU relations, climate crisis and Gaza: why Ed Miliband is fired up by Foreign Office challengesPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorLabour veteran is said to relish role that requires careful negotiation of Trump and impending G20 leadershipSat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTShareExtraordinarily, given the importance of geopolitics, the office of foreign secretary has sometimes appeared a consolation prize in British politics, perhaps reflecting the transfer of responsibility to Downing Street or the Cabinet Office.That is not howEd Milibandviews the job. His allies say suggestions that he nurses resentment after he was deprived of the chance to be chancellor misunderstand his grasp of the policy challenges ahead. “Ed has an immense appetite to get things done and is relishing being in this job,” one says. “Ed will be a policy-driven foreign secretary.”To that end, he is preparing a distinct agenda on relations with the EU over the next decade, Britain’s chairing of theG20next year and the climate crisis. Miliband is also determined to contribute to some of the big debates about shaping the international order of the future – debates that may take him into difficult territory given the volatility of the US alliance.Palestine may take longer to address, partly owing to the Israeli elections and the sudden glimmer of progress overHamas disarmament, but his instincts are clear. In 2014, as Labour leader, he urged his MPs to vote to recognise Palestine.View image in fullscreenThe UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, speaks with his French counterpart, Jean-Noël Barrot, during a visit to the Quai d’Orsay in Paris last week.Photograph: Leon Neal/ReutersAcutely conscious that he is the tenth foreign secretary since William Hague stood aside in 2014, Miliband also arrives without a Foreign Office permanent secretary after thesacking of Olly Robbins, and with some staff on a rolling strike over the large job cuts that Robbins had announced he would impose.But Miliband, working with the newEuropeminister based in the Foreign Office, Hamish Falconer, intends to be closely involved in talks on the UK’s relations with the EU since he regards a successful solution to that relationship as the single biggest question facing the UK. His personal involvement will give the Foreign Office greater influence in the Europe debate than under Keir Starmer’s leadership, when the Cabinet Office was the sole proprietors of negotiations with the EU.Miliband represents a Eurosceptic constituency and remains bound by Labour’s manifesto red lines not to enter the single market or customs union in this parliament. But that does not prevent him from seeking to influence Andy Burnham’s longer-term thinking about where the UK’s relationship with the EU should be in 10 or 15 years. Burnham, Miliband’s aides argue, has shown an openness to ideas on social care and the same openness may apply to issues such as European defence.“Having a closer relationship with Europe is a key foreign policy priority to protect our national security and grow our economy,” an ally said. “Ed will be working in lockstep with No 10 and Hamish Falconer to make this happen. He sees Europe as at the heart of this agenda.”View image in fullscreenHamish Falconer was made minister for intergovernmental relationsandEuropean relations by Andy Burnham.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersFriends also said Miliband wants to find a way to revive the ailing G20, a largely economic multilateral body that has been steadily declining in influence since 2008, when the UKplayed a major role coordinating the response to the financial crashduring Gordon Brown’s premiership.In the latter days of his own tenure at No 10, Starmer appointed Brown to act as his special envoy on global finance and cooperation in advance of the G20, and Brown will retain the role, working alongside Miliband who was one of his advisers while chancellor. Lord Wood, who acted as a foreign policy adviser during the Brown premiership, has also been appointed to the Foreign Office as a minister in the Lords, and will bring experience and intellect to the role.With the UK due to chair the postponed illicit finance summit in December in advance of taking over the G20, ideas such as a global wealth tax and greater transparency in overseas financial holdings areall being promoted. But the secrecy of Britain’s overseas territories has for a decade been a millstone in the UK’s call to combat corruption.Kirsty McNeill, the new international development minister and a former executive director at Save the Children, has been asked to wrestle with the impact of massive aid cuts. She has previously said the UK will not regain credibility on aid unless it sets out a path for returning aid spending to 0.7% of GDP. Aidwill fall to 0.3% next yearandBurnham’s £2 bus fare capis being funded by a raid on the aid budget. The G20 at least provides a creative way for her to build alliances to tackle unjust debts and illicit financial flows.Aglobal wealth tax was proposedduring the Brazilian presidency of the G20 in 2024 after a study commissioned from the French economist Gabriel Zucman. “There is overwhelming public support for this idea,” Zucman said at the report’s launch. “Ten years ago, nobody believed 130 countries would support a minimum tax on multinationals. It was thought of as utopian.”The report said billionaires were paying an average of 0.3% tax on their wealth – less than the rates paid by workers. Zucman said the average wealth of the top 0.0001% of individuals had grown by 7.1% a year on average between 1987 and 2024, increasing the share of global wealth held by billionaires from 3% to 14%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion26:57Why it is so hard to tax the super-rich – videoTrump’s own G20 summit is due in Miami in December, by which time he could be diminished by a reverse in the midterm congressional elections. There has been a slow drop-off in world leaders attending the G20 partly owing to geopolitical rifts overUkraineand questions over its value, but by next year the economic fallout from the war in Iran may require economic and political coordination.Miliband is not, meanwhile, expected to act quickly on Burnham’s admission thatLabourneeded to “do better” on Gaza. Burnham suggested action on trade with illegal Israeli settlements was on his agenda, but Foreign Office diplomats have questioned the enforceability of such a ban.A debate is under way as to whether European states would best help the political parties opposed to the Israeli prime minister in the October elections by imposing fresh sanctions, underlining Benjamin Netanyahu’s diplomatic isolation, or whether he would use international disapproval to his domestic advantage.From Ukraine and Sudan to Gaza: why have hospitals become a target of war?Read moreThe pressure from the Labour backbenches for a more robust policy that treats international law with the same seriousness in the Middle East as the UK does in Ukraine is intense. A letter from 80 parliamentarians coordinated by the MP Kim Johnson called on Burnham to impose comprehensive sanctions on Israel and recognise the findings of the UN commission of inquiry thatIsrael is committing genocide. Burnham has said it is for the international courts to make such determinations.But a consequential question will be how Miliband retains his progressive credibility and yet remains on good terms with the US state department under Trump. Wood, a sceptic about past UK foreign military interventions, strongly opposed the US military attack on Iran.But the need to retain a modicum of US support for Ukraine has, ever since Trump’s election, been seen as an essential UK foreign policy priority, one that has required compromises and often involved working with the recently deceased Republican senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine. That is unlikely to change in the short term.Explore more on these topicsEd MilibandForeign, Commonwealth and Development OfficeUkraineEuropeDonald TrumpAndy BurnhamBenjamin NetanyahuanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Singapore bans Massive Attack for showing Palestinian flag, breaching ban on foreign emblems | Massive Attack | The Guardian
description: Two members given ‘stern warnings’ after concert and barred from returning, with band also excluded from performing in Singapore again, say authorities
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two members given ‘stern warnings’ after concert and barred from returning, with band also excluded from performing in Singapore again, say authorities
Content: Massive Attack in concert at the O2 Academy, Brixton, London, February 2016. Authorities in Singapore said the band would not be allowed to perform there again after a Palestinian flag was unfurled on stage.Photograph: RMV/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMassive Attack in concert at the O2 Academy, Brixton, London, February 2016. Authorities in Singapore said the band would not be allowed to perform there again after a Palestinian flag was unfurled on stage.Photograph: RMV/REX/ShutterstockMassive AttackSingapore bans Massive Attack for showing Palestinian flag, breaching ban on foreign emblemsTwo members given ‘stern warnings’ after concert and barred from returning, with band also excluded from performing in Singapore again, say authoritiesAgence France-Presse in SingaporeFri 31 Jul 2026 23.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish trip-hop bandMassive Attackhas been barred from performing in Singapore after an investigation found two members unfurled a Palestinian flag during a concert, police said.Singapore, known for its tough laws on public speech and assembly, bans the open display of all foreign flags, national emblems or banners without a permit.Two band members who held the flag on stage during a concert on Wednesday were also banned from re-entering Singapore and issued with warnings, police said in a statement late on Friday, without naming the pair.The concert promoter had not responded to an AFP request for comment at time of publication. The band had not issued a public comment.A video circulating online showed two Massive Attack members on stage unfurling a Palestinian flag to loud, prolonged cheers from the audience.After concluding their investigation and in consultation with state prosecutors, police said they “administered stern warnings to both men” and barred them from coming back to the city-state.The media regulator was also probing possible breaches of licensing conditions.“Notwithstanding the event organiser’s prior acknowledgment of the licence conditions, during the performance, two band members held a foreign flag on stage, and one of them also shouted ‘Free Palestine’,” police said.The media regulator “will also not grant any future application for performances by the band in Singapore in view of the entry ban”, police said.The band is known for its criticism of Israel’s military actions in Gaza and has used its popularity to support the Palestinian cause.In April, frontman Robert Del Naja wasamong more than 200 people arrestedat a protest in London’s Trafalgar Square in support of Palestine Action, an activist group banned by British authorities.Singapore is a major concert hub for south-east Asia, having hosted multi-night performances by Taylor Swift, Coldplay, Ed Sheeran and Bruno Mars.The police urged the public, including foreigners, “to refrain from importing foreign politics as this can undermine our social cohesion and the rule of law”.Explore more on these topicsMassive AttackPalestinePalestine ActionMiddle East and north AfricaProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Top mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead after 11 hit by avalanche in Pakistan  | Mountaineering | The Guardian
description: Other members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak have also died, climbing company says
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Other members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak have also died, climbing company says
Content: Nirmal Purja pictured in 2021 after his return from leading the first team to summit K2 in winter.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APView image in fullscreenNirmal Purja pictured in 2021 after his return from leading the first team to summit K2 in winter.Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/APMountaineeringTop mountaineer Nirmal Purja confirmed dead after 11 hit by avalanche in PakistanOther members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak also died, climbing company saysGeneva AbdulSat 1 Aug 2026 09.41 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA world-renowned Nepali mountaineer and former UK Special Forces member has died after being among 11 climbers caught in a deadly avalanche on Pakistan’s Broad Peak.Nirmal Purja was killed leading an expedition of 10 other people on the world’s 12th-highest mountain when an avalanche struck at around noon on Thursday.Elite Exped, the company Purja co-founded, said in a statement: “Today it is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak.”“We have also received confirmation that other members of the expedition sadly did not survive,” it said, without further detail.Purjamade history in 2019 after climbing all 14 of the world’s peaks over 8,000 metresin just over six months. He later led the first team to summit K2, the world’s second-highest mountain, in winter.1:52Nirmal Purja climbs world’s 14 highest peaks in record-breaking 189 days – video report“Records are made to be broken,” the former Gurkha and UKSF membertold the Guardian in 2019. “Someone one day will come along and be stronger. People are only limited by their imagination. If you don’t dream, then you won’t do it. Human beings are capable of doing amazing things.”The expedition included five Nepali climbers, as well as US, Pakistani, Omani and Chinese nationals. Another foreign climber was also part of the group, said Karrar Haidri, the vice-president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan.Elite Exped also confirmed the deaths of other expedition members, including his climbing partners and guides, Pur Bahadur Gurung (Yukta), a Nepali citizen, and Nima Sherpa.“Our deepest thoughts, prayers and heartfelt condolences are with their families, friends and loved ones,” the Elite Exped statement said. “No words can erase the pain of this unimaginable loss, and we ask that everyone respects their privacy as they grieve.”Map of Broad PeakOn Friday, rescuers had said thatfour bodies had been foundand efforts were under way to retrieve them despite the harsh weather. Among the victims were Nadhira Alharthy, the first Omani to climb Everest, and a US climber, Mallory Geis.View image in fullscreenNadhira Alharthy, the first Omani to climb Everest, was also among the victims.Photograph: instagram/alharthynoorTrackers carried by the climbers showed a rapid loss of altitude, suggesting the team had been caught in an avalanche. Purja’s tracker, however, shifted location after the initial rapid descent. The GPS data suggested the avalanche occurred close to 9am local time at 6,579 metres (21,585ft), between camps two and three on the west ridge of the 8,047-metre mountain, the most popular ascent route.View image in fullscreenBroad Peak is the 12th highest mountain in the world at 8,051 metres.Photograph: Naveed Hussain/AlamyThe British adventurer Bear Grylls said the news of Purja’s death was “heartbreaking for so many climbers around the world who had a relationship with this remarkable and unique man”.In the 2023 documentary Finding Michael, Purja and Grylls were enlisted to recover the body ofMichael Matthews, the youngest Briton to climb Everest, who disappeared on the mountain in 1999.Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of them in the special forces. In 2018, he was awarded an MBE by the queen for his achievements in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.He also drew plaudits for twice risking his life to help others. The first time was while descending from Annapurna, when he led a rescue of fellow climber Chin Wui Kin, who had been separated from an accompanying expedition and left without food, water or oxygen for 40 hours. He later died in hospital.Less than a month later, Purja and his team rescued two climbers from a height of 8,400 metres, sacrificing their own supplementary oxygen to the climbers in need.“For me it’s not about ego,” he previously told the Guardian. “It’s about principles. You can’t call yourself a climber and not help in that situation.”The Prince of Wales said he was “truly saddened to hear of the tragic death” of Purja, adding that he “served with distinction” before “becoming one of the world’s greatest mountaineers”.Explore more on these topicsMountaineeringPakistanSouth and central AsiaAvalanchesNepalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Devolution plans strengthen case for written UK constitution, says Burnham | Constitutional reform | The Guardian
description: PM argues for codified model of decentralisation that would fundamentally change centuries-old workings of state
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: PM argues for codified model of decentralisation that would fundamentally change centuries-old workings of state
Content: Burnham is inspired by Germany’s postwar basic law, which equalises finances across the regions.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenBurnham is inspired by Germany’s postwar basic law, which equalises finances across the regions.Photograph: Jeff Overs/BBC/PAConstitutional reformDevolution plans strengthen case for written UK constitution, says BurnhamPM argues for codified model of decentralisation that would fundamentally change centuries-old workings of stateJosh HallidayandAletha AduSat 1 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said his programme of devolution strengthens the case for a written constitution for the UK, a move that would fundamentally alter the workings of the state that have developed over centuries.The prime minister has long believed the UK’s “antiquated” political system needs a dramatic overhaul if opportunity is to be shared equally across the country.The UK is one of only a few major democracies without a written constitution, a document that codifies how a nation is governed within a set of fundamental rules.In a potentially historic shift, Burnham said this weekend that his government’s programme of decentralisation – which includesgiving regional leaders much greater controlover their finances – strengthens the argument for a codified arrangement.“It will increase the case for a constitution because Britain is changing through this,Englandis certainly changing through this,” he said.Burnham said the UK needed to devise a codified model of devolution that works for Wales, Scotland,Northern Irelandand the English regions.“In the end, I think it does start to point towards a new constitutional settlement … with that commitment to equivalent living standards,” he said, adding that his pledge of “good growth in every postcode” was “more than just a soundbite”.Burnham described the further devolution measures outlined on Friday as the most radical departure from Britain’s overcentralised political establishment. The “rewiring” of the UK had “gone to a new level of seriousness” and was centred on shifting decision-making outside Whitehall to mayors and local authorities throughNo 10 North.Tim Bale, a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, said introducing a written constitution would be a “huge departure” for the UK. Historically, most countries did it “in the wake of a revolution or a war that has removed or delegitimised the former regime”.It is unclear how the UK government would go about such significant constitutional change at the same time as pursuingBurnham’s agendaon issues such as devolution, social care and public control of utilities.While it would bring the UK into line with other democracies such as the US, Bale said it could “represent a major constraint on the executive … because it would presumably put the rules of the game beyond the power of parliament to change with a simple majority”.He added: “One of the upsides is that it might better define the competencies of the various levels of government – local, regional and national. But there is no way he will be able to limit it to that.”In his 2024 book Head North, written with the Liverpool city region mayor, Steve Rotheram, Burnham said deep inequality had become entrenched in Britain partly because it had not evolved from a “feudal state” in which power is largely concentrated in Westminster.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on England’s centralised state: Andy Burnham must unbundle it | EditorialRead more“Our failure fully to set out the rules for how the country should be run is one of the principal reasons why Britain is one of the most unequal major countries in the world,” he wrote.“Our unwritten and murky constitutional arrangements have had the effect of hoarding power in a small number of hands – in Whitehall and Westminster and, by extension, in the powerful networks of institutions and vested interests that surround them.”Burnham has cited as inspiration Germany’s postwarbasic law, orGrundgesetz, which stipulates there must be equivalent living standards in all the country’s states, with the wealthier regions redistributing their funds across the nation.Under devolution plans announced last week, by early 2028 regional mayors across England will be able to keep a share of income tax generated in their area.Under proposals to be published in late October, it is expected that economic powerhouses, such as London, Greater Manchester and the West Midlands, will hand some of their share to less prosperous regions, such as Hull and East Yorkshire.Dr Hannah White, the chief executive of the Institute for Government, said: “Adopting a written constitution – of the kind almost every other country already has – would represent a very significant constitutional shift for the UK and be a major exercise. A fully codified constitution would need to go far beyond devolution to encompass all the rules which structure the UK state.”Explore more on these topicsConstitutional reformAndy BurnhamDevolutionLabourWalesScotlandNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Purple reign: how shade became British gardeners’ favourite | Gardens | The Guardian
description: Britons move away from trend of grey paving and pristine lawns in an embrace of colour, with lavender a top choice
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Britons move away from trend of grey paving and pristine lawns in an embrace of colour, with lavender a top choice
Content: More than 11,000 visitors of RHS Garden Wisley’s Hilltop were asked to pick their favourite colour for plants.Photograph: Tim Graham/AlamyView image in fullscreenMore than 11,000 visitors of RHS Garden Wisley’s Hilltop were asked to pick their favourite colour for plants.Photograph: Tim Graham/AlamyGardensPurple reign: how shade became British gardeners’ favouriteBritons move away from trend of grey paving and pristine lawns in an embrace of colour, with lavender a top choiceHelena HortonSat 1 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you manage to spot a garden in bloom this summer, beyond the strips of bleached and torched grass, there may be one colour you see more than any other: purple, the horticultural hue of the season.Plants such as lavender, salvias and catmint are in vogue, according to the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS), which conducted extensive research into the colours Britons best love to see in their gardens.In one experiment at RHS Garden Wisley’s Hilltop, more than 11,000 visitors were asked to choose their preferred shades. Purple flower hues accounted for the strongest preference (26.67%), closely followed by red (25.24%).View image in fullscreenVisitors look at the crops at Warwickshire lavender farm.Photograph: Jacob King/PAThe purple patch has surprisedgardentrend watchers and marks a departure from recent less dramatic trends. Grey hues have been very popular in home and garden design over the last few years.Tom Massey, anaward-winninggarden designer based in London, said clients wanted bright colours, particularly purples. He said: “We’ve moved away from the era of large expanses of decking, paving and lawn towards richer, more naturalistic planting inspired by meadows and natural plant communities.”View image in fullscreenMore natural, colourful garden styles are growing in popularity.Photograph: Ros Crosland/AlamyLaura Carey, who co-owns Carey garden designs with her husband, Joe, has found that purple is the most popular colour with her clients, too. She said: “Purple is a favourite across the board with all of our clients. There are so many purple flowering plants to choose from, including national favourites like lavender, alliums and geraniums.”View image in fullscreenCatmint is also a popular purple plant.Photograph: John Glover/AlamyMassey added: “Purple has always been a hugely important colour in gardens because it combines beautifully with greens, silvers and the buff tones of ornamental grasses. It also attracts pollinators and tends to have a calming quality. Plants like salvias, nepetas, alliums and lavender remain incredibly popular for exactly those reasons.”The popularity of the colour may be related to the emotions it evokes in humans. Other research found that purples and blues evoke a sense of calm and relaxation, and yellows and oranges bring joy.Massey said: “I think people are becoming much more confident with colour generally. You can see this in high-profile public landscapes that have proved hugely popular, such as Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in London, parts of the High Line in New York, and the seasonal displays and borders at RHS gardens like Wisley, where bold combinations of colour are used to create planting schemes that are both beautiful and ecologically rich.”View image in fullscreenSalvia nachtvlinder.Photograph: Elf Photography/AlamyThe findings were published in the study Flower Power: How favourite flower colours shape how we feelinActa Psychologica.Dr Ashby Sachs, a wellbeing fellow at the RHS, said: “Colour is a key consideration when it comes to garden design, but little is known about how it interacts with our sense of wellbeing. That different shades of colour can elicit an anticipated emotional response in people is incredibly useful when it comes to designing spaces for specific purposes and people such as in schools and hospitals.”Explore more on these topicsGardensPlantsnewsShareReuse this content

title: On the ground in the English seaside town rightwing influencers say is being ‘invaded’ | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Some in Dover say their town is being exploited by content creators and politicians, but others claim there is a genuine problem
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Some in Dover say their town is being exploited by content creators and politicians, but others claim there is a genuine problem
Content: Tom Armstrong, who lives in the area, said it was good that rightwing politicians were drawing attention to small boat crossings.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Armstrong, who lives in the area, said it was good that rightwing politicians were drawing attention to small boat crossings.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianImmigration and asylumOn the ground in the English seaside town rightwing influencers say is being ‘invaded’Some in Dover say their town is being exploited by content creators and politicians, but others claim there is a genuine problemKevin RawlinsonSat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you believe rightwing influencers and politicians, Dover and the widerKentcoast has been the site of an “invasion” for years now. And, for an online audience of millions, they and their camera crews have been the vanguard in the nation’s defence.Indeed, if you believe all you see on the algorithms of amateur Channel watchers, the shadow home secretary,Chris Philp, braved a hail of French gunfire as he took to the water in a fishing boat this week; an attempt by the French authorities, he suggested, to deter him in his mission of highlighting the small boats crisis.The inconvenient truth behind Philp’s attempt to self-police our borders is that nothing of the sort happened. The French government said he simply passed by a routine training exercise that involved firing live rounds.With its sloping pebble beach and sunbathers and dog-walkers enjoying the summer sunshine by its marina this week, Dover does not look much like the frontline of a war zone. Are the rightwing figures who regularly visit the town to create social media content exploiting it for their own careers, or are they seeking solutions to a genuine problem? “They’re using Dover a bit,” said one resident, Alison Drake. “People making all these videos and that is not really doing much, is it?”View image in fullscreenThe frontline of a war zone? The Dover seafront, where rightwing influencers and politicians flock to make content for social media about an ‘invasion’.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianSome said that creating tension where there was none before was all part of the plan. “What they’re trying to do is play on fear with all of these stunts,” said Razia Shariff, who runs the Kent Refugee Action Network (Kran), a charity that provides education for refugee and asylum-seeking young people.Whether or not the selfie stick-toting influencers who descend on the south coast need to capture the supposed “invasion” is, for some, a moot point.Some of those living in the area insisted the relentless focus on the issue – and on the region – was at least keeping the problem in the public eye. “They’re letting the people know that the French are not doing anything,” Tom Armstrong said. Armstrong is avowedly anti-immigration and said the “country is being devalued” by it. He said rightwing politicians were helping that cause. “You’ve got to draw attention,” he said. Later, he added: “We’ve got to know the truth.”Philp claimed to have been exposing the small boats crisis during his jaunt across the Channel. While Drake agreed that rightwing figures highlighting the issue might prompt action, she added: “Everyone knows about it, it’s about time they did something about it. They don’t do anything. So, it’s all very well everyone keep going on about it, but no one does anything. They know it’s happening.”View image in fullscreenAlison Drake said despite the attention on Dover, no one was doing anything about the small boat crossings.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianFew people have had more opportunity to solve the small boats crisis than Philp who, as immigration minister in the early 2020s, oversaw a sharp increase in crossings.In contrast, organisations such as Kran are working to alleviate some of the challenges caused by the way migration has been handled by successive governments.The young people Kran helps are taking part in a summer scheme at an academy in Kent this week. Shariff spoke glowingly of some of their predecessors’ achievements. One, she said, had arrived in the UK as a child refugee and now worked as a nurse in local hospitals. “Others have set up their own businesses against all the odds. They get on with their lives and they try.”Carol, who lives in Dover and did not want to give her surname, suggested the focus should be more on the work of organisations such as Kran than on politicians such as Philp andNigel Farage.The Reform leader has repeatedly referred to small boat crossings as an “invasion”. Standing on the Dover seafront in 2024, he described the site as the “frontline of the great national debate on immigration”.Carol did not recognise the picture the Reform leader painted of the town, as she stood on almost the same spot he had occupied two years ago. “I mean, look, it’s pleasant enough,” she said, nodding towards the beach.View image in fullscreenCarol worries that Dover being used as the backdrop for content about small boat crossings could deter tourists from visiting.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/The GuardianPeople there were sunbathing in the warm weather, while children played in the water and others took an opportunity to go out in the sea in small vessels. “I think it is unfair that Dover is headlined in that way. Because you can sit on the beach, enjoy the area.”Carol said it was frustrating that Dover and other nearby towns were so often used as the backdrop for social media content focusing on the small boats crisis and feared it could deter people from visiting an area that needs a lift.“It’s a bit rundown, like many towns. It’s a bit sad. So it’s not a great place to shop, by all means, but the seafront’s lovely. And the surrounding countryside is lovely. I’m sure it isn’t helping. Dover has got that image.”Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumKentChris PhilpNigel FaragenewsShareReuse this content

title: Knickers in a twist: why M&S selling crotchless underwear isn’t as outrageous as it seems | Marks & Spencer | The Guardian
description: Some have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts say
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Some have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts say
Content: In 2024, M&S reported a third of underwear sales were made by people under 30.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenIn 2024, M&S reported a third of underwear sales were made by people under 30.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAMarks & SpencerKnickers in a twist: why M&S selling crotchless underwear isn’t as outrageous as it seemsSome have called it ‘S&M’, but partnership with Ann Summers is less a scandal than another step in a century of evolving underwear trends, experts sayLauren CochraneSat 1 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe news that Marks & Spencer is selling Ann Summers crotchless knickers on their website has been greeted – as might be expected – with outrage online, being described as everything from “tawdry” to“S & M”.But it could be this is just the latest evolution in what the UK’s biggest underwear retailer has available for the smalls drawer. In recent years, the store has sold vastly different options through its own products, ranging from full-brief knickers to thongs, period knickers and those that can be used bywomen who wear stomas. The introduction of other brands in clothing came five years ago, with underwear included. Ann Summers – which is selling bras and chemises as well as knickers on the M&S website – lines up alongside lingerie brands including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein.Catherine Shuttleworth, the chief executive of retail consultancy Savvy, sees it as part of wider strategy. “They’ve started introducing brands to bring them into sectors that probably isn’t their core,” she says. “And this is another one. It’s just a little bit more eye-catching.”View image in fullscreenThe offending crotchless thong being sold by M&S, which has been called ‘tawdry’Photograph: M&SShuttleworth describes M&S underwear as a “national obsession” and there’s little doubt the store remains a must-visit for anyone restocking their underwear drawer. If its long-term popularity might have meant it was perceived as a bit mumsy for younger people, that has changed recently. In 2024, the store reported that people under 30 made up a third of underwear sales – double that of 2023.View image in fullscreenThe Ann Summers knickers are sold on M&S’s website alongside other retailers including Pour Moi and Calvin Klein.Photograph: M&SShuttleworth says the introduction of Ann Summers could be about continuing to engage this demographic. “They are always innovating for every stage of your life,” she says. “And I think this is a gap in their category. Ann Summers is a byword for sex, isn’t it?”This echoes the message coming from the retailer itself. In a statement, an M&S spokesperson said: “Our ‘brands at M&S’ strategy is all about giving customers greater choice through carefully selected third-party brands that complement our existing M&S offer. Ann Summers is one of the latest brands to join [M&S online], helping broaden our underwear and nightwear offer.”There is also, of course, the publicity factor. “It doesn’t really matter whether they sell any crotchless pants or not, we’re all going to be talking about it,” says Shuttleworth. “You might also go online to look. You might not buy those, but you’ll think: ‘I could do with replacing my pants.’”M&Shas sold underwear since the 1920s and fitted bras since 1947. It was the first retailer to sell pre-shrunk cotton underwear in 1965, and by 1976 knickers were the biggest export – nearly 4m pairs were sold internationally every year. Fashion dictated different styles – from the “hip-hugger” styles in the 60s to thongs, whichreached the apex of popularity in the mid-00s.In 2016, the store sold 60m pairs of knickers a year, with Brazilian knickers replacing the thong. The style, which reveals some of the wearer’s bum, made up 10% of those sales. By 2021,thongs were back, thanks to the popularity of low rise jeans. According to the retailer’s website, the No 1 bestseller now is a five-pack of white full briefs.View image in fullscreenExperts have said that M&S have always followed trends, including lace designs a world away from basics.Photograph: PR ImageLorraine Topper, a researcher atThe Underpinnings Museum, argues the reaction around the crotchless knickers is disproportionate – because the store does stock sexier styles along with basics.“M&S have always followed fashion with regard to their lingerie designs,” she says. “For some reason, it’s the multipack of full briefs that sticks in people’s heads when you talk about their underwear, rather than, for example, the beautiful lace designs from the Rosie Exclusively range.”She describes the outrage as “a fuss over nothing … Open-crotch underwear for women was the norm before the 1920s so this type of garment isn’t quite as scandalous as we might first think.”Explore more on these topicsMarks & SpencerRetail industryUnderwearnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘MPs have had their stomachs pumped’: concerns over ‘alcohol-soaked’ culture in Westminster | Politics | The Guardian
description: Alcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report finds
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Alcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report finds
Content: MPs socialise on the terrace outside the House of Commons. Politicians have described how alcohol is readily available throughout the day, including at daytime lobbying events.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/In Pictures/GettyView image in fullscreenMPs socialise on the terrace outside the House of Commons. Politicians have described how alcohol is readily available throughout the day, including at daytime lobbying events.Photograph: Mark Kerrison/In Pictures/GettyPolitics‘MPs have had their stomachs pumped’: concerns over ‘alcohol-soaked’ culture in WestminsterAlcohol is embedded in profession where long hours, loneliness and lobbying are the norm, report findsDenis CampbellSat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 04.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleParliament is “Britain’s last alcohol-soaked workplace” where MPs are offered free drinks as early as midday despite alcohol-related scandals, areport has revealed.Drinking is commonplace and some MPs have had their stomachs pumped after consuming so much alcohol that they ended up in hospital, one disclosed.Alcohol is “embedded” in how Westminster works, driven by loneliness among MPs, socialising in order to meet ministers, and drinks being served at daytime and evening events.View image in fullscreenThe Churchill Room bar on the terrace of the House of Commons.Photograph: Lisa Ryder/AlamyThose are the findings of a survey of 190 MPs and their staff which shows that Westminster’s drinking culture endures, despite rising concern and a string of incidents, including an MP’s researcherallegedly having had her drink spikedin Strangers’ bar in parliament and the revelation that the Labour MP Neil Coyle was at one timedrinking up to 200 units of alcohol a week– the equivalent of 10 pints a night. The spiking led to a police investigation and the temporary closure of Strangers’ bar.The report, by the Institute of Alcohol Studies (IAS) thinktank, said: “The findings suggest that Westminster remains a highly unusual workplace where alcohol is embedded in professional life, networking, lobbying and socialising in ways that would be exceptional in most other UK workplaces.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, visit a pub during a trip to Essex. The report found alcohol was embedded in networking, lobbying and socialising for those working in Westminster.Photograph: Richard Pohle/Pool Times Media Ltd/AP“Participants described alcohol as being available throughout the working day, frequently provided for free, and often intertwined with career advancement.”Twenty-four MPs, 58 Westminster staff and 108 constituency office personnel shared their experiences and views. One MP, describing how readily available alcohol was at Westminster, said: “Going to a meeting at noon and alcohol’s available. Of course, I’m not used to that in my old job.”The free alcohol at events on the parliamentary estate, which organisations arrange to help them lobby MPs, emerged as a particular issue.Another MP said: “Where else in a work environment would you go, unless it was the works Christmas do, and there was free alcohol there for you? It just wouldn’t happen in real life.”A third said: “You can start drinking here from 12 o’clock onwards and go around and consume large amounts of alcohol, and it’s relatively freely available.”A fourth described events as a “legitimised opportunity to drink alcohol”, while a fifth said this routine provision of alcohol helps to create a “casual attitude to drinking”.Hannah Spencer, the Green party MP elected at the Gorton and Denton byelection in February, received a mixed reaction from MPs when in April she labelled Westminster’s drinking culture“unprofessional and worrying”and said it led to cases of “questionable and dangerous behaviour”. She remarked that “you can smell the alcohol when people are in between votes”.View image in fullscreenHannah Spencer said she found Westminster’s drinking culture ‘unprofessional and worrying’ after being elected as an MP this year.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe IAS report also found that:42% of the MPs interviewed had been offered an alcoholic drink at a work meeting or event on a weekly basis during the previous six months; 13% said that occurred daily.22% had concerns about a colleague’s drinking.Parliament’s long and unusual working hours, the loneliness many MPs experience being away from home, the pressures of the job and socialising in order to advance their careers can all act as catalysts for drinking.The report added: “The availability of alcohol was seen to encourage unhealthy behaviour in general, from affecting colleagues’ sleep and stress levels to potentially normalising high-risk drinking, with one MP referring to colleagues having had their stomachs pumped in hospital and going back into Westminster the following day.”Some MPs said the findings should prompt Westminster to rethink its attitude to alcohol. The Labour MP Cat Smith said: “We wouldn’t accept a surgeon operating after a drink or a driver getting behind the wheel – so why should we accept legislators voting on the laws of the land after one?“If we’re serious about being a professional workplace, we have to ask hard questions about practices like late night votes that sit alongside on-tap bars.”Beccy Cooper, who was a public health consultant before entering parliament as a Labour MP in 2024, said the report was a wake-up call. In a foreword to the report, she suggested that parliament should draw up its first formal workplace policy on alcohol.She added: “Two findings stood out to me. Almost one in 10 respondents reported a negative experience because of someone else’s drinking at work and 70% either didn’t know, or weren’t sure, how to raise a concern about a colleague’s drinking.“That combination – real, measurable harm and no clear route to address it – is exactly the kind of gap we need to address.”View image in fullscreenSome MPs said Westminster should rethink its attitude to alcohol and parts of the job such as late night votes that sit alongside bars on-site.Photograph: House of Commons/PAKatherine Severi, the IAS’s chief executive, said Westminster should limit the provision of free alcohol to evening events as part of a renewed drive to make it a more modern workplace, which many MPs and staff support. “Very few professions these days would allow free alcohol from midday, or regularly host outside organisations sponsoring events where drinking is the norm during working hours,” she added.The report also said that the commercialisation of parliament as an events venue contributed to MPs’ drinking.In 2023, parliament’s independent complaints and grievance scheme saidalcohol was a “frequent factor” in its investigationsinto alleged misconduct at Westminster. In its findings of 30 investigations it undertook between 2021 and 2022, it added that drinking in parliament’s array of bars was “leading to intimidating behaviour like shouting and swearing”.In July 2023, Daniel Greenberg, the parliamentary standards commissioner, said alcohol had led to “behaviour problems” at Westminster and suggested the sale of alcohol on the state be kept under review.A parliament spokesperson said everyone working there had been reminded to use alcohol responsibly, but hinted that immediate changes were unlikely. “Any changes to parliament’s provision of alcohol would ultimately be a matter for members to decide on. The estate is a unique working environment that includes public access and events,” they said.“Parliament’s behaviour code makes clear that everyone should be treated with respect at all times, and those who choose to drink alcohol on the estate must do so responsibly.”Westminster’s efforts to promote more responsible drinking include greater provision of no- and low-alcohol products and venue staff’s right to refuse to serve anyone who is, or looks likely to become, intoxicated.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
