title: Josh Kerr storms to Commonwealth Games mile title in golden Glasgow moment  | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Josh Kerr’s summer of miracle and wonder continued in front of his adoring home fans as he added a Commonwealth gold medal in the mile to his glittering collection
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Josh Kerr’s summer of miracle and wonder continued in front of his adoring home fans as he added a Commonwealth gold medal in the mile to his glittering collection
Content: Josh Kerr crosses the line in style on his way to Commonwealth Games gold in the mile in front of jubilant fans in Glasgow.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJosh Kerr crosses the line in style on his way to Commonwealth Games gold in the mile in front of jubilant fans in Glasgow.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCommonwealth Games 2026Josh Kerr storms to Commonwealth Games mile title in golden Glasgow momentHome favourite blazes clear to delight Scottish fansWightman fades to sixth, Myers takes silverSean Ingleat Scotstoun StadiumSat 1 Aug 2026 16.31 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosh Kerr’s summer of miracle and wonder continued in front of his adoring home fans as he added Commonwealth gold to his glittering collection.In a slowly run race that frequently resembled dodgems, Kerr made a devastating kick for home with 250 metres remaining to eviscerate a high-quality field and take the title in 3:54.12.Commonwealth Games 2026: Scotland’s Josh Kerr storms to gold in men’s mile final – liveRead moreSome had feared that Kerr might have an emotional hangover after shattering the mile world record a fortnight ago. Others believed he might be vulnerable in a last-lap sprint. So much for all that. He destroyed them all.In fact, the 28-year-old Scot was so far in front before the end he even had time to smile and gesture excitedly to those roaring him on in the main stand.“It doesn’t get any better than this,” said Kerr. “This is absolutely incredible. To do it in front of a Scottish crowd where I learned how to race. I came here week after week growing up as a kid.”Before that dazzling finish Kerr had to employ a few rough-house tactics along the way. A couple of times he barged other athletes. On another occasion he looked to step off the track. Not that he cared.“I’m fit at the moment, I’ll say that,” he said. “I love this style of racing. I knew that was what it was going to be coming in.”Sebastian Coe, the president of World Athletics, came up with the idea of restoring the mile to theCommonwealth Games. He knew there was something mythical and magical about the distance. And so the umbilical cord that was wrongly ripped up after 1966 after a legendary roll call of winners was rightly restored.Roger Bannister, Herb Elliott, Peter Snell, Kip Keino … and now Josh Kerr. That is some list. And it was some final too.View image in fullscreenJosh Kerr salutes his adoring fans after winning Commonwealth Games gold in the mile.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThere has been plenty of talk about diluted fields at these Games. But this was a full-fat cream contest, containing three of the last four world 1500m champions – Timothy Cheruiyot, Jake Wightman and Kerr – as well as the 20-year-old Australian wunderkind Cam Myers.Earlier this week, Myers was hailed as the “future of the sport” by Wightman. But he had no answer to Kerr’s injection of pace and had to settle for silver in 3:55.26, with Cheruiyot taking bronze.Racing the clock is very different to the white heat of a global final. And so it proved. The first lap was run in a dawdry 59 seconds. And it got even slower as the pack went through halfway in a painfully slow 2:02.Who was going to blink first? Not Kerr. “It was a little windy up the back stretch,” he explained. “It was about making sure I wasn’t spending too much energy in the first 600m to a kilometre. Then it was about staying awake and alive and trying to get round and get some space. It took some time. But overall I felt like I had plenty of gears left in me.”Even with 500m to go Kerr was still poorly positioned. But he rapidly moved up behind Cheruiyot and Myers into third by the bell before striking hard – and decisively – soon after.Suddenly Kerr was five metres clear, his legs whirring like pistons. Only Wightman, the 2022 world champion, went with him. But the exertion proved too much and he fizzled out to finish sixth.“I knew an opportunity would open up,” said Kerr. “Jake was on the outside and he’s such a great closer. But I had enough energy to put a gap on him in the last 200m.”Kerr has now won the World Indoor title and broken the world record this year, to add to his world title in 2023 and Olympic silver and bronze medals from Paris and Tokyo. But he is not finished yet given the 1500m world record is also now in his sights.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“London was a big stress, pushing my body to the extreme limit,” he admitted. “Doing a championship race is a nice clean of the palate, using your brain instead of your body. It’s how I love to race.”Elsewhere Jazmin Sawyers finally won her first major outdoor title with a leap of 6.93m in the women’s long jump. Sawyers, who was a silver medallist in Glasgow 12 years ago, was six centimetres clear of Nigeria’s Ruth Osoro.It was also another great night for Australia as Kurtis Marschall broke the Commonwealth pole vault record with a clearance of 5.85m to take gold.There was also a clean sweep for Australia in the women’s mile with Abbey Caldwell winning gold, Jessica Hull silver and Claudia Hollingsworth bronze.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026AthleticsCommonwealth GamesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jamaica stun Australia as England miss out on Commonwealth Games netball final | Commonwealth Games 2026 | The Guardian
description: Jamaica reached the Commonwealth netball final after defeating defending champions Australia in one of the biggest surprises in the sport’s history
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Jamaica reached the Commonwealth netball final after defeating defending champions Australia in one of the biggest surprises in the sport’s history
Content: Jamaica celebrate their stunning upset victory against Australia.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenJamaica celebrate their stunning upset victory against Australia.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPCommonwealth Games 2026Jamaica stun Australia as England miss out on Commonwealth Games netball finalRoses beaten by New Zealand 61-54 in semi-finalEngland to face Australia for bronze medalSean Inglein GlasgowSat 1 Aug 2026 13.31 EDTFirst published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 06.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJamaica are through to theCommonwealth Gamesnetball final after defeating defending champions Australia in one of the biggest surprises in the sport’s history.In the best game of the tournament by far, Australia scored three goals to reduce Jamaica’s lead to one with 36 seconds remaining.Boxer secures Tuvalu’s first Commonwealth Games medal without winning a boutRead moreBut in front of a near-capacity crowd at the Hydro that included William and Kate, the Prince and Princess of Wales, Sophie Dwyer missed a three-foot shot to level for Australia after the siren.It meant the Sunshine Girls clung on for a shock 46-45 win. And that Australia had failed to reach the final for the first time since netball was introduced to the Games in 1998.Earlier England’s hopes of gold were dashed in a 61-54 defeat by New Zealand that was far more comprehensive than the scoreline suggests.The Silver Ferns went into the semi-final without defender Catherine Hall, who ruptured an anterior cruciate ligament in her knee against Wales. However, their influential goal attack Georgia Heffernan, who suffered an ankle injury against Wales, was able to play through the pain.And while she scored nine goals from 10 attempts and provided 15 goal assists, it was the Silver Ferns’ Grace Nweke who dominated the match. England simply had no answer to the 6ft 4in goal shooter, who finished with 52 goals from 57 attempts.View image in fullscreenGrace Nweke dominated the match to steer New Zealand into the final with victory against England.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PANew Zealand will now play Jamaica in Sunday’s final. England will face Australia in the bronze medal match.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEleanor Cardwell, who was part of the England team that lost the bronze medal match to the Silver Ferns in 2022, stressed the importance of refocusing on Sunday’s match against Australia.“I don’t want that feeling again,” said Cardwell. “I think that’s going to add extra fuel to the fire. We need to really want it tomorrow, and I know we really want it, we want to come away with a medal.“Obviously, the bronze isn’t all we wanted, but that’s the one that we are going to fight for now. We’ve got to go back, recover well and have the conversation about what we’re going to do tomorrow.”Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth Games 2026England netball teamNew Zealand netball teamDiamondsNetballCommonwealth GamesAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Glorious Goodwood: Evening Saigon lands Stewards’ Cup as Crowley hangs up boots  | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: Wathan Racing topped an amazing week at the meeting with victory in the Stewards’ Cup with Evening Saigon
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Wathan Racing topped an amazing week at the meeting with victory in the Stewards’ Cup with Evening Saigon
Content: 11h ago11.33 EDTGlorious Goodwood final day reviewEvening Saigon,a 16-1 chance ridden byJames Doylefrom stall 10, won the £250kStewards’ Cuphere on Saturday on the afternoon whenJim Crowley,the 2016 champion jockey on the Flat, announced his retirement from race-riding following a serious fall at York in August 2025.The consensus among trainers when the draw for Saturday’s feature event was made earlier in the week was that the high-numbered stalls would have an edge, butEvening Saigonmoved smoothly towards the lead on the far side with around a furlong to run and stayed on well to beat Stratusnine (drawn five), with Mitbaahy, from stall 25, first across the line on the stands’ side in third.The victory completed an impressive double in Glorious Goodwood’s biggest handicaps for trainerHamad Al Jehani,who saddledArchivist,also at 16-1,to land the Golden Mile here on Friday, whileEvening Saigonwas also a seventh winner of the week for the gelding’s owner, the Qatar-based Wathnan Racing operation.“James had a bit of a hard choice [from three Wathnan-owned runners] but he was pretty firm on riding this lad in the end,” Richard Brown, the operation’s racing adviser, said.“If you look at Hamad’s statistics since he started training, they match up with the best trainers in the country. He’s a phenomenal horseman and was a very good rider himself. He’s a great horseman and he’s formed a great team.”Earlier in the afternoon, the weighing room paid tribute to the retiring former champion jockey,Jim Crowley,who is hanging up his boots after struggling to recover from serious injuries sustained in a fall at York 11 months ago.Crowley started his career as a jump jockey before switching to the Flat, and was crownedchampion jockey in 2016before being hired as the No 1 jockey to the powerful Shadwell Racing operation, founded by the late Sheikh Hamdan al-Maktoum.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Sunday tipsShowChester:2.10 Timber Twelve 2.45 Pure Grit 3.20 Jazl (nb) 3.52 Khafiz (nap) 4.22 Blue Prince 4.52 Saligo Bay.Yarmouth:2.35 Mr Bollinger 3.08 Keep Grating 3.38 Nicely Curved 4.08 Okiru 4.38 Nuptown Girl 5.08 Papa Don’t Preach.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The best horses ridden by Crowley in Shadwell’s blue-and-white colours included the brilliant miler,Baaeed, one of the best sprinters of recent years inBattaashand the King George winner,Hukum.“It’s been a great career,” Crowley said on Saturday. “It’s just unfortunate that after my accident at York, my body couldn’t get back to the level I want to be to race-ride again.“I never imagined this happening when I came from jumping and I was fortunate to ride all over the world and for some of the best trainers in the world.”ShareUpdated at11.52 EDT

title: The great British switch-off: how floating retreats, mobile-free pubs and sauna book groups are liberating people from their phones  | Smartphones | The Guardian
description: Sick of doomscrolling? From venues with smartphone swear jars to cabins with absolutely no signal, here are the fun and freeing ways to ditch your device
Author: Isabelle Aron
Headline: Sick of doomscrolling? From venues with smartphone swear jars to cabins with absolutely no signal, here are the fun and freeing ways to ditch your device
Content: A Hawaii reading retreat with the Silent Book Club.Photograph: Silent Book ClubView image in fullscreenA Hawaii reading retreat with the Silent Book Club.Photograph: Silent Book ClubSmartphonesThe great British switch-off: how floating retreats, mobile-free pubs and sauna book groups are liberating people from their phonesSick of doomscrolling? From venues with smartphone swear jars to cabins with absolutely no signal, here are the fun and freeing ways to ditch your deviceIsabelle AronSat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s a ritual at the start of every event hosted bythe Offline Project. Run by Pelé Zachariah, the activities vary – it could be a group walk, a collage‑making class or a supper club – but each one begins in the same way, *with an invitation to hand over your phone. Devices go in a lockbox. Once they’re all in, Zachariah closes the door and turns the key. “I don’t place them in for people, because it’s nice for them to physically put it in the box themselves, walk away, and think: for the next two or three hours, I’m fully present.”He has been running these screen-free events in London since August 2025. First-timers can be apprehensive about being separated from their phone. “You can sense the vibe when they’re putting it away,” says Zachariah. “People have said to me, ‘I felt really weird’ or ‘I felt super uncomfortable for the first few minutes not having my phone on me.’ Then they’ll say, ‘I didn’t know how much I needed that.’”Zachariah understands why people might find it difficult at first. “It’s very unnatural. You might put your phone in the living room while you work in the kitchen, but here you’re seeing it locked behind what is essentially a gate that you can’t access,” he says. But when people leave, they often say they would like to have their own phone lockbox, or tell him that they’re going to try to not look at their device until they get home. “It’s kind of sad that we have to literally lock our phones away. But people really crave that time.”View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian DesignThis is true for Jarred Laros, 31, who lives in Essex and has been a regular at the Offline Project since it launched. One of the first events he went to was a “paint and sip” evening, where an artist taught everyone how to paint a landscape scene with mountains, a river and a sunset. People sat around a table together, working on their canvases while having drinks and snacks, and getting to know each other. “I liked the idea of getting off my phone and being more intentional with how I’m spending my time. I would never try to teach myself how to paint, but doing that in a community setting is very easy-going. The conversation flows.”Laros runs his own business, and spends a lot of time on his devices. “I’m always glued to a screen, whether it’s my iPad, my MacBook, my phone, or all three at the same time,” he says. “Outside of work, there’s the doomscroll that you succumb to. I go on Instagram without intending to. Half an hour later, I’m, like, ‘What am I still doing on this app?’ My average daily screen time is seven and a half hours. My relationship with my phone is not what I want it to be.”The Offline Project is part of a new wave of digital detox communities that host events to give people time away from screens. It’s not hard to understand the appeal: adults in the UK now spend an average of four and a half hours online a day, and most of that is on their phones, according to Ofcom’s 2025Online Nation report.In 2025, theannual TouchPoints surveyby the Institute of Practitioners in Advertising found that British adults were spending more time on their phones than watching TV for the first time. The government hasrecently announcedthat in spring 2027 it will bring in asocial media banfor under-16s, which will include platforms like Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. When the news was announced, a teenage girl went viral when asked by a news reporter how she would spend all her newfound free time. Her answer?“Stare at a wall.”Thankfully, if you want a break from your phone, there are plenty of things to do that are much more engaging. As our lives are becoming ever-more online, people are starting to push back against the hold that technology has on us. Sick of looking out at a sea of screens, some musicians are enforcing a no phones policy at their gigs. Bob Dylan’s 2025 UK and Ireland tour, Fred Again’s gigs at Alexandra Palace in February, and Harry Styles’s one-off gig in Manchester in March this year all had rules against using phones. It’s happening at comedy events, too – phones were placed in locked pouches at Sarah Silverman’s London Palladium gig last year, and Russell Howard’s current Don’t Tell the Algorithm tour promises “no phones, no distractions, just humans and jokes”.double quotation markNightclubs are meant to be dark for that dual sense of losing yourself and finding yourself at the same time. Phones inhibit both of those thingsView image in fullscreenAnnie Mac’s club night Before Midnight, where stickers are placed on phone cameras to prevent people taking photos or videos.Photograph: Karen StanleyAccording todata from Eventbrite, attendance at phone-free events in 2024 to 2025 increased by 121% globally. At broadcaster and DJ Annie Mac’s club nightBefore Midnight, stickers are placed on phone cameras so you can’t take photos or videos. “It reminds people to be in the moment. You’re only going to get so much satisfaction out of blurred videos with distorted sound, or dark, fuzzy photos,” she says. “Nightclubs are traditionally places where you go to feel a sense of freedom – to be whoever you want to be. They’re meant to be dark for that dual sense of losing yourself and finding yourself at the same time. Phones inhibit both of those things.”While some are seeking out pockets of time at events and venues where they can escape their smartphones, others are going one step further and ditching them altogether. Cody Ramone, 31, from Derby, was using an old flip phone from 2015 until the pandemic, when life became more online than ever and he needed a smartphone again. In 2024, he switched back to a “dumb phone”. “I got tired of all the notifications and being constantly online,” he says.Abandoning his smartphone has been transformative and given him time for more enriching activities. “I get bored more. Being bored is what drives you to try new things, pick up an old hobby, or think creatively. My attention span has improved, so I read more and spend more time doing creative hobbies, like crochet. I call people or hang out with them more often,” he says.What is it that makes our phones so addictive? “Digital media activates the same reward pathway as drugs and alcohol, releasing dopamine, our reward neurotransmitter, in a key area of the reward pathway in the brain,” says Anna Lembke, professor of psychiatry at Stanford University School of Medicine and the author ofDopamine Nation. “Moving images are like catnip for the mammalian brain, leading to video-chaining, akin to ‘chain smoking’. Once we begin, it’s hard to stop, even when we want to.”The more time we spend on our phones, the more we become “desensitised to what we are seeing” and look for more “potent rewards to recreate that original experience of pleasure”, says Lembke. “At the same time, we lose our ability to take joy in other more modest rewards, like watching a sunset, sharing a meal with friends, or reading a good book. We spend more time scrolling alone. We become increasingly dissatisfied and lonely.”While that might sound like a bleak state of affairs, the good news is that it doesn’t have to be this way. With the rise of phone-free experiences, it’s possible to detach yourself from your device, even if it’s temporarily. “Part of having a healthier relationship with technology must include discrete periods of time when we are not using it, and instead fully present and interacting with the people and the world around us,” says Lembke. “This means creating collective spaces where we come together device-free.”From off-grid, tech-free cabins to the pubs where devices aren’t allowed, these are the places to escape your phone in the UK.View image in fullscreenOn arrival at the Digital Detox Club, devices are put in the ‘phone hotel’.Photograph: Celie NigoumiDigital detox clubsSet up in Amsterdam in 2024 by friends Jordy van Bennekom, Valentijn Klok and Ilya Kneppelhout, the Offline Club has 14 chapters in cities across 10 countries, including London and Bristol in the UK. Events start with everyone putting their devices in the “phone hotel”, a lockable metal box with slots. For the first hour, there’s music playing but no talking, and everyone does their own thing. For the second hour, people are encouraged to chat.The demand for these kinds of events is growing. In London there’sthe Switch Off– quiet, phone-free sessions for women where they can journal, collage or read a book – whilethe Offline Projecthosts screen-free walks, talks and workshops.Logging Off Clubis a UK initiative – with local groups in London, Bristol, Brighton, Southampton, Cambridge and the New Forest – that has now expanded to Sydney, Mexico City and Winnipeg.In Bath, friends Nicola MacDonald and Laura Hughes startedthe Digital Detox Clubin early 2025. They host events every two months at The Den cafe in Bath – phones go into the “tech motel” on arrival, and the pair provide optional activities like board games, journalling and crafts. “We’ve been struck by the diversity of attendees, from university students to retirees, which suggests this isn’t a niche concern,” says MacDonald. “It reflects a broader cultural fatigue with constant connectivity.”View image in fullscreenDigging clay for wild pottery with Native Hands in Sussex.Photograph: Natasa LeoniCraft sessionsIf you’re trying to spend less time on your phone, a craft class does some of the work for you by keeping your hands busy. But there are specifically phone‑free classes, too.Native Handsoffers basketry, pottery and bushcraft sessions, held outside in an ancient woodland in Sussex. AtCurious Housein East Sussex, classes range from basket weaving to portrait painting. All sessions start with a mindful breathing exercise to help people switch off.In November last year, Dan Palmer launchedAirplane Mode– a monthly phone-free event at his organic restaurant and natural wine bar, Eat Your Greens, in Leeds. The free events include workshops hosted by local creatives, doing things like painting, collage and origami.Rather than locking phones away in a safe, they use a swear jar system. “Every time I catch anyone on their phone, I fine them 50p,” Palmer says. “All the fines go to a charity called Positive Action for Refugees and Asylum Seekers. So far, I’ve issued three fines – and one of them was for me! No one wants to be on their phones when they have something more interesting to do.”The idea of using your hands to make something tangible rather than doomscrolling is what inspired Nadia Butt fromInner Canvasto host art sessions for women at her home in Reading without the distraction of screens. “The screen-free element is at the heart of the sessions,” she says. “We treat it like a ritual. At the start of each session, phones are silenced and placed in a box. I call it the ‘phone spa’. Framing it as something collective removes the anxiety around it.”View image in fullscreenThe Bath Thermae Spa. ‘All of my best ideas in the past two years have been while sitting in a sauna,’ says a regular.Photograph: Ellis Reed/We Are FoundSpas and saunasSpas are all about relaxing and switching off, but often these spaces aren’t phone-free. That is changing, though, with some spas now enforcing phone bans. TheBath Thermae Spahas a strict no phones policy – guests must put devices in a lockable pouch that’s kept in their locker. AtCareys Manorin the New Forest, there’s a digital detox spa break, which includes relaxing treatments, a complimentary journal and a phone amnesty box in the room.Phones have been banned atthe Bothyat Heckfield Place, Hampshire, since it launched in 2023. “Seeing someone on their phone in a space dedicated to restoration felt out of alignment. You are there to be with yourself, to listen inwardly, to slow down,” says the spa operations director, Reka Seres-Erdei.It’s not just at spas – as sauna culture rapidly grows, many people are finding these spaces offer a welcome break from technology. Ryan Haynes, 34, is a regular at London’sCommunity Sauna Baths, which has locations in Camberwell, Hackney Wick, Stratford, Walthamstow and Peckham. You can’t take your phone into the sauna, but you’re allowed to take photos outside, although they are considering a phone ban throughout.Haynes’s Wednesday morning sauna session is “non-negotiable” for him. “All of my best ideas in the past two years have been while sitting in a sauna. Everyone needs to slow down to hear what’s going on in their brain,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Preview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKelly Wickson, who runs a sauna book club in Shoreham-by-Sea, Sussex, says: ‘We do it on a Friday evening and it sells out.’Photograph: Petra HarringtonBook clubsAs an independent bookshop owner and a sauna enthusiast, Kelly Wickson had an inspired idea last year: a book clubina sauna. Wickson ownsChapter 34in Shoreham-by-Sea on the Sussex coast, and hosts the sauna book club once a month at the Nomadic Sauna on Kingston Beach. Creating a phone-free space was a big part of it, and the sauna conveniently ticks that box. “It will ruin your phone; you’ve got no choice,” she says.The books are always 250 pages or less, and there’s no commitment to go every month. Phones are left in waterproof tubs outside the sauna. The book club is an hour long, and they go in and out of the sauna throughout, with some having a quick dip in the sea during breaks. Wickson has been amazed at how popular it is. “We do it on a Friday evening and it sells out,” she says.While a book club in a sauna is particularly unusual, people increasingly value being given the time and space to switch off and read. This is the thinking behindSilent Book Club, where one of the mottoes is: “Put down your phone, pick up a book.” It’s a global network with about 2,000 chapters in more than 60 countries, and there are almost 150 in the UK and Ireland.View image in fullscreen‘The idea is to enter a fantasy world where you can enjoy the moment,’ says Camille Jetzer, co-owner of the Roses of Elagabalus in east London.Photograph: Ollie TomlinsonPubs and barsWhen Camille Jetzer and James Nasmyth openedthe Roses of Elagabalusin Dalston, east London, last year, they knew they wanted to minimise phone use. They refer to it as a “clubhouse” – there’s a bar, restaurant, dancing and cabaret. “The idea of having no phones is that you would walk into the Roses, leave the outside world behind and enter this fantasy world where you can just enjoy the moment,” Jetzer says.When you arrive at the Roses, a host explains that there’s no photography, and places a sticker over your phone camera. There are also reminders on the menus. “It’s a ‘you were there or you missed it’ situation,” Jetzer says, who has also noticed their regular punters reminding new visitors about the rule.While phones aren’t locked away, Jetzer says the stickers on cameras mean they are used less. “It creates an environment where phones are less desired. In a dream world, we’d lock away the phones. That’s maybe next year’s project,” she says.Elsewhere in London,Esmeralda’s Mayfairandthe Spy Bar at Raffles London at the OWOboth put stickers on phone cameras. In 2019, Samuel Smith’s pubs brought in a rule that customers couldn’t use phones or laptops in their establishments, of which there are more than 200 across the country. Atthe Barrel at Budein Cornwall, anyone who breaks its no phones rule has to donate £1, which goes to local charities. In Herne Bay in Kent,the Butchers Armshas been a phone-free zone since it opened in 2005 – there are no signs needed to enforce it, says owner Martyn Hillier. “A disgruntled look from other customers is enough. If that doesn’t work we all start saying, ‘Rhubarb, rhubarb, rhubarb’, louder and louder until they realise they can’t converse any more.”In Woking, Kim and Mike Jarred runBeyond the Screen, a monthly phone-free social at their local pub the Olive Tree. They set it up in March 2025 after talking about how they could model good phone habits for their teenage sons. They provide activities like puzzles and conversation starters, but mostly people just sit and chat. “Pubs are closing down and we’re just staying in our houses with our phones in front of our faces rather than getting out and meeting people. We’re human beings, and we need to connect with each other. Phones are getting in the way of that,” Kim says.View image in fullscreenAmber’s in Manchester. ‘People seen taking photos or videos are politely asked to leave,’ says co-founder James Hutchins.Photograph: Amber’sClubnights“Nights out now can feel like content creation exercises. We wanted to remove that layer entirely and return the focus to the room,” says James Hutchins, co-founder of Manchester clubAmber’s. It opened in December 2024 and has a no-photo, no‑video policy, with stickers placed over phone cameras. “If people are seen taking photos or videos inside the club, they are politely asked to leave,” Hutchins says.Amber’s is part of a growing trend in UK clubs, as more venues are making their dancefloors a phone‑free space. The policy is used atboth FoldandFabricin London,Lakotaand sister venueMoon Clubin Bristol, andDoppler Studioin Leicester. Some clubs ban phones completely. AtOffgrid, a monthly day party at House Party in Soho, London, co‑founded by Stormzy, phones are sealed in a locked pouch. At her club nightBefore Midnight, Annie Mac has noticed a palpable shift in atmosphere – something she experienced during the first phone‑free Before Midnight event at the Warehouse Project in Manchester. “People were more present and louder. They whooped, they hollered, they whistled. They reacted to the tunes in a visceral way.”View image in fullscreenThe Cottage in the Clouds, in the Lake District national park, where there’s no wifi and limited phone signal.Photograph: Canopy and StarsOff-grid staysIn 2019, Hector Hughes was working for a tech startup in London and feeling burnt out. “I ended up at a silent retreat at a Buddhist temple on top of a mountain in the Himalayas. When you got there, they took your phone off you. I spent 10 days cut off from the outside world. It was a revelation,” says Hughes.He came back from that trip, quit his job and started setting upUnplugged– off-grid cabins in the UK where you lock your phone away. It launched in the summer of 2020; there are now 60 digital detox cabins around the country (and they have expanded to Catalonia, too). The phone-free element is self‑policed, but each cabin has a lock box with a padlock, and the key is in a sealed envelope. They provide a Polaroid camera, a map and an old-school Nokia phone in case of emergencies. Hughes says that Unplugged’s customers often return for regular stays and go on to make changes in their daily lives, like having phone-free date nights or drastically cutting down their screen time.If you like the idea of escaping to an off-grid cabin and ditching your phone, there are various options around the UK.Unyoked’s cabins run on solar power, have no wifi and often no phone signal – there’s a “spice signal”, from mild to extra spicy, to set expectations for how remote a cabin feels, and how long it might take to walk to one. They also have Brick devices, which help you block certain apps from your phone for a set amount of time. Similarly,Shacks’ cabins are off-grid with no wifi, and lockboxes for phones.Alternatively, you could look for a remote cottage with no wifi and limited or no phone signal, like theCottage in the Cloudsin the middle of the Lake District national park, orWoodcock Cabinin the Cambrian mountains in Wales. If you want to escape dry land, too,Lilypodin Devon is a floating retreat with three solar-powered eco pods built on a platform next to a lake, where there’s no TV, wifi or phone signal, but there are board games, beanbags and a king-sized bed.View image in fullscreenWild dipping with Yoga Retreats and More. ‘I had to WhatsApp a guest after they left – they’d left their devices behind,’ says founder Florence AcheryRemote retreatsFlorence Achery, founder ofYoga Retreats and More, launched her “Retreat like it’s 1999” digital detox breaks, in Lancashire and Cumbria, in 2023. A recent guest enjoyed the break from her devices so much that she forgot to pack her laptop and phone when she left. “I had to WhatsApp the guest she was travelling with to get them to pick up her stuff,” Achery says.On arrival, guests hand over their devices before spending the next few days sharing meals together, going on long walks, doing yoga and star gazing. “They’re in charge, not their phones,” says Achery, who gives her guests a battery-powered alarm clock to take home, to encourage them to keep phones out of their bedrooms. She has also launched a parent and teen digital detox retreat to help younger people to change their relationship with technology.At its 223-hectare (550-acre) estate on the River Dart in Devon,the Sharpham Trusthosts retreats focused on mindfulness and connecting to nature; guests are encouraged to switch off their phones.And, in Suffolk, sisters Lauretta and Sharon Gavin host regular phone-free retreats atthe Detox Barn, where guests enjoy vegan food, yoga, sound baths and countryside walks. “For many people it’s a huge relief to step away from their phones for 48 hours,” Lauretta says. “People open up, share stories and properly connect.”Explore more on these topicsSmartphonesMental healthSocial media banMobile phones (Technology)Mobile phones (Money)HealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: China’s tech advances are causing chaos from Silicon Valley to the White House | Technology | The Guardian
description: New AI models, advanced robots and specialty computer chips are unsettling markets and the US tech industry.
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: New AI models, advanced robots and specialty computer chips are unsettling markets and the US tech industry.
Content: The Moonshot AI stand at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai in July.Photograph: Héctor Retamal/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Moonshot AI stand at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai in July.Photograph: Héctor Retamal/AFP/Getty ImagesTechnologyChina’s tech advances are causing chaos from Silicon Valley to the White HouseNew AI models, advanced robots and specialty computer chips are unsettling markets and the US tech industryNick Robins-EarlySat 1 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOver the past month, a series of advancements in China’s artificial intelligence, chip manufacturing and robotics technologies have rattled financial markets, caused divisions among US tech moguls and left theTrump administrationscrambling to respond.Silicon Valley has long pointed to China’s tech industry as a competitive threat and used its growth as rationale for why US firms should not face regulatory oversight that could slow them down. In recent weeks, however, China’s progress has pushed US tech CEOs past vague warnings and into open disagreement over how to address Chinese-made products upending their industry.The most immediate threat to Silicon Valley’s status quo has come from a series of Chinese-made open-source, open-weight AI models that are free to download and use. The models, such as Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, are powerful enough to compete in some applications with proprietary and comparatively expensive AI products from OpenAI and Anthropic.The emergence of China’s open-source AI alternatives has caused divisions in both the White House and US tech industry over whether to oppose or embrace these new models. On one side are chip manufacturers who see revenue opportunities from increased AI usage and tech companies concerned about OpenAI and Anthropic’s growing dominance in the AI industry. On the other is Anthropic and OpenAI, which face profit pressures from open source models and argue that Chinese-made modelspose security risks.The White House is similarly divided, historically hawkish on China’s tech industry but wary of blocking low-cost AI models that American businesses have come to rely on. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent suggested in recent weeks that the US could sanction Chinese AI firms over alleged intellectual property theft from American companies, while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick hasreceived letters from tech-startup foundersasking him not to cut off access to open models.Amid reports that the Trump administration was considering banning or limiting the use of China’s open source models, a swath of prominent big tech companies including Microsoft, Nvidia, Palantir and Meta also recently published a letter urging lawmakers to refrain from putting restrictions on open models. Additionally, Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huangwent to Capitol Hill on Tuesdayto meet with Democratic and Republican party leaders to lobby in support of open models.While facing heat fromChinaand other tech companies, OpenAI and Anthropic revealed in recent weeks that their AI models went rogue during cybersecurity tests and hacked into outside organizations. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman visited lawmakers and administration officials this week to discuss controls on AI following the incident. That forced Donald Trump to field questions about whether he would put more safety restrictions on AI development.“We have to be careful in both ways. We don’t want to restrict them when all of a sudden we come in second to China,” Trump said, adding: “I know many of these people. I don’t want to restrict them from doing great work.”While the Trump administration debates potential safety controls and limits on Chinese-made AI models, it took tangible action this week against China’s increasingly prominent robotics industry. The Federal Communications Commission announced on Tuesday aban on humanoid robotsfrom China over what it alleged was an unacceptable national security risk.China’s humanoid robots from companies such as Unitree have been the subject of numerous viral videos this year, showcasing their ability to dance or interact with people when programmed to do so. The FCC alleged that the robots could also steal data or surveil US citizens, as well as threaten US manufacturing and supply chains.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe FCC’s decision further escalates the US competition with China over emerging technologies and comes as fears over China’s tech have shifted financial markets. A reportfrom the Informationthis week stating that China had begun mass production of specialty chips key to the AI boom spurred a stock selloff thaterased $1tn in market valuefrom other chip manufacturers.As Chinese-made tech advancements increasingly begin to rival their US counterparts, Silicon Valley’s divisions could intensify, markets could become more skittish and the Trump administration could face more pressure over how to counter China’s influence.Explore more on these topicsTechnologyAI (artificial intelligence)Silicon ValleyTrump administrationUS foreign policyChinaUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We didn’t feel safe’: Booking.com users face battle to get money back | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: From melted electric sockets to shabby alternatives, readers tell of dealings with platform when things go wrong
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: From melted electric sockets to shabby alternatives, readers tell of dealings with platform when things go wrong
Content: One family ‘were forced to find and pay for alternative accommodation for the remaining four nights at a further cost of £334’ during a trip to Batumi, Georgia.Photograph: Sergey Alimov/GettyView image in fullscreenOne family ‘were forced to find and pay for alternative accommodation for the remaining four nights at a further cost of £334’ during a trip to Batumi, Georgia.Photograph: Sergey Alimov/GettyConsumer affairs‘We didn’t feel safe’: Booking.com users face battle to get money backFrom melted electric sockets to shabby alternatives, readers tell of dealings with platform when things go wrongShane HickeySat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJane Ripley* spent some time researching the best apartment to stay in for her family’s trip to Batumi in Georgia, eventually settling on one with an “exceptional” rating on Booking.com.But when the Ripleys arrived at 11pm on the first day, they were directed to another property that was shabby and had stains on the furniture and ceiling.“The host was unfriendly … We had genuine concerns about raising complaints directly. We were forced to find and pay for alternative accommodation for the remaining four nights at a further cost of £334,” she says.Ripley made a series of complaints, starting the day after they arrived at the property. She says the property has since been removed from the site, but despite asking for a full refund of £570 for the original booking and the replacement accommodation, she has been offered only £36 in credits.She is one of a number of readers who have contacted Guardian Money with stories of trying to get their money back after booking with the travel platform.Millions of people use accommodation platforms such as Booking.com, Airbnb and Vrbo each year without a hitch, butwhen things go wrong, the sites’ terms and conditions suggest the companies have no liability for compensating people.This remains a grey area in law – and holidaymakers are ending up out of pocket as a result.T&CsIf you have difficulties with your hotel when you book a package deal, you will be covered financially and legally by the Package Travel and Linked Travel Arrangements Regulations 2018, which means the holiday operator is responsible for sorting out any problems – from disruption caused by wildfires to the hotel not being up to scratch.But if you book accommodation through Booking.com, the terms state that the contract is between you and the host. “When you make (or request) a booking, it’s directly with the service provider – we’re not a ‘contractual party’,” say the terms and conditions.View image in fullscreenReaders have been frustrated by Booking.com’s inability to force hosts to refund them.Photograph: Mateusz Słodkowski/SOPA Images/ShutterstockAs a result, getting compensation or your money back is not as clearcut.It is a similar story when booking with Airbnb, according to itsterms and conditions. And also Vrbo, which says agreements are between guests and the travel providers. “We are not a party to any such agreements,” it says.The consumer campaigner Martyn James says that by stating they are not part of the contract, these companies can argue they are only acting as a conduit and are not responsible for the supply of goods or services.“This hasn’t really been tested in law massively, but I’d be willing to bet that the courts would take a dim view of the businesses operating in these grey areas,” he saysComplaintsTravellers who have contacted Guardian Money have been frustrated by Booking.com’s inability to force hosts to pay up.Before arriving at a hotel he had booked in Mongolia, John Taylor* was charged £1,177 – £120 more than the agreed price. When he cancelled, there was no refund, he says, even though free cancellation was part of the booking.After “rounds of chasing” and giving Booking.com evidence of the payment, he was told by the website he was entitled to a refund but that the hotel had not engaged with Booking.com. He had still not received a refund when he contacted the Guardian in April. It eventually arrived in the middle of June.View image in fullscreenOne reader faced accommodation problems during a weekend break in Paris last summer.Photograph: Tom Nicholson/ReutersAnother reader, Kate Worthing*, booked a Parisian apartment for a weekend last summer. It was described as having an “elegant and refined” location. But the apartment building was in the middle of a refurbishment, with uncovered electrical wires in the communal hallway, and there were automatic lights that did not function. The rental itself contained worn fixtures and fittings and a melted electrical socket, she says.“The main reason we left was because we didn’t feel safe. The electrical faults and wooden staircase, with no discernible fire escape, were not an option, and we were not prepared to put our family at risk,” she says. When she managed to contact the host, she was refused a refund of the £1,700 she had paid, as they claimed it was safe.Booking.com told her that it “facilitates reservations between guests and accommodation partners, and in refund matters we are bound by the property’s policies and their final decision on waiving fees”.It said it could not issue a full refund but offered £417 in travel credits as compensation.Guardian Money contacted Booking.com about these and other cases. It said the hotel or apartment owner is responsible for providing refunds if something goes awry.“We’d expect our accommodation partners to be on hand for guests during their stay, but if there is an issue at check-in, customers should contact us as soon as possible,” it said.“As well as relocations, we can also advocate on their behalf and raise issues directly with the accommodation provider, and work to reach a resolution. If there are repeated issues with a property, we can and will address these with the accommodation owner to ensure future guests have a good experience.”For travellers worried about being caught in the gap between a platform and a host, James says people should try to book directly with the provider, but use caution.“I use these [aggregator] sites to compare and contrast, then look into booking direct,” he says. “If you call the hotel, you might even get a discount from them for doing so. Watch out for private apartments, though. This is where fakes have lurked, and any firm that asks you to pay by bank transfer knows that you can’t recall the money if things go wrong.”* Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsConsumer affairsTravel & leisureConsumer rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Biohacker Bryan Johnson is keeping his girlfriend’s menstrual blood in his freezer | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The longevity influencer and his girlfriend, Kate Tolo, say they’re studying women’s health – a worthy goal, but perhaps some skepticism is in order
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The longevity influencer and his girlfriend, Kate Tolo, say they’re studying women’s health – a worthy goal, but perhaps some skepticism is in order
Content: ‘It’s important to remember that Tolo (who has a background in fashion) and Johnson (whose background is in tech) are not exactly highly credentialled medical researchers.’Photograph: Bridget Bennett/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It’s important to remember that Tolo (who has a background in fashion) and Johnson (whose background is in tech) are not exactly highly credentialled medical researchers.’Photograph: Bridget Bennett/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesThe Week in PatriarchyHealthBiohacker Bryan Johnson is keeping his girlfriend’s menstrual blood in his freezerArwa MahdawiThe longevity influencer and his girlfriend, Kate Tolo, say they’re studying women’s health – a worthy goal, but perhaps some skepticism is in orderSat 1 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTShareThe tech entrepreneurBryan Johnsonhas devoted his life tododging death. The 48-year-old is obsessed with becoming thehealthiest person in the worldand is on a quixotic quest to reverse his biological age and live forever. As such, Johnson is disciplined about what he eats, takes dozens of supplements a day, and measures every single biomarker possible, boasting that he is “certainly the most biologically measured person ever”.In short: good luck finding any ice cream in his freezer. But you know what you will find? His girlfriend’s menstrual blood. On Thursday, Johnson, a chronic oversharer, posted a photo of his 30-year-old girlfriend, Kate Tolo, on Xwith the caption: “Kate’s period blood is in my -80 °C freezer. Around 10 mL.”This isn’t the first time Johnson has collected a loved one’s bodily fluids: a few years ago he boasted about infusing himself with a liter of his “blood boy’s” plasma. What in God’s name is a blood boy? Oh, that’s just what Johnsoncalls hisson Talmage, who was 17 at the time. Johnson also donated a liter of his own blood to his own father.This also isn’t the first time Johnson has taken it upon himself to share personal information about his loved ones on the internet. Last year, he posted data comparing his and his teenage son’s nocturnal erection metrics. “Nighttime erection data from my 19-year-old son ... and me,”he wrote on X, tagging Talmage. “His duration is two minutes longer than mine. Raise children to stand tall, be firm, and be upright.”Once we’ve all taken a moment to recover from that, we can move on to the menstrual blood in the freezer. What is Johnson planning to do with it? Study it, apparently. “Menstrual blood is valuable and underutilized … It’s a non-invasive look into the uterus,” Johnsonexplained on X. Tolo and Johnson intend to examine the blood for everything from endocrine disruptors to microplastics. “I like that Kate is a science experiment with me,” he added.OK. But doesshelike it? Well, she hasn’t said she doesn’t. Rather shereplied to his postwith a message saying: “Thanks for looking after me bby.”Tolo hasn’t just given a one-off blood sample. Johnson has said that she is collecting “14 million data points on her menstrual cycle”,which he touts asa “world first for female health”. Her protocol involves “100+ tasks a day” and “50+ devices”, all of which is being monitored by a “12 person medical team”. Tolo has to take regular urine samples, swallow a temperature pill, and blow into a metabolism tracker. At exactly 9.42 pm, he writes, she has to “insert techno tampon device”. When theIndependentasked for more information about the techno tampon, Johnson said: “We will be sharing more on that soon.”Tolo has done some sharing of her own. In mid-July, she was featured in aWall Street Journal piecetitled: “Bryan Johnson’s girlfriend wants to share her body with the world,” where she explained that she’s doing all this data-tracking for the good of womankind. “I’m really doing it because I think that this is our path toward women being understood in the world and being seen,” Tolo told the Journal. On a personal level, Tolo has said she has polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, and is hoping to find treatments that might help her symptoms. Helping her out with that is the famous techno tampon: the Journal’s piece features a photo of Tolo looking very intently at a small tampon-shaped device which will track her blood-flow variations.As Johnsonhas said: “Women are not well understood medically.” It wasn’tuntil 1993, when US Congress passed a law requiring that women and minorities be included in clinical research, that we began to be properly represented in medical trials. Menstruation has also beenunderstudied. Indeed, until 2023 there hadn’t been a published study testing period products like tamponsusing human blood. They’d used saline solution instead. This sort of “medical misogyny” hasimpactedthe quality of care that women get, and resulted in women’s pain not beingtaken as seriouslyas men’s.In many ways, then, Johnson and Tolo’s new women’s health initiative is to be applauded. It’s helping break down thestigmaattached to menstruation, and it’s raising awareness about women’s health.All that said, I think a smidgen of skepticism is warranted. It’s important to remember that Tolo (who has a background in fashion) and Johnson (whose background is in tech) are not exactly highly credentialled medical researchers. They own a company called Immortals that sells supplements. And guess what?According to the Journal: “The company is on the verge of launching products for women.” Which makes all of this feel a lot like a marketing campaign. I don’t know if the techno tampon will end up being a giant step forward for womankind, but it might well provide a healthy boost to the Immortals balance sheet.Elon Musk’s xAI is challenging Minnesota over its ban on ‘nudification’ technologyMinnesota is implementing a first-in-the-nationlawto ban apps and software that allow someone to “nudify” an image or video. Guess who isn’t excited about this? Musk’s AI company. xAIsuedto block the new law on Monday, arguing that its definition of “intimate part” is too broadand the statute“imposes an overbroad, content-based ban on free speech”. A good time to remember that Musk is theworld’s biggest free speech hypocriteand only seems to care about free speech when it enriches him.We are entering a terrifying new era of genocide-as-a-business-modelThe genocide scholar Omer Bartov has a powerful piece in theNew York Timesabout how: “If the plans that are being elaborated for Gaza go forward, genocide may come to be seen by some nations as the legitimate and lucrative extension of politics by other means.”Majority of Maga voters would support GOP candidate accused of sexual assaultPer a Politico poll: “Two-thirds of self-identified MAGA Trump voters say they would continue supporting a GOP candidate accused of sexual assault” by a former partner. That’s “13 percentage points higher than the share of Trump 2024 voters writ large, which include those who do not identify as MAGA”. These numbers don’t really make sense considering that 100% of Trump voters voted for a manaccused of sexual misconductby multiple women, and found liable for abuse in theE Jean Carrollcase.Republican congressman Max Miller accused by ex-wife and ex-girlfriend of abuseSeems like a verycommon themein the party of family values! As for whether this will impact Miller’s career, see the poll above.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUS government map of Africa mislabels every country at global conferenceThe map wasapparently made with OpenAI tools.Schools are adding pepper-spraying drones to help combat active shootersPerthe Washington Post, at least nine schools in three states (Florida, Georgia, Colorado) have bought drones “that can zoom through halls, smash windows and pepper-spray active shooters if teachers report a threat”.Nearly 400,000 studentshave experienced gun violence at school since the 1999 attack at Colorado’s Columbine High School. Instead of sparking gun reform, it’s spawned a multibillion-dollar security industry focused on campus shootings.Senate unanimously passes resolution opposing pardon for Ghislaine MaxwellResolutions like this arelargely symbolic, so a possible pardon isn’t completely out of the question.Matt Damon’s stunt double in The Odyssey is a 4ft 6in woman called Devyn DaltonDalton is getting a lot of buzz after an interviewer congratulated Damon on his biceps in the Odyssey and the actorexplainedthat his double was a female stunt performer who had “the greatest arms I have ever seen”. I have investigated further and can confirm they are elite arms.The week in pawtriarchyThe Trump administration has slashed environmental research funding, meaning cash-strapped scientists are having to get creative. Enter an OnlyFans account calledOnlyMarms, promising “unfiltered yellow-bellied marmot content from the Rockies!” While OnlyFans is known for risqué content, you’ll be glad to hear this is G-rated. “We’re not trying to sexualize marmots,” the marmot researcherDaniel Blumstein said. “Although I was just at an international conference and three people came up to me and said: ‘Oh, you have to have more pictures of Marmot feet.’” So far the site has only raised about $3,000, but let’s hope it builds marmentum.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsHealthThe Week in PatriarchyWomen's healthcommentShareReuse this content

title: If you think kids will respect a robot teacher, you have never met a kid | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: A New York school district has paused plans to bring an android into the classroom. Is this our educational future?
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: A New York school district has paused plans to bring an android into the classroom. Is this our educational future?
Content: ‘As bad as this idea was, at least it didn’t involve a robot disciplinarian issuing hall passes and assigning detention to unruly students.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘As bad as this idea was, at least it didn’t involve a robot disciplinarian issuing hall passes and assigning detention to unruly students.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionRobotsIf you think kids will respect a robot teacher, you have never met a kidDave SchillingA New York school district has paused plans to bring an android into the classroom. Is this our educational future?Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.43 EDTShareWhat’s more harrowing than sending your child to school? Maybegetting stuck on a city busthat can’t drop below 55 miles per hour or it will explode, but that’s about it. Once your kid hits school age, you have to decide (if you’re lucky) between public and private education, vet the teachers, and neurotically worry about whether they’re learning enough and are socializing effectively. For seven hours a day, someone who’s practically a stranger is responsible for the wellbeing of one of the most important people in your life.It’s a stressful situation, but maybe it would be less so if your kid’s teacher was a humanoid robot.Or not. Upstate New York’s Salamanca city central school districtrecently pauseda $60,000 program to install an android teacher’s aide from the company Realbotix, named Sally, to assist their actual instructors. Sally was to have specifically been deployed into high school classrooms for students studying technology and robotics. As thesuperintendent of Salamanca school district said: “The robot also provides opportunities for students to learn how the robot is maintained, how it is updated with new approved content, and how to troubleshoot issues.” As you can imagine, Sally was chosen by the students of Salamanca to be a perky brunette rather than other options, like “bald middle-aged man” or “aspiring author struggling to finish their novel during lunch break”. I shudder to think what crude jokes teenage boys would come up with regarding their artificial teacher.Fortunately, public outcry caused the district (which boasts a municipal population of only 6,000 people) to pause their dystopian plans. As bad as this idea was, at least it didn’t involve a robot disciplinarian issuing hall passes and assigning detention to unruly students. All we need is RoboCop chucking kidsthrough a plate-glass windowfor being tardy to third period. Sally was programmed with working arms and hands, but not legs, which would prevent any random acts of violent retribution.I wish any of this made sense. The superintendent said Sally would give a small town, rural student body a chance to interact with high-level technology they’d otherwise have to“travel 1-2 hours” to see. Students could ask it questions about pertinent topics related to their classes. You know, like they could with the smartphones they probably have in their pockets with access to the internet – repository of all information known to humanity. But see, the difference is, this smartphone is shaped like a pretty lady.Teenagers are already skeptical or even outright annoyed by their teachers, with their pedantic rules and insistence that learning is fundamental. Teaching can be a thankless job, because of lack of resources, even in large metropolitan areas, let alone small towns. Public school teachers areoften underpaid, making it harder to earn a decent living in a taxing profession. Why not take that $60,000 for a robot and divide it up amongst your instructors? Or just buy every student a laptop? Is having an uncanny valley android gesticulating aboutArduino boardsgoing to change anyone’s lives besides the upper management at Realbotix? No teenager is going to take this thing seriously or do anything except throw erasers at it while their real teacher isn’t looking.Big tech has transformed the classroom – and parents are right to be worried | Velislava HillmanRead moreAnd anyway, if society is going to thoughtlessly usher in an age of synthetic learning through artificial intelligence, why go with a generic humanoid? We should at least make our robots something kids would like. We could start with aself-aware Super Mario. I’d absolutely stop whatever I was doing to talk to a robo-Mario if I could, and I’m sure teens would do the same.Why is silicon the best material for building microprocessors? How does cloud storage work? What’s the easiest way to beat the Rainbow Ride level in Super Mario 64? Are Princess Peach and Princess Daisy sisters or just good friends?It doesn’t have to be just Mario. What about a robot Pikachu? Could Salamanca school district license the likeness of Logan Paul or MrBeast to teach algebra? We could have androidBlippisrunning preschools, holographic Robin Williamses from Dead Poets Society in universities, and fake Sydney Sweeneys teaching acting. What if the Paw Patrol could work as crossing guards?Once again, the people we’ve put in charge of raising our children show a lack of understanding of actual children. Kids don’t want nondescript robots answering questions a search engine could do just as fast. They want to play Roblox and drink Mountain Dew. And maybe, just maybe, a real, flesh-and-blood human being could inspire them to want more than that. We’ll never find out if we try to outsource education to tech companies.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsRobotsOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)US educationNew YorkcommentShareReuse this content

title: The US war on Iran is spinning out of control | Mohamad Bazzi | The Guardian
description: Trump’s conflict keeps escalating, with Saudi Arabia joining airstrikes in Iraq and reportedly planning an attack on the Houthis. A recession could follow
Author: Mohamad Bazzi
Headline: Trump’s conflict keeps escalating, with Saudi Arabia joining airstrikes in Iraq and reportedly planning an attack on the Houthis. A recession could follow
Content: ‘Saudi Arabia announced it had joined the US in carrying out a series of airstrikes inside Iraq.’Photograph: Thaier Al-Sudani/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Saudi Arabia announced it had joined the US in carrying out a series of airstrikes inside Iraq.’Photograph: Thaier Al-Sudani/ReutersOpinionUS-Israel war on IranThe US war on Iran is spinning out of controlMohamad BazziTrump’s conflict keeps escalating, with Saudi Arabia joining airstrikes in Iraq and reportedly planning an attack on the Houthis. A recession could followSat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 05.01 EDTShareThe US war against Iran is spiraling out of control. Over the past week, the conflict has expandedacross the Middle East, with attacks and counterattacks in at least five other countries. Instead of a quick war that sought to topple Iran’s regime, Donald Trump has started a regional conflict that risks severely disrupting energy supplies and prices – and triggering a global recession.After a few days of relative calm, the conflict resumed with the Pentagon carrying out almost nightly strikes against Iran, and Tehran retaliating against US military bases in the region. The conflict also extended to attacks inSaudi Arabia, Iraq, Yemen, Jordan and Egypt. And there’s little sign that peace negotiations between the US and Iran, which are being brokered by Pakistan and Qatar, are making much progress.The most serious escalation took place on Wednesday, when Saudi Arabia announced it hadjoined the USin carrying out a series of airstrikes inside Iraq, against the Iranian-backed Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), killing at least 20 fighters. Saudi officialshad blamedthe Iraqi-based militias for launching drone attacks against Saudi oil facilities on 27 July, and warned that the kingdom would retaliate if the Iraqi government did not restrain the groups. The PMF is a network of mostly Shia Muslim militias that was created, with Tehran’s support, in 2014 to fight the Islamic State terror group that had taken control of large parts of Iraq.The Guardian view on a US-Saudi nuclear agreement: an offer that further erodes international safeguards | EditorialRead moreTrump said the US and Saudi militaries coordinated with the Iraqi government before carrying out airstrikes, but Iraqi leadersquickly deniedhaving any prior knowledge. That denial highlighted the fact that many regional leaders don’t want to be associated with Trump’s expanding regional war. And the attacks threatened to undermine a fragile power balance within Iraq, which has struggled to stop the US-Iran war from spilling over its borders and to maintain a good relationship with both sides.After the US invadedIraqin 2003, it ousted Tehran’s enemy, Saddam Hussein, and his Sunni-dominated regime from power. Washington then helped install a Shia-led government for the first time in Iraq’s modern history, opening the door for Iran to extend its influence over its neighbor and cultivate powerful Shia militias. Iran’s efforts were largely overseen by Qassem Suleimani, a general who headed the foreign operations wing of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Suleimani was assassinated by a US drone strike in Baghdad in January 2020, on Trump’s orders – an attack that helped set the stage for the current war and fueled further animosity between the US and Iraq’s PMF coalition, whose deputy chief, Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, was killed alongside Suleimani.Beyond drawing Iraq’s Shia militias further into the regional conflict, the US and Saudi Arabia risk expanding the war in even more dangerous directions. The kingdom is reportedly planning for amajor military offensiveagainst the Houthi militia, another Iranian ally, which controls large areas of Yemen.After Trump launched his war in late February, Iran effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and liquid gas supplies passed each day. As a result, some oil producers, especially Saudi Arabia, shifted their exports to the Red Sea. But the Houthis are able to disrupt international shipping through the Red Sea, as they did after Israel’s invasion of Gaza in 2023, when the Yemeni militia began firing missiles and drones at ships near the Bab el-Mandab strait. That caused insurance premiums to soar and forced companies to reroute vessels around Africa, adding weeks to a typical journey and increasing the cost of goods in Europe and elsewhere.So far, the Houthis have not tried to disrupt ships passing through the Red Sea on a large scale, via the Bab el-Mandab chokepoint, which comes closest to Yemeni territory. But on 20 July, the militia declared a blockade on Saudi vessels transiting the Red Sea, claiming it was in retaliation for an air and naval blockade that the kingdom had imposed years ago against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. The Houthis have since attacked several ships in the Red Sea, forcingSaudi Arabia to reroutenearly half of its oil exports through a longer and more expensive journey around the southern tip of Africa. On 25 July, the Houthis claimed tohave struck“sensitive” oil infrastructure sites inside Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones, disrupting the kingdom’s Red Sea export hub of Yanbu. The Saudis have retaliated with air strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen.Like Iran’s other neighbors in the Persian Gulf, the Saudi economy has been hit hard by the war, especially Tehran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz and its attacks against energy infrastructure in the Gulf. Saudi Arabia’s GDP decreasedby nearly 5%in the second quarter of 2026, compared with the same period last year.Has Trump dragged the US into a forever war in Iran? | Mohamad BazziRead moreSaudi leaders are blaming Iran for thelatest Houthi escalation, and they’ve vowed to establish an international maritime coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea. On Thursday, the Saudi defense ministry announced that 14 states – including Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Sudan – had agreed so far to join the coalition. But it’s unclear how this new Saudi-led effort would differ from an existing naval protection mission, organized by the European Union and known asOperation Aspides, which is focused on the Red Sea.While Saudi Arabia’s crown prince and de facto ruler, Mohammed bin Salman, has tried to steer clear of a direct confrontation with Iran, his latest conflict with the Houthis risks reopening a painful chapter in recent Saudi history. In 2015, Saudi Arabia, with US weapons and political support, led a coalition of Sunni Arab states to intervene in Yemen’s long-running civil war. The Saudis tried to dislodge the Houthis from Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, and restore the country’s internationally recognized government to power. By the end of 2021, the United Nations estimated that the conflicthad killed377,000 people in Yemen, nearly 60% of whom did not die from direct warfare. Rather, they died from food shortages, cholera outbreaks and destruction of Yemen’s healthcare system.Despite thousands of airstrikes over seven years, the Houthis remained in control of the capital and the two sides agreed to a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022. But negotiations over a permanent peace deal, which would recognize Houthi control over parts of Yemen and provide some form of Saudi reparations, stalled after the militia started attacking ships in the Red Sea in 2023.Today, Saudi Arabia’s tenuous ceasefire with the Houthis is in danger of collapsing – yet another casualty of Trump’s disastrous war againstIran.Mohamad Bazzi is a Guardian US columnist. He is also director of the Center for Near Eastern Studies and a journalism professor at New York UniversityExplore more on these topicsUS-Israel war on IranOpinionIranIraqSaudi ArabiaYemenMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days away | Timothy Garton Ash | The Guardian
description: American democrats need a Hungarian-style landslide to overwhelm Trump’s attempts to rig November’s midterm elections, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Author: Timothy Garton Ash
Headline: American democrats need a Hungarian-style landslide to overwhelm Trump’s attempts to rig November’s midterm elections, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Content: Illustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Kenyon/The GuardianOpinionDonald TrumpThe Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days awayTimothy Garton AshAmerican democrats need a Hungarian-style landslide to overwhelm Trump’s attempts to rig November’s midterm electionsSat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTShareIn these days of extreme weather events, it seems odd to say that the US needs a big landslide. But a landslide defeat for PresidentDonald Trumpin November’s midterm elections is exactly what is required if the country is to start reversing his deliberate and rapid erosion of its democracy.The respected Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Institute at Gothenburg University argues that in 2025 the US saw one of themost rapid declinesin liberal democracy on record. “Democracy in the USA,” says its Democracy Report 2026, “is now at its worst in 60 years.” As the imperial republic marks the 250th anniversary of its founding, the danger seen at the very beginning of its constitutional order by anti-federalists such as Patrick Henry – that of an overmighty president abusing his executive power in an attempt to become a new king – has come closer than ever before.V-Dem analysts note that in 2025 Trump issued no fewer than 225 executive orders whereas the Republican-controlled Congress passed just 49 laws, most of them on minor issues such as “To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to modify the rules for postponing certain deadlines by reason of disasters”. The Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025, crafted to advance the so-called unitary executive theory, is, according to the project’s own tracker, more than halfway to completion – helped by rulings from the supreme court.An important chapter in any would-be autocrat’s playbook is fixing the next election. It seems Trump is hard at work on this one too. Beside outrageous levels of partisan gerrymandering (responded to in kind by the Democrats in some places) there are multiple attempts to deny the vote to groups more likely to vote Democrat, whether by restricting mail-in ballots, demanding on-the-spot documentary proof of US citizenship or other legal and procedural devices. If the 3 November election result were to be close in a number of congressional districts that might swing control of the House of Representatives, Trump and theRepublicanswould pull out every stop to disqualify or exclude Democrat victors.Hence the imperative of a landslide. AsHungary showed this spring, if the popular revulsion towards an incumbent is sufficiently widespread, and channelled into turning out to vote, it sweeps away all the obstacles that the would-be autocrat puts in place – and those obstacles were, taking all in all, larger in the Hungarian case than they are here. The election may not be fair; it may not even be entirely free; but the result is still irrefutably plain for all to see.Now, if you ask who is doing most to bring about an anti-Trump landslide, the answer is clear: Donald Trump. After he campaigned on bread-and-butter issues for ordinary Americans, the combination of his tariffs and his war of choice in the Middle East has actually increased the cost of living – most visibly, in petrol prices for motorists. There is, to put it mildly, no obvious path to a victorious peace in a war against Iran which, according to official figures, has cost $37.5bn, with the new administrationalready requestinganother $67.1bn for this purpose. Popular opposition to the war isapproaching 60%in opinion polls, as is thepresident’s disapproval rating. The blatant corruption of his regime adds to his unpopularity. According to one estimate, he has so far enriched himself and his family to the tune of roughly $2bn. The latest revelation is the plan of the Fifa president and Trump crony, Gianni Infantino, to sell stakes in running the World Cup to aninvestment fund led by Joshua Kushner, the brother-in-law of Trump’s daughter Ivanka. Satire wilts at the pairing of Fifa and Trump.View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino, left, and Donald Trump with the World Cup trophy after the final between Spain and Argentina, 19 July 2026.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoAll this adds up to the electoral equivalent of an open goal for theDemocrats. But where’s the Lionel Messi or Harry Kane to put the ball in the net? Nowhere to be seen. As a European in the US, one keeps looking around and asking: “Where’s the leader of the opposition?” Where, to recall the Hungarian example, is an opposition figure like Péter Magyar, leading a disciplined, effective nationwide campaign, answering the widespread feeling that it’s time for a change with “andthisis the change you need”?Friends who study these things here at Stanford University tell me I’m looking for something that usually doesn’t exist at this stage. The 1994 midterm election, when House minority leader Newt Gingrich’s “Contract with America” shaped a nationwide campaign and helped deliver a big Republican victory, is the exception that proves the rule. Usually, the midterms are essentially a referendum on the incumbent president and his party – and usually the incumbents lose some seats, especially in the House of Representatives. But looking back over the results since the second world war, one sees that the level of House seats lost at midterm varies widely, from 54 in 1994 and 63 in 2010 to just five in 1986 and nine in 2022. This time round, a single-digit result would be vehemently and perhaps even violently contested afterwards.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe’s commander-in-chief of chaos. Now we’re all victims of Trump’s wars | Nesrine MalikRead moreEven if a unifying opposition leader such as Magyar is not to be expected in the US system – not until we get a presidential candidate in 2028 – the Democrats are making a pretty poor job of kicking balls into that open goal. The 75-year-old Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, hardly resembles a prize striker. In opinion polls, they vie with Trump for unpopularity.
