Much of the energy is with democratic socialists like New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, but can they win in places like Michigan or Wisconsin? The New York Times columnist and podcaster Ezra Klein has toyed with the notion that this very diversity might be a strength: you need one kind of candidate in Kansas and another kind in Seattle. Horses for courses. But getting the wrong candidate in just a couple of the 35 Senate seats up for grabs this time seems likely to cost the Democrats their already slim chance of flipping the Senate as well.What’s at stake here is not the future of the Democrats; it’s the future of democracy. A normal midterm change in control of the House is the absolute minimum needed to start checking, if not actually reversing, the unprecedented erosion of liberal democracy under Trump. That check will come partly through Congress’s constitutional powers to control government funding, to investigate and to impeach. If there’s an electoral landslide, however, it will come even more through the psychological shift, as Trump begins to look like his own worst nightmare – being a “loser”. For that very reason, the man who would be king will try first to prevent, then to circumvent and delegitimate a Democrat-controlled House with all the means at his disposal. Nonetheless, this would be the end of the beginning.Last summer, I wrotea columnarguing that Americans had 400 days to save their democracy. It’s now little more than 90.Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS midterm elections 2026US politicsDemocratsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: My highly educated Uber driver’s heartache underscores how transactional Australia’s visa regime has become | Julianne Schultz | The Guardian
description: Belonging is hard when gaining citizenship is so expensive. The state has just become a regulator of the market
Author: Julianne Schultz
Headline: Belonging is hard when gaining citizenship is so expensive. The state has just become a regulator of the market
Content: ‘He wanted to belong but, like many visa holders, felt his presence was conditional – buy the visa, pay the fees, do the shitty jobs, don’t get above your station.’Photograph: Posed by model; PixelsEffect/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘He wanted to belong but, like many visa holders, felt his presence was conditional – buy the visa, pay the fees, do the shitty jobs, don’t get above your station.’Photograph: Posed by model; PixelsEffect/Getty ImagesOpinionAustralian immigration and asylumMy highly educated Uber driver’s heartache underscores how transactional Australia’s visa regime has becomeJulianne SchultzBelonging is hard when gaining citizenship is so expensive. The state has just become a regulator of the marketSat 1 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 19.23 EDTShareI had scarcely closed the door of the Uber that saved me from getting drenched in the sleety Melbourne rain when the driver asked, “Are you a professor?”“Well, yes,” I replied. But the question took me by surprise, most drivers barely notice their passengers. It wasn’t a bad guess; I was outside a university. “Are you a student?” I asked the young driver.He had been. Now like many international graduates, he was driving, trying to make ends meet while searching for a job in the specialised field of engineering he had successfully studied at vast expense.“While I was studying, I had a well-paying job in aged care – now this,” he told me. “I’d have to do a master’s to get to that level and even then, I don’t know if I’d get a job here. I really like Australia but might just go back to India.”His heartache was palpable. This is what the transactional nature of Australia’s complicated visa system can feel like.At my friend’s citizenship ceremony, I was moved by the quiet pride in the faces of new Australians | Shadi Khan SaifRead moreI had spent the day in a room with a politically diverse group of scholars, policy analysts, former politicians and activists discussing why immigration had become such a toxic issue and what might be done to restore trust.Now this young man put flesh on the bones of the analysis. The gap between the dispassionate policy talk and the lived reality was huge. He wanted to belong but, like many visa holders, felt his presence was conditional – buy the visa, pay the fees, do the shitty jobs, don’t get above your station.In the seminar room the range of views reached to the outer edges of the political debate.Some argued that a much more discriminatory policy should be adopted, banning people on the grounds of religion or country of birth, prohibiting international students, massively reducing visas for low-paying jobs. Others argued that the pathways to citizenship for temporary visa holdersshould be made easier, that the spouses of Australian citizens should not be counted as “immigrants” and that the data that provedimmigration was a net economic positivebe respected.The default mode of partisan blame has reached new heights since the Liberal party allowed itself to be spooked byOne Nation’s confected outrage. But the problems ascribed to immigration are not all the fault of the Albanese government.The truth is that immigration policy and, more recently, its lived reality of multiculturalism, have been a bipartisan construct since Australia became a nation. White Australia and its demise, postwar migration, multiculturalism and dual citizenship were supported by both major parties.Over the past three decades the replacement of a primarily unskilled and family reunion migration policy with one based on skills and a complex range of (expensive) visa categories, buttressed by stronger character tests, greater ministerial discretion, deportations and offshore detention has been the work of both parties.The shortcomings of this system are clear: dependence on temporary visa holders for a vast range of essential (low-paid) jobs, rent-seeking exploitation of the visa system by some employers and universities, reliance on the market to provide housing and infrastructure without a clear population policy.And so the hysterical anti-immigration rhetoric that has swept the world has now gained a foothold in this settler society of immigrants.Even as a child I remember earnest conversations that celebrated the article of faith that Australia’s immigration system was unique. People came to work in designated jobs and were initially accommodated in migrant hostels, before often moving into one of the many homes the state housing commissions built at scale. Their children attended comprehensive public schools. They were encouraged to become new Australians and citizens, their families followed and attachment grew.They were not transient guest workers.Now millions are. A transactional ethos has been built into the immigration system; the state is just a regulator of the market.When racism is so entrenched in Australia, could paying lip service to multiculturalism do more harm than good? | Anhaar KareemRead moreThe nostalgia for the “good old” migration system (under the white Australia policy) and complaints about the current regime ignores this structural change that has been embraced on economic grounds by both major parties.Each new skilled arrival has a positive impact on the budget. When the target number is cut, they need to be offset by increased fees or cuts elsewhere.The cost of visas for students, backpackers, partners and othersjumped by 25% in July. Australia now has the most expensive partner visas, costing at least $11,710 – up to 10 times more than comparable visas in Canada, the UK and the US.Belonging is hard when it is so expensive.John Howarddisliked multiculturalismas a policy, but Philip Ruddock, his long-serving immigration minister, consulted widely and oversaw the transition to a more skilled and diverse immigration intake. Last year, as anti-immigration rallies disrupted cities,Ruddock wrote of his despairat the “failure of political leadership to restore honesty, transparency and discipline to migration policy”.A lack of honesty on both sides leads to public cynicism and emotional manipulation. Ruddock wrote: “Australia risks squandering one of its greatest assets: an immigration program that has built prosperity, enriched our society and renewed our nation for generations.”Blame is not a solution, nor is policy timidity. Honesty is crucial.Julianne Schultz is the author of The Idea of AustraliaExplore more on these topicsAustralian immigration and asylumOpinionAustralian universitiesMigrationAustralian politicsAustralian citizenshipAustralian economycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Manchester mayoral result holds the key to the future of progressive politics  | Neal Lawson | The Guardian
description: Voters on the left may be fragmented – but they will pull together behind a convincing cross-party message, says Neal Lawson, director of cross-party campaign organisation Compass
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Voters on the left may be fragmented – but they will pull together behind a convincing cross-party message, says Neal Lawson, director of cross-party campaign organisation Compass
Content: ‘When second preferences kicked in, it’s estimated that about seven in 10 progressives who had backed other parties piled in behind Craig.’ Labour's Bev Craig with a supporter at the Manchester mayoral vote count on Friday.Photograph: Gary Roberts Photography/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘When second preferences kicked in, it’s estimated that about seven in 10 progressives who had backed other parties piled in behind Craig.’ Labour's Bev Craig with a supporter at the Manchester mayoral vote count on Friday.Photograph: Gary Roberts Photography/ShutterstockOpinionPoliticsThe Manchester mayoral result holds the key to the future of progressive politicsNeal LawsonVoters on the left are more fragmented than ever – but they will pull together behind a convincing cross-party messageThe author is director of the cross-party campaign organisation CompassSat 1 Aug 2026 08.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.51 EDTShareThe results of the election for a new mayor to succeed Andy Burnham inGreater Manchestershow progressives standing at the threshold of a new era. But only if they work together.The new mayor,Bev Craig, was elected using the supplementary vote, which uses voters’ second preference if no one wins more than half the vote in the first round. Despite the Burnham bounce, Labour received only 47% of the vote in the first round, well down on Burnham, who never achieved below 63% in his three campaigns. But when second preferences kicked in,it’s estimated that about seven in 10progressives who had backed other parties piled in behind Craig.This confirms that we live in an age of bloc politics; left v right. Few now shift between blocs, but many move parties within their respective bloc. The Manchester mayoral vote saw the progressive bloc consolidate behind Labour, just as it did for Andy Burnham in Makerfield, but they backed the Greens inGorton and Dentonearlier in the year andPlaid Cymruin a Senedd byelection at the end of last year.Two things are happening at once in this progressive bloc: voters are becoming more promiscuous in who they really support and highly disciplined in how they actually vote. Voters seem to be backing the progressive candidate best placed to beat the right, but only when the candidate is deemed sufficiently progressive. This amorphous mix of progressive voters appears to be capable of ruthlessly flocking around the same candidate.Given that UK politics is likely to remain incredibly fragmented, two challenges face progressive parties and voters, in winning and governing. Within this fragmented bloc lurks the danger of “progressive tragedies”, where a majority progressive vote splits and lets the right bloc through. The bloc, rather than the party, that now wins today is the one that most efficiently organises its total vote.But it’s not just the quantity of the progressive vote that matters, it’s the quality. While majorities can be won on a small percentage of the vote, as in the general election in 2024, these victories don’t deliver strong government, because people are merely backing the least bad option. As soon as the going gets tough, this negative support melts away. Unless Burnham can reach and maintain something more like 40% backing, governing will remain treacherous.View image in fullscreen‘He built a long-term cross-party consensus in Manchester.’ The prime minister, Andy Burnham, with the newly elected mayor, Bev Craig, on Saturday.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PALabour has been in this doom loop of failure for too long. Because it decides to go it alone and not work with other progressive parties, it can only win under first past the post by appealing to centre-right voters. This means promising little or no change. With no mandate for radical change, Labour sets itself up to fail and wonders why it loses the red wall, Scotland, Wales,support from Muslim votersand nowinner-city seats.The clever move would be to mobilise the country’s whole progressive majority based on a transformative offer. This fragmented landscape can and must be woven together in a way that combines values, policies and electoral performance.There are good omens for this, starting with Burnham himself. He built a long-term cross-party consensus in Manchester, which was the basis for sustained state and private sector investment and the fastest-growing economy in the country. His experience of the supplementary vote, where to secure second preferences he had to listen and engage with non-Labour voters, led him to back a fully proportional voting system.But the mobilisation of any latent progressive majority requires deeper roots than just transactional electoral politics. This is why Burnham’scross-party move on social carematters. While he should haveinvolved the Greens, he recognises that some big issues need a broad and permanent consensus. This principle should be extended, not least to delivering a low-carbon economy. Processes such as this build trust across parties and reveal just how much progressives have in common.Problems still abound. Progressive consolidation works in byelections where media attention and polling send a signal to voters about who to back. But unless progressives work out how to organise their bloc in a general election, the chaos of many progressive tragedies will ensue.In this regard, it’s Clacton that shows the way. It is woeful that the progressive parties have all pulled out, leaving the voters of Clacton with no serious choice about who represents them. As in Tatton in 1997, where theanti-corruption journalist Martin Bell stoodagainst the sitting Tory MP and won, moves should have been made to field a credible centre-right independent to challenge Reform.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, a critical precedent has been re-established, that these so-called “national” parties don’t always put up candidates. Now they’ve stood aside, they can repeat it. Why stand a candidate in a seat that you have no hope of winning and by doing so only make it more likely that the national populist right wins? At the next election, local parties should be empowered to decide whether to stand or not.The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s speech: Rewiring Britain needs Westminster to give up real power | EditorialRead moreThe change to unlock all of this is proportional representation (PR), the promise of which massively helps consolidate the progressive vote at the next election. Burnham and the Labour party staunchly back it. Combined with manifesto promises from the Liberal Democrats and the Greens, a super-majority for change could transform our political system for good. This is why the vote in the Commons on 2September on an elections bill amendment setting up a national commission to pave the way for PR is a critical litmus test of Burnham’s commitment to a new politics for a new society.British politics has never been more volatile and will continue to be so. Yes, the Burnham bounce is welcome. But will it last? No one should think the resourceful and ruthless British right will simply sit back and let progressives win. They will unite the right if they must.As ever, the people are ahead of the politicians. If the parties can catch up and stop their self-defeating tribalism, then progressives won’t just beat Reform – they will beat the causes of Reform.Neal Lawson is director of the cross-party campaign organisation CompassExplore more on these topicsPoliticsOpinionGreater Manchester mayoralty byelection 2026Greater ManchesterMayoral electionsLocal politicsProportional representationByelectionscommentShareReuse this content

title: In the battle of Elon Musk v the press, we can’t let truth be the loser | Jane Martinson | The Guardian
description: The trillionaire Tesla owner has called the editor of the Economist a ‘traitor to the west’ after a clash-filled interview. How should the media respond? asks Guardian columnist Jane Martinson
Author: Jane Martinson
Headline: The trillionaire Tesla owner has called the editor of the Economist a ‘traitor to the west’ after a clash-filled interview. How should the media respond? asks Guardian columnist Jane Martinson
Content: A screen in Times Square, New York City, shows an image of Elon Musk, 12 June 2026Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA screen in Times Square, New York City, shows an image of Elon Musk, 12 June 2026Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockOpinionElon MuskIn the battle of Elon Musk v the press, we can’t let truth be the loserJane MartinsonThe trillionaire Tesla owner has called the editor of the Economist a ‘traitor to the west’ after a clash-filled interview. How should the media respond?Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 07.31 EDTShareElon Musk’slong interview with the editor of the Economistis as good a representation as any of the current clash between two worlds. In one corner, the editor of an 182-year-old news organisation which promotes economic liberalism and freedom. In the other, the world’s first trillionaire, who spreads misinformation to his hundreds of millions of followers on his own social media platform. The bout is a masterclass in the challenges journalists face in a new world of AI, fact avoidance and online aggression.The flash points in Zanny Minton Beddoes’ conversation with Musk start with definitions. Musk says that the people Minton Beddoes calls “far-right” and “fringe” (she mentions Germany’s AfD party) are in fact just “normal people”. They clash over whether the speed of his cuts to USAID led to unnecessary deaths in developing countries – she believes his claim that it didn’t defies not only statistics but the evidence from her reporters on the ground. Asked if he is racist, he cites the fact he has four children with a woman who is “half Indian”. In an awkward exchange, when asked by Minton Beddoes whether he is anti-Muslim, Musk says he is against “people coming to a country with antithetical views … I’m against rape and murder.”The tone shifts when Minton Beddoes accuses Musk of spreading misinformation about Europe and particularly her home town, London, telling him that the statistics show that it is a safer place to live than most large US cities. She appears genuinely irritated that he rejects all evidence that violent crime is far lower than he says and grooming gangs are not terrorising the streets. After she asks if he understands why this makes people loathe him, it becomes a playground spat. Musk points out that with so many followers on X, he must be popular. Besides, “they hate you far more than they hate me”. She admits to the media losing trust.The exchange says a lot, not just about both participants and what they believe in, but also the state of our current media ecosystem. To use the metaphor of the summer, if the interviewwere a Homeric quest, the editor would be trying to get back to a place of truth and safety while Musk would be the angry sea god unleashing violent storms and monsters after the challenge was seemingly over.That dynamic was mirrored in the response. The interview appears to end with the two agreeing to disagree; they even continue to chat while Musk has his photo taken. When Minton Beddoes promoted the interview on X, Musk then reposted it, adding “zany interview with Zanny”. She liked this so much she reposted his repost. After some of his followers posted rude things about the media he piled in on “the reality distortion nightmare mirror that is the legacy mainstream press”. By the weekend, hewas calling her a “traitor to the west”. On Thursday, she confessed to being “bemused” but not scared by the “more and more aggressive” response. She has learned not to look at online comments,she told Radio 4’s Media Show. “If you scroll through them and read hundreds of things saying how awful you are, it’s not very pleasant, so don’t do it.”View image in fullscreenZanny Minton Beddoes, the Economist’s editor-in-chief.Photograph: Felix Clay/The GuardianIt seems particularly timely to see what lessons can be learned from all this, given the latestgovernment-backed investigation into the safety of journalistsfound that many admitted to self-censoring reports on contentious issues such as rightwing protest for fear of being attacked. Throwaway vitriolic comments about journalists are directly linked to increased aggression online and off, the report found. Female journalists bear the brunt of this aggression.The shift to online and video journalism, the increasing celebritification if you will, has made more journalists identifiable, and therefore afraid for their safety. Again, Minton Beddoes is a great example of this given that the Economist, famous for the anonymity of its writers, has recently moved into far more video content. The Insider – the platform on which she interviewed Musk – is a weekly interviewlaunched last September; guests have included Benjamin Netanyahu and Tucker Carlson, so Minton Beddoes is no stranger to combative subjects.Musk’s view of truth is the reason the exchange feels more important than similar confrontations. Asking powerful people questions and continuing to try to find the answers even when they react badly is the essence of what journalism is. In her short response to newsletter subscribers this week, Minton Beddoes promised to double down on the issues raised in the interview. She told them to look forward to new reports examining the facts surrounding the impact of shutting down USAID, the number of victims of grooming gangs in Britain and the amount of violent crime in European cities – all topics she had clashed with Musk over.The news business has not always behaved as ethically as it should andtrust levels are at an all-time lowand falling across the developed world. But data and on-the-ground reporting are the only ways to beat misinformation. You can claim that it’s just too dangerous to walk around in Britain,as Musk did– despite having not visited for several years – or you can find the data which suggests that homicide rates in general and even knife violence crimes are far lower than in major US cities, as the Economistdid in a social videoliked 73,000 times.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOwnership of his own platform and infinite riches may give Musk a loudspeaker, but this old-fashioned reporting is the kind of public service the world needs. Especially if Musk really is the Cassandra he says he is and artificial intelligence is going to best humans within a decade, making it even harder to keep a firm hold on reality.Jane Martinson is a Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group. As the Marjorie Deane professor of financial journalism at City St George’s, University of London, she has a connection through a charitable foundation to Zanny Minton Beddoes, who is chair of trustees. She writes in a personal capacityDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The hill I will die on: Games are the opposite of fun, and I’d ban them for anyone over 12 | Emily Watkins | The Guardian
description: Get your balls, pucks, Scrabble boards and packs of cards away from me – all I want is space to be together, ideally with a coffee or a glass of wine, says writer Emily Watkins
Author: Emily Watkins
Headline: Get your balls, pucks, Scrabble boards and packs of cards away from me – all I want is space to be together, ideally with a coffee or a glass of wine, says writer Emily Watkins
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/2024 Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/2024 Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onBoard gamesThe hill I will die on: Games are the opposite of fun, and I’d ban them for anyone over 12Emily WatkinsGet your balls, pucks, Scrabble boards and packs of cards away from me – all I want is space to be together, ideally with a coffee or a glass of wineSat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.06 EDTShareThe other day, I met a friend at the park for a catch-up. After 45 minutes of blissful note-swapping – my newtabi shoes, his new boyfriend – he pulled out a pair of ping-pong paddles and indicated a nearby table. “Fancy a quick game?” We are no longer speaking.I’m joking, but only sort of. As far as I’m concerned, games of any sort ought to be illegal once everyone present is over the age of 12. I will make grudging exceptions for professional athletes, because apparently they’re earning a living, and realistically there is very little chance of me being asked to join in with, say, the Wimbledon final. But when it comes to anything less formal, the risk of being corralled is just too high: bat those balls, pucks, packs of cards, spinning bottles and Scrabble boards away from me, please.Truly, there is no social situation made better by adding a game. In a setting with people I know and love, it feels like a cruel and unusual punishment to have organic conversation curtailed by something ghastly likeArticulate!And although structured activities are often wheeled out for groups of strangers, that’s even worse – because now not only am I playing a game, but doing so with a bunch of people I don’t know, and I want to die.Let’s go round the office and introduce ourselves with two truths and a lie! Let’s get each of the hens to write down their favourite thing about Milly and she can guess who wrote what! Let’s stick pins in our eyes!skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Radio 4’s Today programme has become really annoying since I left | John HumphrysRead moreIn axing games, I’m not advocating for anything to replace them. On the contrary, all I want is space to be together, ideally while clutching either a coffee or a glass of wine, depending on the time of day. Don’t start thinking that activities that bridge that divide – pub quizzes, for instance – are an exception to my furious veto, either; they’re actually the most dire of all, the Uncanny Valley of organised fun. All the cues – friends, booze – are there for a lovely time, then suddenly,shhhhhh!, it’s the music round and Ollie takes this onevery seriously.Speaking of which, I’m fully aware that there exists a whole cohort who feel just as strongly as I, only in the opposite direction. I have encountered them in the wild – frothing at the mouth as they chastise you for putting your card on the left instead of the right or whatever – and frankly, they frighten me. Maybe I envy their strength of feeling. I’m not sure I’ve ever felt that righteous about anything, but it looks energising.Am I pathologically uncompetitive? Has my lack of interest in games birthed a unique ineptitude at almost every single one? Yes and yes! Nonetheless, my years on the sidelines have made one thing abundantly clear: the real fun begins as soon as the games stop. As I said to my friend at the park: put the paddles down and get me a glass of pinot, please.Emily Watkins is a freelance writer based in LondonDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Like Burnham, I was an altar boy. His Catholic upbringing is shaping the way he governs | Julian Coman | The Guardian
description: With a prime minister raised in a tradition that emphasises our mutual dependency, we may finally have a leader who can address the anomie gripping our country, says Guardian associate editor Julian Coman
Author: Julian Coman
Headline: With a prime minister raised in a tradition that emphasises our mutual dependency, we may finally have a leader who can address the anomie gripping our country, says Guardian associate editor Julian Coman
Content: Liverpool Metropolitan Cathedral.Photograph: Ian Dagnall/AlamyView image in fullscreenLiverpool Metropolitan Cathedral.Photograph: Ian Dagnall/AlamyOpinionAndy BurnhamLike Burnham, I was an altar boy. His Catholic upbringing is shaping the way he governsJulian ComanWith a prime minister raised in a tradition that emphasises our mutual dependency, we may finally have a leader who can address the anomie gripping our countrySat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.05 EDTShareLike Andy Burnham, I was once an enthusiastic altar boy, although I don’t recall competing to be at the front with the communion plate as the prime ministerapparently did. Much of my motivation had little to do with piety. The tips received for serving at weddings were often very generous and I got on well with Father Jerome, an engagingly worldly monk from Ampleforth who shared my passion for Manchester United.I’m five years older than Burnham, but the atmosphere of the small-town northern Catholicism we grew up with will have been much the same.The second Vatican council’s reforms, responding to the social changes under way since the 1960s, were “democratising” the tone and style of worship, and traditionalists were mourning the sidelining of the old Latin mass. The huge success of Pope John Paul II’s groundbreakingvisit to Britainin 1982 – the first by a reigning pontiff – had made the faith seem more mainstream and less rarefied. Politically, most Catholics voted Labour, and the large number of Celtic surnames in parish registers testified to a demographic significantly different from Anglican congregations, which were both more English andmore Tory.Burnham is the first British prime minister to have been raised in this kind of environment, and he has been explicit about its influence upon him. To which the response of many secular well-wishers may well be polite indifference. Catholicism gets abetter press among progressivesthese days, as Rome takes a stand against the cruelties and excesses of Maga-style xenophobia and nationalism. But most liberals would be wary of any Catholic proselytising in areas beyond migration and human rights.They should look deeper. Like Burnham, I lapsed – in my case when I went to university and started looking for different kinds of truths in western Marxism and leftwing social theory. But unlike Burnham, I went back to the church in my 30s. So I have watched with some fascination as the significance of the new prime minister’s cradleCatholicismhas been pondered beyond the confines of the religious press.Two weeks into Burnham’s premiership, it is already clear that something important is at stake here that meshes with Burnham’s conventionallypolitical critiqueof “40 years of neoliberalism”. He himself talks of “a direct read-across between what I was learning at … church and Labour values”, which might sound a bit broad brush and a bit obvious, in a “be kind” type of way. In fact it is anything but, and it matters that the church was a Catholic one.During the 1980s – the decade Burnham has pledged to “roll back” – Margaret Thatcher did not attempt to disguise thetheological rootsof a political vision that emphasised self-reliance and theProtestant work ethicas primary virtues. The Methodist worldview she inherited from her lay-preacher fathertranslatedinto a strident individualism, and a contempt for the collectivist institutions and ethos of the postwar welfare society. As Thatcherassertedin the first phase of her premiership: “Economics are the method; the object is to change the soul.”As she evangelised, the surplice-clad Burnham wasimmersed in the Catholic resistance to this harsh new social doctrine, digesting and disseminating the sermons of the archbishop of Liverpool, Derek Worlock. Based on the social teaching of papal encyclicals, Worlock’s politics (and those of his Anglican counterpart, David Sheppard) emphasised fraternity, solidarity and mutual obligation. “I am my brother’s keeper,” he observed in 1990. “And he’s sleeping pretty rough these days.”Cut to Burnham’s first bigpolicy announcement, when he vowed to use his premiership to end rough sleeping across the country. Commentary, understandably enough, has focused on the practical difficulties he encountered in delivering a similar pledge in Greater Manchester as mayor. But just as important is the message it sent about priorities: in the early morning of his first day in the country’s highest office of state, Burnham made a point of going to talk to homeless people on the streets of central London.The Catholic church would call this the “preferential option for the poor”, a way of systematising the gospel idea that the last should be first. In the ethical architecture ofCatholic social teaching, it is accompanied by other pillars designed to protect people from both an overmighty technocratic state and the moral indifference of the market. Subsidiarity, the idea that power should not be hoarded at the top but devolved downwards, is clearly at the heart of nascent Burnhamism. The dignity of work, elaborated upon in papal encyclicals such as John Paul II’sLaborem Exercens, has been at the core of our angst-ridden debates about the legacy of deindustrialisation and the future of AI.The clue is in the word “social”. Thatcher’sassertionthat “there is no such thing” as society channelled a Protestant emphasis on individual responsibility. It revealed a perspective with a lineage going back to post-Reformation distrust of a Catholicism that, with its smells, bells and rituals, inserted its clerics between the believer and their Bible. Burnham’s much-quoted naming of his chief influences as “Everton FC, the Labour party and the Catholic church” indicates a quite different sensibility; one which finds meaning and truth in relationships and social institutions, and is at heart convivial. His determination to present the crisis in social care as an issue to becollectively faced and resolvedcomes from the same source.One could go on. Burnham’slove of Philip Larkin, a (self-described “agnostic”) poet who captured the pathos and sadness – but also the beauty – in ordinary lives, is of a piece with an understanding of the world that is not obsessed with individual achievement and material wealth. It was Labour’s grievous error in the 90s and 00s to succumb to the meritocratic, aspirational creed, alienating vast swathes of its traditional support that looked to the party for different, associational values.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and morePreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham’s Catholic upbringing appears to have provided him with convictions that allowed him to emerge relatively intact from that heretical turn. The intriguing possibility is that as a result, the country finally has a prime minister able to understand the deeper origins of the anomie gripping a country in which former sources of social solidarity are under threat, or have already disappeared. The nation’s discontents are of course eminently practical, with the cost of living and the degradation of public services taking their place at the top of the list. But they can also be attributed to a sense that the common good – another concept of Catholic social teaching – has been chronically neglected in many ways, in an unbalanced, unequal society.That is a moral issue about the way we live now, as much as it is a technical policy challenge. If Burnham’s stint as an ambitious altar boy can help him resolve it, it will be good news for a largely secular nation.Julian Coman is a Guardian associate editorDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Gregg Araki on sex, film and queer resistance: ‘All the terrible shit in the world is because of sexual repression’ | Gregg Araki | The Guardian
description: As his 12th feature film, I Want Your Sex, hits theaters, the cult gay film-maker is as fired up as ever
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: As his 12th feature film, I Want Your Sex, hits theaters, the cult gay film-maker is as fired up as ever
Content: Gregg Araki at the Los Angeles premiere of I Want Your Sex on Tuesday.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APView image in fullscreenGregg Araki at the Los Angeles premiere of I Want Your Sex on Tuesday.Photograph: Richard Shotwell/APGregg ArakiInterviewGregg Araki on sex, film and queer resistance: ‘All the terrible shit in the world is because of sexual repression’Owen MyersAs his 12th feature film, I Want Your Sex, hits theaters, the cult gay film-maker is as fired up as everSat 1 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIs straight sex the most perverse sex of all?Gregg Araki’s new film makes a convincing case. Titled I Want Your Sex, the movie is a deliriously fun and often hilarious study of desire, power and art that features bondage, full-frontal and a vagina made out of pink chewed-up bubble gum. “For me, it is a very queer story,” the director says, speaking the week of the film’s release in a video call from his Los Angeles home. “It’s a take on kink and alternate sexuality that goes right across the straight-queer spectrum.”While it is not the first heterosexual movie by Gregg Araki – that honor goes to his 1995 acid trip of a road movieThe Doom Generation– it features the new queer cinema pioneer’s starriest cast in years, perhaps in a sign that Hollywood at large has caught up to the cult director’s anarchic vision. Forty years into his career, we still want Araki’s sex: the film is set to reach the director’s biggest audience to date, opening to 700 US screens this week, a stunning figure for an independent film and a wider opening than recent films by indie veterans likeNicolas Winding RefnandJim Jarmusch.Today, the director is in a buoyant mood; he wears a striped tank top and looks at least two decades younger than his age of 66. “The world’s so fucked up right now with wars andICEand fucking genocides that I want to put a little queer joy and positivity into the world,” he says.The film follows Elliot (Cooper Hoffman), a puppyish 23-year-old college graduate whose ambitions in life amount to a vague goal to start a podcast. After he starts working as an assistant for the brash, sexually carnivorous artist Erika (a turbo-chargedOlivia Wilde), he instantly falls under her spell, leading to a polymorphous parade of sexual epiphanies as he becomes, as he says of one of Erika’s artworks, “a slave to this vagina”.‘Beautiful and terrifying’: the best American LGBTQ+ books, chosen by Samuel R Delany, Kaveh Akbar, Eileen Myles and moreRead moreThere’s an infectious sense of mischief to I Want Your Sex, helped by an ensemble cast that includesCharli xcxas Elliot’s dorky girlfriend, whose idea of a good time between the bedsheets is poring over a neurology textbook, as well asJohnny KnoxvilleandMargaret Choas detectives who interrogate Elliot after a body is discovered floating face-first in a swimming pool. My favorite might be Zap, played by Mason Gooding, who cuts down Elliot’s claim of being “queer adjacent” by retorting: “Have you ever sucked a dick?” Araki has a soft spot for the character too. “He’s very much my snarky sensibility,” the director says.The film was initially scheduled to shoot after Araki wrapped promotion forWhite Bird in a Blizzard, a 2014 drama starringShailene WoodleyandEva Green. Back then, the script was something like “a comic50 Shades of Grey”, he says, with a female intern seduced by her male boss. But after initial funding fell through, the project was put on ice, and when Araki revisited the script after making 2019’s teen TV comedyNow Apocalypse, he worried it felt tone-deaf in the wake of#MeToo. “I started to feel uncomfortable with the [script’s] image of a woman getting dragged around by the hair, even in a consensual situation,” he says. “I don’t want to kink-shame anybody, but as a man, I didn’t really want to put that image out there.“That’s when I got the idea to flip the sex roles and make it a male sub and a female dom,” he says. “I’ve always been a very hardcore feminist from the time I was in film school in the late 70s, so the Erika Tracy character became much more interesting to me.” The script further crystallized in the wake of a 2022studythat found that gen Z were having less sex than previous generations. “When Erika says [to Elliot]: ‘Your generation’s all about Fomo and you’re missing out on the sexual part,’ that was kind of my reaction to that article,” he says.View image in fullscreenOlivia Wilde and Cooper Hoffman in I Want Your Sex.Photograph: Courtesy of Magnolia PicturesThe day before our interview, the Hollywood trade magazine Varietytweetedan Araki quote predicting that gen Z will inevitably “regret” not having sex out of fear of getting hurt. While some readers got defensive, others seemed to take it as a metaphorical kick up the butt. “He’s so right let me start fucking for real,” wrote one young cinephile.When I mention the reaction, Araki seems thrilled about getting people talking. “That is one of the most exciting things about the movie to me,” the director says. “I don’t want to lecture anybody, but I want to open up a conversation.“I don’t want to sayallof gen Z, but a certain number of gen Z live a sheltered life and don’t go out much,” he continues. “It’s like [they have] a fear of making a mistake, or being uncomfortable or of having an experience that’s not wonderful. A lot of those experiences arenotwonderful! The first time you ever get your heart broken or someone cheats on you, it really rocks your world. I just can’t imagine going through life without that experience.”Araki thinks that sex is missing in movies, even the ones that are ostensibly all about it. “There’s this whole talk about [cinema’s] sexual renaissance withBabygirlandPillion,” he says. “But I didn’t find Babygirl sex-positive at all. The way that the Nicole Kidman character gets punished for exploring her own desires made me a little uncomfortable.”The hockey-themed gay TV showHeated Rivalryhas also been accused of sanitizing sex for the female gaze. “Uh huh,” Araki says with a slight frown. I’m surprised to learn that he is a big fan, but he doesn’t seem to mind a little debate. “I thought the sex scenes were well-handled and not really watered down,” he says. “It’s kind of what a lot of my sex scenes are: ‘R-rated HBO’. You don’t see genitalia but it’s as explicit as you can be without crossing the line into adult entertainment.”View image in fullscreenAraki and the cast of I Want Your Sex at the film’s  LA premiere.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersAmid its fiesta of raunch, there’s a sly sweetness to I Want YourSex. Despite Elliot’s initial reservations, it seems that Erika unlocks the young man’s unexplored desire to fulfill orders. At times, the pair’s rapport is surprisingly touching, even if there are signs this won’t end well. “I kind of like being your toy,” he tells her moonily over lunch as she nonchalantly drags on a cigarette.‘I feel both thrilled and ruined by this’: Olivia Wilde and Edward Norton on making sex comedy The InviteRead more“I based Cooper’s character on myself when I was in my early 20s and trying to figure out what my sexual identity was,” Araki says. (The director now identifies as gay but was in a public relationship with actor Kathleen Robertson in the late 90s.) Meanwhile, Erika is partly inspired by post-fame Araki, with much of her dialogue culled from the director’s own past interviews. Before shooting began, he told Wilde that there was no room for nerviness on his set. “I was like: ‘Whoever plays this part needs to be completely fearless and not give a fuck about what people think,’” he says. “She was like: ‘That’s what I want to do.’” (Between this andThe Invite, Wilde has emerged as one of the most fun actors to watch this summer.)The director has always taken audiences out of their comfort zones. Araki’s breakout feature The Living End featured a then unprecedented sex scene between the film’s HIV-positive gay lead characters, while 2004’s Mysterious Skin unflinchingly examined the after-effects of childhood sexual abuse in a film anchored by career-best performances from a youngJoseph Gordon-Levittand future Oscar-nominated directorBrady Corbet. He says that the key to his relationships with actors is trust: “I’m not a director that is like: ‘OK, here’s how you’re going to act this scene.’ Once I find the right person and they’re in front of the camera, I just let them have at it.”View image in fullscreenAraki’s 2005 film Mysterious Skin starred Joseph Gordon-Levitt.Photograph: Courtesy of TLA ReleasingWhile Wilde and Hoffman’s chemistry is both explosive and often outrageously funny, I Want Your Sex is just as cutting in its satire of the commercial art world. Erika’s art is frankly hideous, with her gallery space full of garish pop-feminist sculptures and photography that would be bought by a finance bro trying to impress his co-workers with his hip bona fides. Araki, perhaps a little generously, describes the character as a cross betweenRobert Mapplethorpeand the “pure provocation” of Madonna circa Sex, the 1992 top-shelf publication that caused much pearl-clutching for its graphic content. Has society gotten any more open-minded about sex, 34 years later?‘Coming out in the 90s? You might as well say ‘I love cock!’’ Nathan Lane on gay life, Broadway and defying stereotypesRead more“In America, things are worse than they’ve ever been,” Araki says. “The level of puritanical tyranny, repression and cancelling of trans people … it is awful right now. That’s why the movie ends with the Jessie Ware songFree Yourself. I’m old school in a sense: I absolutely believe in ‘make love, not war.’“So much of the hatred, the misery and the aggression and the violence and all the fucking terrible shit in the world right now is from this weird sexual repression,” he goes on. “My movie is my version of Free Yourself, you know what I mean? The sentiment of the song is very positive, inclusive and progressive – the opposite of this culture of oppression and fascism with the dictatorship of our current administration.”He feels fundamentally hopeful about the next generation, despite wishing they would get laid more. “Whenever we do screenings in New York, [the audience is] all these Letterboxd kids,” he says, referring to the social platform for movie fans. “And they’re very sophisticated cinephiles –Charli xcxis one of them! They have very discerning taste in auteurs. It really gives me hope that this younger generation seeks out films that are not your standard popcorn multiplex movies.”View image in fullscreenCharli xcx and Hoffman in I Want Your Sex.Photograph: Courtesy of Magnolia PicturesWhile a recentGlaad reportfound that LGBTQ+ inclusion is at a three-year low in films from the 10 largest distributors, Araki says that queer cinema is in great shape if you know where to look. “At Cannes this year, it was like abonanzaofqueermovies,” he says. “It’s amazing that that is the state of where we are at. That’s kind of where the queer new wave came from in the first place, way back in the early 90s where all of us – Todd [Haynes] and Gus [Van Sant] and I – were just kids.”Araki says that he can see some similarities between LGBTQ+ life today and that of the early 90s. He leaves me with this slightly grim but necessary thought. “Because of the Aids crisis, queer people were kind of being exterminated, so there was a need for expression,” he says. “I think that exists today as well. Queer film-makers that can see the writing on the wall, and that the right wing in this country are not going to stop at trans people. We’re not safe.“It’s very important to be able to have a queer voice and be unfiltered about it,” he says. “That’s where almost all my movies come from. You know, that’s the magic.”I Want Your Sex is out now in the US, on 27 August in Australia and on 28 August in the UKExplore more on these topicsGregg ArakiComedy filmsComedyLGBTQ+ rightsOlivia WildeHeated RivalryCharli xcxinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ​What makes a good comic novel? Andrew Sean Greer on the joy of funny writing  | Comedy | The Guardian
description: The Pulitzer-winning author of Less and Villa Coco explores the art of writing humour – plus 10 of the best novels to make you laugh
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Pulitzer-winning author of Less and Villa Coco explores the art of writing humour – plus 10 of the best novels to make you laugh
Content: Comedy​What makes a good comic novel? Andrew Sean Greer on the joy of funny writingThe Pulitzer-winning author of Less and Villa Coco explores the art of writing humour – plus 10 of the best novels to make you laughAndrew Sean GreerSat 1 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTShareView image in fullscreenIllustration: Javi AznarezIn March 2020, when the mayor of San Francisco instructed all citizens to remain in their houses due to a pandemic, the first thing I did was order all the books of Agatha Christie. I was not alone; I think many of us immersed ourselves in reliable narratives to drown out the chaos. It did not matter if it ended in marriage or murder; the reliability was what mattered. Later when I realised I would need to hole up for some time, my reading shifted to a different kind of novel. And because, like Christie, our world has an endless supply of new terrors, it is the comic novel that still fills my reading hours.Nobody knows what a comic novel is. And once you start discussing it, all the fun runs out. EB White compared it to dissecting a frog (you’re left with innards and a dead frog) but I would compare it to turning all the lights on at a party: everyone looks terrible and you’ve ruined the party. Most would agree, of course, that Wodehouse wrote comic novels, but I turn to books hardly anybody would classify that way – Moby-Dick by Herman Melville, for instance – that yet seem to me to be a hoot. I think they are books thatdecidesomething is funny, as Jerry Seinfeld once defined comedy. In Moby-Dick, it’s a coin nailed to a masthead. In Vladimir Nabokov’s Pale Fire, it’s the worst best poem you’ve ever read. And yet we feel we’re getting at something the most solemn narratives aim for: an understanding of the human condition, of grief, of love, of death. All the big stuff. The comic novels I love are books that could just as easily have been tragedies. It is simply that the author hasdecidedit’s funny.It’s something I learned from a wise friend of mine who once, after I angrily related a publishing story of mine, responded: “That’s not a very funny story.” I was shocked. And then I understood that I had not processed the story at all, and was serving this dish to her raw. I had to learn to turn an old outrage into a funny story. And then she would be willing to listen. I did learn to do this. And I have put the very scene I have described to you into my latest novel. A comic novel, if you like.I have written both comic novels and novels where you would not crack a smile – serious novels, I suppose. And I can relate that, for me, writing the comic ones is a much more pleasant, though very different, kind of work. But the plots are no funnier than the serious ones. See if you can guess which one is comic and which is serious:A young woman in 1952 San Francisco joins with her husband’s gay lover to remove obstacles to her liberation and gain a small fortune.A middle-aged writer travels across a troubled United States while struggling to maintain his recently renewed relationship with a younger man.Even if you guessed, you see my point: I have to decide it’s funny. And that takes double-processing. Like blond hair at the salon. First, I work out the hardships and frustrations of the characters as realistically, even tragically, as possible. People die in comic novels. Sometimes the world ends, or sometimes just the world we thought we knew, and I have to consider the real reactions of my characters because, after all,theydon’t know it’s a comedy. Second, I begin to write it as if it’s all just a funny story. That takes a great deal of struggle and sometimes feels impossible.double quotation markWhen writing comedy, a whole feast of words is spread before you: hullabaloo, brouhaha, hubbub and chivaree. Chivaree!In my last novel,Less Is Lost(that’s the one about the middle-aged writer), I found myself sitting with my notes on visiting three forced labour plantations in the American south. There was nothing humorous about them, yet I didn’t want to cut them; I knew my protagonist had to confront that part of American history. But then I read over the notes of my final visit and realised thatIwas the comedy: myself and the other white visitors, showcasing our guilt and anxiety through statements that were utterly absurd. In fact, I ended up portraying the visit almost exactly as I had it in my notes … but with a different emphasis. Is it “funny”? No. Is it “comic”? Definitely. Why? I don’t know. I don’t know. I can’t explain it any better for fear of turning on the party lights.In writing my latest novel,Villa Coco,I had a much easier time, since I was working off notes in my diaries from my time living in Tuscany, and those notes were already blond hair in a salon; I made a promise to myself that I would turn each day’s events into a “funny story”. And yet, in a way, I found myself sifting through these stories for the other thing: the real feeling. Because there was the death, in those days, of a dear friend. A turn of seasons. A broken heart. All the things I would have previously put down in my diary now had been expunged, and though I had processed them into lovely stories, the job (as a novelist now and not a diarist) was to get to the hardships and frustrations of my characters. Because, to me, comedy is only great fun if it is about something hard and true.“I don’t think of you as writing a comic novel,” a writer friend told me. “I think of you as working through something in whatever way you have to.” He meant that my books are not “about” women in 1952 or middle-aged writers or olive harvests in Tuscany. They are about marriage and growing old and the terror of death. It is just that, in a comic novel, those issues are temporarily resolved, often in a flagrantly artificial fashion. As if to say: life is a vale of tears, and there’s no fixing it, but just for fun let’s fix this one small piece. Let’s decide, briefly, to lift the weight of being. You can’t successfully do that, I think, without being honest about it first.View image in fullscreenTuscany, Italy, an inspiration for Andrew Sean GreerAnd yet – what a lovely time I have working on these books. Because everything has to be processed in this way, each awful moment of the day becomes more material for comedy. Thus I become, somehow, more resilient; a trip on the sidewalk is no less embarrassing than before but, instead of trying to play it off, I laugh with anyone who notices (and peopledo notice). What would normally be a dull wait at a bus stop (or a mind‑numbing trip through the internet) becomes a delightful experience with my notebook. “Cheese rolling contest May 20,” I might copy down from a poster, “Prize is the wheel of cheese.” Or “lady in black sequined dress yelling at a mailbox at nine in the morning. I think she mailed her purse by mistake.” I am not a person who particularly lives in the present tense, but comedy forces me there. A good place to be.Language also achieves a new richness. People assume writers think about plot or characters, in the way they assume painters or photographers think about their subjects. But painters think about paint. Photographers think about light. And writers think about words. There is something so utterly delicious about being able to make use of words that are otherwise forbidden to touch. I don’t mean curse words; I mean fancy ones. Take for instance something like “noise”. In a serious novel, you would have to say “down the street came a noise”. Anything more elaborate would be a red flag of pretentiousness. So you settle for the austerity of “noise” and move on. But when writing comedy, suddenly a whole feast of words is spread before you: hullabaloo and brouhaha and hubbub and chivaree. Chivaree! Banging pots and pans together to publicly shame a citizen or tease a newly married couple! What a word! My language has not become simpler by writing comedy; it has become zestier. And if, like me, words are your favourite medium, it is akin to tomatoes finally coming into season after months of cabbage and kale.Villa Coco by Andrew Sean Greer review – fun in the Tuscan sunRead moreNo wonder what some consider the very first “novel” was one of the most rip-roaring, slapstick comedies around: Don Quixote. Chaucer himself was not above a fart joke, and Shakespeare could never resist a pun. There is a grand tradition, in fact, of great writers dabbling in comedy – Philip Roth, Saul Bellow, Thornton Wilder – and I think there is something about having seen the darkness that pulls so many to laughter. Certainly, in these difficult times, with endless apocalyptic films and novels appearing, many of us find ourselves picking upStella Gibbons’ Cold Comfort Farminstead.There is something dear and beautiful about the comic novel, something to love. A friend to hold your hand when the lights flicker out and tell you a story until they come back on again. And, for those of us who write them, a way to feel our way forward down the tunnel into the light. I know that it was a solace to imagine a much younger American man, finding himself delivered to a rural Tuscan train station that he says is “so fanciful one might unwrap it and find it was chocolate”. And to be seated next to a princess who cannot understand him because she has not mastered “the American dialect”. And throw a wild animal into his window at night. And make the septic tank overflow. All to get at a simple truth: the world is trouble, and full of sorrows, and we will not get out alive.But look closely: it is, in fact, made of chocolate.Villa Coco by Andrew Sean Greer is published by Sceptre. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Ten novels to make you laughCold Comfort Farmby Stella GibbonsThis is a satire of a genre that no longer even exists (the rural English romance) because it erased it with its perfect sense of humour.Pomp and Circumstanceby Noël CowardThe queen is coming to visit a far-flung island nation and everyone is aquiver.Pninby Vladimir NabokovThe poignancy of Nabokov’s tortured Russian academic makes one fall in love with poor Pnin.Bech: ABook by John UpdikeThe first of a series of books about a Philip Roth-like novelist adrift in the world. Like Nabokov, a wordsmith having great fun with the English language.The Selloutby Paul BeattyA brilliant example of taking the most serious of subjects – slavery in America – and turning it completely on its head.I Capturethe Castleby Dodie SmithI reread this book annually and both laugh and shed tears over the fate of our teenage narrator, Cassandra, whose diary this is.View image in fullscreenOur Man in Havanaby Graham GreenePersonally, I prefer Greene’s “entertainments” to his serious fiction, from Travels With My Aunt to this wonderful case of mistaken identity.Little Me: The Intimate Memoirs ofThat Great Star of Stage, Screen and Television, Belle Poitrineby Patrick DennisFrom the writer of Auntie Mame, a deliciously deluded memoir of an absolute nobody, complete with photographs!The Pursuit of Love/Love in a Cold Climateby Nancy MitfordEccentricity and delight mix with heartache in this classic fictionalised version of her famous family.Don Quixoteby Miguel de CervantesHilarious from beginning to end, and the sequel is even better, because suddenly Don Quixote and Sancho Panza are famous because everyone has read the first.

title: A forgotten Victorian children’s book helped me grieve my father | Culture | The Guardian
description: The stories in Mrs Leicester’s School, written by a woman who killed her own mother, were suffused with grief, and finally triggered mine as I was teaching a class of students
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The stories in Mrs Leicester’s School, written by a woman who killed her own mother, were suffused with grief, and finally triggered mine as I was teaching a class of students
Content: Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreenIllustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningCultureA forgotten Victorian children’s book helped me grieve my fatherThe stories in Mrs Leicester’s School, written by a woman who killed her own mother, were suffused with grief, and finally triggered mine as I was teaching a class of studentsChris TownsendSat 1 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen my dad went into hospital for what would be the final time, shortly before Christmas last year, I had been finishing up a lecture series on early children’s literature for the university where I teach. My dad had had a drinking problem practically my whole life, but his alcoholism had worsened across decades. Then suddenly, after years of poor health, his liver just gave up on him. He was dead within days.Shortly after his death I was due to lecture on a relatively forgotten book of stories for children called Mrs Leicester’s School, mostly written by the English writer Mary Lamb but with parts by her more famous brother, Charles. I was not prepared for how moved I would be by the simple message of one of the stories. That often bizarre and sometimes grim collection of tales for pre-Victorian boys and girls changed the way that I, an almost 40-year-old man, think about grief.My lecture began with the Lamb siblings themselves, who were reasonably successful writers in their time; any branch of Waterstones will still carry their Tales from Shakespeare. But Mary is better known today because she killed her own mother with a knife in 1796, during a breakdown. Charles intervened, but their mother couldn’t be saved. Mary was spared imprisonment because Charles pledged to become her legal guardian. They took up writing children’s books.The fact that Mary killed her own parent coloured my first encounter with Mrs Leicester’s School, which is far more emotionally intense than any kids’ book ought to be. Many of the children who act as the narrators of the stories have lost parents; several of the stories directly concern their experiences of loss.I was especially struck by the story of Elizabeth Villiers, or The Sailor Uncle, which I focused on for my lecture, delivered to two dozen 20-year-olds in a dusty theatre. It begins after the young Elizabeth’s mother has died. She doesn’t think of her death as a cause for tears, as she has never seen her father cry; he mostly locks himself in his study.double quotation markI started talking about it in a lecture to my students. At one point, I realised I was cryingThat changes when her “sailor Uncle” returns from sea, and Elizabeth takes him to his sister’s grave, where he is struck by an “agony of grief”. This in turn sets off Elizabeth’s father. The “very first day I ever saw my father weep”, she tells us, became the day she “first learned my mother’s death was a heavy affliction”. Elizabeth, upset, blames her uncle for bringing painful feelings into her home. Nevertheless, he is kind to her and when he eventually heads back to sea, Elizabeth realises that she will miss him terribly.It was this part of Lamb’s story that really got to me when I narrated it to my students that morning. Elizabeth’s father sits her down, dries away the tears she’s shed for her uncle, and says to her: “Let it be a lesson to you to be as kind as possible to those you love; and remember, when they are gone from you, you will never think you had been kind enough.”At this point in my lecture, I realised I was crying, and had been for some time. My students were aware, but, rather than laughing with embarrassment, they were rapt. One girl, who also had cheeks shining with tears, looked straight at me and simply nodded, slowly.Lamb doesn’t spell it out, but the father is finally working through his grief. He has exited the locked study of his repressed emotions. Grief is a complicated thing, and always distinct in its complications, but what we shared in that lecture theatre was a recognition of the power of literature to make grief shareable, and somehow bearable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe sense of loss we feel for those we love, Lamb’s little book tells us, reminds us that there are many kinds of love that make life worth living in the first place. When my dad died, my grief was complicated by the fact that I long ago felt I’d lost him; I’d been grieving for years, and I wasn’t sure I had any tears left. Mrs Leicester’s School helped me see that I did.Did a cultural moment prompt you to make a major life change?
