title: From TikTok to signing with Kesha, Boy Throb say they’re for real – and serious about a US visa | Music | The Guardian
description: ‘The people’s boy band’ are petitioning the US government for an ‘extraordinary abilities’ visa for singer Darshan Magdum, who lives in India
Author: Rosalind Adams
Headline: ‘The people’s boy band’ are petitioning the US government for an ‘extraordinary abilities’ visa for singer Darshan Magdum, who lives in India
Content: From left, Evan Papier, Anthony Key and Zachary Sobania of Boy Throb, at the group's first concert at the Bowery Ballroom in New York City, New York, on 12 May.Photograph: Shuran Huang for the Washington Post via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFrom left, Evan Papier, Anthony Key and Zachary Sobania of Boy Throb, at the group's first concert at the Bowery Ballroom in New York City, New York, on 12 May.Photograph: Shuran Huang for the Washington Post via Getty ImagesMusicFrom TikTok to signing with Kesha, Boy Throb say they’re for real – and serious about a US visa‘The people’s boy band’ are petitioning the US government for an ‘extraordinary abilities’ visa for singer Darshan Magdum, who lives in IndiaRosalind Adamsin New YorkSat 1 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe screams of hundreds of fans waving glowing pink orbs grew louder as one member of Boy Throb appeared on stage at Irving Plaza inNew YorkCity earlier this month.Singer Darshan Magdum wasn’t there in person – he was calling from India while his visa application to enter the United States remained in limbo. With his face projected across a large screen on stage as he spoke through Zoom, he told the crowd: “I’m so sad that I can’t be there with you all tonight.”“Hell yeah, Darshan!” someone yelled. At one point, chants of: “Visa! Visa! Visa!” rippled through the crowd.“When Darshan was on screen, I needed to, like, spiritually send him love,” said Kenzie, 30, who went to the show with a few of her friends.Magdum’s immigration journey has become a key part of Boy Throb’s lore, driving millions of viewers to their videos and in the process converting them into genuine fans. Dubbing themselves “the people’s boy band”, Boy Throb formed last fall, choosing their name from fan suggestions and posting their rise onTikTok. The other members are Evan Papier, Anthony Key and Zachary Sobania, who all live in Los Angeles. Dressed in matching pink sweatsuits evocative of Amy Poehler’s “cool mom” character in Mean Girls, Boy Throb began posting videos explaining the dilemma of their fourth band member being stuck in India.Magdum submitted his application for an O-1 visa that’s designated for people with extraordinary abilities in December. Internet personalities haveincreasingly appliedfor the visa as social media has shifted the nature of fame in recent years. One of Boy Throb’s first goals was to reach a million followers to support his application.In early videos, Boy Throb sang covers of familiar pop hits, replacing lyrics to persuade the US government to approve Magdum’s visa. In one post, Boy Throb and some fans protested outside a local television station in Los Angeles, chanting: “Hey, hey, ho, ho, write about our Indian bro.” Within a month, they had a million followers on TikTok.View image in fullscreenA photo of Darshan Magdum in the phone case of a Boy Throb fan, at the Bowery Ballroom in New York City.Photograph: Shuran Huang for the Washington Post via Getty ImagesBut when video of their first gig performing at a nursing home surfaced last year, some commenters wondered if it was all just a gag. The band responded in a social media post that they had received some unkind messages asking if they were “satire”. Though their videos could be silly and fun, they were earnestly trying to make it as artists, they said.Papier and Key have both previously auditioned for American Idol while Sobania studied guitar and music production at the Berklee College of Music. Magdum already has a large following for his falsettocoversof songs from PinkPantheress and Lady Gaga.“We’re not going to let this negativity stop us, in fact we’ve been actively using it as fuel to prove the haters wrong, which is why we’re currently in the process of creating ORIGINAL music!” they wrote.By the night of their July 2026 show in New York, they had released several original songs, including“Can’t Stop the Throb”, “Number One Boy” and “DJ Turn It Down” featuring Kesha. The pop star signed Boy Throb to her independent label, Kesha Records, and brought them on stage at the Bonnaroo music festival in June. “These boys have stolen my heart,” shetoldthe crowd.Ever the optimists, Boy Throb decided to call their three-stop tour the Rehearsal Tour, considering it a practice run before Magdum joins them in the US. The night of the show, fans Rose and Alley were debating which merch to purchase before the concert began. Among the items for sale were the band’s signature pink sweatsuits for $119 as well as T-shirts that read “Not Satire” and “Boy Throb Is Real”.While some on Reddithavetheorizedthat the comedian Nathan Fielder is behind Boy Throb, others have dismissed this. But whether there is a more elaborate comedy bit behind the group hardly seems to matter any more, said fans at the show.“Either way, it’s a good cause. Get Darshan his visa,” said Rose, 26. “I feel like they’ve proven they’re a legitimate band. Look at all the people here.”“And low-key their songs are good,” added her friend Alley, 27.Even as Magdum remains in India, his status remains a point of levity. Before the concert began, there was already a life-size cutout of Magdum smiling in his pink tracksuit on stage. Papier, Key and Sobania kicked off the show with an a capella version of the national anthem, holding their right hands on their hearts as an image of the American flag waved behind them.As patriotism and American flags have become increasingly associated with the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign and protectionist policies, Boy Throb offers people a different way to celebrate both the country and the value of immigration – all through a bubble-gum-pop lens.“We’re living in a unique hell right now and I love this subversion of it,” said one fan after the show. “It’s nice to be part of something so positive.”In March, Boy Throb shared with fans that the government had requested more information to support Magdum’s application. “Begging for press solely to improve an immigration beneficiary request is not indicative of an organization or an establishment that has a distinguished reputation,” thelettersaid.Later, Boy Throb connected with Jonathan Grode, an immigration lawyer based in Pennsylvania, who submitted additional paperwork to support Magdum’s visa application.“This case really caught my attention because they knew that they had people with talent, they knew they had people with an idea, but they let the fame come before the recognition of the ability,” said Grode.“It fundamentally begs the question of: how is fame created?”View image in fullscreenFrom the top, Zachary Sobania, Evan Papier and Anthony Key, with a cardboard cutout of fellow member Darshan Magdum, before the group’s concert on 12 May.Photograph: Shuran Huang for the Washington Post via Getty ImagesWhile the one million followers was one of their first achievements, the Irving Plaza show revealed the confidence they’ve gained as performers in recent months. The choreography was spirited, their vocals strong and the playful use of props and pop-ins from Magdum added to the fun of the show.“I’m really proud of them. I think part of following boy bands is just seeing how they grow more successful over time,” said Zyn, 31, who was thrilled with how much the group had improved after the show.“They’ve always been genuine. It’s more just convincing other people that they’re genuine,” added her friend Hannah, 26.While their catalogue of songs is still limited, the packed venue didn’t stop cheering from their opening medley of songs about New York City through covers of Chappell Roan’s Pink Pony Club and their original singles. They wrapped up the night performing an unreleased song about being your squeaky-clean boy, playfully swinging bath towels between their legs to more whoops from the audience.“If they can get the crowd going like that, they’re real,” said Eric, 31, after the show. He considered himself a casual fan who had only seen a couple of their videos before attending the concert with some friends. “It was very infectious and fun. I am fully on board.”As fans spilled out onto the street after the show, the merch table was nearly cleaned out. Both the Boy Throb Is Real and Not Satire shirts were sold out.Explore more on these topicsMusicUS immigrationPop and rockKeshaNew YorkTikTokfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A towering piece of monoculture’: how The Odyssey discourse has dominated this summer | The Odyssey | The Guardian
description: Christopher Nolan’s smash hit epic has continued to excite and enrage everyone from rightwingers to academics, an old-fashioned throwback to a uniting big-screen event
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Christopher Nolan’s smash hit epic has continued to excite and enrage everyone from rightwingers to academics, an old-fashioned throwback to a uniting big-screen event
Content: Matt Damon in The Odyssey.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenMatt Damon in The Odyssey.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyThe Odyssey‘A towering piece of monoculture’: how The Odyssey discourse has dominated this summerChristopher Nolan’s smash hit epic has continued to excite and enrage everyone from rightwingers to academics, an old-fashioned throwback to a uniting big-screen eventPeter Bradshaw reviews The OdysseyThe Odyssey: jaw-dropping action, dark magic and dolphin cameos – discuss with spoilersGo woke, get rich: why rightwing hate campaigns don’t affect the box officeJesse HassengerSat 1 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf a high-profile academic isreviewing a movie for the London Review of Books, that movie in question must be making some kind of mark on some kind of culture. And if people are actually reading a movie review in the London Review of Books, and writing thinkpieces in disagreement or favor of said movie or its review, that movie may actually be a cultural phenomenon.The Odyssey: jaw-dropping action, dark magic and dolphin cameos – discuss with spoilersRead moreNormally, volume of discourse about a movie should not be mistaken for a sign that people are actually seeing it. Sometimes online factions just have a bored fixation not shared by the rest of the world. ButChristopher Nolan’sThe Odysseyhas some major receiptsat the box office, too: the movie has already outgrossed Oppenheimer, Nolan’s last movie, itself a shockingly popular movie for adults. Though The Odyssey’s audience skewed male in its first weekend, by its second its gender split wascloser to 50/50, suggesting reach beyond the stereotypically male-driven action-adventures. It’s also reaching out to older moviegoers, an endangered demographic in a summer where under-25s have driven the success ofObsessionandBackrooms. Three-quarters of The Odyssey’s audience has been over 25, while memes inspired by the movie (most popular:Matt Damon’s anguished face portraying Odysseus listening to the sirens’ song andRobert Pattinson’s slimy suitor demanding that “someone get these BEGGARS out of here!”) have indicated that younger people are paying attention too.All told, The Odyssey fast closing in on a billion dollars worldwide, and the number of movies that have done this without superheroes, sequel hype or a whole lot of animation is vanishingly small. This is the strange, rarified air that Nolan’s film now occupies. Meanwhile, exactly those other types of movies traditionally aiming for that territory – superhero movies such asSupergirl, remakes includingMasters of the UniverseorMoana, animation films likeToy Story 5andMinions & Monsters– have failed to catch on more broadly. Some have bombed, some have underperformed and some have become seemingly frictionless billion-dollarsmashes, but none feel like true events. Though an incoming mega-smash featuringSpider-Manreinforces that sometimes audiences will still rush out for the right familiar superhero, Nolan’s movie still stands outin a summerthat may have seen tides turn against IP.Of course, The Odyssey is also, in its way, a form of IP;it’s a storythat almost everyone purports to at least kinda-sorta know, even if the specifics are lost somewhere in the halls of high school. Nolan’s big-budget adaptation of the Homeric epic has emerged as a towering piece of monoculture that throws back to pre-fragmentation days. Or, at very least, back to less preordained smashes including Barbie or Top Gun: Maverick, IP projects that seem to dig deeper into audiences’ psyche than other, more preordained blockbusters.Go woke, get rich: why rightwing hate campaigns don’t affect the box officeRead moreSpecifically, these kinds of monocultural events stand in opposition to so many 21st-century box office hits that manage to make tons of money while still feeling like a niche. This waspioneeredbytheTwilight movies, which would make $700m worldwide like clockwork without ever feeling like an all-demographics smash, but there are plenty of hit superhero movies that also qualify: movies that a lot of people who like that sort of thing saw, without convincing infrequent moviegoers (whose infrequency has seemingly only grown post-pandemic) to show up. Even aless expectedsmash such asA Minecraft Movieisn’t exactly a unifying force across demographics. Call it the difference between Avatar (massive worldwide phenom that seemed to reach across demographics) andAvatar 3(big hit for the not-insubstantial group of people who have been watching every Avatar movie, but nothing your grandparents likely went out for).It’s tempting to classify The Odyssey’s cultural success as reminiscent of a pre-internet time, and in some ways it is, befitting its connections to old-fashioned sword-and-sandal epics of the 1950s. Yet it’s really a convergence of old-fashioned monoculture and more newfangled discourse explosion. Rather than a superhero movie generating endless rewritings of the same nerd-to-normie translations (who was that character and are they going to be in the next superhero thing?) and glorified spoilers (is there a post-credits scene? And while we’re at it, can you describe it for me?), here is an R-rated movie, based on an epic poem, aimed at adults, prompting essays from film critics, academics and amateur Nolan scholars. It’s movie discourse fit for a 200-student freshman seminar, writ even larger.View image in fullscreenTom Holland, Matt Damon and Christopher Nolan attend The Odyssey premiere in Mumbai.Photograph: Prodip Guha/Getty ImagesThat might sound dismissive in its own way. But as tediously rancorous as the Very Online versions of these discussions can be, fueled by sometimes-insufferable Nolan acolytes and their equally disagreeable opponents, with the bonus unwelcome intrusion of afailed pre-release rightwing culture war, there’s at least a trackable rationality to a lot of post-release Odyssey discourse. Is it even something like ... healthy cultural-studies debate?! At first, the classicist and, most crucially, Odyssey translator Emily Wilson seemed to be forming a surprise backlash (given that Nolan had cited her translation’s opening line as inspiring his work) with her London Review of Books piece, focusing on the director’sdeviationsfrom the text, what she sees as thematic inconsistencies and simplifications, and some potential blind spots in race and gender. This then turned into an internet-fueled critique of an academic’s analysis of film, which some felt included some misreadings of certain characters, scenes and ideas.Some of the exchanges feel like a turf war between classics and film – are academics not encouraged to weigh in on movies using a different framework? Are mainstream film critics not encouraged to defend their sometimes (often) less rigorous discipline from those who feel confident dipping into it because of the subject matter? Other discussions have emerged (or re-emerged) from within the film community, reviving questions about whether the most popular name-brand writer-director in the world gives the short shrift to his female characters.Anne Hathaway’s Penelope joins her two other Nolan characters, from The Dark Knight Rises and Interstellar, as some of the strongest in his filmography. But it’s undeniable that Nolan tends to characterize hisfemale leadsas wives or wife figures, and some haveopinedthat the new movie’s wealth of women feel marginalized in ways they aren’t in the millennia-old original text.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayPreview latestEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOdyssey debates have touched exhibition, too: is Nolan’s film, shot entirely on IMAX cameras but only available to be shown in that native format in a few dozen theaters worldwide, placing undue emphasis on a more elitist form of spectacle? Or is he simply providing a level of showmanship that causes demand to outstrip a symbolically meager supply?View image in fullscreenAnne Hathaway and Tom Holland in The Odyssey.Photograph: Melinda Sue Gordon/Universal Pictures/APThe sheer volume of back-and-forth can be wearying – even (especially?) for pop-culture writers who make their living generating reviews, essays, thinkpieces and follow-ups off of the biggest hits of the day. Here’s a bummer stat from my own experience: since the beginning of this year’s summer movie season, there have been at least half a dozen discussion-worthy movies I haven’t written about in any great detail, because of middling-to-low demand. On the other hand,I’vewrittenaboutThe Odyssey and Obsession, this summer’s other major cultural phenom, close to a dozen times put together. I’m grateful for the work – and for the existence of popular movies that can withstand more robust and varied discussion than a 700-word, thumbs-up-or-down review. On the other hand, a new genuine monoculture threatens to simply refine which handful of movies generates 90% of coverage. (At least the “ending explained” industrial complex will have a chance to examine endings that might actually bear analysis, as The Odyssey in particular does.)‘An intermission is a must’: why Greek cinemas are adding a loo break to The OdysseyRead moreWhat’s most striking about the Odyssey discourse, however, is that even amid some built-in rancor or disdain, people actually seem excited to engage in it, rather than listlessly scrolling through it on their way to the next tempest in a teapot. That hybridization of old-school monoculture and more technologically enhanced saturation – unlike those 1950s epics and realImax availabilitynotwithstanding, both the movie and discussion of it feels nearly as accessible as a streaming series du jour, and probably more rewarding – doesn’t feel like astroturfing, but an actual post-release excitement that’s rarer and more fun than pre-release hype. (You have to be truly excited to successfully wring memes from the carefully controlled images of a Nolan film.) Even that ginned-up faux-outrage about the movie’s diversity became amusingly sporting with the gradual and merry realization that most people trulydo not care about what infuriates Elon Musk. The movie that a vocal minority insisted was bringing about the destruction of the west, or whatever they were prattling on about, has turned out to be a great unifier – not necessarily of opinion, but towards a reminder that going to the movies and talking about them after, rather than casting about for what else is on, can still feel like a vital part of living in the world.Explore more on these topicsThe OdysseyChristopher NolanAction and adventure filmsHomerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best theatre to stream this month: Self Esteem dazzles with Teeth ’n’ Smiles | Stage | The Guardian
description: Rebecca Lucy Taylor leads David Hare’s rock’n’roll drama, Michaela Coel tells us Chewing Gum Dreams and Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo stars in a murder mystery
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Rebecca Lucy Taylor leads David Hare’s rock’n’roll drama, Michaela Coel tells us Chewing Gum Dreams and Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo stars in a murder mystery
Content: Rock revival … Rebecca Lucy Taylor in Teeth ’n’ Smiles.Photograph: Jono WhiteView image in fullscreenRock revival … Rebecca Lucy Taylor in Teeth ’n’ Smiles.Photograph: Jono WhiteThe best theatre to stream this monthStageThe best theatre to stream this month: Self Esteem dazzles with Teeth ’n’ SmilesRebecca Lucy Taylor leads David Hare’s rock’n’roll drama, Michaela Coel tells us Chewing Gum Dreams and Stranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo stars in a murder mysteryChris WiegandSat 1 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeeth ’n’ SmilesLike a time capsule crowbarred open, its fug filling the auditorium, this year’s 50th anniversary production of David Hare’s dramaabout a 60s rock band’s unravellingmade for a fascinating evening. The tunes by brothers Nick and Tony Bicât – plus Rebecca Lucy Taylor AKA Self Esteem’s new number,Maggie’s Song, which expertly matches their milieu – have been collected on acast recordingbest played on repeat. Altogether now: “Don’t let the bastards come near you. They just want to prove you’re sane.”Chewing Gum DreamsIn September, London’sTheatre503 and tiata fahodziwill revive Michaela Coel’s sparky, name-making monologueChewing Gum Dreams. OnNT at Homeyou can see Coel herself perform this whirlwind tour of a 14-year-old girl’s world, from the top deck of the 67 bus to nightclubs, chemists and the classroom.Romeo and JulietAfter 14 years at the helm, Antoni Cimolino steps down as artistic director of Canada’sStratford Festivalthis season (Jonathan Church takes up the role in the autumn). Cimolino began as an actor and the archive ofStratfest@Homeincludes his 1992 Romeo, opposite Megan Porter Follows from Anne of Green Gables.Marco da Silva Ferreira: F*cking FutureOur critic Lyndsey Winship detected “a somewhat 3am vibe” to Portuguese choreographer Marco da Silva Ferreira’s “subtly intoxicating” protest dance piece when it visited Sadler’s Wells East in June. Available onArte.tv, captured at the Lyon Dance Biennale in 2025.View image in fullscreenBlockbuster … from left: Joe Bolland as Guildenstern, Hiran Abeysekera as Hamlet and Hari Mackinnon as Rosencrantz in Hamlet at the National Theatre.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHamletHiran Abeysekera’s irreverent Prince of Denmark wears a Blockbuster Video sweater and now you can rent his performance with aNational Theatre at Home subscription. Filmed at the Lyttelton theatre, Robert Hastie’s production was part of Indhu Rubasingham’s opening programme, with Francesca Mills’s Ophelia roundly praised.The Pansy CrazeMason Alexander Park hosts an epic series celebrating queer performers through the ages – not just theeponymous 1930s partiesbut also the Elizabethan era – in what is billed as blending “the dazzle of a cabaret with the intimacy of a piano bar”. Laverne Cox, Jesse Tyler Ferguson and Sasha Velour also star. FromAudible.Murder at the GatesStranger Things’ Gaten Matarazzo – who makes his West End debut in Rent in September – can be heard onthis new musical concept albumby Steven Sater and James Bourne. It revolves around an heiress’s murder mystery party that goes spectacularly wrong.HumoRafaela Carrasco’s flamenco ballet is the story of 19th-centurycigarreras– the women who made and sold cigars – unfolding in both factories and at fiestas, exploring their fight for emancipation. On a stage dressed with just a few flowers and chairs, it’s richly atmospheric with the ensemble sometimes puffing away. title: Singapore bans Massive Attack for showing Palestinian flag, breaching ban on foreign emblems | Massive Attack | The Guardian
description: Two members given ‘stern warnings’ after concert and barred from returning, with band also excluded from performing in Singapore again, say authorities
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Two members given ‘stern warnings’ after concert and barred from returning, with band also excluded from performing in Singapore again, say authorities
Content: Massive Attack in concert at the O2 Academy, Brixton, London, February 2016. Authorities in Singapore said the band would not be allowed to perform there again after a Palestinian flag was unfurled on stage.Photograph: RMV/REX/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMassive Attack in concert at the O2 Academy, Brixton, London, February 2016. Authorities in Singapore said the band would not be allowed to perform there again after a Palestinian flag was unfurled on stage.Photograph: RMV/REX/ShutterstockMassive AttackSingapore bans Massive Attack for showing Palestinian flag, breaching ban on foreign emblemsTwo members given ‘stern warnings’ after concert and barred from returning, with band also excluded from performing in Singapore again, say authoritiesAgence France-Presse in SingaporeFri 31 Jul 2026 23.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish trip-hop bandMassive Attackhas been barred from performing in Singapore after an investigation found two members unfurled a Palestinian flag during a concert, police said.Singapore, known for its tough laws on public speech and assembly, bans the open display of all foreign flags, national emblems or banners without a permit.Two band members who held the flag on stage during a concert on Wednesday were also banned from re-entering Singapore and issued with warnings, police said in a statement late on Friday, without naming the pair.The concert promoter had not responded to an AFP request for comment at time of publication. The band had not issued a public comment.A video circulating online showed two Massive Attack members on stage unfurling a Palestinian flag to loud, prolonged cheers from the audience.After concluding their investigation and in consultation with state prosecutors, police said they “administered stern warnings to both men” and barred them from coming back to the city-state.The media regulator was also probing possible breaches of licensing conditions.“Notwithstanding the event organiser’s prior acknowledgment of the licence conditions, during the performance, two band members held a foreign flag on stage, and one of them also shouted ‘Free Palestine’,” police said.The media regulator “will also not grant any future application for performances by the band in Singapore in view of the entry ban”, police said.The band is known for its criticism of Israel’s military actions in Gaza and has used its popularity to support the Palestinian cause.In April, frontman Robert Del Naja wasamong more than 200 people arrestedat a protest in London’s Trafalgar Square in support of Palestine Action, an activist group banned by British authorities.Singapore is a major concert hub for south-east Asia, having hosted multi-night performances by Taylor Swift, Coldplay, Ed Sheeran and Bruno Mars.The police urged the public, including foreigners, “to refrain from importing foreign politics as this can undermine our social cohesion and the rule of law”.Explore more on these topicsMassive AttackPalestinePalestine ActionMiddle East and north AfricaProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a perfect finale for French super-soldier thriller The Sentinels  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The first world war drama has been a thrill throughout. Plus, the uneasy story of the Berlin Olympics in 1936. Here’s everything to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The first world war drama has been a thrill throughout. Plus, the uneasy story of the Berlin Olympics in 1936. Here’s everything to watch this evening
Content: Action men … The Sentinels on BBC Four.Photograph: BBC/Caroline Dubois/Federation Studio France/Esprits Frappeurs/CANAL+View image in fullscreenAction men … The Sentinels on BBC Four.Photograph: BBC/Caroline Dubois/Federation Studio France/Esprits Frappeurs/CANAL+TV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a perfect finale for French super-soldier thriller The SentinelsThe first world war drama has been a thrill throughout. Plus, the uneasy story of the Berlin Olympics in 1936. Here’s everything to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Alexi Duggins,Hollie RichardsonandEllen E JonesSat 1 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 1 Aug 2026 01.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Sentinels9.50pm, BBC FourThis French counterfactual thriller about lab-grown super-soldiers in the first world war has sustained itself convincingly; as the final two episodes drop, the political intrigue and action sequences dovetail perfectly. The mission to free Mazauric is in jeopardy – which is worrying as it’s clear that everything depends upon it.Phil HarrisonSussex: Jewel of the South Coast7pm, Channel 5Exactly why this show opts for a title that risks alienating viewers from every other county on the south coast is hard to fathom. This instalment of the continuing profile takes in a lifeguard, a Chichester cleric working to preserve her cathedral, and farmers making artisan cheese.Alexi DugginsBoléro at the Proms7.55pm, BBC TwoRecorded on the day of the World Cup final, the Spanish National Orchestra made its Proms debut with Ravel’s Boléro. Under chief conductor David Afkham – his neck wrapped in a Spain football scarf – they also performed Rodrigo’s Concierto de Aranjuez and Manuel de Falla’s The Three-Cornered Hat. Nick Mohammed presents.Hollie RichardsonHitler’s Games: Berlin 1936 in Colour8pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenConflicted memories … Marlene Owens in Hitler’s Games: Berlin 1936 in Colour on Channel 4.Photograph: Woodcut“One hundred thousand spectators rose at once doing the Hitler salute and shouting ‘Heil Hitler’.” Historians help to tell the story of the Berlin Olympics in 1936, along with the offspring of competitors such as Jesse Owens, Audrey Brown and Jack Beresford. They share their family members’ conflicted experiences of wanting to represent their countries at an event that was Nazi propaganda.HRThe Staircase10.55pm, ITV1For all of its plotting contrivances, this drama about Michael (Colin Firth) and his attempts to prove that he didn’t murder his wife Kathleen (Toni Collette) is tense and gripping. The DA’s office builds the case against Michael – handily for the prosecutors, details about his past emerge that could do their job for them.PHGhosts Australia10.55pm, BBC ThreeA double bill of laughs with the ghoulie squad down under. Kate may be getting used to her spooky housemates – including Lindy the 80s aerobics instructor and Satan the 90s biker – but will they behave when her mum, Mel, unexpectedly comes to stay? Worse still, Mel is threatening to move in.HRFilm choiceHeretic, 9.35pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenIn his villain era … Hugh Grant in Heretic on Sky Cinema Premiere.Photograph: Kimberley FrenchSophie Thatcher (Yellowjackets) and Chloe East (The Fabelmans) play a pair of unworldly Mormon missionaries who arrive at the door of an avuncular Englishman hoping to make a new convert. That Englishman, however, is played by Hugh Grant – once a foppish romcom idol, now deep into his villain era – and what at first seems like a playful willingness to debate religion turns into something much more terrifying. With a script by A Quiet Place co-writers Scott Beck and Bryan Woods to work with (the two also co-direct), Grant commands the screen with glee. It’s a career-best performance, with enough dark miracles to fully restore your faith in A24’s waning horror output.Ellen E JonesLove Me, 10.25am, Sky Cinema PremiereMillennia have passed since humanity’s extinction, and on Earth’s half-frozen ocean a smart-tech-enabled buoy (Kristen Stewart) floats alone, emitting a “waiting to connect” signal. One day this is answered by a passing satellite (Steven Yeun), and together the devices search the internet, hoping to derive an understanding of life and love from this oddly incomplete record. First-time film-makers Sam and Andy Zuchero combine animation and live action into awe-inspiring visuals – and it’s funny too!EEJLive sportCommonwealth Games, 8.30am, TNT Sports 2Day nine in Glasgow features netball, cycling, boxing and bowls.Golf: Women’s Open, noon, Sky Sports GolfDay three from Royal Lytham.Horse Racing: Glorious Goodwood, 1.15pm, ITV1Includes the Coral Stewards’ Cup.Cycling: Tour de France Femmes, 2.30pm, TNT Sports 1Giro d’Italia winner Demi Vollering is a big favourite for the race, which starts in Lausanne.Scottish Premiership Football: Aberdeen v Hearts, 5.15pm, Sky Sports Main EventLast season’s unlucky losers visit Pittodrie in the first week of fixtures.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Exploring Rabat, Morocco – this year’s Unesco World Book Capital | Morocco holidays | The Guardian
description: Rabat is a gorgeous seaside city with great food and culture, but for book lovers there’s an added incentive to go this year
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rabat is a gorgeous seaside city with great food and culture, but for book lovers there’s an added incentive to go this year
Content: The Kasbah of the Oudayas in Rabat boasts tremendous views.Photograph: Sergio Formoso/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Kasbah of the Oudayas in Rabat boasts tremendous views.Photograph: Sergio Formoso/AlamyMorocco holidaysExploring Rabat, Morocco – this year’s Unesco World Book CapitalRabat is a gorgeous seaside city with great food and culture, but for book lovers there’s an added incentive to go this yearBen AitkenSat 1 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first book I read willingly was Bridget Jones’s Diary. I was 19. Up to that point, I hadn’t been much of a reader. I’d been more into football, or Baywatch, or Robin Budd in the year above – anything really. Given the choice between reading a book and staring at a wall, I would have plumped for the latter.After finishing my A-levels, I worked in a barbecue restaurant in Portsmouth – which is where I found Bridget Jones. The book was lying around in the staffroom. I picked it up and read a few pages, and then a few more, and then a few more. It felt exciting. Like I’d met someone. Like I was suddenly in a relationship. Over the next few days, I remember cancelling nights out so I could go to bed and read. My mum thought I was depressed.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian GraphicsIt hardly matters what book gets you going. For Jeanette Winterson, it was the Book of Deuteronomy.For David Nicholls, it was Tales from Moominvalley. What matters is that a book gets you going. Throughout my 20s, I worked as a carer, but I was always reading and scribbling on the side. I became a published author seven years ago. It’s not an overstatement to say that Bridget Jones changed my life. That books did.So when I learned that 2026 wasNational Year of Reading(a UK-wide campaign intended to promote the importance and joy of reading) and that Rabat was to be this year’sUnesco World Book Capital(a rotating designation intended to promote the importance and joy of reading), I packed a few volumes and set off for Morocco’s capital. I was hoping for a cultural adventure, and perhaps a tagine, in this ancient seaside city perched scenically between Casablanca and Tangier.View image in fullscreenBen Aitken in Rabat, Morocco.Rabat was made the capital of Morocco in 1912, at the beginning of the turbulent 44-year period when the country found itself under the thumb of the French. The first thing I saw of the city was the New Town, or Ville Nouvelle, which was laid out in the 1920sà la française, meaning it looks nothing like the huge medieval medina that’s just up the road.From the central train station, I proceeded to the solar-poweredMohammed VI Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, where the permanent exhibition – Shifting Horizon(s) – does exactly what it says on the tin. Highlights include the abstract paintings ofMohamed Melehiand a provocative photograph byLalla Essaydi. Part of a series calledBullet Revisited, the latter shows a woman covered head to toe in gold bullets, and is a powerful indictment of the violence women suffer.I walked north to the medina, an irregular network of narrow streets lined with small shops flogging mint, slippers, strawberries andsabon beldi, a black soap made from the flesh and oil of olives. The medina was busy but calm. Not once was I asked to consider a carpet or sample a sardine. Indeed, I felt rather invisible. In this respect, the customer service was uncannily French.I followed my nose to the Kasbah of the Oudayas, an enchanting district of low whitewashed houses. Built on high ground in view of the ocean, this former royal citadel was ideally placed to spot visitors on the horizon, and greet them appropriately.After checking into a riad on Rue Bazou, I descended a flight of stone steps to the beach, a modest curve of sand where scores of people were playing football and volleyball. I crossed the cooling sand and climbed on to the breakwater to better observe a neon sun sink slowly seaward, as a lone surfer, way out in the offing, sought inch-perfect swell.View image in fullscreenEnticing streets in the Kasbah of the Oudayas.Photograph: Adam Smigielski/Getty Images/iStockphotoI took a pew at the beachsideRelais Marinrestaurant. I didn’t deliberate over the menu. Like casserole and paella, tagine is a dish in two senses; both the cooking vessel and the meal, on this occasion a confusion of lamb, almonds and prunes in a delicious gravy that, with time, had reduced to a bold, flavourful pesto, which I mopped up with chunks ofkhobz(Moroccan flatbread). I could have eaten another.The next morning I went to the Cafe des Oudayas. Situated next to the Andalusian Gardens – a wonderful place full of orange and pomegranate trees – this alfresco cafe offers three things: mint tea, biscuits and an excellent vantage point.As I eked out the tea, I watched a boy poised on the edge of a towering rock, 30 metres above the Bou Regreg river. Goaded by his friends, he meant to jump, but he hesitated for minutes in the intensifying sun. His dive, when it finally came, was a thing of beauty – a wide and graceful arc, shapely, immaculate, somewhat divine, almost unreal. The gallery held its breath until he re-emerged – to be met with disingenuous disdain.“La poule a attendu une éternité!”(The chicken waited for ever!) Lads, eh?View image in fullscreenA bookseller presides over his stock.Photograph: Nur Photo/Getty ImagesOn a whim, I boarded an electric tuk-tuk, one of 60 in the city. I asked the driver to take me directly to theChellah, a medieval necropolis that also houses what’s left of the Roman city of Sala Colonia, but, knowing best, the driver instead went out of his way to show off his home town, swinging by St Peter’s cathedral and a nightclub calledAmnesia, where Morocco’s king is said to have boogied back when merely a prince.The Chellah – when I finally got there – did not disappoint. After doing a round of the picturesque ruins, I climbed to a gorgeous onsite cafe and ordered the couscous. Befitting tradition, the dish comprised a pyramid of seven vegetables, a moat of couscous, a jug of broth and some meaty treasure hidden within the veg. It was unmistakablybon.If one requires beer in Rabat, one heads toLe Dhow, a bar and restaurant on a boat moored in the shadow of the kasbah. Sitting on the upper deck, I savoured an ice-cold pint while chatting with a British undergraduate studying at theUniversité Internationale de Rabat. I asked if she felt comfortable in the city. “It’s been fine,” she said. “Some men have said hello. One asked for a photo. To be honest, I’ve experienced a lot worse in Worcester.”I’m just going to come out and say this – don’t go to Rabat because it’s this year’s World Book Capital. Despite my best efforts, the exact nature of the 300-plus events the city is purportedly going to run during its year as WBC remain a mystery to me. Instead, go to Rabat because it’s an excellent city.C’est simple.On my final evening, I chanced on a humble bookshop in the medina – Bouquiniste El Azizi. Of the hundreds of preloved books assembled in the diminutive space, a dozen or so were in English. Among them was Bridget Jones’s Diary. I picked it up and read a few pages – and then left it for someone else to stumble on, and perhaps break their duck with.On leaving the shop, I noticed a sign:Les livres prennent soin de nous. Books take care of us. The sentiment strikes me as the right note to finish on.Ben Aitkenis the author of Shitty Breaks: A Celebration of Unsung Cities, £9.99. title: Meera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for oyster mushroom burgers with five-spice slaw | Burgers | The Guardian
description: These roasted oyster mushrooms are meaty, savoury and chewy, made even more satisfying in a south-east Asian-style dressing
Author: Meera Sodha
Headline: These roasted oyster mushrooms are meaty, savoury and chewy, made even more satisfying in a south-east Asian-style dressing
Content: Meera Sodha's oyster mushroom burgers with five spice cabbage.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenMeera Sodha's oyster mushroom burgers with five spice cabbage.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.Meera Sodha recipesBurgersMeera Sodha’s vegetarian recipe for oyster mushroom burgers with five-spice slawThese roasted oyster mushrooms are meaty, savoury and chewy, made even more satisfying in a south-east Asian-style dressingMeera SodhaSat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot every plant makes a great burger filling. You might think pulses or potatoes for heft, but the lack of texture and propensity to mush can be unsatisfying. This is where mushrooms excel; they trade in satisfaction. Roasting them brings out their natural umami and removes water content, leaving them chewy, caramelised and occasionally crisp. They can also make friends with the most unlikely of ingredients, like they have here with peanut butter, soy, agave and sesame.Oyster mushroom burgers with five-spice cabbageWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appNow, two types of agave syrup are available in the supermarkets: dark is richer, more caramelly; lighter is simpler and more neutral. If you only have or can find light, use that. These mushrooms can be cooked on skewers on a barbecue, but do so over indirect heat under a watchful eye.Prep10 minCook30 minServes4For the mushrooms600g oyster mushrooms60g smooth peanut butter2 tbsp toasted sesame oil1 tbsp dark agave syrup2 tbsp red or brownmiso1½ tbsp light soy sauce1 tbsp apple cider vinegar3 garlic cloves, peeled and mincedFor the five-spice cabbage200g white cabbage, finely shredded5 spring onions, trimmed, greens and whites finely shredded½ tsp fine sea salt½ tsp ground five-spice1½ tbsp apple cider vinegar15g coriander leaves, finely chopped1 tbsp mayonnaise, plus extra to serve4 brioche burger buns, to serveHeat the oven to 240C (220C fan)/475F/gas 9, and line two trays with baking paper.If your mushrooms are in big clumps, break them gently into individual mushrooms and put them in a large bowl. Put the peanut butter, sesame oil, agave, miso, soy sauce, vinegar and garlic in a small bowl, stir until you have a smooth sauce, then pour this over the mushrooms.Using your hands like claws in an arcade machine, carefully toss to cover all the mushrooms in the sauce. Spread the mushrooms over the two trays, then bake for 12-15 minutes, until all the liquid has dried out and the edges are charred, then remove from the oven.While the mushrooms are cooking, make the slaw. Put the cabbage and spring onions in a big bowl, sprinkle over the salt and scrunch with (clean) hands. Mix through all the other salad ingredients.To assemble the burgers, split and toast the brioche buns – one minute in a toaster works well. Spread one cut side of each bun with mayo, pile on a quarter of the mushrooms, then top with some slaw. Repeat with the other burgers, clap on the lids and serve.Explore more on these topicsBurgersMeera Sodha recipesFoodVegetablesMain courseVegetarian food and drinkNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content
